*Laṅkāvatāra-hṛdaya-mudrā-pratītyasamutpāda*.
This scripture is the commentary of the Elder of Leifeng. Using the fangs and claws of the Chan school, he entered the lairs of the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* and *Yogācāra* traditions.
He lamented the desolation of scholastic learning and grieved over the superficiality of the Chan gate;

indeed, this was the course of events since he retired to Kuangfu in the year of Kǐsī (1233), when he observed the world with a chilled heart and resolved his will in response to the times. Thus, it was from this that he hung his gourd at Jinjing and leaned his staff against Yuyue.

As for Yuan, when he inquired into the realization of the Dharma, his mind was as serene as a calm ocean; when he looked up to admire the noble reclusion of the *Jia-dun*, his stature rose like a towering mountain.

Like Dizang Chen, he plowed the fields to earn his daily meal; like Xianzhi, he stood while reciting and walked while reading. With a cold stove and a chilly hearth, he upheld the total transmission of the Great Dharma;
amidst tangled thorns and disordered threads, he relied on the blade of wisdom to sever them alone. In these respects, he truly combined the virtues of the ancients.

Thus it was. Upon returning to Ling in the year Wuxu, I was unable to proceed from Yumen back home the following year. During the years Ren and Gui, I spent my days seeking further instruction on the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) with my younger brothers, including Shijian.

We took the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as our fundamental text, pointing out that the "primordial spirit" (*ādi-puruṣa*) and the "self" (*ātman*) were not to be indiscriminately included within the "jewel of nature.

By doing so, we suddenly realized that even such absurdities as "tortoise hair" and "oil from sand" were merely the spontaneous dispelling of deluded attachments. Consequently, I extended [this realization].

The essential purport thus reveals the conditions for this commentary, which perfectly accords with the core of the Mind-school while incorporating the names and characteristics of the Perfect teaching.

It not only serves as a stabilizing pillar against reckless Chan, but also inspires those in the lecture halls. Its creative genius transcends the ordinary, merging the ocean of meaning at its profound source; its divine mechanism remains deep and silent.

Having resolved numerous difficulties regarding half-verses, with weary countenances and perspiring hands, I have collated and searched through the texts. Beholding the brilliance of the Great Meaning, I rejoice that these subtle words have not fallen into oblivion.
The Teaching thus supports the fundamental principle; I have traced the *Biezhuan* (Separate Biography) to its four fascicles and recognized it as being identical to the *Zang* (Canon).
Supporting the Great Mind to transcend the Two Vehicles—this is truly the application of the supreme mind, gazing with concern upon the evils of the times.

This is the work of one who has done so. Therefore, throughout this commentary, whenever there is a profound discourse that penetrates the principle, or a point that captures the essential core of the sūtra—whereby one perceives the *zong* (the fundamental school) through the literal meaning and text, and fuses the literal meaning and text with the *zong*—I have ventured to mark these out for the instruction of future students.
Just as the four rivers all flow into the ocean while not a single bubble remains, it is incumbent upon those reading the text to clarify their eye of wisdom.

Regarding the name of the mountain: this mountain is composed entirely of *laṅkā* jewels; therefore, it is named after its precious substance. The mountain is located in the South Sea and is the dwelling place of yakṣas.
Because the king of that region invited the Buddha to preach the Dharma upon the mountain, it was also named after the mountain [of the invitation].
It is called the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. The Great Being Zao Bo said: "This sūtra was preached on Mount Laṅkā in the Southern Sea.
When the Tathāgata’s carriage reached the foot of the mountain, the Yakṣa King Rāvaṇa and the Bodhisattva Māndārava, riding in a palace of lotus flowers, [approached him]."
They came to invite the Tathāgata to enter the mountain and preach the Dharma. That mountain was steep and lofty; looking down from it, one beheld the great ocean, and it had no gates or entrances.

Only those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are capable of ascending there. This symbolizes the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi*), wherein there is neither cultivation nor realization.
Only then can one ascend. Looking down at the great ocean represents the clarity of the ocean of the mind: stirred by the winds of sensory objects, the waves of consciousness surge;
when one realizes that objects are fundamentally empty, the ocean of the mind becomes naturally still.

When both mind and objects are tranquil, there is nothing that is not illuminated—just as when the great ocean is windless, the sun, moon, and constellations appear with brilliant clarity. This sutra is intended for Bodhisattvas whose roots of virtue are matured.
It is taught that the seed-consciousness and the karmic consciousness are the Tathāgatagarbha, which differs from the two vehicles that extinguish consciousness and seek quiescence;

it also differs from the Bodhisattvas who practice emptiness through Prajñā and delight in the progressive excellence of emptiness. It directly clarifies that the substance of consciousness is, by its very nature, entirely true.

It then becomes the functioning of wisdom (*jñāna*). Just as when there is no wind over that great ocean, its reflections are clear and penetrating, so too when the ocean of the mind does not waver, the winds of objects are not distinct;
simply by being able to realize the truth, consciousness (*vijñāna*) becomes wisdom. Zao Bo was certainly deeply conversant with the essential tenets of the *Laṅkāvatāra*.
This sutra was first translated during the Liu Song dynasty by Guṇabhadra, consisting of four fascicles, titled [the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*].
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-ratna* was later retranslated into ten fascicles by Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei dynasty, titled *Rulengjia*.
During the Tang dynasty, Śikṣānanda, along with Fuli and others, translated it into seven fascicles, titled *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra*.
Although the Tang translation is concise and direct, it ultimately does not equal the lofty, ancient, profound, and vast style of the Song translation. Therefore...
From antiquity until the present, it has remained as it was first translated. During the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, the Great Master Bodhidharma crossed the sea and arrived in Wei.
He sat facing a wall at Shaolin and, having transmitted the Dharma to the Patriarch Huike, said: "In this land, only the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* can serve to seal the mind;
I entrust it to you as well. From that time on, the *Laṅkāvatāra* became the secret treasury of the Chan school. Now, as for the practitioners of Chan...
It is hollow and superficial; it is lamentable that there are those who have never even unrolled the scroll throughout their lives.

Seeking its interpretation within the field of doctrinal studies (yixue), one finds only Zongle and Fuyi, who were commissioned by imperial decree to compile a commentary at the beginning of the Hongwu era; later, during the late Wanli period, there is the *Biji* (Notes) by Deqing;

and in the Chongzhen era, the *Yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning) by Zhixu. Aside from these, there are few instances to be found. As the Great Master Bodhidharma once said regarding this sutra: [text continues].
"Five hundred years later, it will instead become a study of mere names and forms. To reflect deeply upon these words, I am truly filled with profound shame and trepidation.
The Great Master likely meant that our school’s transmission had been lost; how could this be anything other than a matter of human failure?

Since the year Shunzhi Xinchou (1661), when my late Preceptor Hua passed away, and the following year when my late Preceptor Dari followed him in death, I have spent the two years of the Ren and Gui cycles merely pursuing the pleasures of worldly existence.
All at once exhausted [his worldly concerns], he settled briefly at Leifeng Peak and soon moved to Ji’ān. Riding upon his long-held aspiration, he simultaneously answered questions on Chan;

this was merely for his own satisfaction and he did not dare show it to others. He only reflected that the Dharma is in its nascent stage: what is called "seeing one's nature" is nearly identical to the *puruṣa* (the divine self);
the path of transcendence is no different from the primordial darkness. It does not arise of itself, yet it is not non-arising; the words of the Sage are complete.
In this regard, there are those who fail to comprehend dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) and consequently fall into nihilism, arbitrarily destroying the Dharma according to their own whims;

compared to those who are merely obstructed by names and characteristics, the merit and fault of these two are as vastly different as heaven and earth. This sutra directly points to the seed-consciousness (*bījavi-jñāna*)—the karmic consciousness—as the *tathāgatagarbha*.
It truly possesses both delusion and awakening; otherwise, if one takes the "flowing stream" (*pravāha*) to be one's own mind, it would conversely become the consciousness that gives rise to birth.

This has been thoroughly and clearly elucidated in the Commentary. Regarding the scriptural passages and treatises cited, I have selected only those that are proximate to the principle and mutually illuminate one another.

As for the "turning words" (*jīyǔ*), I have treated them with particular gravity. Now, a "turning word" serves as the pivotal mechanism for shifting from the realm of existence, while a "teaching" (*jiào*) provides the ultimate destination beyond words. Since this is precisely the profound discourse, I shall not decline to clarify it.

This is refuted. To employ merely such language of total eradication to obscure the profound essence of the True Teaching (zhenquan) and to misrepresent the meaning of names and phrases—how can this be anything other than the confusion of "wu" and "an" into "ma"?
At such a time, this is the malady of Chan, wherein it becomes difficult to distinguish the authentic from the spurious. Our Great Master was the first to inaugurate the teaching of wordlessness.
This is transmitted together in four fascicles. My humble and anxious concern is that you, along with all future generations of the world, may reverently uphold these compassionate instructions.
This is the first part of the "Essential Heart of All Buddha-Speech" (Sarvabuddhapravacanahṛdaya).
The nature of the Dharma-realm is fundamentally devoid of awakening or delusion; it is the categories of sentient beings that distinguish the true from the false.
True and false both originate in the one mind; delusion and awakening are manifested through the myriad dharmas. There are no separate dharmas, yet they appear as if present before us;

there is no different mind, yet it clearly forms a continuous succession. This is truly because the ultimate truth fails to awaken and deluded movement gives rise to conceptualization. To penetrate this delusion...
The Original Truth knows that the true reality is extinguished; therefore, the twelve classes of beings attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
When deluded views cause the flux of phenomena, the thirty-two marks manifest as ordinary appearances, thereby becoming inverted conceptions. Thus, our Great Awakened World-Honored One...
They cast off precious and noble garments to don tattered and soiled clothing; they point to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as ignorance and label that which is like an illusion as falsehood.

The faculties, the body, and the vessel-world are partitioned according to the capacity of their respective sentiments; the land of retribution and the transformation-body are differentiated based upon the mirror of wisdom.
Just as a mirror reflects both the beautiful and the ugly, the forms of things appear within it; yet the formless emptiness is the luminous foundation.
Quiescence is like the moon that comes and goes according to others; it is only people who perceive it themselves.

The bright orb suspended in the void is without deficiency, yet when one uses beauty or ugliness to compare it to the luster of a mirror, or follows its coming and going to scrutinize the lunar essence, this arises solely from the optical defect of the eyes.
This is not something the sagely wisdom can remain silent about. In signless, empty luminosity, how could there be room for verbal expression? It is simply said to be neither ugly nor—

The beautiful face is suspended in the void like the bright moon; there is no need to point it out. I speak only of neither coming nor going, hoping that by encountering this before one's eyes, the mind may be awakened.
I fear that one might discard the moon to stare only at the finger. Because the finger is ugly, I have just now spoken of "going.

Yet, when one exhausts the analysis of the mirror’s light, its ugliness has no beginning; what further need is there for beauty? When one investigates the moon’s essence, its traces of coming are formless; how much less can there be a "going"?
From what source? Both the beautiful and the ugly are illusory; the substance of the mirror is fundamentally empty. Coming and going are entirely void; the nature of the moon is originally bright.
This is why the one hundred and eight phrases sever all verbal explanations. What meaning is revealed in this very moment?

By investigating the arising and ceasing of the eight consciousnesses, one sees that beginningless falsehood has no cause. True wisdom is fundamentally without discrimination, yet it results in non-awakening.
The mind is fundamentally quiescent, yet failing to maintain the numinous source, it instead becomes a consciousness of deluded movement.

When the mind does not give rise to consciousness, one is eternally in nirvāṇa amidst the flow of existence; when consciousness does not depart from the mind, one needlessly undergoes birth and death within the ever-abiding.
A single film over the eye causes a thousand flowers to disorient the sky; a single delusion blinds the mind, causing myriad emotions to obstruct wisdom. Once the film is removed, the eye remains.
When the flowers have faded and the sky is clear, the deluded interpretations of the mind vanish and the spirit is relinquished, so that wisdom shines brightly.

Yet, if one remains confined by the boundaries of intellect within the realm of emotion, then every exercise of wisdom is but emotion; the mind becomes darkened within the ocean of consciousness, such that the entire mind is nothing but consciousness.

Through inconceivable perfuming and transformation, the fundamental limit of birth and death is difficult to know; as for the various causes of all delusions, how can the continuity of the faculties and consciousness ever cease? If...
If one does not conceal that true consciousness, one will inevitably give rise to erroneous calculations regarding the cause of birth.

Flowing through delusion as the cause, there arises the convergence of eye-consciousness, form, and light; yet this "superior subtlety" is still but consciousness. How is this different from the folly of [seeking] tortoise hair or sand oil?

To falsely calculate existence and non-existence renders cause and effect void. This is entirely due to failing to understand what is manifest before one, taking it to be something separate, or perhaps never having even attempted to do so.
To perceive the beginning is to erroneously conjecture about the primordial darkness. Indeed, the mind has no prior limit; whatever manifests belongs entirely to deluded beings.

Consciousness does not depend on subsequent conditions, yet it merely discerns initial appearances, all of which arise like illusions. To weary of birth and incline toward quiescence is to extinguish grasping.
It is not difficult to see the end of the realm of appearances; by abandoning the delusory and realizing the true, one achieves the antidote.

Yet, one has not yet thoroughly investigated the beginning of arising and ceasing, which is why awakening is non-differentiated while delusion has degrees of depth. The mind has neither difference nor sameness, whereas consciousness has its limits.
Therefore, the ocean-treasury of the storehouse consciousness is inconceivable; the awakened mind is eternally abiding, and within both birth-and-death and nirvana, there is no creator.

The distinctions between the holy and the ordinary are empty manifestations; they are what appear through deluded thought. That which is traversed by holy wisdom—the faculties, objects, mind, and consciousness—is not separate from the single reality.
The boundary between delusion and awakening is ever distant; within the nature of True Suchness, emotional perceptions remain distinct.

The reason for the ascent and descent among the six realms of existence lies within the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Within this, the paths of wisdom branch into many divergences according to the relative heights and depths of the four noble causes.
While the eight consciousnesses merely possess the error of delusion, reaching the point where waves surge and boil, the moist nature of the ocean water remains ever-present.
The seven evolving consciousnesses fundamentally lack a true cause. Though they may be as deep, clear, tranquil, and still as a profound pool, the momentum of their refined currents never ceases.
Thus, the state of profound stillness does not depart from the boundary of consciousness; this clarifies how contact gives rise to sensation. Waves are entirely water;
this points to the gate of non-duality for the ignorant. True reality transcends words; advance in practice toward the place of self-awakening and investigate it thoroughly.
Ultimately, compassion and wisdom perfect the three marks at the source of self-awakening; they purify the manifest flow and transcend the five dharmas beyond the reach of thought.
To abandon this fundamental school is to fall into false views. Failing to realize that what appears is the manifestation of one’s own mind, one falsely posits a cause for birth.
To know thoroughly that all phenomena return to emptiness is yet to sink into nihilism, like tracing the origin of a hare’s horns.
When the analysis of the ox-horn reaches its conclusion, one begins with mutual dependence, yet ultimately finds it to be without cause.

Because emptiness depends on form, and because form depends on emptiness, their distinctions are clearly manifest. By removing form, emptiness is clarified; by removing emptiness, form is clarified. The process of inclusion and exclusion is thus perfectly distinct.

How could one know that they manifest all at once? Within a dream, how could there be before and after? Since the two aspects are without difference, who would distinguish "this" from "that" upon waking?

If one awakens, it is a total awakening; having realized that delusion is empty, what need is there to destroy or eliminate it? If one is deluded, one does not know one's own delusion; it is only because of the sense faculties (*indriya*) that there is suddenness or gradualness.

Departing from the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the sense bases (*āyatana*), one attains the gate of liberation and cessation (*nirodha*). By enumerating giving (*dāna*), morality (*śīla*), and patience (*kṣānti*), the waves [of phenomena] are revealed.

This is the path of the *pāramitās*. It shatters the mundane sentiments that cling to the aggregates (*skandhas*), rejects the heterodox doctrines of causelessness, and points to the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) within dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
It shows how false thoughts arise from delusion, demonstrating that these sentiments do not exist as inherent entities.

Guiding one back to self-awakening (*pratyātma-vidyā*), it allows for an immediate entry into the state beyond words, abandoning the mind of subject and object that clings to external conditions, and clarifying the characteristics of ultimate differentiation.

Regarding the explanation of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*, there are neither two nor three vehicles. Śrāvakas know this according to reality, yet they merely distinguish between different causes.

Bodhisattvas do not forget their original vows and thus still guard against the bliss of quiescence (*śāntisukha*). Even the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is not within the realm of the two vehicles.
The eternal is inconceivable. How could it be the same as the external paths that rely on causal conditions? Self-awakening is the true cause;
it possesses real self-nature, whereas impermanence and changing characteristics merely fall within the realm of discursive thought. Fundamentally abiding, it does not belong to seeing or hearing;

yet when it encounters the objects of cognition, one consequently takes awakening and transforms it into an object. Holy wisdom transcends all discrimination. Do not be deluded by the present thought. Only then will you see that principle cannot be expressed through words.

The mind does not realize its own nature; as it evolves through successive cultivation, the various vehicles each establish their respective seed-natures (*gotra*). It is not that they lack Buddha-nature; rather, they are gathered by the spiritual power of the vehicle.

Even those with the disposition of *icchantika* possess causes and conditions. Thus, one knows that delusion and awakening share the same objective conditions, yet the minds of the ignorant and the wise differ.

The holy and the ordinary are of one reality, yet they are distinguished by their perceptions and conceptions. Just as with the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), one perceives them as a self, while another perceives them [as empty].
There is no self. From this point on, the true meaning diverges significantly. As for mind, intellect, and consciousness: if they are different dharmas, they are identical;

if they are different dharmas, they are distinct. The essence of awakening has never undergone change. By shattering attachments, one returns to reality; yet in its nature, there are three aspects. Because of the notion of "self," it is shown to be non-existent.

Wisdom thus becomes twofold: penetrating the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, one realizes that names and marks are themselves suchness (*tathatā*), and that the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of phenomena means that deluded thoughts are themselves correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).

Just as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) depends upon dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), one manifests a form-body (*rūpa-kāya*) before others, enters into the illusory nature of all phenomena, and does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence. Thus, one travels universally through all lands, universally gathering in all sentient beings. And...
It is not extinction. It reveals the profound meaning; how could it fall within the realm of verbal expression?
To counteract the discriminating mind, it is said that there are no objective realms. To eliminate the notion of selflessness, it is termed the gateway of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Do not dwell upon expedient means; it is solely the dharma of internal realization. Profoundly deep and utterly empty, it is not something manifested by words and speech.
Progressing ever higher, one attains the practice of self-awakening, which transcends the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*) and surpasses these three branches.
It manifests within the moon reflected in water and the shadow; it emerges beyond both establishment and denial. Among the four types of *dhyāna*, the noble joy consists of only three:

emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Of these, the Truth of Reality (*tattva-satya*) is most perfectly accordant. [It is characterized by] sensation, tranquility, and internal awareness.

The body can only be realized through silent, intuitive penetration. It dissolves the ice of birth-and-death within the mind, intellect, and consciousness, restoring the water of nirvāṇa within the Tathāgatagarbha.
This matter of the emptiness of self-nature is neither annihilated nor eternal; it is like an illusory flower blooming from awakening—neither destroyed nor dying.
Therefore, any perception of nirvāṇa apart from this self-nature belongs to the realm of causes and conditions; it is merely a verbal expression, like an illusion.
The Dharma of this [teaching] is such that it constantly abides within birth and death, identical to delusion and confusion; yet, in its very place, there is no arising and no intrinsic nature.

Therefore, it is called "non-arising. Because it is non-arising, it is said to be like an illusion. Being like an illusion, it is beyond fault. This is the realm of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, which cannot be expressed in words.
Since its non-arising nature is free from all attributes, it is not something known by non-Buddhists or those of the Two Vehicles; therefore, it is treated as a cessation of discourse. (4)

The fruit does not transcend the mind-measure (*cittamātra*). The two types of awakening discern *nirvāṇa*. Apart from the *ālayavijñāna*, there is no nature of concealment; apart from non-awakening, there is no *ālayavijñāna*.
The seven evolving consciousnesses are fundamentally unborn from the beginning; discrimination merely increases non-awakening. Non-awakening conditions arising, and false marks of existence manifest.
Awakening to delusion arises from confusion; such is the nature of the perfected reality (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*). Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time...
In essence, it is the One Vehicle. Within both the mundane and supramundane realms, there has never been a duality of self.

By transmitting the realization that deluded thoughts lack inherent nature, and by investigating the principle that self-awakening is not something external, one finally understands that the mind does not give rise to conditions, and conditions do not give rise to the mind.

When both mind and conditions are simultaneously extinguished, quiescent illumination pervades as many grains of sand as there are in the Ganges. As phenomena and principle merge, emptiness and existence are revealed within the Ocean Seal Samādhi. One.
The ground is all grounds; all grounds are one ground. Realizing that phenomena are unborn, one merges images within the water and mirror;

following the nature to give rise to function, one enumerates types within the space of luminosity. One cuts off the Arhat’s attachment to external forms and destroys the awakened body of those with a mind.
In the Buddha there is no self or other; the Dharma is uniform across past and present. This is the ultimate.

There is not a single word [of inherent existence]. It is only in accordance with the various categories of beings that the three bodies (trikāya) first appear. If one clings to the notion that they exist, one conversely falls into the error of causelessness (*ahetuka*).
If one relies upon their non-existence, one establishes a doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*). The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is fundamentally unborn;

yet, while its false appearances do not obstruct dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), its nature and characteristics are quiescent—how, then, can a mind that grasps at existence find a place there? While cause and effect are clearly manifest, it is difficult to empty away the karma of non-action. Existence...
There is nothing that is not reckoned. Upon first entering one's own school, one employs skillful means according to the capacities of beings;

it is impossible not to speak. Through the school, one reveals the teaching; through the teaching, one attains the school. The manifold unreality is itself the foremost reality. Self-nature is fundamentally empty;

the place where deluded thoughts arise is precisely where deluded thoughts do not arise. How could they be distinct as they follow conditions? "One arises" and "one does not arise"—these are established by false views.
Falsehood. The four characteristics and the four equalities are non-dual in true awakening. Entering the meaning through words, the Sūtras reveal the source of the mind.
Discerning consciousness clarifies wisdom; the stage of the Tathāgata is attained solely through self-realization.
All dharmas have the mind as their intrinsic nature. Abiding within the inner mind, there is no characteristic of transformation. All continuities are realized through awakening.

The cause is that only by returning to original enlightenment does one possess knowledge as it truly is. To speak of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) while obstructing false conceptualization, or to speak of the existence of nature (*svabhāva*) while distancing oneself from fear, are neither discourses that reach the ultimate nor teachings that accord with skillful means;

they should not be established as formal tenets. Only when the self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are clarified is this not a lack of wisdom. False imagination and non-cognition are distinct from one another.
The teaching of definitive meaning (nītārtha) aims at that which precedes words. When practice attains its essence, awakening transcends the realm of principle.

To grasp meaning by relying on language is to misrepresent names and phrases; to reach the divergent paths of dharmas is to eliminate worldly discourse. One should simply know how to remain detached from words and phrases.

Yet it is not silence. Furthermore, when one recognizes that the mind is far removed from all conditions and does not fall into annihilation, then the true and the false, which exist in mutual dependence, are suddenly fused;
the subject and object of this remedial process both cease, resulting in liberation according to reality, known only through self-realization.
Non-abiding nirvana is the equality of all phenomena; it is neither cause nor effect. It is that which the Tathāgata knows and awakens to:

having self but no other, being both form and dharma. How could the wondrous response of all Buddhas be empty and devoid of meaning? That there is no nature does not mean non-existence; that there are different names does not mean existence.
Because it is not non-existent, it is the nature of non-arising, which does not perish along with conditions. Because it is not existent, it is non-extinguished.

The Dharma does not arise dependent on conditions, nor does it perish following conditions; yet for the sake of sentient beings, I speak of non-arising. It does not arise dependent on conditions, nor does it perish;
yet for the sake of sentient beings, I speak of non-perishing. Through the provisional application of skillful means, I establish the chapters and phrases of the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, one who excels in the meaning is first called "one of great learning. Contemplating this, I offer a profound warning to the foolish: do not hold to views.
These characteristics are the reality of the nature of delusive thought. They transcend the chain of causal links; thus, the wisdom of discernment is empty.

These two kinds of evil views arise solely from delusion regarding all phenomena. The subtle mind within the three realms of existence dwells only within self-awakening; it is neither permanent nor impermanent.

It is determined that there is no intrinsic nature. Regarding what is included or not included, these distinctions depend on the individual. To perceive the differing characteristics of phenomena still belongs to the meditative stillness of the Two Vehicles.
Even with the recollection of one’s original vows, one must still await the sustaining awakening of the eighth stage. The dream of crossing the river has already awakened.
The light of the blazing fire begins to pervade; there is no longer any abiding. Ultimately, how does this differ from the initial mind?

The Buddha-ground is suddenly adorned; initial awakening is thus the most supreme. It transcends the constant state of non-arising and differs from that empty space. It is that which is attained through skillful means.
Not produced by different causes, its self-nature is inherently stainless. Yet, through non-awakening, it becomes the cause for the various realms of existence.

Sustained by the seven transformations, the fault of residual habit-energies remains despite the absence of a self. The nature of the *ālaya* is fundamentally without birth or cessation; adventitious defilements appear as if there were turbidity or clarity.
Entering from the conventional into the ultimate, one provisionally relies upon the five dharmas; through wisdom and purity, one realizes that there is but the single mind. (3)
The Buddhas of the world transcend worldly expectations and establish their own unique realization; they are not like the udumbara flower [rare and elusive].
Their untainted habitual tendencies do not conform to the doctrine of momentariness. Abiding in the True Dharma, they view all things as if they were *gandharvas*.

They distinguish between the provisional and the real within the Six Perfections, mutually illuminating the three types of Buddhahood. They lead the followers of the Two Vehicles to ultimate fruition and exhort those in the three realms of existence toward purity.
All these belong to provisional teachings and are spoken for the sake of transformation. If one discusses the fundamental abiding, there is no language at all;

it speaks only of that which is not a vehicle, causing one to awaken to clarity by oneself. Fundamental enlightenment is pure, requiring no merit or effort; its self-nature is adorned and how could it tolerate defilement?
This is what is called the luminosity of fundamental wisdom and the fulfillment of discerning prajñā. From beginning to end, from root to branch, they converge at the ultimate limit.
As for what is spoken: in sum, the Great Way leaves no trace; it dwells solely within the present moment. The ultimate principle is forgotten in the heart; it does not lie beyond kalpas.
Therefore, at Mahādeva’s Cave, the room was closed off, and at Vaidalya, the mouth was sealed. To speak without speaking, one reveals the vast array of all phenomena;
to hear without hearing, one unifies a thousand opportunities within stillness. As soon as one involves oneself in conceptual thought, one has already fallen into error.
In the present age, people merely seek a point of reference and vainly boast of that which transcends all things.

Therefore, it is said that on such-and-such a night he attained Buddhahood and on such-and-such a night he entered Nirvana, yet in the interval he did not speak a single word. The fundamental limit of birth and death and the fundamental limit of Nirvana—how could there be two distinct streams in accordance with reality?
The marvel lies in not knowing; the fault likewise lies in not knowing. To be deluded by this "non-phrase" is itself the awakening to this "non-phrase."

The entire body is within the dream; the place of awakening does not shift from amidst the mundane bustle. Amidst the various conceptualizations, the turning of the faculty lies only within the glance of the mirror.
Like water containing the moon, inner and outer are simultaneously fused; like a mirror meeting the void, the tranquil light penetrates through to the core.
From antiquity until now, from day throughout the night, it does not become more radiant because there are people.

Flattery! How could the void kalpa ever diminish the empty luminosity? Those who lose it share the same mental cognition as those who possess it; those who attain it do not alter what is heard or seen.
One must know that it exists—what use is it to claim it does not? Does a mani jewel become confused by the five colors? Is the complete form hidden from the many blind?
To preserve the truth and discard the false is difficult to avoid being like the cutting off of cranes or the lengthening of ducks.

To criticize [this view] is like blocking the light at a window; how can one avoid the reproach of leveling mountains and filling ditches? Therefore, the eight consciousnesses are fundamentally void, and the five dharmas are all provisional.

The two selves are falsely grasped, and the three natures are erroneously established through mutual dependence. Though there are thousands of differences and myriad distinctions, they do not exceed a single delusion.
From the beginning to the end, tracing it back and following it through, it ultimately returns to the present thought. One may thus believe that the direct path is nothing other than this.
Master Zongchi reached the ultimate end: beginning in non-awakening and concluding in non-awakening, it was like milk in water, difficult to distinguish.

When the sage washes away the sentiments of the ordinary, and the ordinary discards the views of the sage, the soot within the black is easily discerned. How could one know that when emotion is forgotten, wisdom merges;

when conceptualization is exhausted, the essence becomes perfect? Therefore it is said: "The Great Way is right before one's eyes. How could the ultimate principle be sought through the passage of kalpas?
Part Two: The Outer [Introduction]. Section One: The Introductory Division. Subdivided into two. △ First, the Prologue to the Occasion of the Sūtra:
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling on the peak of Mount Laṅkā by the shore of the Southern Sea, adorned with various kinds of precious flowers.
For the sake of adornment, he was accompanied by a great community of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas who had come from various diverse buddha-fields.
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possessed mastery over immeasurable samādhis and sported with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati was their leader; all the Buddhas had personally poured water upon his head in the consecration.

He thoroughly understands the meaning of the objective realm as a manifestation of his own mind. To various types of sentient beings, he universally manifests through various mental forms and immeasurable gates of liberation according to their respective categories.
He has attained ultimate penetration into the five dharmas, the three self-natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness.

At the assembly following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda requested the Buddha to establish a standard for the compilation of the various sūtras, asking with what they should begin. The Buddha replied that they should begin with:
“Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling...”. This subsequently became the universal formula for all sūtras.

This sūtra points directly to the fact that the present sense organs, bodies, and the world-receptacle of sentient beings are all manifestations of the mind alone; they are like dreams and illusions, and are not real.
It is not non-existent. A single moment of non-awakening, and all phenomena manifest simultaneously; when one realizes this within that very place, the one mind is without differentiation.
This is the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which is not known by those of the Two Vehicles or the external paths.
Therefore, at this opportune time, all the great Bodhisattvas present in the assembly who had come together with [the Buddha] have attained mastery over samādhi.

They sport with supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*). Skillfully understanding that which is manifested by their own minds, they employ skillful means (*upāya*) to deliver sentient beings according to their various mentalities and forms.
They have attained ultimate penetration into the five dharmas, the three natures (*svabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and selflessness (*anātman*).

They are capable of hearing and receiving the Tathāgata’s foremost definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), falling neither into the net of doubt nor being deluded by any heterodox causes or inferior teachings.
That which causes delusion and confusion—the various great assemblies that gather together—are all manifestations of the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).

They are not like those śrāvakas of fixed nature who are incapable of rising [to this realization]. Therefore, this dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) accords with the fundamental purport of this sutra: that all is mind-only (cittamātra).
This is also a manifestation of correspondence. △ Next, the verse of praise by the appropriate recipient:

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, together with Māti Bodhisattva, having traveled through all Buddha-fields, by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and—
He praised the Buddha in verse:
"The lands of all Buddhas are, in fact, the lands of sentient beings. This Bodhisattva is able, within the daily activities of sentient beings, to penetrate the realm of the Tathāgata;
that is to say, he sees all forms as the form of the Buddha, and hears all sounds..."
All these are the voices of the Buddha. They travel through all lands, for all such lands are the buddha-fields of the Buddhas.
By means of this, they receive the spiritual power of the Buddhas above and stimulate the faculties of those in the assembly below. All praises of the Buddha contain the meaning of the sūtra;
there can be no other underlying intent.
The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky; since wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
All phenomena are like illusions, far removed from mind and consciousness; since wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Far removed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, the world is ever like a dream. Wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet gives rise to great compassion.
The world is like a flower in the sky; all phenomena are like illusions.

The world is ever like a dream—this is the daily activity of sentient beings, wherein they suddenly perceive the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata, which is beyond the reach of wisdom to grasp as either existent or nonexistent.

The Tathāgata, out of compassion for these sentient beings who cannot awaken by themselves and who, following their own mind and consciousness, falsely calculate existence and non-existence (eternalism and nihilism), gives rise to great compassion and employs skillful means to deliver them.
The Bodhisattva, having deeply grasped this intent, uniquely reveals the essential purport of the entire sutra in his praise of the Buddha;
this constitutes a correct understanding of its meaning.

Knowing that both persons and phenomena lack self (*pudgala-nairātmya* and *dharma-nairātmya*), and that afflictions (*kleśa*) and their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) are eternally pure and signless (*animitta*), one gives rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cling to a self within the aggregates (*skandha*), whereby afflictions arise based upon this clinging. Those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) contemplate the non-self of the aggregates, yet they have not yet forgotten the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Both of these states belong to delusion; there is no difference of depth between them. This refers to the non-self of persons and phenomena, and the afflictions...

"Afflicting you with flames," yet [the mind] is eternally pure of itself; these are originally all words of praise for the Buddha. However, they actually refer to ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, whose essence is entirely empty.
This is truly due to a lack of awakening, whereby they falsely perceive the cycle of birth and death. The Tathāgata, knowing this deeply, gives rise to compassion to deliver them.
Although there are no sentient beings who attain extinction, the ten inexhaustible phrases of his original vows are vast and profound.

Listen. Examining the three subtle states: first, based on non-awakening, the mind moves; this is called the "phase of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*). Second, based on movement, there is the capacity for seeing;

this is called the "phase of transformation" (*vivartalakṣaṇa*). Third, based on seeing, objects falsely appear; this is called the "phase of manifestation" (*pratibhāsalakṣaṇa*). These three belong to the eight consciousnesses and constitute the beginningless, false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Subsequently, based on the phase of manifestation, one discriminates in response to objects, forming the six coarse states, the first of which is the "phase of cognition" (*jñānalakṣaṇa*).

The co-nascent attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) relies on wisdom (*jñāna*). When thoughts arise therein without interruption, it is called the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*). This constitutes the conceptual attachment to phenomena (*dharma-vikalpa*).

Although these two types of self-attachment belong to the seven consciousnesses, their root is capable of seeing [the object] most clearly; yet because they arise based on non-enlightenment (*avidyā*), they are the most subtle.

Even in the eleventh stage (*bhūmi*), there still remain two aspects of ignorance regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa-moha*); therefore, they are not within the range of perception for those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

That which is known is precisely this *jñeyāvaraṇa* (obscuration of the knowable). Third, based on mindfulness, the arising of attachment is called the "characteristic of grasping" (*parāmarśa-lakṣaṇa*); it is the innate grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*).
Fourth, based on grasping, the arising of conceptualization is called the "characteristic of naming" (*nāma-paryāya-lakṣaṇa*); it is the discriminative grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha-vikalpa*).

These two forms of grasping at a self give rise to all fundamental afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*), and they also belong to the seven consciousnesses. However, they are distinguished according to their respective objects.
Because it is that which is grasped and maintained, the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) are able to eliminate and sever the person-self (*pudgala-nairātmya*) through their contemplation;

however, they do not sever the dharma-self (*dharma-ātman*) of the seven consciousnesses. Master Xuanzang attributes the conceptualized (*vikalpita*) aspect to the six consciousnesses and the innate (*sahaja*) aspect to the seventh consciousness.

Nevertheless, this [text] infers the cause of its arising and thus refers to it collectively as the "seven consciousnesses. The five [aggregates] rely on afflictions to create karma, which is termed "arising" (*utthāna*).

The characteristic of karma consists of the six types of karmic reliance and the retribution they attract; this is termed the characteristic of being bound by suffering. These two belong to humans and devas.

However, the three subtle and six coarse characteristics in their entirety all arise from non-awakening (*abodha*). Upon awakening, they are entirely empty—what is called eternally pure and signless (*animitta*).
There is no nirvāṇa in anything; there is no Buddha who has attained nirvāṇa, nor is there nirvāṇa within the Buddha. It is far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened.
Whether existence or non-existence, it is entirely free from both.
The first four verses state that the daily activities of sentient beings are entirely the realm of the Tathāgata.

This means that the *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata is not different from the birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) of sentient beings; therefore, it is said that "all things have no *nirvāṇa*. If there were such a thing as *nirvāṇa*, [it would be distinct].
It would be better to have no birth-and-death at all. Since there is birth-and-death, there must be sentient beings in birth-and-death.
Because there are sentient beings who enter birth-and-death, there must be Buddhas in nirvana. Because there are sentient beings who enter birth-and-death, there are Buddhas who enter nirvana.
Thus, the subject of awakening and the object of awakening clearly exist in mutual dependence. How can one know that all sentient beings [are inherently enlightened]?
Having entered parinirvāṇa, there is no further nirvāṇa; the Tathāgata perceives this clearly and is thus able to accord with the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are both like dreams and illusions. Having severed the mind of subject and object, one does not fall into the views of existence or non-existence.
The unsurpassed, truly real is not to be measured by the scope of thought or calculation.
It is the tranquil contemplation of the Muni; this is the departure from birth. This is called non-grasping. It is pure in this life and in future lives.
The Dharma-body is without nature and without birth; it is neither mind nor consciousness.
This Sage is quiescent, suddenly transcending all views and signs of arising and ceasing. If one contemplates in this way, all grasping is severed in a single kṣaṇa.

From that very moment, the eyes open wide, and until the end of the future, pure mindfulness will naturally succeed one another. This is what the Great Mirror [Huineng] meant by "the preceding thought..."
It is not born; the subsequent thought does not perish. This is because it praises the Buddha and points people toward this [reality] for them to fix their eyes and ears upon.
The first introductory section is concluded.
II. The Main Body (Zhengzongfen). Divided into two parts: First, directly pointing to that which is beyond words and transcends verification—vast, subtle, and wondrous. First...
The Dharma-gate of the Single Meaning. Divided into two parts. △ First, the one hundred and eight questions.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāmati had praised the Buddha with verses, he declared his own name: "I am named Mahāmati;
I have attained mastery in the Mahāyāna. Now, by means of one hundred and eight points of meaning, I respectfully inquire of the Most Honored and Supreme One."

The Bodhisattva declares himself to have attained mastery of the Mahāyāna, wishing that those of the present and future generations may know that the meaning of what he asks is entirely essential to the One Vehicle (ekayāna) and not merely the distinctions of other vehicles.
The Knower of the World, having heard those spoken verses, surveyed the entire assembly and addressed the sons of the Buddha, saying:
"O you sons of the Buddha, now ask whatever you desire; I shall explain for you the realm of self-realization."

This realm of self-awakening is that which has been realized by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. Although it is investigated and elucidated throughout the four fascicles with repeated analysis, it does not exceed this [point] in total; therefore, it is revealed at the outset.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having received the Buddha’s permission, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and asked in verse:
“How does one purify thought? How does thought increase? (The Wei translation says: “How does one purify all cognitions?
By what cause do cognitions arise? “How does one perceive delusion? How does delusion increase? (The Wei translation...)
Question: By what cause is there delusion? By what cause does delusion exist? For what reason are there lands, transformations, marks, and various non-Buddhists?
How is there the sequence of non-perception? Why is it called "non-perception"? (The Wei translation says "quiescence and sequence";
the Tang translation says "and the sequence of no-shadow").
"Recollection" refers to deluded cognition. "Delusion and confusion" refer to non-awakening. Since True Suchness is devoid of intrinsic nature, through non-awakening it undergoes deluded movement;

as soon as the afflictions of views arise, there is thus deluded cognition. Desiring to purify deluded cognition, one must exhaustively investigate the origin from which that deluded cognition arises.
Desiring to awaken from non-awakening, one investigates the source of this non-awakening; only then does one come to know that True Suchness (Tathatā) is without inherent nature.

This is the secret intent of all Buddhas, and it is precisely what should be asked at the outset. "Kṣetra" refers to the land or realm; "transformative marks" refers to all the manifested appearances of the six realms of existence.
First, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are mentioned, followed by the emergence of "no-suffering. This is intended to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.
Furthermore, "non-appropriation" refers to the tranquility of the Muni, who does not appropriate a single dharma and is free from all reflected images.
Next, there are the successive stages, which refer to the distinctions within unconditioned dharmas.
Why are they called "sons of the Buddha"? To what state does liberation lead? Who is bound, and who is liberated? What are the realms of dhyāna? How do the three vehicles arise?
I pray that you will explain these for me. From what do dependent origination and its conditions arise? What is the agent, and what is the acted-upon?
What is the simultaneous diversity of discourse? What is growth? (The Tang translation says: "How do all existences arise?
What are the formless attainments and the meditative absorption of cessation? What is the cessation of perception? By what cause does one awaken from concentration?
How do the activities of going, coming, and maintaining the body arise? How does present discernment occur? And how are the various stages produced?
"Where does liberation go? This is intended to reveal that for the Muni, there is neither bondage nor liberation; thus, it is further asked, "Who binds and who is liberated?

To say there is no liberation or bondage is merely the deluded vision of those who are either confused or awakened. "Dhyāna-bhūmi" (the realm of meditation) refers to the various meditative concentrations of both ordinary beings and sages.
"Pratītyasamutpāda" (dependent origination) refers to phenomena produced by causes and conditions. "Kāraka-kṛtya" (the agent and the action) refers to the doer and the deed.
"The fruit of the karma that has been performed" refers to the various divergent explanations, which point to the heterodox teachings of non-Buddhists.

"Growth" refers to how the causes and effects of the three realms of existence increase. "Formless attainments" refers to the four spheres of emptiness (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). "Cessation absorption" refers to the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
The cessation of perception refers to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

Awakening from meditative concentration refers to why the Tathāgata awakens from concentration to initiate various activities and manifest the going and staying of the body. Manifesting discrimination refers to presently teaching various distinct dharmas.
Producing the stages refers to establishing the characteristics of the practices of the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Who is it that destroys the three realms of existence? What is their body, and where is it located? To what place do they go when reborn? Who are these most excellent sons?
By what cause do they attain supernormal powers, as well as mastery and samādhi? What is the nature of the mind in samādhi? O Most Excellent One, please explain this to me.

"Destroying the three realms of existence" (*tribhava*) refers collectively to the three vehicles (*triyāna*) exiting the existence of the triple world. Having exited the triple world, where do they abide?
What kind of bodies do they receive? To what places are they reborn? It is said that the sages of the three vehicles alike exit the triple world;

however, their bodies and lands differ, and their manifestations and transformations are distinct. "The Supreme Sons" (*varaputra*) refers to the various bodhisattvas. "Supernatural powers" (*abhijñā*) refers to...

The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). *Samādhi* is a translation of "correct reception" (*samyak-pratigraha*). Regarding the "mind of *samādhi*": this refers to the mind abiding in *samādhi*, as well as the relationship between the mind and *samādhi* in terms of their identity or difference.
What is called the "storehouse" (ālaya)? What are the mind (manas) and consciousness (vijñāna)? What are birth and cessation? How does one see and then return [to the source]?
(The Wei translation says: "By what cause does one see all phenomena? By what cause does one sever what is seen? What is the lineage (gotra)? What is non-lineage and the measure of mind (cittamātra)?
How are the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) established, as well as the meaning of non-self (anātman)? Why is there no sentient being (sattva)? Why is there...?

According to worldly convention, "store" (ālaya) refers to the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna); "mind" (manas) refers to the seven consciousnesses; and "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to the six or five sensory consciousnesses.

"Arising and ceasing" refers to the arising and ceasing manifested by the various faculties and consciousnesses. "Viewing" refers to the view of arising and ceasing. "Returning" means returning to the state of non-viewing. This is the same [as the preceding].

Within this single mind, there is the distinction between the storehouse consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) and the mental consciousness; there is the difference between seeing arising and ceasing and seeing non-arising and non-ceasing.
This delusion and awakening, as well as all that is false and illusory, are entirely non-existent. Regarding "lineage" (gotra): the lineage of the three vehicles refers to those with potential;

"non-lineage" refers to those without potential, indicating the non-Buddhists and the icchantikas. Regarding "mind-measure" (citta-mātra): it means that while the mind is one and the same, each [perceives] differently.
There is a measure. To establish characteristics is to speak of the characteristic of self; this is not the meaning of "self," which refers to the characteristic of non-self.
"Sentient beings" is merely another way of speaking regarding the characteristic of self; that is to say, within the dharma of self there are no sentient beings.
Why, then, are they said to exist in conventional truth?
How is it that the views of annihilationism and eternalism do not arise? How is it that the Buddha and the non-Buddhists are not contradictory in their characteristics?
What will become of the various diverse schools in future ages? What is emptiness and what is its cause? And how does momentary destruction occur?
The views of annihilationism and eternalism are both the false views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). To see that these two views do not arise is what is called the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha and the non-Buddhists are neither identical nor different; this is spoken from the perspective of the universal equality of the one mind.
"Different schools" (*nānā-nikāya*) refers to the fact that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his disciples compiled the sūtras into various distinct collections.

If the mind is fundamentally equal and there is nothing outside of the Buddha, why is it that we, the disciples of the Dharma, instead hold divergent views? "Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) refers to the fact that the nature of all phenomena is empty.
If one observes all phenomena directly before one's eyes, why is it said they are empty? "Momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) refers to the subtle [nature of existence].
It is mindfulness; moment after moment it does not cease, yet it does not abide for even a single kṣaṇa. This is not something known by those lacking wisdom.
How is it that the womb-born arises? Why is the world unmoving? For what reason is it like an illusion, a dream, and a city of the gandharvas?
The world is like a mirage in the heat, and like the moon reflected in water. For what reason are the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the wings of awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) taught?
Why is there turmoil in the lands? And why do beings perceive existence?
"Born from the womb" refers to the birth-and-death of sentient beings through the breaking up of their aggregates.

"The world is immovable" means that while lands repeatedly change, the true nature remains eternally abiding. "Illusion," "dream," "gandharva city," "mirage," and "moonlight on water" collectively serve as metaphors for the unreality of both sentient beings and the world.
As for the phrase "why is it so?": it refers to the birth-and-death of sentient beings and the world.
The shifting and flowing of the realms manifest clearly before us; yet, as for those who speak of them as being like illusions or dreams, who indeed would recognize this?

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and *bodhi* both refer to right wisdom—that is, that which awakens to the nature of illusions and dreams. As for the "disorder of the land," it refers to the shifting and flowing of the land.
To perceive this shifting and flowing as having real existence is because sentient beings lack wisdom and falsely perceive it as substantial.
There is. What is this? It is the state where awakening and delusion are far apart.
Why is there neither arising nor ceasing? The world is like flowers in the sky. How does one awaken to the world? Why speak of being free from words?
Who is it that is free from false conceptualization? In what way is the analogy of space [applied]? How many kinds are there of reality as it is? How many perfections of the mind are there?
For what reason does one traverse the stages? Who reaches the state of non-apprehension?
"Neither arising nor ceasing; like flowers in the sky"—all these refer to the world. The world is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing, yet it is seen falsely as arising and ceasing.
It is fundamentally like flowers in the sky, yet it is seen falsely as being real. This state of existence depends upon awakening.
To awaken to the world is precisely to awaken to this world—which is neither arising nor ceasing and is like flowers in the sky. Once awakened...
The world is thus understood to be like an illusion; one does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence, for it cannot be reached by verbal expression.
Therefore, it is called "detached. Once detached from verbal expression, conceptual discrimination is suddenly stilled. All phenomena are like empty space;

seeing their fundamental true nature, one reaches the other shore, traverses all the stages (*bhūmi*), and arrives at the state of non-reception (*anupādāna*). This is what can be realized through gradual succession.
This is because he wishes for the World-Honored One to clearly reveal [the truth]. How many kinds are there in reality? They are: the *tathatā* (suchness) that is realized;

the distinctions between the three vehicles (*triyāna*); and the minds of the various *pāramitās*, which likewise divide into three vehicles according to whether one attains liberation from birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
What are the two kinds of selflessness? How is the flame purified? How many types of knowledge are there? How many are the natures of sentient beings' precepts?
Who gives rise to the various natures of jewels, such as mani-gems and pearls? Who gives rise to all languages and the various natures of sentient beings?
Among the two types of selflessness, the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is the most subtle; therefore, it is emphasized by repeating the words "thusness" (*tathatā*).

Thusness is precisely the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which pertains to the grasping at phenomena. Regarding wisdom (*jñāna*), there are fundamental distinctions; regarding ethical discipline (*śīla*), there are those of the bhikṣu and the bodhisattva.
The nature of the maṇi jewel belongs to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*); the nature of language belongs to the sentient-being world (*sattva-loka*).
Within the questions, these may refer to the vessel-world, the sentient-being world, or the supramundane; they may concern the Buddha, his disciples, the ignorant, or outsiders.
These are not fixed in their sequence, nor are they necessarily presented in a systematic arrangement at once; rather, they may be treated according to the circumstances.
Regarding the attainment of meaning through speech: one must know that all distinctions arise from the single true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
they are like illusions, inconceivable.
Who has revealed the fields of knowledge and the arts? How many types of *gāthā* are there—the long verses and the short stanzas?
How many kinds are there of becoming? What is called "treatise" (śāstra)? [The Tang translation says: How many different types of principles are there? How many distinctions are there in explanation?
How do food and drink arise, and how do various desires arise? What is meant by "king"? What are the wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) and minor kings?
How does one protect the kingdom? How many kinds of devas are there? What is meant by "earth"? What are the lunar mansions (nakṣatra)?
As well as the sun and moon, the practitioners of liberation—how many kinds of these are there? How many kinds of disciples are there? What is an ācārya?
And how many kinds of Buddhas are there? Furthermore, how many kinds of births are there? (The Tang translation says: "How many kinds of Tathāgatas are there?
The same applies to the accounts of their previous lives.")

The fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) refer to the five sciences: first, grammar (*śabdavidyā*); second, the science of crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*); third, the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*);

fourth, the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), which refers to the examination and determination of what is erroneous and what is correct; and fifth, the inner science (*adhyātmavidyā*), which refers to the detailed exposition of the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*). The first three are external treatises (*bāhyaka-śāstra*), while the latter two are internal.
This is an internal treatise (*abhidharma*). *Gāthā* is translated as "verse" (*gātha*); it refers to long hymns composed in short metrical lines, all of which are spoken within the *sūtras*.

"Treatise" (*śāstra*) refers to the establishment of the principles explained therein; it is distinguished by being an internal or external commentary. This question asks: how many kinds of discourse are there?

[The topics include] food and drink, sensual desire, human kings, the various devas, the great earth, the constellations, the sun and moon—these generally refer to the two categories of sentient beings and their environment (*bhājana-loka*).
"Worldly names and characteristics" refers to such things as practice, disciples, preceptors (ācārya), Buddhas, and birth; these are called the distinct names and characteristics of the supramundane.
"Practice" applies to all three vehicles. "Disciples" include both bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. "Preceptor" (ācārya) is translated as "model" or "standard."

There are five kinds of modes of conduct (*ācāra*). First, "birth," which refers to the manifestation of the events of birth by the Tathāgata, who attained Buddhahood after practicing over many lifetimes.

As for Māras and the various heterodox teachers (*tīrthika*), how many kinds are there of each? Furthermore, regarding their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and their minds (*citta*), how many kinds are there of each?
What is the measure of conventional designation? (The Tang translation says: "How is it merely a provisional assumption?
I pray that the Most Victorious One will explain: what are emptiness, wind, and clouds? What is mindfulness and intelligence? What constitutes forests and trees?
What constitutes creeping vines and grasses? What are elephants, horses, and deer? How are they captured? What constitutes the base and lowly? By what cause is one base and lowly? What is [this]?
Six sections [of the cycle] encompass [this]. What is an icchantika? Men, women, and those who are neither male nor female—how are these all born?

"Nature" (svabhāva) and "mind" (citta) both refer to the faculties and desires of sentient beings; "provisional measure" (prajñapti-mātra) refers to the provisional designation based on the measurement of the nature of the mind.
"Mindfulness and intelligence" refers to worldly intelligence. Six sections encompass [this]. In the Western Regions, two months are reckoned as one [season].
Section. There are six periods in a year. One is *cchanda*, translated as "faith" (*śraddhā*); *ti* is translated as "not possessing. This means not possessing faith.
This also concerns the inquiry into the distinctions between the names and characteristics of the sentient beings and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
What is the regression of cultivation? What is the arising of cultivation? By what dharma does the meditation master establish what kind of person?
How do sentient beings arise in the various realms of existence? What are their characteristics and what are their types?

In the practice of cultivation, there is progress and there is regression. "Arising" refers precisely to progress. Regarding the methods of dhyāna, there are differences between the sudden and the gradual;

regarding the faculties of persons, there is no uniformity in their magnitude. These are the distinctions within the supramundane. "The various realms" refers to the six destinies and the four modes of birth.

"Characteristics" and "categories" refer to the characteristics and categories of the various realms of existence; they are the world of sentient beings, which, through illusion and delusion, branches out into many paths.
What constitutes wealth? By what cause is wealth attained? What constitutes the Śākya clan? By what cause does the Śākya clan exist?"
What is the Ikṣvāku lineage? Supreme Honored One, please explain. What is the long-suffering ṛṣi? How does he provide instruction?
How does the Tathāgata appear at all times and in all lands, surrounded by the most excellent sons, in various names, forms, and classes?
Why does one not eat meat? Why was the consumption of meat prohibited? For what reasons do various classes of beings eat meat?
This concerns the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane. O Śākyas, of the Ikṣvāku lineage:
in the past, during incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there was a Bodhisattva who was the crown prince of a kingdom; he renounced the throne for the sake of the Path and followed the Brahmin Gautama.
He studied and changed his surname to Gautama. Later, he returned to reside at the Ikṣuvāḍa Monastery outside the city.
There, he was wounded by a bandit, and blood flowed upon the ground. Mahāgautama perceived this with his divine eye and traveled to the monastery by means of his supernormal powers.
He took the blood and placed it in vessels on either side, instructing them: "If this practitioner is sincere, the blood shall be transformed into human beings. Subsequently...
In the tenth month, blood from the right side became male and from the left side became female; they subsequently became the Ikṣvāku lineage.

Later, King Yima gave birth to four sons by concubines who were slandered by the legitimate queen. The king banished them from the country, and they dwelt in the Forest of Straight Trees on the Snowy Mountains.

Their mother followed them there and arranged marriages for each of them, whereby they eventually established themselves. When the king heard of this, he was filled with joy and spoke these words: "These..."
A true son of the Śākya can establish himself; for this reason, he is called a Śākya. "Śākya" (釋) is translated as "capable," meaning that he possesses talent and ability.
The fourth son was named Śobhita (莊嚴), who was the one from whom King Śuddhodana received his lineage. Regarding the phrase "all times and lands":
it means at all times and in all lands, manifesting universally according to the various types of beings.
Some are shaped like the sun and moon; some like Mount Sumeru or a lotus flower. There are lands with the supreme marks of lions, situated sideways or inverted over the world.
Some are like Indra’s net, or composed entirely of various precious gems; others have the forms of the lute, the hourglass drum, or various kinds of flowers.
Some are devoid of the light of the sun and moon; such [worlds] are immeasurable.
Sumeru and the Wondrous High Mountains govern the four continents as a single world-system. Padma refers to the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*).
Siṃha is the most excellent among worlds. There are worlds that are tilted and worlds that are inverted; these include all those that are superior and inferior.

It is like Indra’s net (*indrājāla*). *Indra* is translated as "Emperor" (*di*). An Emperor’s net consists of a thousand pearls, each pearl interpenetrating the others; this expresses inexhaustibility.
The sun and moon, the lute (*vīṇā*), the hourglass drum (*tūṇava*), flowers, and fruits are all forms and characteristics of the world.
"Precious jewels" means that the world is composed of precious jewels. "Devoid of the light of the sun and moon" refers to stainless radiance that does not depend upon the sun and moon.
What is the transformation Buddha? What is the retribution-born Buddha? What is the suchness Buddha? What is the wisdom Buddha?
Why does one not attain equal and perfect enlightenment in the desire realm? For what reason does one attain bodhi at the Akaniṣṭha heaven, having transcended desire?
When the Sugata has entered parinirvāṇa, who shall uphold the True Dharma? For how long will the Teacher of Gods remain? And for how long will the True Dharma abide?
How many kinds of *siddhāntas* and views are there? Furthermore, regarding the divisions of the *vinaya* for bhikṣus, what are they and by what causes and conditions do they arise?
Those sons of the Most Victorious Ones, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Śrāvakas—by what cause do they undergo a hundred transformations?

How is it that they are free from a hundred receptions? The "Transformation Buddhas" (nirmāṇakāya) consist of thousands, tens of thousands, and billions of bodies; these are transformations according to the various types of beings.

The "Great Transformation" (mahānirmāṇa) refers to the *Rocana* of a thousand fathoms, who manifests for Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage; this is also called the "Retribution Body for Others" (*parasaṃbhogakāya*). "Suchness" (*tathatā*) and "Wisdom" (*jñāna*) both refer to the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*).

Suchness, original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), wisdom, and initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*): these constitute one’s own retribution. It is the unification of the initial and the original, the dual fusion of principle and wisdom.
Vairocana attained the path of Bodhi in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven and not in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in order to demonstrate that one attains purity by departing from desire.
Who shall uphold the True Dharma? This refers to those of what kind of faculties and inclinations.

Only then is one fit to transmit and uphold the True Dharma (*saddharma*). The duration for which the Buddhas abide in the world and the duration for which the True Dharma abides in the world each vary—being long or short—according to the causes and conditions of both oneself and others.
*Xi* (悉) means "all" or "pervasive. *Tan* (檀) is translated as "giving" (*dāna*). *Jian* (見) refers to the "capacities" (*indriya*) of those who are the recipients.
This refers to the fourfold nature shared by the Tathāgata’s pervasive teachings and the capacities of the sentient beings who receive them: first, the world... [text continues].
1. The *dhātu-siddhānta* (the standpoint of elements) yields the benefit of joy; 2. the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedies) yields the benefit of extinguishing evil;

3. the *pudgala-siddhānta* (the standpoint of persons) yields the benefit of generating goodness; 4. the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth) yields the benefit of awakening to principle. Vinaya.
*Fǎnlǜ* (Revising the Vinaya). "Bhikṣu" refers to one who upholds the Vinaya. "Causes and conditions" refers to the causes and conditions for the formulation of the precepts.

"A hundred transformations" and "a hundred non-receptions" refer to the distinctions between Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas. "Transformations" refers to the cycle of birth and death through transformation;

as long as one has not yet reached the stage of Buddhahood, one still dwells in the realm of skillful means, transforming the coarse into the sublime. "Non-reception" refers to the absence of [grasping].
The remaining nirvana is realized by all three vehicles.
What is mundane penetration? What is supramundane? And what constitutes the seven stages? I pray that you will explain these for us.
How many kinds of saṃgha are there? What constitutes the schism of the saṃgha? What is the science of medicine (cikitsā-śāstra)?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions [is it taught]—[the Tang translation says: "What are sentient beings? and explains the science of medicine at length]?

Bodhisattvas on the fifth stage engage with worldly affairs to benefit sentient beings; this is called mundane supernatural power (*laukika-abhijñā*). Upon reaching the seventh stage, when the causes of birth are both exhausted, it is only then termed supramundane (*lokottara*).

Regarding the *saṃgha*, there are those of the Mahāyāna and the Two Vehicles. To "destroy the *saṃgha*" refers to violating the discipline (*vinaya*) and violating right view. The Buddha is likened to a skilled physician;
that is, the Tathāgata manifests transformations according to conditions, providing medicine according to the illness, just like a skilled physician of the world.
For what reason, O Great Muni, did you utter such words: "Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni are I"?
Why did you speak of annihilation and permanence, as well as of self and non-self? Why do you not at all times proclaim the true meaning?
Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, you have analytically taught the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*).

For what reason [do you speak of] the forests of men and women, the *harītakī* and *āmalaka* trees, Mount Kailāsa and the Iron Ring Mountains (*cakravāḍa*), the various mountains such as Vajra, adorned with immeasurable jewels, and filled with sages and *gandharvas*?
Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and I—regarding these as past and present, self and other, there is not the slightest distinction between them;
this is the true teaching. Yet, when one further speaks of permanence and annihilation, or of self and non-self, it is because one extensively analyzes the mental capacities of sentient beings:
