The first kind alone arises from non-awakening (*abodha*) and serves as the causal principle for the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). This clarifies that consciousness is not separate from the mind;

it is solely due to non-awakening that the characteristics of consciousness are suddenly formed. Therefore, it is said: "Where the water flows, the waves of the evolving consciousnesses arise from the storehouse consciousness."

Water is a metaphor for the mind (*citta*). The torrential current and the waves are metaphors for the two consciousnesses: the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). "One's own mind" refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind.

This *tathāgatagarbha*-mind manifests as grasping due to non-awakening (*abodhi*). "Grasping" refers to the two divisions of the perceived object (*nimittabhāga*) and the perceiving subject (*darśanabhāga*).
The act of seeing is the grasper (*grāhaka*), and the appearance is the grasped (*grāhya*). If there were no non-awakening (*abodha*), then the mind would incur the fault of producing consciousness.

This beginningless falsehood is that which is manifested by non-awakening; because it is manifested by non-awakening, it transforms into what resembles objective realms, thereby forming the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of form and so forth.
Consciousness possesses the functional capacity to cognize objects, and it naturally engages in discrimination; this is called the self-nature of consciousness.
It is their nature. When there is a desire to see, attention is immediately directed toward it; that is to say, the four sensory objects of the floating faculties rush out and flow toward forms.
Mahāmati, just as with visual consciousness, all the sense-faculties arise simultaneously with every atom and pore, yet they arise in accordance with their respective objects.
It is also like this. For example, it is like a bright mirror manifesting various forms and images. Mahāmati, it is like a fierce wind blowing upon the waters of the great ocean.
This refers to the eight consciousnesses arising either simultaneously or gradually. "Simultaneous arising" means arising all at once; "following sequence" means gradual arising.
The sense organs and pores are the "roots" (indriya). The atoms are the "objects" (viṣaya). As with visual consciousness, one may use the eye as an analogy for all other forms of consciousness.
Each consciousness is distinguished as either sudden or gradual; in all cases, consciousness manifests based upon roots and objects. Therefore, it is said, "it is likewise so.
To understand the purport of this analogy, one should look at the two lines beginning with "For example" below. Regarding the "sudden":
Just as a single consciousness may simultaneously take multiple objects as its conditions, or when multiple objects are present together, multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously;
so too, just as a single consciousness may gradually take various objects as its conditions, or when objects appear sequentially, the various consciousnesses arise gradually.

Furthermore, regarding the five sensory consciousnesses, it can be said that when the five sense-objects are all present together, they arise simultaneously. However, in the case of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), even when the five sense-objects are encountered, it can only take them as its conditions gradually.
These five consciousnesses involve both the sudden and the gradual, whereas the mental consciousness involves only the gradual and lacks the sudden.

Nevertheless, all of them are triggered by the faculties and objects, and the substance of consciousness manifests accordingly. The "substance of consciousness" refers to the true nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Therefore, the substance of consciousness is likened to a mirror or the ocean, while the faculties and objects are likened to forms and wind. Forms and wind are inherently devoid of cognition; the mirror and the ocean remain as ever clear and reflective.

Only through non-awakening does one perceive differentiation; only then does one realize that the five sensory consciousnesses (pañca-vijñāna-kāya) function identically to the eighth consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna).

Although they interact with their respective sense organs and objects, they remain free from conceptual discrimination and analysis, remaining perfectly intact. This state exists solely within the realm of delusion.
In a single moment, it flows into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*). Once missed in the blink of an eye, it can no longer be apprehended.

The winds of external objects toss the ocean of the mind, and the waves of consciousness flow without interruption. Due to the causes—the characteristics of what is produced, whether distinct or non-distinct, and the characteristics produced by the conjunction of karma—one becomes deeply attached through conceptualization.
Because one cannot discern the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and so forth, the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*) arise.

Mahāmati, one should know that the simultaneous arising of those five bodies of consciousness, through the mutual cognition of differentiated and segmented characteristics, is the cause of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
This refers to the eight consciousnesses being mutually causes for one another—neither identical nor different—arising collectively through the activation of karma. Thus they exist.

This is the distinction. "The ocean of mind" refers to the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness). "The winds of external objects" refers to the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). "The waves of consciousness" refers to the seven consciousnesses.
Because the winds of the objects of the six sense-fields toss and stir the ocean of mind, the waves of the seven consciousnesses do not cease.
As for "the characteristics produced by causes," they are neither different nor not different. "Causes" refers to the true consciousness; "characteristics produced" refers to—

The transformation of the two consciousnesses within the *ālayavijñāna* means that they are not different because they share the same true nature (*tathatā*). Yet, they are not non-different because each has its own specific object.

However, generally speaking, due to the arousal of karma through non-awakening (*abodha*), all the consciousnesses simultaneously combine to produce this "phase of arising" (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*) of karmic activity.

Deeply immersed in attachment, one is unable to comprehend the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of form (*rūpa*) and so forth; thus, the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) evolve. As for the self-nature of form and so forth...
"Nature" refers to the fact that form and so forth have the internal consciousness manifesting them as their nature; they appear as if present before one, yet in reality they do not exist.
"That which is concomitant with those five groups of consciousness" means that when the five consciousnesses arise, there is a simultaneous mental consciousness that arises together with them.
Due to the differentiation of causal conditions, conceptualization arises; this mental consciousness (manovijñāna) further takes the five sensory consciousnesses as its cause.

Thus one knows that, failing to realize the Tathāgatagarbha, deluded movement constitutes karma, giving rise to the two divisions of the perceiving subject (darśana-bhāga) and the perceived object (nimitta-bhāga).

These two divisions of subject and object are the manifesting characteristics of the arising of karma. Because the perceiving subject manifests the object, the sense organs and their objects are formed; furthermore, by means of...
The faculties and objects give rise to consciousness, which then initiates differentiation. The ocean waves are fundamentally the same; the winds of the objects are not distinct.
It is simply that one fails to realize this, and thus the marks of karma continue on their own. There is nothing further to point out.
That body transforms. It does not form the thought: "I am mutually the cause for one another" (the Wei translation says:

"The five consciousnesses and the mental consciousness do not form the thought that they are reciprocally causes for each other"). Rather, it transforms through the attachment to the false imaginings manifested by one's own mind;

yet these various [consciousnesses] transform together while their characteristics are distinct, discriminating objects and distinguishing their respective segments. Thus it is said that they transform (the Tang translation says:).
Regarding the objects manifested within one's own mind, conceptualization and attachment arise simultaneously; they lack any distinct characteristics, as each perceives its own respective object.
This clarifies that the eight consciousnesses are, from the very beginning, unborn; they do not change while following conditions, yet they do not change as they follow conditions.
"That body" refers collectively to the eight consciousnesses. These eight consciousnesses are mutually dependent on one another, yet they do not form conceptual thoughts.

This means they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Because they lack intrinsic nature, although they falsely give rise to conceptual constructions and each perceives its own object, the mind does not know karma, and karma does not know the mind; their essential substance is quiescent, and all differentiated characteristics are exhausted.

This is what is called the transformation of the attachment to false conceptualizations manifested by one's own mind, wherein those various mutually exclusive characteristics arise together. (Tang Translation)

The characteristic of disintegration is the characteristic of non-differentiation. It is precisely because the characteristic of differentiation arises in its own place and perishes in that very place that the characteristic of non-differentiation also manifests from time to time.
However, due to a lack of awakening, one merely perceives one's own respective objects within the distinctions of the segmented [world]. △ Third, exhausting the ultimate limit of the *ālayavijñāna*.
It is like a practitioner who enters dhyāna-samādhi; the subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) continue to evolve, yet they do not perceive this, and thus they think:
"Consciousness has ceased, and only then have I entered the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). In reality, consciousness does not cease when one enters absorption;

it does not cease because the seeds of habitual tendencies have not been extinguished. It is said to cease only because the conditions for its evolution and its grasping are incomplete. Mahāmati, it is just as...
This subtle storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the ultimate limit; except for the Tathāgatas and the Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages,
no one— including Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or practitioners of external paths— can fathom or fully comprehend it through the power of the samādhi and wisdom they have attained.
The flowing and ceasing of the eight consciousnesses cannot be fully understood through the cessation of sensation alone. Objects are fundamentally empty, and their grasping is likewise false.
Both concentration and distraction, as well as movement and stillness, all belong to discrimination and fall within the boundaries of consciousness.
This refers to failing to recognize the cause of the continuous flow [of existence], thereby abandoning birth and hastening toward extinction; all such states are merely within delusion.
△ Fourth, revealing that what is manifested by one's own mind is the true reality, free from delusion.

The characteristics of the remaining stages consist of wisdom and skillful means, the analytical determination of phrases and meanings, and the maturation of the most supreme and boundless roots of goodness.
Having abandoned the false fabrications of the delusions manifested by one's own mind, one dwells in mountain forests in meditation, practicing the lower, middle, and superior levels.

Thus, one is able to perceive the continuous flow of the delusions of one's own mind, receive the empowerment of the Buddhas in immeasurable lands, and attain the power of mastery and the three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).

O sons of the Buddha, my spiritual friends: they have completely transcended the false conceptions of the mind, thought, and consciousness, which are the self-nature realm manifested by one's own mind;
they have transcended the ocean of birth and death, karma, craving, and ignorance—causes such as these.
Therefore, Mahāmati, practitioners should draw near to the most excellent spiritual friends.
This statement intends to exhaustively reach the limit of the *ālayavijñāna* and bring one’s own mind to fulfillment.
By means of the power of wisdom, one skillfully resolves all phrases of ultimate meaning; thus, one is able to leave behind the false delusions manifested by one’s own mind.
Once one can leave behind these false delusions, one finally realizes that the continuous flow of one’s own mind arises entirely from non-awakening (*abodha*). If...
Upon reaching the state of non-awakening, one immediately awakens to one’s own mind, no longer being carried away by the realms of deluded sentiment.
One naturally abides in the ocean of the mind, which is the sphere of profound tranquility, and is taken into the care of the Buddhas, dwelling as a child of the Buddha. Such is the natural law.

Regarding those false conceptions of the self-nature realm manifested by one’s own mind—namely, the mind, thought, and consciousness—the false conceptions manifested by one’s own mind are all the self-nature realm.

When one thoroughly realizes that these self-natures are entirely without distinction, then all karma and delusions of birth and death appear like a dream due to confusion; upon awakening, they vanish just as a dream does, without requiring further effort.
"Transformation" means to transcend utterly. Thus, one knows that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not perceive even a single dharma as being the body, karma, or something separate from a master;
yet there is still a state of separation. This is unlike the Two Vehicles, for whom birth-and-death, afflictions, and karma truly exist as characteristics to be abandoned.
Nor is it like the heterodox outsiders, who hold that everything is unobtainable. And yet...

It is not necessary to depart from them. This [teaching] is not the most supreme knowledge; it cannot deeply penetrate the principle that there is only true consciousness (*vijñāna*) and no other consciousness.
Therefore, it indicates that one should draw near to them. The "ocean of birth-and-death" refers to the suffering of the karma of birth-and-death.

Regarding "karma, craving, and ignorance": "karma" is the fundamental ignorance that initiates karma; "craving" is the desire that moistens the branches [of existence]. Ignorance is... [text fragment ends].
It is clarity. The absence of knowing is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). △ Fifth, the verse on the differentiation of the eight consciousnesses, which gives rise to self-awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: "For example, like a vast ocean wave, which arises from a fierce wind;
the great billows surge through the dark abyss without a moment’s interruption. The ocean of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is eternally abiding; its objective realms..."
"Stirred by the wind, the various waves of consciousness surge and arise.

This is a general verse summarizing the causes and conditions for the transformation of the *ālayavijñāna*. The great ocean is used as a metaphor for the *ālayavijñāna*; the fierce wind is a metaphor for the objects of the six sense-fields;

and the waves are a metaphor for the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). With the *ālayavijñāna* as the cause and the sensory objects as the condition, the seven consciousnesses come into being.
The body undergoes transformation;
there are various colors such as blue and red, as well as conch shells, milk, rock honey, bland flavors, and manifold flowers and fruits.

The sun and moon and their radiance are neither different nor not different. Just as waves arise from the waters of the ocean, so it is with the seven consciousnesses: they arise in conjunction with the mind.

This verse further clarifies that the five sense objects—form and so forth—are neither different nor non-different [from consciousness], thereby demonstrating once more that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are likewise neither different nor non-different [from the storehouse consciousness].
Blue and red represent the object of form; conch shells and cowries represent the object of sound; milk, honey, salt, and the bland represent the object of taste;

flowers represent the object of fragrance; and fruits represent the object of touch. These five objects are all manifestations of internal consciousness, just like the sun [reflecting in various vessels].

The moon and its radiance are neither different nor not different; this serves as a metaphor for the relationship between the evolving consciousnesses and the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which is like that between the waters of the ocean and the waves—neither different nor not different.
Just as the waters of the ocean transform and various waves arise, so too do the seven consciousnesses arise in conjunction with the mind.

That is to say, within the locus of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), various consciousnesses evolve; it is by means of that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that one conceptualizes the meanings of various signs.
There are eight unchanging characteristics; even the signless is itself signless. Just as with the waves of the ocean, there is no distinction between them;
so it is with the various consciousnesses and the mind—no difference can be found.

This verse reiterates the first four lines by using the waves of the ocean as a metaphor for the arising of the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) in conjunction with its manifestations.

This leads into the final two lines, which state that [all phenomena] ultimately return to the fundamental storehouse consciousness, wherein various cognitions (vijñānas) arise through transformation.

As for the final eight lines, they mean that although no characteristics of the transformation of the various cognitions can be apprehended, it is nevertheless by means of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) reflecting upon them—without destroying conventional designations—that the eight [consciousnesses] exist.

[This is] the Ear[-division]. The preceding "Chapter on Arising and Ceasing" states: "The manifest consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*) and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*) are mutually causes for one another through their characteristics of being subject to destruction or not.

This is because both the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) possess two characteristics: being subject to destruction and not being subject to destruction.

That is to say, while the aspect of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) is subject to destruction, its own true nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) is not. This long passage [in the present text] says: "And those respective characteristics of destruction..."

They function simultaneously. The verse states: "The unimpaired characteristics are eight. This refers generally to all consciousnesses functioning while deluded regarding the Truth; it indicates that their entire substance is entirely the Truth.

Since the entirety of the Truth is without differentiation, one should speak of them as "unimpaired" (*abhinna*). Since they arise through the differentiation of delusion regarding the Truth, one should speak of them as "impaired" (*bheda*).
That these two are used interchangeably is precisely for the purpose of giving rise to awakening. Since they arise from delusion regarding the Truth, differentiation occurs.

They are distinct, yet it is like flowers appearing before one who stares fixedly; within them, there is neither the characteristic nor that which is characterized. Therefore, it is said that "non-characteristic is also non-characteristic.

Furthermore, just as seawater and its waves share the same nature of water and are without distinction, one deeply understands that all consciousnesses share the same true nature and are likewise without identity or difference.
Delusion follows the appearances of consciousness, while awakening reaches the essence of the unreal.

"Mind" (*citta*) is named for its function of accumulating (*saṃcita*); "intellect" (*manas*) is named for its function of extensively accumulating. The various "consciousnesses" (*vijñāna*) cognize their respective objects; these are said to be five based on the manifestation of their present objects.
Furthermore, each of these eight consciousnesses individually cognizes its own object. Since they are seen to be of the same essence and without difference, there are merely different names.
The eighth is called "mind" because it can receive habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) and can store seeds; this is what is meant by "accumulation."
It is karma. Seventh, that which constantly and critically deliberates upon the internal person and phenomena is called the *manas* (mind).

It maintains these two types of grasping and extensively acts as the cause for karma, further perfuming the *ālayavijñāna* so that it cannot attain purity; therefore, it is said to "extensively gather and accumulate. The latter six are equally termed "consciousnesses" (*vijñāna*).

That which discriminates the five sense-objects (*viṣaya*) of the past and present and operates through the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is called the *mano-vijñāna* (mental consciousness); it functions in relation to the present.
The objects that can manifest the five sensory realms are called the five consciousnesses.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva asked in verse: "Blue, red, and all other forms and images cause sentient beings to give rise to various consciousnesses."
"Just as with the various phenomena that are like waves, how is it that you wish only for me to explain this? Mahāmati,
fearing that sentient beings will not realize that the objects before them are manifestations of internal consciousness and are not [externally] existent,

yet arise from the delusions of the seven evolving consciousnesses and are thus not non-existent, [I teach] that there are presently existing forms capable of producing [cognition], such as blue or red."
Thus, the consciousnesses that currently arise are like waves upon the ocean; in this regard, the subject and object are distinct, yet it is said they are neither different nor not different.

As for the statement "without characteristics, yet also without characteristics," why is this? It is because [the author] intends for the World-Honored One to clarify that both subject and object are manifestations of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra), and that there is nothing else existing apart from them.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse: "The various colors, blue and red, and all such waves do not exist at all.
It is taught that the mind is the accumulation of karma in order to awaken ordinary people. That karma does not exist at all; it is detached from what is grasped by one's own mind.
Since there is nothing grasped and no grasping, it is the same as those waves. The body is established through experience; this is the manifest consciousness of sentient beings. Regarding that:
The manifestation of all karma is like the waves upon water.
This verse concerns the subject-object relationship of mind and objects: both are merely manifestations of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*). Blue and red represent all forms;
the waves represent all cognitions. All are empty and non-existent. Yet, despite being non-existent, they are designated by the name "accumulated karma."
As for "mind," it is intended to let ordinary beings know that all karmic fruits are created solely by the mind;
therefore, it is said that "the mind is called the collector of karma" in order to awaken all ordinary beings. Yet, even this collected karma is unattainable;
thus it is said, "that karma is entirely non-existent. Due to the failure of one's own mind to realize this, there are falsely grasped objects, like [the hairs seen by] those with cataracts.
It is like flowers in the air seen by a diseased eye. These flowers and the eye originally do not reach one another; therefore, it is said that they are detached from what is grasped by the mind.
Since the empty flowers grasped [by the eye] are already detached, the cataract in the eye that grasps them is likewise fundamentally non-existent.
Just as with those waves—the waves are entirely water—it is said that "that which is grasped has nothing to grasp," which is the same as the case of the waves. Manifestation...
The preceding sense organs, bodies, and the vessel-world are all manifestations of consciousness alone.
The manifesting consciousness and the manifested sense organs, bodies, and vessel-world are like the waves upon water; they are neither one nor two.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva spoke again in verse: "The nature of the great ocean’s waves can be discerned by their surging;
The storehouse consciousness and its karma are likewise—why is it not perceived?"
In this verse, the ocean and its waves can be easily distinguished; however, the *ālayavijñāna* (the storehouse consciousness) and karma, which serve as their metaphors, are difficult to perceive.
"Karma" here refers to the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse: "Ordinary people lack wisdom; the storehouse consciousness is like a vast ocean.
The characteristics of karma are like waves; through these analogies, the truth is understood."
Ordinary beings lack wisdom and cannot be addressed with direct truth; therefore, the treasury and its turning are used as metaphors, hoping that they may achieve self-awakening.
This cannot be demonstrated through ultimate reality. Consequently, in the subsequent text, there is again the question of why the truth is not spoken.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again spoke in verse: "When the sun rises, its light shines equally upon beings of inferior, middling, and superior capacity.
So too does the Tathāgata illuminate the world; for the sake of the ignorant, he speaks of reality. Having already categorized all dharmas, why does he not speak of the ultimate truth?"
This statement says that the Tathāgata appears in the world to reveal, cause others to awaken to, and lead them into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision of all things;

yet he does not directly reveal the ultimate reality, but instead classifies the various dharmas. What is the intent of this? "Classifying" refers to dividing [the teachings] into the ninefold or twelvefold divisions.
How could one know that the three vehicles and five vehicles taught by the Tathāgata are all merely... [the first stage].
The single ultimate truth is such that sentient beings, lacking wisdom, cannot be pointed directly toward it; thus it must be shown indirectly.
Although there is no separate meaning, there is a great "timeliness" [for this approach]. The following text specifically clarifies this intent.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse: “If one speaks of reality, that mind has no reality.
Just as the waves of the ocean, images in a mirror, and dreams— All appear simultaneously; so too are the objects of the mind.

Because objects are not simultaneous, karmic activity arises in succession. That which cognizes is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which intends is the mental faculty (*manas*); And as for the five [sense-consciousnesses]...”
This is manifested without any fixed order. It is like a master painter and his disciples who spread out colors to depict various forms;
my teaching is also like this. The colors themselves originally possess no patterns; they are neither the brush nor the canvas.
Yet, for the sake of delighting sentient beings, they are interwoven in a variegated manner to paint all manner of images.
The Tathāgata does not speak of reality because the minds of sentient beings lack reality. That which exists yet is not seen is equivalent to non-existence.
If one wishes to point directly to what is manifest before one's eyes, it is neither mind nor consciousness.
It is like using five colors to show to those who are blind; the Tathāgata acts regarding that which is not mind, yet points to it as mind, and thus compares it to a sea-mirror.
Regarding that which is not consciousness, he points to it as consciousness, and thus compares it to the waves of the sea and the images in a mirror.
These refer to the eight consciousnesses transforming to give rise to various consciousnesses, all appearing simultaneously and instantaneously. The seven evolving [consciousnesses] rely upon...

They manifest according to their objects; when the objects are not complete, they appear sequentially. The differentiation of the six consciousnesses, the mental attention of the seventh consciousness, and the engagement with sensory objects by the five consciousnesses all appear in succession, yet without a fixed order of priority.
This is precisely why the Tathāgata cannot directly reveal the ultimate reality, but instead employs skillful means to guide sentient beings—just as a skilled painter [proceeds step by step].

This is like applying colors to depict forms. If it were for the mind to await awakening, or for consciousness to await emptiness, how could such transcendence of emotion and severance of conceptualization be the application of the great wisdom? To have awakening and delusion is merely what the ignorant delight in seeing.
What is called "color" has no pattern; it is neither brush nor silk. Yet, in order to delight sentient beings, one cannot help but produce this.
Speech is a provisional practice; reality is beyond names and words. Discernment pertains to the beginner's stage; cultivation reveals the truth.
The state of true self-awakening is free from both the perceiving subject and the perceived object. This is taught for the sake of the Buddha’s sons;

it is merely designated as "truth" through verbal expression. Yet when one reaches the actual truth, there is only a silent resonance, like a person drinking water who knows its coldness or warmth for themselves.
That which is known by oneself cannot be explained by names or signs; therefore, in contrast to verbal expression, it is [described as such].
This is distinct. It is true self-awakening, obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Both the subject that awakens and the object awakened to are not within the realm of the senses.
This may be spoken of for the sons of the Buddha, but it is not easily explained to those of beginner’s capacity.

The foolish engage in extensive conceptual proliferation; all such varieties are like illusions. Though they appear, they lack reality; thus they are described in various ways. These are designated according to specific circumstances;
what is taught is not what is appropriate for them, and thus it is not taught to them. This applies to each and every one of those who are sick.
Just as a skilled physician prescribes according to the specific case, so the Tathāgata teaches sentient beings according to their inclinations and capacities.
This is not the domain of conceptual construction, nor is it the portion of the śrāvakas; it is what the Compassionate One has taught as the domain of self-realization.
The Tathāgata provides extensive analytical explanations for the sake of the foolish; therefore, all various phenomena are like illusions.
Although they appear yet lack reality, he could ultimately not help but speak of them in their various forms. Such provisional designations according to circumstances were truly unavoidable.

If he were to speak of the ultimate reality too hastily, it would simply be inappropriate for those listeners. This is just as a skilled physician treats a patient; it is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s skillful adaptation.
"The minds of sentient beings correspond to the measure of what is known through deluded thought (*vikalpa*). This refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

"The Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings"—here, "compassion" means responding to their minds according to their capacities. "Compassion" is the realm of self-realization (*pratyātma-gati*), which is not within the scope of ordinary worldlings or those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
6. Directly demonstrating the three characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to know the manifestation of his own mind—the realm of false discrimination consisting of the grasped and the grasper—he should leave behind crowds, worldly customs, and sleep;
throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, he should constantly awaken himself and practice skillful means.
He should also distance himself from the doctrines and discourses of those with evil views, as well as from the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding the characteristics of the vehicle: one should thoroughly penetrate the characteristics of the false conceptualizations that appear from within one's own mind.

This is an exhortation to practice according to the teaching. For all objects of false conceptualization—both the grasper and the grasped—arise from a lack of awareness regarding the manifestations of one's own mind;
thus, although one dwells amidst all such objects, this manifest cognition remains [unrealized].
Although it has been shifted, while one remains in the state of delusion, one is unable to perceive it; therefore, it is said:

"If you wish to know the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of your own mind—the realm of false discrimination consisting of the grasped and the grasper—you should leave behind clamor and sleep, and constantly awaken yourself during the first, middle, and last watches of the night.
This is precisely awakening to your own mind. The direct perception of one's own mind is easily realized in a quiet place."
Furthermore, the evil views of externalists and the deluded teachings of the two vehicles increase false conceptualization and run counter to one's own mind;
by distancing oneself from both, one finally realizes that all marks of false conceptualization are manifestations of one's own mind.
Thus they arise and thus they cease. This is the direct and expedient method for cultivation.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has established the characteristics of wisdom and dwells therein,
they should diligently train in the three aspects of the higher noble wisdom.
Wisdom. Regarding non-awakening: if one does not awaken to one's own mind, then although one is in the midst of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one cannot abide therein.
Once awakened and abiding, as for the three characteristics of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) that still remain, they shall be simultaneously eliminated through enlightenment;
thus the compassionate vows will be fulfilled. This is illustrated by the following passage.
What are the three characteristics of noble wisdom that one should diligently cultivate? They are: the characteristic of non-existence;
the characteristic of the sphere of the self-vow of all Buddhas; and the characteristic of the ultimate realization of noble self-awakened wisdom.

Having attained these through practice, one is able to abandon the mental state of the "lame donkey" of wisdom and attain the eighth stage of the Supreme Son (Bodhisattva). Thereupon, regarding those three aforementioned characteristics—
"Born of cultivation, Mahāmati. As for the mark of non-existence, it refers to the marks of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and externalists; these are born from their respective practices.
Mahāmati, as for the mark of the sphere of one's own vows, it refers to what is born from the cultivation within the sphere of the original vows of all previous Buddhas. Mahāmati."

Regarding the ultimate characteristic of the noble wisdom of self-realization: it is the absence of conceptual attachment to the characteristics of all phenomena; it is the attainment of the body of the illusion-like samādhi;
and it is the arising of the practice that advances toward the stage of the Buddhas. Mahāmati, these are called the three characteristics of noble wisdom.
If one accomplishes these three characteristics of noble wisdom, one can reach the ultimate realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization. Therefore, Mahāmati...
Wisdom. One should diligently practice and study the three characteristics of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

Upon the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is completely severed; all mental activity ceases and nothing further arises. This resembles the wisdom of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), which is termed "the wisdom of the lame donkey.
It is only upon entering the eighth stage that this is abandoned. As for the characteristic of non-existence (*anupalambha-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the two vehicles.

This is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). A bodhisattva abides in the marks of wisdom, yet still employs the meditative tranquility (*śamatha*) of the two vehicles to purify subtle attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
This constitutes not losing skillful means (*upāya*), rather than being attached to real dharmas. Regarding the marks of the former Buddhas' own vows, the *Śrī-mālā-sūtra* states:

"For those who have not yet crossed over the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), cause them to cross over the truth of suffering; for those who have not yet understood the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), cause them to understand..."
To understand the Truth of Suffering’s origination; to establish those not yet established in the Truth of the Path;
and to attain the Truth of Cessation not yet attained—these four great vows rely upon both the Separate and Perfect Teachings, taking as their object the two types of the Four Noble Truths:

conditioned and unconditioned. This is the characteristic of the self-vows of the Buddhas of the past; the Bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind differs from that of the Two Vehicles. It is the realization of the Sage through self-awakening.

Regarding the characteristic of the ultimate realization of wisdom (*jñāna-paryanta-lakṣaṇa*): it refers to the realization of the objective realm as the manifestation of one’s own mind in all places;

the penetration of all phenomena without obstruction; the attainment of the illusory body (*māyā-deha*); and the perfection of the stage of Buddhahood (*buddha-bhūmi*). This is precisely the wisdom of differentiation (*viśeṣa-jñāna*).
Although it is not called "differentiation," it is termed the "ultimate of noble wisdom" (*āryajñāna-paryanta*) because it is the fundamental basis for the culmination of differentiation.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, the youth Sudhana traveled through one hundred and eleven cities to study the bodhisattva path.
Finally, upon arriving at the abode of Maitreya, he was again instructed to return and see Mañjuśrī. [Maitreya] declared:

"All those spiritual friends you previously encountered, the bodhisattva practices you heard, the gates of liberation you entered, and the great vows you fulfilled—all these were due to the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī."
"O Śūṣila, in all places, one attains ultimate perfection. Therefore, know that after the characteristics of wisdom in the preceding abodes, one then diligently cultivates the three characteristics.
When these three characteristics are accomplished, it is likewise simply called 'being able to reach the ultimate realm of the noble self-realized wisdom.
This is because the fundamental wisdom illuminates all distinctions; thus, it is ultimately without distinction."

[End of section] The first part above clarifies the causes and effects, as well as the heterodox and orthodox, regarding the eight consciousnesses, thereby concluding the demonstration of the self-awakening of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

The second part demonstrates that the five dharmas (*pañcadharma*) are devoid of self-nature (*svabhāva*) and self (*ātman*), distinguishing them from the vehicles of the two *śrāvakas* and externalists (*tīrthika*), thereby revealing the causes and effects of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
This is divided into three sections. The first clarifies the five dharmas, which is further divided into nine parts. The first is Mahāmati’s question.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of great bodhisattvas, [recited] the *Sūtra on the Discrimination of the Self-Nature of the Objects of Noble Wisdom*.
Empowered by the majestic spiritual authority of all Buddhas, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, we pray that you will expound for us the *Sūtra on the Discrimination of the Self-Nature of the Objects of Noble Wisdom*, which is the basis for the discrimination of the one hundred and eight phrases."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, based on this discrimination, explains how Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter into the imagined nature of self-characteristics and common characteristics.
Because he explains the imagined nature through discrimination, they are able to thoroughly know and universally observe the selflessness of persons and phenomena,
purify their delusions, illuminate the various stages (*bhūmi*), and transcend all sounds.
Having heard of the Pratyekabuddhas and the bliss of the various meditative concentrations of the non-Buddhists, they observe the inconceivable sphere of activity of the Tathāgata.
They definitively abandon the five dharmas and the self-nature (*svabhāva*), becoming well-adorned with the wisdom of the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
They give rise to illusory spheres of experience, ascend to the Tuṣita palaces of all Buddha-fields, and so forth, up to the limit of form (*rūpa-kūṭastha*).
This concludes the section on the celestial palaces. [The text states: "One attains the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharma-body.
This question concerns the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) in order to reveal holy wisdom (*āryajñāna*) and to distinguish it from erroneous views.

For it is due to delusion regarding one's own nature that false imagination arises; thus, within the ground where self and other are fundamentally non-existent, notions of self and other suddenly appear simultaneously.
The marks manifest instantaneously as forms, just as when the visual consciousness first perceives color, it attains the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the visual consciousness;

yet, as soon as one falls into conceptual discrimination, they become the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). These are all the realms of deluded thought and non-awakening. All Bodhisattvas enter into this.
Yet, they demonstrate all the various distinctions between the mundane and the supramundane, established through the formulation of one hundred and eight propositions.
If one realizes that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has no distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this constitutes the domain of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

One thereby attains the realization that neither self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) nor common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) can be apprehended. Furthermore, all bodhisattvas do not abandon any of the various [phenomena] belonging to the mundane and the supramundane.
Through these distinctions, one attains the profound elucidation of the one hundred and eight non-positions (*apada*).

This is what the Tathāgata has analyzed and taught as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of deluded thought (*vikalpa*). By means of this analysis, one realizes that deluded thought has no separate self-nature;

thus, one first understands that self-nature is fundamentally without a person and fundamentally without phenomena. Because there is neither person nor phenomenon, one is able to purify and eliminate delusion.
One conceives [of these stages] yet does not exert diligent effort; one illuminates the various grounds yet remains unimpeded by their perfect interfusion.
One transcends the bliss of the deluded external dhyānas and enters the sphere traversed by the Tathāgatas. What is called "delusive attachment" is immediately and suddenly empty.

Wisdom is like the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), yet it is not substantially existent either. This wisdom of the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas arises from delusive conceptualization.
Regarding the self-nature: one clarifies the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*). All adornments are, in fact, the adornment of one’s own mind.
This means that by transforming the delusory objects manifested by one’s own mind, one manifests lands as an illusion and ascends to celestial palaces as an illusion;

without departing from one's own mind, one attains the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, which is ultimately and eternally abiding. △ Second, refuting the false calculations of the non-Buddhists regarding existence.

"No. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There is a class of non-Buddhists who, through the conceptual attachment to the notion of 'nothingness,' perceive that because causes are exhausted, there is the idea that a rabbit has no horns.
They think that just as a rabbit has no horns, all phenomena are likewise so. Mahāmati, furthermore..."

Other non-Buddhists perceive the various qualities (*guṇa*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and substantial entities (*dravya*), seeing them as distinct and separate according to their shapes and spatial positions.

Having seen this, they become attached to the notion of "transverse dharmas" that do not exist—like the horns of a rabbit—and conceive the thought that "oxen have horns. Mahāmati, they fall into these two views.

Not understanding that it is the measure of the mind, they increase the proliferation of false imaginings regarding the objects of their own minds. They establish the measure of the roots of false imaginings through the experience and enjoyment of the body.
Mahāmati, the nature of all dharmas is likewise so; being free from existence and non-existence, one should not form conceptions thereof. Mahāmati!
Furthermore, if one forms the notion that a rabbit has no horns while departing from both existence and non-existence, this is called a false notion.

Because it arises from dependent observation, one should not form the notion that a rabbit has no horns. Even down to the analysis of the nature of things into subtle atoms, nothing can be apprehended.
Mahāmati, since the realm of the noble ones is free from such [dualities], one should not form the notion that a cow has horns.
This demonstrates that because they do not comprehend the self-nature of deluded thought (*vikalpa*), there arise the false calculations of the heterodox paths.

Deluded thought arises from the mind-measure (*citta-mātra*) of non-awakening (*a-prabodha*). The mind is not a state of movement; it is through non-awakening that delusion is produced. This delusive production is not existent, and its cessation is not non-existent.
Both existence and non-existence are dualistic delusions that merely increase non-awakening; they are not the fundamental mind-measure. Therefore, they do not understand.

The characteristic of arising begins with ignorance, whereby one erroneously clings to the sensory faculties and inevitably falls into the view of eternalism; yet even if one observes the exhaustion of causes, one again sinks into the view of annihilationism.
This notion of "a rabbit having no horns" and "an ox having horns" arises from the conceptualization of mutual dependence.
Even while within the True Dharma, it is not easy to suddenly and directly transcend this state, for as long as the fundamental mind-ground has not reached full perfection, [one remains bound].

The deluded emotions of non-awakening are difficult to exhaust. Though one clearly knows that what is manifest before one is not existent, and that the vast void is not non-existent, at the very moment of thought, one has not yet glimpsed this;
thus, silent conceptualizations secretly nourish themselves. This is what is meant by being detached from existence and non-existence, yet still forming the notion of a rabbit’s horns.

In short, the contemplation of emptiness arises because one is stalled in attachment to existence; only then does one come to believe in the realization of illusion—how could there be any further need for non-existence? There is no such thing as "non-existence."

If it can be attained, then even non-existence would have nothing from which to depend. What is called the "separation from the realm of the sages" ultimately means one should not form the notion that a cow has horns.
As for the exhaustion of the causes of awakening, it is like the Sāṃkhya teachers who exhaust eighty thousand kalpas.
In profound stillness there is no cognition; one clearly knows that all phenomena before one ultimately reach exhaustion and are identical to the horns of a rabbit.
"Elements" (*mahābhūta*) refers to the four great elements. *Guṇa* is translated as "reliance" (*āśraya*). *Dravya* is translated as "dust" (*rajas*).

"Transverse phenomena" refers to the various phenomena arranged in a disordered manner, such as the Lokāyatika masters who perceive the four great elements as having atoms (*paramāṇu-rajas*) as their generative cause, because they exist.
All phenomena are presented in various arrangements, each distinct from the others; therefore, one conceives of the non-existence of a rabbit's horn while forming the notion that a cow has horns.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, is it not the case that those who have attained freedom from false conceptualization perceive [things as they truly are]?"
Having perceived the characteristic of non-arising, one investigates through inference and deliberation. Does one then say that the arising of false discrimination is "non-existent"?
To perceive the characteristic of non-arising means to see that the horns of a cow cannot be obtained, and thus the characteristic of existence does not arise.

By means of this inference, one does not give rise to false discrimination. This is the reason for the nihilistic calculations of the Tīrthikas; we wish for the World-Honored One to explain it in detail.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not because of the failure to observe that one says 'non-existent' regarding the non-arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Why is this?

Conceptual construction arises dependent upon that [object]. One gives rise to conceptual construction based on those horns; because conceptual construction arises based on the horns, it is therefore said to be dependent."
Because of this cause, they are neither different nor non-different. One does not speak of "non-existence" regarding horns based on the failure to perceive them;

rather, such views—whether seeing existence or non-existence outside the sphere of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*)—are all causes of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Therefore, one should abandon them. Deluded conceptualization relies upon the horn to calculate existence and non-existence;
thus, taking the discrimination of existence and non-existence as a cause is not the correct cause. This is because it is distinct from... [the true nature].

They are not different; they are all merely conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Based on the horn, the conceptualization of existence arises; this is "not different. Based on the horn, the conceptualization of non-existence arises; this is "different.
Both are causes of conceptualization and are equally without reality. Therefore, one who attains the objective realm of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) [transcends them].
One certainly does not observe them and thus does not give rise to the false imagination that "there are no horns.
Mahāmati, if the false imagination were different from the horns, it would not arise dependent upon the horns.

If it were not different, then because it is dependent upon them—even when analyzed and sought down to the level of subtle atoms—it is entirely unfindable; for it is not different from the horns, and therefore it too [is non-existent].
It is not a nature. If both are without nature, what dharma and for what reason could one say they do not exist?

Mahāmati, if one says there are no horns because they do not exist, or observes them as existing and thus says the rabbit has no horns, one should not form such a conceptualization. Mahāmati, this is because it is based on an incorrect cause.
Thus, when one speaks of both existence and non-existence, neither is established.
This refers to the proponent of non-existence who relies on the "cause arising from horns" as a premise; subsequently, because that cause is found to be unreal, what was posited becomes empty.
Therefore, one should not form such a conceptualization. The point is this: if the imagined nature were different from the horns, it would not depend upon the horns;
if it were not different from the horns, then it would depend upon them. Now, if we analyze the horns themselves down to the level of atoms, they cannot be found.
Since its existence is not distinct from these horns, its very nature cannot even be definitively established. If existence is not its nature, then that—
Non-existence is also not a nature; both are devoid of nature. What thing or what dharma in the world could be said to be non-existent?
To see non-existence and say "there are no horns," or to see that existence cannot be apprehended and say "there are no horns"—this basis for existence and non-existence should not be conceptualized.
That which is not the correct cause refers to failing to attain the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas, whether in terms of existence or non-existence.
These two views are both merely conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), Mahāmati.
Furthermore, there are other non-Buddhist views that cling to the substance, form, and spatial dimensions of matter and emptiness;
they fail to properly understand the limits of space and thus give rise to the false discrimination of a view regarding spatial boundaries, asserting that matter is separate from space.
This passage refutes the view held by certain non-Buddhists who ultimately claim that things exist without a cause yet depend on conditions; therefore, one must completely abandon such views.
They cling to the notion that form is distinct from space, asserting that the four great elements and atoms can produce all phenomena.
This arises merely from their failure to properly understand the boundaries between form and empty space, giving rise to all manner of false conceptualizations.
Mahāmati, space is form; it enters into the categories of form. Mahāmati, form is space; it is established by the nature of the container and the contained.

One should understand that the phenomena of form and emptiness are to be distinguished through conceptual differentiation. Mahāmati, when the four great elements arise, their own characteristics are each distinct;
they do not abide in space, yet it is not that space does not exist within them.
Regarding "entering according to the nature of form": there is not a single phenomenon in the world that can exist apart from space, nor is there any that is not entered by space.
"Holding" refers to the space that holds; "held" refers to the form that is held. There is likewise not a single phenomenon in the world that is not held by space.
This establishes the intrinsic nature of form and space; it should be understood accordingly.
This is what is known. If one holds that form exists because of emptiness, or that emptiness exists because of form, this is merely the deluded view of ordinary people and non-Buddhists.
To examine the meaning of form and emptiness: they arise simultaneously and manifest all at once through the delusion of the True Nature into consciousness;

there is no sequence of before and after, nor any distinction between self and other. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Obscuration becomes emptiness; the binding of emptiness becomes form. It further states: "Emptiness arises from Great Enlightenment."
It is like a single bubble arising from the ocean. The minute dust-motes of the realms of outflows are all produced in dependence upon space.
Now, to be attached to form or attached to space is to be deluded regarding the limits of the Middle Way; one does not transcend discursive thought (*vikalpa*).

Only when one awakens to what is manifested by one’s own mind does one first realize that all manifested realms are collectively identical to the events of a dream. Within a dream, the empty space and the sensory faculties (*indriya*) appear vividly before one; this is form.
This is emptiness. It is still a conceptual discrimination. Only after awakening does one know that it is produced by the perceptions of consciousness and is neither existent nor non-existent.
The four great elements have distinct individual characteristics; although they do not abide in empty space, that which enters and is supported by them is beyond all discrimination.
This is because [the opponent] reckons the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the four great elements to be the cause for the arising of all phenomena; therefore, the following analogy is stated:
It is for the sake of clarifying this.
It is thus, Mahāmati: one observes that the cow has horns, and therefore concludes that the rabbit has no horns.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, if the horn of a cow is analyzed into atoms, and those atoms are further analyzed as not remaining for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), then what is there to observe such that one says [the rabbit] has none?
If one says that one contemplates other things, those phenomena are likewise so.

Ultimately, even the reckoning of non-existence arises because of the reckoning of existence; they are established through mutual dependence and are not the true characteristics of existence or non-existence.
If non-existence were not reckoned because of existence, then one might as well split a cow’s horn into atoms, and further split those atoms...
It does not abide for even a single moment. Since this "corner" (characteristic) is absent, by what could one observe and manifest its lack of characteristics?
Therefore, know that for those who reckon there are characteristics, those characteristics do not abide;

and for those who reckon there are no characteristics because characteristics do not abide, then the absence of characteristics has nothing to be manifested, nor can it abide. When both existence and non-existence do not abide, [one is] directly beneath.
"What is this state? To observe other things means to infer from the horns of one's own cow.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:
"You should abandon the false views and deluded imaginings regarding rabbit horns, cow horns, space, form, and color. You, all you Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas, should contemplate your own minds."
Manifesting as deluded thoughts, he enters [the world] to become the most excellent son of all buddha-fields, instructing them through the skillful means of the manifestations of his own mind.
This concluding statement indicates that one should abandon the dualistic delusions of existence and non-existence and directly contemplate "mind-only. Thus, the Bodhisattva...
If one can observe the manifestation of one's own mind and see all realms of deluded thought manifested by one's own mind—

arising all at once through the confusion of mind into consciousness— as being entirely like illusions and transformations, one will immediately and completely transcend the characteristics of existence and non-existence,
form and emptiness, and so forth. Thereafter, with an illusion-like body, one enters an illusion-like buddha-field to serve all Buddhas.
"Son, by means of the skillful method that is like an illusion, I teach and instruct you regarding the manifestation of one's own mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Form and the rest, as well as the mind, do not exist; yet form and the rest nourish the mind.
The body, experience, and establishment are the manifestations of the *ālayavijñāna* for sentient beings. The mind, the intellect, and consciousness are its own nature."
The Dharma has five aspects: non-self, the two kinds of purity, that which is taught by the Proclaimer, and the mutual arising of long, short, existence, non-existence, and so forth.
Because of non-existence, existence is established; because of existence, non-existence is established. By analyzing phenomena down to atoms, the false imagination of form does not arise.
This is the locus established by the measure of mind (*cittamātra*), which is not favored by those with evil views, as it is not the sphere of discursive thought or the Śrāvakas.

It is likewise so, as taught by the Savior: this refers to the realm of self-realization, wherein form and other such phenomena fundamentally do not exist within the mind; rather, the mind arises and is nourished in dependence upon form and the rest.
However, since the mind has no form or other such qualities, from what do the manifest sense organs, bodies, and the vessel-world arise to serve as the supports for the mind?
This is because, due to delusion regarding the Truth, the storehouse consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) manifests all that is seen by sentient beings.
Since these appear due to delusion, the Tathāgata extensively explained the mind (citta), intellect (manas), mentation (vijñāna), the five dharmas, the three natures, and the two [selflessnesses].
The various types of selflessness are also designated according to one's delusions in order to provide names and characteristics that enable definitive discernment.

This is just like the views regarding the length, shortness, existence, or non-existence of form and so forth; these are established through mutual dependence, such as perceiving existence based on non-existence, or perceiving non-existence based on existence.

All these are matters within delusion; they lack self-nature altogether. If one does not give rise to any discrimination regarding all objects of conceptualization, but dwells solely in the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of what is manifested by one's own mind—this realm of self-awakening is that which the Tathāgata, the Savior of the World, has taught.
Those with evil views do not delight in it, claiming it is not the realm of ordinary beings or Śrāvakas. △ Third, showing purity.

Setting aside the sudden and gradual [approaches], at that time Mahāmati Bodhisattva, for the sake of purifying the stream of manifestations within his own mind, again requested the Tathāgata, saying to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, how does one purify the stream of manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings? Is it sudden or gradual?"

"Self-mind-manifestation-stream" (*svacittadṛśya-saṃtāna*) refers to "manifestation" (*dṛśya*), "active functioning" (*samudācāra*), "stream" (*saṃtāna*), and "continuous flow" (*pravāha*; i.e., the continuous flow of the active functioning of the eight consciousnesses).
The preceding section clarified the realm of false discrimination manifested by one's own mind;

this section addresses how one who has realized that all active functioning and flows are manifestations of their own mind may employ skillful means to purify them—whether by sudden or gradual means. This constitutes the fifth [section].
The Dharma is right knowledge.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Purification is gradual, not instantaneous, just as the mango fruit ripens gradually and not instantaneously.
The Tathāgata’s purification of the stream of manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings is likewise gradual, not instantaneous. It is like a potter..."

The construction of various vessels occurs gradually, not instantaneously. In the same way, the Tathāgata’s purification of the stream of manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings is likewise gradual, not instantaneous.
It is like the great earth, which gradually produces the myriad things, rather than producing them all at once.
The Tathāgata’s purification of the stream of manifestations from the minds of all sentient beings is likewise gradual, not instantaneous.

Just as a person learning music, writing, painting, or various other arts achieves proficiency gradually and not instantaneously, so too is the Tathāgata’s purification of the stream of manifestations from the minds of all sentient beings: it is gradual, not instantaneous. It is like a bright mirror.

All signless forms and images appear instantaneously. In the same way, the Tathāgata purifies the stream of mental manifestations of all sentient beings, and likewise instantaneously manifests the pure realm that is signless and devoid of any existence, like the orbs of the sun and the moon.

It instantaneously illuminates and displays all forms and images. In the same way, for the sake of sentient beings who wish to be freed from the afflictions of the habitual tendencies of their own mind’s manifestations, the Tathāgata likewise instantaneously displays the supreme realm of inconceivable wisdom.

Just as the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) instantaneously discerns and knows the manifestations of its own mind, as well as the bodies, their establishment, and the objects of experience, so too do those various *nirmāṇakāya* Buddhas.
It is likewise so. It suddenly ripens the realms where sentient beings dwell by establishing practitioners in that Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Just as the Dharma-Buddha creates the Nirmanakaya-Buddha, its radiance shines forth, illuminating the noble path of self-realization.
It is likewise so. Regarding the existence or non-existence of intrinsic nature within the characteristics of phenomena, he illuminates and causes the extinction of evil views and false imaginings.

This is discussed primarily in terms of the principle of sudden awakening and sudden cultivation, while simultaneously encompassing both the sudden and the gradual; it concerns the Buddha and sentient beings as a whole.
The original delusion of true consciousness manifests its entirety as all manner of false appearances, not through gradual stages.
Thus, one awakens to the fact that delusions have no cause and suddenly perceives that the self-nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing.

All false minds cease instantaneously and simultaneously, without any waiting. This is the principle of sudden awakening and sudden eradication, as found in the first stage of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s Ten Abodes.
By means of the samādhi of non-action, one’s own essence accords with the truth. Afflictions are but adventitious dust; they possess no inherent nature whatsoever.
There is only the true essence and its function, free from greed, anger, and delusion. Spontaneously, one is a Buddha—this may be called sudden enlightenment and sudden cultivation.
Yet, the progression through the stages and grounds remains strictly orderly. The twenty-five wheels of Perfect Enlightenment extensively open up skillful means, and thus it is said:

Only those who possess sudden awakening do not follow along with phenomena; thus one knows that the principle of the Perfect and Sudden is clearly seen by the Tathāgata, and the faculties and desires of sentient beings are also clearly seen by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the provisional and the real are both exalted, and the Dharma-methods of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time are identical.
Yet, when one infers the Buddha’s fundamental intention, there is only the sudden and no gradual; this is also based on the manifestation of one's own mind.
This is the measure. It is devoid of all falsehood; such is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When awakening occurs, delusion is extinguished;
once awakened, delusion does not arise. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "There is only the path of the One Vehicle; it is spoken of as three for the sake of differentiation. This is the definitive principle.
It is like a bright mirror or the orbs of the sun and moon, which suddenly manifest forms and images that lack inherent characteristics, because both the mirror and the sun and moon are empty.

This clarifies the meaning. It is like the Tathāgata suddenly revealing the characteristics of the non-existent, pure, and inconceivable wisdom, so that sentient beings may know that what appears to their own minds is a mere manifestation (*svacittadṛśyamātra*). It is fundamentally empty and luminous, and fundamentally free from defilement.

One suddenly abandons the faults and afflictions of habitual tendencies all at once, rather than through gradual cultivation. Thus, by means of the *ālayavijñāna*, one suddenly discerns and knows that which is produced by one's own mind.
Regarding the use of the present root-body and the vessel-world as metaphors: this refers to the mind that manifests in the daily activities of sentient beings.
Originally, there exists such pure wisdom-function that illuminates and comprehends all things simultaneously, without any sequence of before or after.

Therefore, based on this, the Buddha-Tathāgata, at the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha), brings all sentient beings to maturity instantaneously, without the need for laborious expedient means. Furthermore...
Regarding the use of the *dharmakāya* as a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya*: this refers to the inconceivable activity of the Tathāgata.

Just as light shines forth to enable the noble ones who have realized self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) to recognize the essence of their own Dharma, so too does the light shine forth, allowing them to suddenly abandon all evil views of existence and non-existence;
furthermore, there is no distinction [between these two lights]. In short, the essence of the nature is light, and its function is light.
It distinguishes between delusion and awakening. In delusion, the root-body and the vessel-world appear in an instant, leaving no room for waiting.
In awakening, the lands of Dharma, Reward, and Transformation are ultimately majestic and pure; how could they require cultivation?

There are indeed many gates to turning delusion into awakening, yet when awakening is identical to delusion, there is nothing at all to be taught or shown. Entering the sudden from the gradual is likewise the Buddha’s last resort.
...[the ear]. △ Fourth, showing the distinctions in the wisdom and teachings of the three Buddhas.

Mahāmati, the Dharma-āśraya Buddha (translated in the Tang version as the Buddha who flows from the nature of phenomena) teaches that all dharmas enter into their own-characteristics and common characteristics;

that they have the habitual tendencies manifested by one's own mind as their cause; and that they have the attachment to the self-nature of continuous false discrimination as their cause, [resulting in] various [distinctions].
In reality, it is like an illusion; various conceptual attachments cannot be found.

All phenomena presently manifesting—whether characterized by specific or general marks—arise from the seeds and habitual tendencies of one's own mind, giving rise to the continuous attachment to the appearances of active delusive thoughts.
Manifested from other-dependent seeds, these various [phenomena] are like illusions. Delusory...
When one calculates and examines what is currently active and grasped, nothing of various kinds can be found. This dependent origination is non-arising;
through delusion one attains awakening, purifies the Buddha-lands, and brings sentient beings to maturity. Therefore, this is that which was taught by the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Buddha).

As for the *dharmakāya* (Dharma Buddha), it is the intrinsically pure awakening. This intrinsically pure awakening is possessed by both sentient beings and Buddhas alike; yet, while they are deluded...
If one is deluded, it is total delusion; if one awakens, it is total awakening. It does not depend on knowledge or views, nor does it borrow from merit or achievement;
it is the natural state of the self-nature (*svabhāva*). Relying upon the Buddha refers to the *prajñā* (wisdom) that flows forth from the Dharma-Buddha.

Originally born from the self-nature, it in turn illuminates the self-nature, adorning the body and the land—this is what is called the "Retribution" [Buddha]. As for the "Transformation" Buddha, it refers to responding to and transforming beings according to their various types, pervading everywhere.
It enters into all things. The land of the eternally quiescent light of self-nature (*svabhāva*) serves as the land of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*), which is not known by others.

The land of the reward Buddha (*vipākabuddha*) is the land of other-enjoyment (*parasaṃbhoga*), shared with Bodhisattvas of the ten stages; it is where the noble and the ordinary dwell together, and this is precisely the land of the transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*).
They enter according to their respective types, and what they perceive differs for each. What the Dharma-Buddha teaches is that self-nature has no basis;

what the Reward-Buddha teaches is that dependent origination lacks intrinsic nature. The Transformation-Buddha, observing faculties according to their inclinations, has no fixed teaching; yet even this is presented in brief.

In principle, they should interpenetrate one another. The Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body are neither three nor one; this is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of both the person and the land. The same applies to their explanations.
Even within the causes and effects of humans and devas, there exists the principle of the Unsurpassed, Right, and True [Enlightenment].

As it is said in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, when the Tathāgata sometimes speaks of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), people take it to be ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); and when the Tathāgata sometimes speaks...
That which is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is regarded by people as worldly truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Furthermore, the Four Truths are common to the three vehicles;
thus, they cannot be definitively fixed.

Moreover, Mahāmati, by clinging to the nature of dependent origination (paratantra-svabhāva), one gives rise to the characteristics of the nature of conceptual construction (parikalpita-svabhāva). Mahāmati, it is like a craftsman...

A magician, relying on grass, wood, tiles, and stones, creates various illusions, manifesting the diverse forms and colors of all sentient beings and giving rise to various false conceptions; yet those false conceptions are likewise devoid of reality.
Based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one gives rise to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

It is like a magician who, relying upon grass, wood, and so forth, conjures forms and colors and thereby gives rise to various false imaginings. Since the dependent nature is itself illusory, the imagined nature is likewise established as empty.
Thus it is, Mahāmati. Based upon the dependent origination nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arises.

It consists of various minds of conceptualization, various characteristics and activities of conceptualization, and the habitual tendencies of attachment to conceptualization; this is the manifestation of the characteristic of the imagined nature.
Mahāmati, this is called the teaching of the Dharma by the Buddha based upon [the dependent nature].

Based on this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the nature of false conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) manifests; this refers to the source from which the deluded thoughts before one arises.
However, when investigating its origin, it fundamentally depends on beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

That which manifests as dependent origination is what is called the various minds of deluded thought and the various characteristics of the phenomena of deluded thought. Once dependent origination has manifested, it is further able to trigger habitual tendencies.

"Vital energy (qi) is the continuous succession of deluded thoughts; therefore, it is called 'the habit-energy of attachment to deluded thoughts. How could one know that this habit-energy arises entirely from non-awakening?
This dependent origination is, in its very immediacy, unborn. When one realizes that objects are nothing but mind, deluded thoughts have nowhere to lodge.
This is the meaning conveyed by one's own nature."
Mahāmati, as for the Dharma-buddha, it is established and functions as the objective realm of the noble ones’ self-realization, free from the self-nature and characteristics of the mind.

To be "free from the self-nature and characteristics of the mind" means to be free from the characteristics of phenomena associated with one’s own mind. Once the characteristics of the mind are abandoned, awakening occurs.

As soon as its essence manifests, it is without master and without support; it is neither mind nor object. At this point where speech and thought are severed, it can only be known through direct realization.
This is the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
Mahāmati, as for the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha), he teaches generosity, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, as well as mind and wisdom.

He establishes the analysis and observation that transcends the views of non-Buddhists and the view of formlessness, by means of liberation from the characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas), and the characteristics of consciousness (vijñāna).
The six pāramitās instruct bodhisattvas; by departing from the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas), they attain the gate of liberation.

This is taught commonly to all three vehicles, wherein they all discern the characteristics of consciousness and establish their own respective paths. This differs from the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), who mistake consciousness for the mind.
It gives rise to the perception of consciousness within the formless realm.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the Dharma-Buddha, he is free from objective referents; with the cessation of objective referents, all activities, faculties, means of knowledge, and characteristics are extinguished.
It is not the realm of attachment of ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or followers of external paths who cling to the mark of a self.

It is established as the ultimate distinctive characteristic of the noble ones' personal realization. Therefore, Mahāmati, it is the ultimate distinctive characteristic of the noble ones' personal realization.
One should diligently practice and study. One must eliminate what is seen as a manifestation of one’s own mind.
