Mahāmati, as for the teaching on "nature" (svabhāva), it is for the purpose of encompassing birth and death; for the purpose of destroying the view of non-existence and the view of nihilism;
and for the purpose of causing my disciples to encompass various karmic conditions for taking birth. Thus, by means of the nature of sounds, one teaches the encompassing of birth and death.
Nature is the Dharma. When the Buddha speaks of the existence of dharmas, it is to cause his disciples to understand the causes that sustain birth and death;
thus, he refutes the nihilistic view of causelessness. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The karmic actions of sentient beings are neither permanent nor annihilated."
Yet one obtains the retribution. Although [dharmas] perish moment by moment, nothing is lost; although there is no agent, there is action;
although there is no experiencer, there is retribution. Although the experiencer perishes, the fruit does not vanish.
Without deliberation or cognition, it exists through combination. Although all sentient beings proceed together with the twelve links of dependent origination, yet...
It is not seen, nor is it known. Because it is neither seen nor known, it has no beginning or end; this is why the Buddha spoke of the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
"Sound" refers here to names and phrases, meaning that while there is the grasping of phenomena, these are likewise empty and merely verbal expressions.

This is intended to further demonstrate that one's karmic activities stem from delusion; if one awakens, one is immediately detached from such natures. Nirvāṇa is spoken of for the sake of sentient beings; it is not [an entity].
This is for the sake of the awakened; it cannot be explained to those whose deluded attachments are not yet exhausted.

Mahāmati, the teaching on the characteristics of the self-nature of illusion is for the purpose of abandoning attachment to the characteristics of self-nature. [Those who have not heard this] fall into the characteristics of the evil views of fools, hoping for what they desire;
they do not know that all is the manifestation of one's own mind, and they are attached to the characteristics of self-nature arising from causes and conditions.

I teach that all phenomena have the nature and characteristics of an illusion or a dream, so as not to allow foolish people with evil views and aspirations to become attached to themselves, others, or any phenomena.
One should see things as they truly are in their proper place; to formulate incorrect doctrines otherwise, Mahāmati, is to fail to see all phenomena as they truly are in their proper place.
To see all phenomena as they truly are in their proper place means to transcend the manifestation of one's own mind.
Illusion has no intrinsic nature; it is manifested solely by the mind. Its manifestation is like a dream or an illusion, and thus it cannot serve as the productive cause for any phenomena.

This is why it destroys the hopes and attachments of the foolish. In its state of suchness, it refers to all phenomena manifested by one's own mind as being illusory, neither falling into existence nor non-existence, nor into subject and object. These are what are called "all phenomena."
It is the true nature (*dharmatā*). Only when not perceiving a single dharma does one see the true nature. This is the realization that the objective realm is the manifestation of one's own mind;
it is a state of correspondence realized through direct experience alone.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Non-arising is the absence of intrinsic nature; The existence of intrinsic nature..."
It encompasses birth and death. One observes them as being like illusions and so forth; one does not form conceptual constructions regarding their marks.
All dharmas lack an inherent nature of arising. To falsely engage in activity is to undergo birth and death.
Birth and death are like illusions, yet they are sustained by conceptual construction. That is to say: they do not arise from themselves, nor are they non-arising; they are without arising.
Dependent Origination. Dependent origination is non-arising. One who awakens to this may transcend and attain it spontaneously.

The preceding ten sections have demonstrated that all phenomena are eternally abiding and like illusions, thereby concluding the revelation that the self-nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is non-arising.
Eleven: Demonstrating the Attainment of Meaning Beyond Words; Ceasing External Delusions; Discerning the Awakening Mind; and Establishing *Nirvāṇa*. This section is divided into five parts.
△ First, it is shown that meaning is attained beyond words.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of the body of names (*nāma-kāya*), the body of phrases (*pada-kāya*), and the body of syllables (*vyañjana-kāya*). (The Wei translation says: "I shall explain the characteristics of the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables.

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who skillfully examines the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables enters accordingly into the meanings of those names, phrases, and syllables, and swiftly attains [Buddhahood].
Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Having awakened to this, one awakens all sentient beings. Mahāmati, as for "name-body" (nāma-kāya), it refers to the establishment of names based on things;
this is called the name-body. As for "phrase-body" (pada-kāya), it refers to phrases that possess a body of meaning.
The ultimate determination of intrinsic nature is the "name-body" (*nāmakāya*). As for the "phrase-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), it refers to that which manifests names;
this is called the phrase-body. Furthermore, the phrase-body refers to length, shortness, height, and depth.

Moreover, the "sentence-body" (*padakāya*) refers to tracks, such as the tracks left by elephants, horses, humans, beasts, and so forth, which receive the name "sentence-body. Mahāmati, as for "name" and "phrase," they are... [with]... by means of...

"Name" refers to the four formless aggregates; therefore, it is called "name. Because its own characteristic manifests, it is called "form. These are termed the bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).
One should study the definition and boundaries of the characteristics of these bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes.

The preceding statement—that verbal expression does not reveal the ultimate truth (paramārtha)—is intended to lead one into the meaning, the phrases, and the structural forms [of the teachings], so that one may swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This means that neither non-verbal expression is the ultimate truth, nor is that which is expressed the ultimate truth;
rather, the ultimate truth is the state of bliss of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), which is entered through verbal expression. Thus it is said.
One knows that what is entered through verbal expression is the phrase of the definitive ultimate of intrinsic nature.
Once one has entered the definitive ultimate, what is expressed by verbal expression is insufficient to manifest it; yet, the means by which this is realized is likewise through verbal expression.
This is called "using a wedge to extract a wedge," which one should carefully observe. Regarding the establishment of names based on phenomena:
it is like naming a vessel a "jar" based on water, clay, human labor, and the tools used to produce it. Regarding the ultimate determination of intrinsic nature:
it is like relying on the phrase that all phenomena are like illusions to realize that all phenomena ultimately lack any inherent nature.
The *tathāgatagarbha* is the meaning of *tathatā*. Characters have varying lengths; phonemes have varying pitches.
One derives names from characters, and characters accumulate to form phrases—this is what is called "manifesting names and phrases.
"Tracks" refers to observing tracks to know that they were traversed by elephants, horses, humans, or beasts; this is like observing phrases to arrive at their meaning. The four formless [realms]...

The aggregates (*skandha*) refer to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. By means of the names "feeling," "perception," "mental formations," and "consciousness," one comes to know the four formless aggregates.

Just as by observing points, strokes, long and short [vowels], and high and low tones, the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of written characters manifest, so too does one enter the meaning of the ultimate reality through the bodies of phrases, sentences, and phonemes—namely, the swift attainment of Bodhi and self-awakening.
This is for the purpose of awakening others. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The distinctions between the body of names, the body of phrases, and the body of phonemes—fools and ordinary people cling to them, like an elephant sinking into deep mud."

The verse rebukes the ignorant outsiders who, failing to know that meaning is attained by departing from words, are instead turned about by the realm of conceptualization, like an elephant mired in mud;
it expresses deep compassion for them. △ Second, showing the cessation of debate to clarify that meaning does not reside in words.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, in a future age, those who possess wisdom—having transcended the views of identity, difference, both, and neither, as well as the characteristics of "mine" and the meaning of the "all-pervading"—will question those lacking wisdom.
Those [lacking wisdom] will then reply: "This is not a correct question," namely, whether form and so forth are eternal or impermanent, different or not different;

and likewise regarding *nirvāṇa* and the conditioned (*saṃskāra*), the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*), the quality (*guṇa*) and the qualified (*guṇin*), and the creator (*kartṛ*) and...
[They] create. They see what is seen: gross objects and subtle atoms; cultivation and the cultivator.

Regarding such reciprocal characteristics and similar questions, the Buddha declared them "unanswered" (*avyākṛta*) and ceased the discussion, saying: "This is not something that those deluded people can know, because they lack the wisdom derived from hearing.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has spoken thus in order to cause them to be free from states of fear."
It is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). It is not explained as being determinate. Furthermore, it is not taught for the purpose of ceasing the speculative views and doctrines of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Regarding "ceasing discourse," this is one of the four types of discourse and has two meanings: first, it ceases the indeterminate discourse of non-Buddhists by not providing a determinate explanation;

this is because they are deluded and lack wisdom, and so that they may be freed from their fear [of the truth]. Second, it ceases false discourse. [The second point] concerns those whose faculties are not yet mature.
As for "the matured": it is because they have been led to abandon attachment; because they have attained silent realization beyond words; and because of the timing and conditions.
Therefore, if one were to pose questions regarding the Tathāgata’s meaning that transcends the four propositions to those who lack wisdom, they would inevitably provide incorrect answers.
Instead, they would engage in numerous difficult inquiries concerning the mutual interplay of subject and object regarding the various marks of form and so forth. This...

The Buddha declared this to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); therefore, I shall desist and not engage in further discussion. Because those deluded people lack knowledge and are deficient in wisdom derived from hearing, if one were to provide a definitive explanation for them, they would inevitably give rise to fear.
This is because the profound meaning of emptiness, which transcends the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*), is not a domain where consciousness can settle.

Should they fall into the four propositions, it would again become mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), increasing their false views. It is for this reason that the Tathāgata [remained silent] for the sake of future generations.

"World" (*loka*) refers to the exhortation. "Form and so forth" (*rūpādi*) refers to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding permanence and difference among all phenomena (*dharma*) within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

"Nirvāṇa and conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the practices capable of realizing nirvāṇa. "Characteristic and characterized" (*lakṣaṇa-lakṣya*) refers to the defining characteristic and that which is defined.

"Basis and based" (*āśraya-āśrita*) refers to the support and that which is supported. "Primary matter and derived matter" (*bhūta-bhautika*) refers to the primary elements and that which is derived from them. "View and that which is seen" (*dṛṣṭi-dṛśya*)... [text fragment ends]
"Seeing" refers to the seer and the seen. "Dust and subtle dust" refers to the subtle particles of a lump of clay.
"Cultivation and the cultivator" refer to the self of persons and the self of dharmas. These exist in mutual dependence; they are empty and lack substantial reality, and thus cannot be recorded.
Therefore, they are called "unrecordable" (avyākṛta).
"Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists speak thus, asserting that the life-principle is identical to the body; such are their indeterminate doctrines (*avyākṛta-vāda*).
Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists are deluded and propound indeterminate doctrines regarding causes; this is not what I teach.

Mahāmati, what I teach is the departure from the grasped and the grasper, wherein false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise. How then could there be any cessation for them? Mahāmati, if there were grasping..."
Regarding those who are grasped by conceptual attachment: because they do not understand that [the world] is the manifestation of one’s own mind, they are restrained from it.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas teach the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the four kinds of formal responses (vyākaraṇa).
Mahāmati, as for the "restraint through non-response," I teach it from time to time for those whose faculties are not yet matured, but not for those who are matured.

This clarifies the reason for the teaching of the *avyākṛta-vāda* (the doctrine of the indeterminate). Life is the root of birth and death; taking this as one's body constitutes the formation of causes and effects.
This is the "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) of non-Buddhists, not what was taught by the Tathāgata—yet they claim it is what was taught by the Tathāgata.

Free from the grasped and the grasper, false conceptualization does not arise; yet, the reason [the Buddha] did not directly teach "Mind-Only" was because [beings] were attached to causes and did not understand that [all things] are manifestations of their own minds, and thus he ceased [such discourse].

However, among the four types of formal declarations used by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas to guide sentient beings, the cessation of formal declaration is intended not only for non-Buddhists, but also for those whose faculties are not yet mature.

As for "the matured": when the time has not yet arrived, one must not increase their conceptual expressions. When the time is approaching, one merely intends to awaken them through words beyond [literal] meaning;
that is to say, one only negates what is wrong, rather than stating what is right. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"It is like the ruddy sheldrake and the *liunti* bird, which dwell and roam together, never parting from one another. The Tathāgata refers to distinct dharmas as such.
Suffering is one thing; pleasure is another thing. Permanence is another thing; impermanence is another thing. Self is another thing; non-self is another thing.
When the time comes, the principle will reveal itself of its own accord.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, all dharmas are free from being produced; they do not arise from causes and conditions, and because there is no agent, all dharmas are unarisen.
Mahāmati, why are all natures devoid of intrinsic nature? Because when one examines them through self-reflexive awareness, neither their specific nor their general characteristics can be apprehended;
therefore, it is said that all dharmas are unarisen. Why are all dharmas ungraspable?

That which comes cannot be brought away; by virtue of its own and common characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), when one wishes to bring it here, there is nowhere from which it comes, and when one wishes to take it away, there is nowhere to which it goes.
Therefore, all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are devoid of bringing or taking. Mahāmati, for what reason are all phenomena not extinguished?

Because the intrinsic nature and characteristics of things do not exist, all dharmas are unattainable; therefore, all dharmas are not subject to cessation. Mahāmati, for what reason are all dharmas impermanent?
It is because their arising as characteristics possesses the nature of impermanence; for this reason, it is said that all dharmas are impermanent. Mahāmati, for what reason are all dharmas permanent?
It is because their arising as characteristics possesses the nature of non-arising; since non-arising is permanent, [all dharmas] are permanent.
To say that all phenomena are eternal is a statement intended to cease further debate. All phenomena are unarisen, because they are devoid of subject and object and lack an agent.
All phenomena lack intrinsic nature, because neither self-characteristics nor common characteristics can be apprehended. All phenomena have no coming or going.

Because the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) have no point of origin from which they come and no destination to which they go, all phenomena are non-extinguished.

Because they lack the characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), all phenomena are impermanent. Because the arising of their characteristics is itself the nature of impermanence, all phenomena are eternal; for that which arises is precisely non-arising.
Because impermanence itself is eternal. To examine these six meanings in detail, there is only non-existence (*anupalabdhi*). Apart from non-existence, no further discourse can be admitted;

therefore, it is called the "Cessation of Discourse" (*vādasthāpana*). By means of this, one restrains all heterodox schools (*tīrthika*), and by means of this, one specifically demonstrates the profound meaning (*gambhīrārtha*).
The profound mystery of the Tathāgata can only be realized through silent resonance.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "There are four kinds of discourse: the categorical, the counter-interrogative, the analytical, and the conclusive.
These are employed to subdue the various non-Buddhists. [They address] existence and non-existence, and arising from self or other—[the views of] the Sāṃkhya."
The Vaiśeṣikas hold that all things are entirely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). He has thus demonstrated that which is discerned by the Perfectly Awakened One:
its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be apprehended; because it is free from verbal expression, it is said to be devoid of intrinsic nature.

"Directly" (*ekāṃśa*) means answering straightforwardly. "By counter-questions" (*paripṛcchā*) means answering through cross-examination. "By analysis" (*vibhajya*) means answering with detailed exposition. "By setting aside" (*sthāpanīya*) means answering by leaving the matter aside.
"Saṃgha" refers to the twenty-five *tattvas* established by the Sāṃkhya school. "Vaiśeṣika" refers to the six categories (*padārtha*) established by the Vaiśeṣika school.
Regarding "causes and non-causes," they lack any real meaning and cannot be explained; one can only say that they do not exist.

It is simply their nature. ○ Third, the specific four fruits. Because they emerge from true awakening, they are divided into six. △ First, the question regarding the distinctions among the four fruits.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I only pray that you will explain for us the various..."

The stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). The general characteristics of the distinctions among the paths of the stream-enterer, as well as the skillful means (*upāya*) regarding the paths of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and the arhat (*arhat*), which a bodhisattva mahāsattva must thoroughly understand.

Having discerned this through knowledge, they teach the Dharma to sentient beings in such and such ways— namely, the characteristics of the two kinds of selflessness, the purification of the two hindrances,
and the crossing over the characteristics of the stages until reaching ultimate penetration.
They attain the inconceivable, ultimate realm of all Tathāgatas, like a mani-jewel of manifold colors, skillfully benefiting all sentient beings by means of the objective realm of all phenomena.
With inexhaustible body and wealth, he sustains and nurtures all beings.

He asks about the characteristics of the four fruits in order to clarify the relationship between the four fruits and the stages of awakening (bodhisattva-bhūmi), both in their commonalities and distinctions.

For the sake of sentient beings, he analyzes and reveals them so that they may abandon the two obstacles of persons and phenomena, realize the two kinds of selflessness, transcend the characteristics of the various stages, and attain penetration into the Buddha-ground.
Ultimate adornment. Attaining the wish-fulfilling jewel, one liberates others through the state of non-existence.
The realm of all dharmas refers to the realm of non-existence. ○ Second, listing the three types of *srotāpanna*. This is divided into two parts.
△ First, showing the characteristics of the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it. I shall now speak for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed listen and receive [your teaching]. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are three kinds of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterers), distinguished by the fruits of the *srotāpanna*.
What are the three? They are the inferior, the middling, and the superior. The inferior [attains] at most seven more births. The middling...
As for those who attain parinirvāṇa in this very life, there are three types: those who attain parinirvāṇa upon being born, and those who attain parinirvāṇa while still in that state.

These three types possess three fetters—namely, the inferior, the middling, and the superior. What are these three fetters? They are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Through the progressive advancement of these three fetters, one attains the state of an Arhat.
*Śrotas* is translated as "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). *Srotāpanna* is translated as "cultivation," meaning the cultivation of the outflow-free.

Furthermore, *śrotas* is translated as "stream," and *srotāpanna* is translated as "entering against," meaning entering against the stream of birth and death. It is also translated as "entering," meaning entering the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*).

Regarding the superior, middling, and inferior [faculties], there are two types: sharp and dull. Those of dull faculties return seven times among gods and humans before attaining parinirvāṇa in their present life.

This refers to those of the sharpest faculties. Regarding these three types of persons who sever the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), the Chinese translation lacks the terms "inferior," "middling," and "superior.

Nevertheless, the severance of the fetters is also distinguished by the sharpness or dullness of their faculties; therefore, it is said that there are distinctions among the three fetters. △ Second, showing the distinctions in the severance of fetters by the *srotāpanna*.
Mahāmati, there are two kinds of self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): namely, that which is innate (*sahaja*) and that which is conceptualized (*parikalpita*).

It is like the conceptualization of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the conceptualization of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). For example, based upon the dependent nature, various attachments to the imagined nature arise.
Because they are neither existent nor non-existent, and because they lack reality as the characteristics of conceptual construction, the deluded ones conceptually construct them in various ways.

The attachment to the self-nature and characteristics of perceptions is like the mirage of a thirsty deer perceiving water; this is the false view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
By means of the non-self of persons (pudgalanairātmya), they grasp at the absence of intrinsic nature and sever their long-standing attachments born of ignorance.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is of two kinds: innate (*sahaja*) and discriminative (*vikalpita*). "Discriminative" refers precisely to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). This discriminative aspect belongs to the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
Although it extensively encompasses all internal and external phenomena, it nonetheless falsely calculates existence and non-existence based upon the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

It is like a phantom person arising from conditions, manifesting various marks such as male or female, bending and stretching; it gives rise to the discrimination of all sentient beings, yet in reality [it is devoid of substance].

It is neither existent nor non-existent; it is entirely devoid of substantial reality and is merely the mark of false imagination. It is like that thirsty deer who falsely perceives water in a mirage.
This *srotāpanna*, through the wisdom of the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), contemplates the lack of intrinsic nature in what is grasped and thereby achieves its eradication.
According to this, the *srotāpanna* abandons two kinds of afflictions and does not fall into the causal views of external paths, yet he still relies upon the person.
Because the wisdom of selflessness eliminates the nature of grasping, the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) is not within their scope.

Mahāmati, as for that which is co-emergent, it refers to the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) held by stream-enterers (srotāpanna), because the four aggregates (skandhas) of one's own body and those of others lack the characteristics of form.

Because form arises from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*upādāya-rūpa*); because they are mutually causal and mutually defining; and because the primary elements and form do not aggregate [independently].

When a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) contemplates the categories of existence and non-existence, they do not manifest, and thus the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is severed. When the view of a self-identity is severed in this way, craving does not arise.
This is called the characteristic of the view of a self-identity.

They arise simultaneously and belong to the afflictions of thought (*citta-kleśa*). Śrāvakas attain liberation by analyzing the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as empty; that is, they realize that the four aggregates—feeling and the others—have no perceivable form or characteristics.

As for the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it depends upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derivative matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced from them; these are mutually integrated, lacking any distinction between self and other.
Thus, they remain far removed from the false views of existence and non-existence, and the conceptualization of craving does not arise. In total, this constitutes two kinds of abandonment.

This is called the abandonment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Mahāmati, as for the characteristic of doubt: because one has attained the characteristic of correctly seeing the Dharma, and because the two previous kinds of false conceptualization regarding the view of a self-identity have been abandoned, doubt regarding the Dharma does not arise.
One does not give rise to the view of another as a Great Teacher regarding what is pure or impure. This is called... [the abandonment of doubt].
The marks of doubt are severed by the *srotāpanna*.

One who attains the mark of "good vision" refers to the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*). Having departed from the causes of existence and non-existence, one perceives the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
This is what it means to have realized the Dharma and seen it well. The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is thereby severed, and doubt does not arise. There are three kinds of doubt:

doubt regarding the Dharma, doubt regarding oneself, and doubt regarding others. One who has realized the Dharma and seen it well does not doubt the Dharma, for the view of a self has already been severed.
Thus, one does not doubt oneself. Not doubting the Dharma and not doubting oneself, one likewise does not doubt others;
that is to say, having eliminated the two doubts regarding the Dharma and oneself upon encountering others, one does not give rise to the notion of another being a Great Teacher elsewhere.
The phrase "for the sake of purity or impurity" is a term of doubt.

Mahāmati, regarding the clinging to precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*): why does the *srotāpanna* not cling to precepts? It is because he clearly perceives the characteristics of suffering in the places where one is reborn;
therefore, he does not cling. Mahāmati, "clinging" refers to the way foolish people resolutely undergo ascetic practices for the sake of the pleasure of material requisites and thus seek rebirth.
He does not do so, except for dedicating [his merit] toward the excellence of self-realization and being free from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

The practice of the means of the characteristics of untainted dharmas and the upholding of the factors of morality (śīlāṅga) is called the stream-enterer’s abandonment of the grasping at the characteristics of morality.
To seek birth in a pleasant realm and thereby grasp the factors of morality constitutes the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa). This is all that the stream-enterer upholds.
All are for the sake of supreme self-awakening; because they dedicate themselves to untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmic practices, attachment to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is severed.
The stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) severs the three fetters, and greed and delusion do not arise. If a stream-enterer were to think, "I am not possessed of these fetters," there would be two faults:
falling into the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the failure to sever the various fetters. Mahāmati said:
The Buddha said, "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has spoken of many kinds of craving. Which among them is the craving that must be severed? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is the fondness for women, being entangled in and greedily attached to them, and through various means committing evil deeds of body and speech while seeking pleasure in the present."

The seeds for future suffering do not arise. Why is this? Because one has attained the bliss of the correct reception (*samādhi-samāpatti*) of meditative concentration; therefore, that [suffering] is severed.
It is not through the severance of craving for nirvāṇa that it is severed.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* says: "Could a srotāpanna have such a thought as, 'I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna'?
Subhūti replied: "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A srotāpanna is called one who has entered the stream, yet in reality there is nothing entered.
And so on, until: "If an arhat were to have such a thought as, 'I have attained the path of arhatship'..."
This constitutes being attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. One should know that such a person forms the notion of having severed their fetters;
they have fallen into the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and have not severed the various fetters. A srotāpanna has severed only craving for sense-desires.

If there were craving for nirvāṇa, then the four fruits would remain unattained. Samādhi and right reception arise from the correct vision of the Dharma; this is what is called samādhi and right reception.
It obstructs that craving so that it may be severed in the present; this is because the *srotāpanna* has not yet exhausted the afflictions of thought (*citta-kleśa*).
[End of] the above section listing the three types of *srotāpanna*. △ Third, showing the characteristics of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Mahāmati, what are the characteristics of a Sakṛdāgāmin? It refers to the sudden illumination of the characteristics of form and the characteristics of the arising of false discrimination;

because one sees that such characteristics do not arise and has clearly perceived the marks of the progression toward dhyāna, one returns once more to this world to reach the limit of suffering and attain nirvāṇa. (The Tang translation says:)
That is to say, one who does not fully comprehend the characteristics of form yet gives rise to conceptualization of form, and having gone once to and fro,
skillfully cultivates the practice of dhyāna and reaches the limit of suffering by attaining parinirvāṇa— for this reason, he is called a Sakṛdāgāmin.

"Instantaneously illuminating the marks of form and the marks of the arising of delusive thought" means that upon this one return, one thoroughly understands that the conceptualizations produced by the marks of form do not arise.
This "conceptualization" refers to the afflictions of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), not the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*).

"Skillfully seeing the direction of dhyāna" refers to the meditative concentration realized through skillfully seeing the Dharma. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The person who is a Sakṛdāgāmin..."

Binding the mind to cultivate the Way for the purpose of severing greed, hatred, delusion, and pride—with this binding of the mind, after one more coming and going, they exhaust the limits of suffering and enter parinirvāṇa. △ Fourth, showing the characteristics of the fruit of Anāgāmin.

Mahāmati, what is meant by an Anāgāmin? It refers to one who, having seen the faults of the views regarding existence and non-existence concerning the characteristics and nature of form in the past, future, and present, causes such false conceptualizations not to arise and severs the fetters (saṃyojana). (The Tang translation states:

"It means that regarding the characteristics of form in the past, future, and present, one gives rise to the discrimination of views of existence and non-existence; yet the latent tendencies (anuśaya) do not arise, and one forever abandons all fetters. Furthermore...
One who does not return is called an Anāgāmin.
An Anāgāmin is able to perceive the faults arising from the conceptualization of the forms and characteristics of the three periods of time, and thus exhausts all such conceptualization.
"Permanently abandoning all fetters" refers here to the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*). There are seven types of *anāgāmin* parinirvāṇa.
First is "parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarā-parinirvāyin*), which means attaining nirvāṇa in the interval after leaving the desire realm but before reaching the form realm.

Excluding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state possess sharp faculties. There are two types of those who attain parinirvāṇa through practice (*abhisamskāra-parinirvāyin*):
first, those with diligence but no mastery over meditative concentration; second, those with indolence yet mastery over meditative concentration.

According to this, they merely perceive the faults of conceptual discrimination and do not speak of the bliss of dhyāna; this should be understood as referring to those of sharp faculties and diligent effort. △ Fifth: Showing the Arhat.
The characteristics of the fruit of the Hīnayāna. Mahāmati, an Arhat is one who has fully accomplished the various dhyānas, samādhis, liberations, powers, and clarities;

[for whom] afflictions, suffering, and false conceptualizations no longer exist as substantial entities. (The Tang translation reads: "That is to say, the various dhyānas, samādhis, liberations, powers, and supernormal faculties have all been perfected. Afflictions...")
Because suffering and its conceptual proliferation are forever exhausted, he is called an Arhat.

An Arhat is one who has nothing further to learn (aśaikṣa). By means of the fivefold Dharma-body—consisting of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—he has reached the further shore.
He has eternally severed the causes for birth throughout the three periods of time and has also eliminated the aggregates of the body within the three realms.
"It means: 'Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; there will be no further existence. 6.
Distinguishing the Arhats from those who have transcended through awakening.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One speaks of three kinds of Arhats. Which of these is being referred to here?"
"Arhat, World-Honored One, is one who has attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility? Or is it a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva manifesting as an Arhat through skillful means?
Or is it a transformation created by a Buddha? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is a Śrāvaka who has attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility."

It is not otherwise. Others practice the bodhisattva path, and through the power of skillful means and fundamental vows, they manifest birth within great assemblies for the purpose of adorning the Buddha’s retinue.

Mahāmati, they teach various doctrines regarding the realm of conceptual construction—speaking of attaining fruits and attaining dhyāna—and because all such things as entering dhyāna are utterly transcended, they manifest the attainment of self-realization.

The attainment of the fruit through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the mind is called "attaining the fruit. Furthermore, Mahāmati, one who wishes to transcend the realms of the dhyānas, the immeasurables, and the formless should abandon the marks of the direct perception of what is manifested by one's own mind.

Mahāmati, it is not the case that the meditative attainments of cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) transcend the direct perception of what is manifested by one's own mind.
Why? Because there is still the measure of the mind (*citta-mātra*).

The aforementioned term "Arhat" refers to those of fixed nature within the three vehicles who belong to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), rather than to Bodhisattvas manifesting in form or Buddhas appearing as emanations.

When Bodhisattvas or Buddha-emanations teach various doctrines among deluded sentient beings—speaking of attaining fruits or attaining meditative concentrations—they do so entirely without subject or object (*grāhya-grāhaka*), in order to demonstrate that these are merely the manifestations of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*). This is what is meant by "attaining the fruit."
The "marks" (lakṣaṇa) differ from the fixed nature [of the dharmas]. They encompass all common activities and lead one forward into the Mahāyāna.

Therefore, those who wish to transcend the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments of the mundane world must depart from the marks of the self-manifesting cognition of their own minds (*svacittadṛśyamātra*).

Furthermore, even the supramundane attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*) belongs to the measure of the mind; it is not the case that transcending the self-manifesting cognition of one's own mind is otherwise [i.e., still within the realm of the mind].

The subsequent passage, which states that "if one awakens, one attains liberation," refers precisely to this. One statement says "attaining the manifestation of one's own mind" (svacittadṛśya-pramāṇa), and another says "being free from the manifestation of one's own mind.
"Attaining" has the meaning of "awakening," and "awakening" is synonymous with "being free."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The various dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and the cessation of all sensation and perception—within the Mind-Only (*cittamātra*), none of these exist.

The fruit of *srotāpanna*, the *sakṛdāgāmin* and *anāgāmin*, as well as the *arhat*—all such states are the delusions of the mind. For the meditator, the meditation, and its objects, there is only the knowledge of their severance."
Seeing the True Reality (*satyadarśana*). This is merely the measure of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). If one awakens to this, there is liberation.

The practitioner of meditation (*dhyāyin*) and meditation (*dhyāna*) constitute the subject that enters and the object entered. Since there is both subject and object, there is an objective sphere (*ālambana-viṣaya*) for the meditation.
[One] abandons [it]; [one] abandons the origin (*samudaya*). [One] knows [it]; [one] knows suffering (*duḥkha*). By knowing suffering and abandoning the origin, the True Reality seen is not...
Transcending the measure of the mind. "Awakening" refers to awakening to the fact that all is the manifestation of one's own mind; through such awakening, one is suddenly liberated from it.

Only by transcending the manifestation of the mind does one truly realize the manifestation of the mind. The above three [sections] distinguish the four fruits, having concluded the emergence of true awakening.
Fourth, the awakening of the discerning mind is divided into three parts: △ First, the formal demonstration of the characteristics of the observing awakening.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of cognition: namely, investigative cognition (*pratyavekṣaṇika-jñāna*) and cognition established through the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of false discrimination (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*).

Mahāmati, as for investigative cognition: it refers to that cognition which investigates the nature and characteristics of self-nature, and finds them unattainable when analyzed beyond the four positions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
This is called investigative cognition. Mahāmati, those four positions refer to being free from [the notions of] identity, difference, both, and neither.
Neither together, nor existent, nor non-existent, nor neither existent nor non-existent, nor permanent, nor impermanent—these are called the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Mahāmati, that which is free from these four propositions is called all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). Mahāmati, one should study and practice the investigation of all phenomena by means of these four propositions.
That all sentient beings fail to attain the noble wisdom of self-awakening is entirely due to their failure to understand that all phenomena before them are manifestations of mind alone;
they give rise to false conceptualizations, and as soon as such conceptualization occurs, they are immediately encompassed by the four logical extremes (*catuskoṭi*).
If one can observe that all phenomena are free from the four extremes and cannot be apprehended, the deluded thoughts of one's own mind will naturally subside.
The essence of awakening is self-so. Whether moving or still, appearing or disappearing, it is without dependence and without a master;

it has no conscious cognition, yet nothing remains unilluminated; it is without self or other, and admits of no placement. This is what is called "attaining liberation through awakening," which is the observation of awakening that one should cultivate and study.
Regarding the discernment of the nature, its own-nature, and its characteristics: this refers to [the discernment] regarding all phenomena...
Regarding the characteristics of the essence of dharmas: one must examine and select with precision to discern their reality or unreality, so as not to be deluded by what appears before the eyes;
only then can one transcendently and suddenly leave them behind. △ Second, showing both the characteristics of delusive thought and awakening, thereby clarifying the holy bliss of self-awakening.
Mahāmati, what is the awakening that consists in the grasping, attachment, and establishment of the characteristics of false imagination?
It refers to the grasping of the characteristics of false imagination and the attachment to the unreal characteristics of the four great elements—solidity, moisture, heat, and motion.

Based on these, one establishes [doctrines] through attachments to propositions, reasons, characteristics, and examples, which are themselves unreal. This is called the awakening that consists in the grasping, attachment, and establishment of the characteristics of false imagination.

These are called the two aspects of awakening. If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes these two aspects of awakening, they will reach the ultimate realization of the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*).
Being well-versed in skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they attain the awakening of non-existence (*nirabhilāpya-bodhi*) and examine the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*).

Upon attaining the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), they enter one hundred samādhis, obtain the distinguished samādhis, behold one hundred Buddhas and one hundred bodhisattvas, and know the limits of the past and future.

Each involves the events of a hundred kalpas. His light illuminates a hundred buddha-fields. He knows the characteristics of the progressively higher stages. His great vows are sublime; his spiritual powers are sovereign.
Having received the empowerment of the Cloud of Dharma, he shall attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening. He skillfully binds his mind to the ten inexhaustible phrases.
Maturing sentient beings, they are adorned with various transformations and radiances. They attain the samādhi of the noble joy of self-awakening.
They point to the four great elements—solidity, moisture, motion, and heat—and [discern] all unreal characteristics based upon these four great elements as being falsely conceived by themselves.
It is grasped and established through conceptual differentiation. For example, based on the characteristic of earth, one might formulate a syllogism as follows:

"This is a substantially existent phenomenon" is the proposition (*pakṣa*); "because it is solid" is the reason (*hetu*); "like diamond" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). This constitutes the characteristic of unreal conceptual differentiation.

This is a false grasping, conceptualization, and establishment. If one can thoroughly comprehend these two kinds of awakened characteristics, then such [characteristics] are merely the deluded awakening and discrimination of the ignorant outsider;
such are my own dharmas, which, when observed through self-awakening, are found to be non-existent.
Only now do I know that all phenomena before one’s eyes arise entirely from one’s own mind, appearing delusively through non-awakening;
what appears is solely one’s own mind, without any separate causal characteristics. Knowing they have no separate existence, one realizes they all stem from non-awakening.
Within this non-awakening, there is no agent—this is what is meant by "no person. Outside of non-awakening, there is no other cause—this is what is meant by "no phenomenon. This...
The two types of selflessness are thus ultimately realized. Observing in this manner, conceptual discrimination is suddenly stilled.
One naturally becomes skilled in means and, through the mind that realizes non-existence, understands the stages of practice and enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Therein, one attains hundreds of thousands of distinct samādhis and simultaneously perceives and enters, all at once, the boundless lands of the ten directions and three periods of time. This is the fundamental [attainment].

May his spiritual power be sovereign and unimpeded, traversing all stages and transcending the empowerment of the Cloud of Dharma to reach the ultimate Dharma-body of the Tathāgata’s self-awakened realization.
Relying upon ten inexhaustible roots of goodness, he universally manifests transformation bodies to teach others in succession without end,
yet never departing from the state of supreme bliss that abides in the noble wisdom of self-awakened realization.
△ Third, showing the excellence of the four great elements and derived matter. Entering into contemplative observation:
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be skilled regarding the four great elements and derived matter.

How is it that a bodhisattva is skilled regarding the four great elements and derived matter? Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva forms this realization: "That which is the ultimate truth consists of the four great elements..."
"Non-arising" (the Tang translation says: "Those great elements are truly non-arising"). One observes that those four great elements do not arise.
Having observed thus, one realizes the limits of names, marks, and false conceptualization; that the limits of what is manifested by one's own mind are external natures that lack inherent existence.
This is called the limit of false conceptualization manifested by the mind, namely, the triple world. One contemplates those four great elements and their derived matter.

The nature is detached. The four propositions are universally pure. It is free from self and what belongs to self. It abides in its own characteristics and segments according to the true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*). Its unarisen own-characteristic is established.

This teaching skillfully leads to the observation and realization of the derived matter produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The four great elements refer to earth, water, fire, and wind.
Derived form refers to visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility. Those who realize that ultimate truth refer to the ultimate truth of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
What is meant by the ultimate truth of the four great elements? It means that the four great elements have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);

they appear to exist through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), yet when discrimination has not arisen, the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is eternally quiescent. Thus, the current names and characteristics within the triple world are all merely portions of one's own mind.

It is apart from conceptualized characteristics. Yet this eternally quiescent *dharmatā* does not arise or cease due to discrimination. Therefore, one should know that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced by them are pure without remainder;

they are free from the four extremes (*catuṣkoṭi*), free from "self" and "what belongs to self," and abide within the reality of the *dharmas* that possess their own inherent characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Abiding in the reality of the *dharmas*, they establish the inherent characteristics of distinct segments, which are non-arising.
Dharma-patience is accomplished in its own place.
Mahāmati, how do those four great elements give rise to derived matter? It is said that the great element of the delusion of moisture gives rise to the internal and external water element;
the great element of the delusion of capability gives rise to the internal and external fire element; and the great element of the delusion of movement...
The internal and external wind elements arise, severing the great elements of the false conceptualization of form. The internal and external earth elements arise;
form and space coexist. Clinging to false truths, the five aggregates accumulate, and the derived matter of the four great elements arises.
The four great elements arise from deluded imagination (*vikalpa*), giving birth to the internal and external four elements.
That is to say, the moisture of deluded imagination constitutes the water element, giving rise to the internal and external water realm. Earth, fire, and wind are likewise so.
This is because, through being deluded regarding one's own mind, deluded imagination arises; it is not produced by a cause, nor is it non-existent. Nor does it...
It can act as the generative cause for others. The non-Buddhists falsely speculate that the five great elements can produce the eleven sense organs;

they do not realize that form and space have, from time immemorial, been suddenly manifested through a lack of awakening. The *Buddhaśikhara Sūtra* states: "The nature of the ocean of awareness is tranquil and perfect;

this perfect tranquility makes awareness fundamentally wondrous. When primordial luminosity shines and produces objects, once those objects are established, the luminous nature itself vanishes. Thus, delusion arises."
Falsely, there is empty space; based on space, worlds are established. When thought clarifies, it becomes the land; when cognition arises, it becomes sentient beings.
Yet they erroneously claim that both form and emptiness can act as causes; therefore, this is a false truth.
Mahāmati, as for consciousness, it continues into other realms of existence because it takes pleasure in various traces and objective spheres.

Mahāmati, the four great elements such as earth, and the derivative forms produced from them, have conditions consisting of the four great elements; they do not have those [four] great elements as their conditions. Why is this?

Because the nature, form, characteristics, location, and the application of effort are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); thus, the great elements are not produced. Mahāmati, regarding the nature, form, characteristics, and location...

The means employed arise through conjunction; they are not formless. Therefore, the characteristics of the derived matter of the four great elements are the false imaginings of externalists and are not mine.

Following the preceding discussion on the arising of the false imaginings of the four great elements, there further emerge the four modes of birth within the various realms of existence, all of which result from a lack of awakening.
They appear falsely; it is not that those four great elements can act as the cause of their arising. Consciousness is, in fact, deluded thought (*vikalpa*).

Since the four great elements are manifested by internal consciousness, and this nature of consciousness further delights in perceiving various forms and appearances, it is able to continue through other realms of existence (*gati*).
Thus, one knows that the forms and appearances both within and without the three realms initially arise through the transformations of consciousness and thought. Since they arise from...
The continuity of consciousness and perception does not have those four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as its generative cause. The four great elements arise from false conceptualization;

therefore, it is said that while there are conditions for the four great elements, the four great elements themselves cannot again act as a generative cause. Thus, it is said that they do not have those four great elements as their condition.
Furthermore, earth and the other elements each possess their own intrinsic nature, each possesses its own form and appearance, and each possesses its own spatial orientation and function.

This is acceptable. Although [the aggregates] lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are not devoid of form and color (*saṃsthāna-varṇa*). How could form and color possibly act as a cause for form and color themselves?

Much less could they act as a cause for the formless aggregates (*arūpa-skandha*). This would be a great error. Therefore, it is said that this is the deluded conceptualization of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika-vikalpa*), and not my own Dharma.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates (*skandha*). What are the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates? They are the five aggregates. What are the five?

They are form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Among these, four aggregates are non-material; that is to say, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Mahāmati, as for form (*rūpa*), the four great elements and the derivative forms each have distinct characteristics.

Mahāmati, it is not that non-form (*arūpa*) possesses the number four, like space. For example, Mahāmati, space transcends numerical characteristics; it is free from numbers, yet through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one speaks of "one space.

Mahāmati, in this same way, the aggregates (*skandha*) transcend numerical characteristics; they are free from numbers, free from existence and non-existence, and free from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Numbers—
Regarding "marks" (lakṣaṇa): these are the conventional expressions of foolish people, not those of the noble ones (ārya).
Furthermore, one analyzes the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the five aggregates (skandha), seeing that the four great elements (mahābhūta) cannot produce the five aggregates.

This is because it is said that the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) arises from the four great elements; for the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) still possesses the number four and each has its own distinct characteristic. Up to... [text continues]
There are no form-aggregates and no fourfold enumeration; they are like empty space. That empty space is free from the characteristics of enumeration, and even the name "empty space" does not exist;
it is only through false conceptualization that one speaks of "one empty space. The aggregates are likewise so.

It is free from numerical characteristics and free from the four propositions of existence and non-existence; therefore, to claim that the four great elements can produce [phenomena] is surely the false view of the non-Buddhists.

Likewise, to claim that form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness possess real self-characteristics that can be apprehended is also the deluded attachment of foolish people, not the teaching of the noble ones.
Examining this analysis of the intrinsic nature of the five aggregates, although one may see...

The four great elements cannot give rise to the five aggregates; yet, it is directly pointed out that the five aggregates are free from all characteristics and free from the four propositions of existence and non-existence, for their very substance is unborn.
Mahāmati, the noble ones are like illusions, appearing in various forms and colors, yet free from the conceptualization of difference or non-difference.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, they are like dreams, reflections, or the body of a person, because they are free from difference or non-difference. Mahāmati, the realm of noble wisdom appears as the manifestation of the false imagination of the aggregates (*skandha*).

This is called the characteristic of the self-nature of the aggregates; you should eliminate it. Having eliminated it, you shall preach the Dharma of tranquility and sever all [attachments to] Buddha-fields.

"Mahāmati, when the various non-Buddhists speak of tranquility, they refer to the purification of the view of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and the entry into the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
Having entered the Immovable Stage, one attains mastery over immeasurable samādhis and the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), as well as the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*).
One thoroughly penetrates the ultimate state, attaining power, clarity, and sovereignty, thereby rescuing, gathering in, and benefiting all sentient beings, just like a great [cloud]."
The earth supports and nurtures all sentient beings; likewise, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva universally rescues all sentient beings.

The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are like an illusion, being neither different nor non-different [from their nature]. To realize their own characteristics as they truly are is called the "approach of noble wisdom" (*āryajñāna-gati*).

Not realizing their own characteristics and falsely engaging in discrimination is called "delusive thought" (*parikalpita*). Although they share these same five aggregates, the distinction between delusion and awakening lies therein.
Therefore it is said: "The destination of noble wisdom is the same as that of deluded imagination; it is what manifests. The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya: "Form is impermanent.
By extinguishing this form, one attains the eternally abiding form of liberation. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise impermanent.
By extinguishing this consciousness, one attains the eternally abiding consciousness of liberation. Form is suffering. Because..."
One extinguishes this form and attains the form of liberation and peace. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Form is emptiness; by extinguishing this empty form, one attains the form of liberation that is not empty.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Form is non-self; by extinguishing this form, one attains the true [self] of liberation.
My form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus.
Therefore, one should know that what is to be eliminated and extinguished is precisely these five aggregates (skandhas) which are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
As for what is taught after their extinction, it is the teaching of these five aggregates of liberation: eternally abiding, blissful, non-empty, and truly self.
This is what is called the Dharma of tranquility. Ordinary worldlings regard form as the self;
within phenomena that are impermanent, non-self, impure, and without bliss, they falsely perceive permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Fools maintain that there is a self apart from form.

To counteract these ordinary worldlings, [the teaching] further shows that within phenomena of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, they falsely perceive impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.

All these are mere conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). By extinguishing these conceptual constructions and departing from the fourfold formulation of difference and non-difference, one realizes the inherent quiescence of phenomena and the vision of the selflessness of dharmas (*dharmanairātmya*).

Being pure and without remainder, one immediately enters the eighth stage, the Immovable (*Acalā-bhūmi*), accomplishes immeasurable samādhis, attains the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*), and possesses the power of mastery and unimpeded supernatural faculties like those of a magical illusion, just like the great earth.
It universally nurtures all sentient beings. Indeed, from non-awakening arises false discrimination, which constitutes delusion and confusion.
When one awakens to the source from which discrimination arises, one realizes it is entirely nothing but one's own mind. All delusions and confusions are like illusions and dreams;
they are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*). This very discrimination becomes wondrous observation. As it is said: "Ordinary people see duality; the wise understand."
They are realized; their nature is non-dual. [This concludes] the first four sections, which demonstrate the selection of the awakened mind.

Fifth, the demonstration of the establishment of *nirvāṇa*, divided into three parts. △ First, the separate enumeration of the *nirvāṇas* of externalists and the two vehicles, in order to manifest the *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of nirvāṇa among the various non-Buddhists. What are these four? They are: (1) the nirvāṇa of the self-nature of things being neither existence nor non-existence;

(2) the nirvāṇa of the self-nature of various characteristics being neither existence nor non-existence; (3) the nirvāṇa of the realization that the self-nature of specific characteristics is neither existence nor non-existence;

and (4) the nirvāṇa of the severance of the continuous flow of the aggregates through their specific and general characteristics. These are called the four kinds [of nirvāṇa] of the various non-Buddhists.
"Nirvana is not what I have taught. Mahāmati, that which I have taught is the cessation of the discriminating consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*);
this is called nirvana. (The Tang translation states: "Mahāmati, that which I have taught is the cessation of the *parikalpita-manovijñāna*; this is called nirvana.")
First, four kinds of nirvāṇa are enumerated in order to refute false causes and false effects; subsequently, the true nirvāṇa of our own Dharma is presented.
Regarding "the nature, self-nature, and non-nature": the Sāṃkhya teachers deludedly regard this as the principle of primordial darkness (*avyakta*), from which consciousness (*buddhi*) arises.
From awakening arises the notion of "self," which ultimately reverts to the principle of *avyakta* (the unmanifest). Regarding the various characteristics, natures, and non-natures:

this clarifies that the masters of the *Sāṃkhya* school postulate that the Great Brahmā (*mahābrahman*), time (*kāla*), space (*dik*), the primal limit (*pradhāna*), space (*ākāśa*), and the self (*ātman*)—these seven principles—are eternally abiding and capable of producing all phenomena, such that all phenomena ultimately return to these eternal abodes.

As for the awakening to the non-nature of one's own characteristics and one's own nature: *Note: The original text contains the term "冥諦" (míng dì), which refers to the *avyakta-tattva* (the principle of the unmanifest) in Sāṃkhya philosophy.*
The Teacher of the World (Lokāyatika) maintains that all phenomena, such as form and mind, have the atoms of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as their cause.
Specifically, he takes the most subtle and luminous aspect within the four great elements—the essence capable of cognition—as the mental factor (*cittadharma*).

He asserts that all sentient and insentient things possess this atomic essence of cognition as their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); this is what is meant by "clinging to all cognition."

This is nirvana. As for the cessation of the continuous flow of the various aggregates (skandhas) as they mutually condition one another: this "continuous flow" is precisely the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).
When the aggregate of formations ceases, this profound stillness and lack of agitation is not true quiescence; it is like a torrential stream.
It appears tranquil and still; what is called "penetrating the profound and merging with the profound" returns to the limits of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The followers of the Two Vehicles do not realize that these are manifestations of their own minds; thus, they conceive of Nirvana upon the cessation of the continuity [of mental states], yet they never depart from consciousness.

In the Nirvana of the Tathagata, deluded consciousness ceases—that is, discriminative consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*) ceases. This discriminative consciousness arises from being deluded regarding one's own mind.
Arising without awareness, one realizes that [the world] is a manifestation of one’s own mind; when discrimination no longer arises, this is itself nirvāṇa.

Self-awakening is the cause, and the cessation of consciousness is the fruit. This statement regarding the cessation of consciousness clarifies the cause by means of the fruit. △ Second, showing that the cessation of the consciousness of deluded thought is itself nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, do you not establish the eight consciousnesses? The Buddha said, “I do establish them.

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “If they are established, why is it that one is liberated from the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) and not from the seven consciousnesses? The Buddha told Mahāmati, “It is because of that cause.”

Furthermore, because of that object-condition (*ālambana*), the seven consciousnesses do not arise. As for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*): it arises from the habit-energy (*vāsanā*) produced by attachment to the segmentation of objective realms;

it nourishes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). It is accompanied by the *manas*, which consists of the thought-impulses (*cetanā*) attached to "I" and "mine," arising solely from causes and conditions.

Without destroying its own characteristic marks, it takes the storehouse consciousness as its cause. By attaching to the objective realms manifested by one's own mind, the collection of minds (*cittasaṃghāta*) arises, with each acting as a cause for the other in a continuous succession.
It is like the waves of the ocean: blown by the wind of objects manifested from one's own mind, they arise and cease in the same way.
Therefore, when the *manovijñāna* ceases, the seven consciousnesses also cease.
The Tathāgata has already answered by establishing the eight consciousnesses; yet Mahāmati alone harbors the doubt that they are not separate from the seven consciousnesses.

This is because, being deluded regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*, its entire substance becomes the consciousnesses, and the consciousnesses in their entirety are the *garbha*. Therefore, the eight consciousnesses cannot be separated [from it].
However, the eight consciousnesses falsely give rise to the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), thereby forming the "self" of the seventh consciousness; this delusion should be severed.

[The text] fails to recognize that the sixth consciousness acts as the cause for the eighth consciousness, while the eighth consciousness acts as the condition for the sixth, and that the seventh consciousness arises in dependence upon them and lacks intrinsic nature.
This serves to reveal the error of [viewing] the mental consciousness [alone] as the culprit. Below, the two meanings of cause and condition are elucidated to establish this proof.

The seven consciousnesses do not arise; therefore, the manas-consciousness (manovijñāna) should be extinguished. The manas-consciousness grasps external objects and realms, falsely engaging in discrimination and thereby triggering habitual tendencies (vāsanā).
This further adds delusion to the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna). From this, the seven consciousnesses and the manas arise simultaneously.

One calculates "I" and "mine," and contemplates causes and conditions as they arise in succession. Yet, in reality, the seven consciousnesses and the storehouse consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) share the same Tathāgatagarbha, which is the indestructible true nature. Arising from delusion regarding this truth, they possess no dual substance.

This clarifies that while the six consciousnesses act as the cause for the eighth consciousness, the seventh consciousness arises dependent upon them and lacks any inherent self-nature. [The] storehouse consciousness...

As the cause, the six sense-objects—which are the objective realms of one's own mind—are manifested. The six consciousnesses, based upon these, engage in grasping and attachment, giving rise to the collection of the seven consciousnesses.

This clarifies that the eight consciousnesses serve as the conditions for the six consciousnesses and that the seventh consciousness arises in dependence upon them, lacking any inherent nature of its own.

Through the successive unfolding of causes and conditions, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) becomes the source of transgression, just as waves arise from the ocean of the mind. By means of the six consciousnesses—
Driven by the winds of objective realms manifested from one’s own mind, there arise birth and cessation. If the six consciousnesses cease, then the mind and intellect naturally come to rest;

it is like a great ocean when there is no wind—the reflections of these objects become clear and transparent. However, this is entirely due to delusion regarding the measure of one's own mind (*svacittamātra*); the perceived and the perceiver arise together.

One perceives and clings to this as the "intellect" (*manas*), and conditioned by the arising of forms, the consciousnesses are produced. If one awakens to the fact that these are merely manifestations of one's own mind, [the delusion ceases].
In all objective realms, conceptualization does not arise; views and attachments gradually subside. The Tathāgatagarbha-mind is, upon reflection, perfectly quiescent (*parinirvṛta*).
Now, as for the statement that awakening to the measure of one’s own mind is *nirvāṇa*: Buddha-nature is the cause and *nirvāṇa* is the fruit.
That which is the cause and not the fruit is called Buddha-nature; that which is the fruit and not the cause is called *nirvāṇa*. Now...
Speaking in terms of the fruit, it is said that "consciousness ceases.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The nature of my nirvāṇa is not something produced, nor does it possess characteristics.

It is the cessation of the consciousness that is the flame of false discrimination; therein lies my nirvāṇa. That [consciousness] has its causes and its objects of clinging; such is the intended meaning."
The body is equally established; that which provides its cause is the mind, serving as the support for consciousness.
Just as when the great flow of water is exhausted, waves do not arise, so too when the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) ceases, the various forms of consciousness do not arise.

Nirvāṇa has no intrinsic nature, nor does it involve grasping or abandoning. It is merely that which is manifested by one’s own mind; it is the cessation of discursive thought and perception—this alone is Nirvāṇa.

Although the eight consciousnesses act as causes and the six consciousnesses act as conditions, and the sevenfold mental body undergoes transformation, these modes of dissolution arise simultaneously.
It is only the objects of the six sense-fields manifested by the mind that appear as if they were present before one, serving as the objects for the consciousnesses.
It continues without interruption; it is not that one has realized one's own mind, for conceptualization is difficult to still.
It is like when the great flow of water is exhausted, the waves no longer arise. This refers to the cessation of consciousness, where the ocean of mind remains as it is.
△ Third, exhausting the distinctions of deluded thought to reveal that wisdom is the fulfillment of the ocean-like fruit of true nirvana.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the general characteristics of the discrimination of the self-nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva-vikalpa-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

If you and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thoroughly understand these general characteristics of the discrimination of the self-nature of conceptualization, you will transcend conceptualization and reach the noble realization of self-awareness (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

You will clearly perceive the common path of the outsiders (*tīrthika*), and by awakening to the cessation of the conceptualization of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka-vikalpa*), you will be liberated. (The Tang translation reads: "Thoroughly knowing...")

This meaning transcends all false conceptualizations and realizes the realm of noble wisdom. It understands the teachings of the non-Buddhists and remains far removed from the dualistic discrimination of grasper and grasped.
Regarding the various marks of dependent origination, one abandons the activity of the nature of false conceptualization and no longer engages in such conceptualizing.
It was stated above that when deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and consciousness are severed, this is termed *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva here desires to exhaust the various distinctions of conceptualization and directly, instantaneously depart from them, reaching the state of the noble self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). Since dependent origination is fundamentally without two dharmas, awakening to delusion is likewise not two minds.

By exhausting delusion, one finds it has no cause; by awakening to enlightenment, one realizes it is not something separate. Only upon reaching the point where subject and object are both severed does one finally know that [it is identical to the ultimate].

The non-Buddhists share the same dependent origination, yet they practice within the sphere of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); it is precisely this that is revealed by the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).
Mahāmati, what is the common characteristic of the discrimination of the imagined nature? It refers to the discrimination of verbal expression and the things expressed.

Conceptualization (*vikalpa*), conceptualization of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vikalpa*), conceptualization of benefit (*guṇa-vikalpa*), conceptualization of self-nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), conceptualization of cause (*hetu-vikalpa*), conceptualization of views (*dṛṣṭi-vikalpa*), conceptualization of accomplishment (*siddhi-vikalpa*), conceptualization of birth (*utpāda-vikalpa*), conceptualization of non-birth (*anutpāda-vikalpa*), conceptualization of continuity (*prabandha-vikalpa*), and conceptualization of bondage and non-bondage (*bandha-abandha-vikalpa*).

These are called the general characteristics of the discrimination of the self-nature of conceptualization. Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of speech (*abhilāpa-vikalpa*)? It refers to various kinds of exquisite sounds.

The sound of singing and chanting, which involves attachment to beautiful music—(the Tang translation says: "to be attached to various beautiful sounds and words")—is called the conceptualization of verbal expression (*abhilāpa-vikalpa*).
Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of the object expressed (*abhidheya-vastu-vikalpa*)?

It refers to the intrinsic nature of the object expressed, which is known by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*); based upon that, verbal conceptualization arises. This is called the conceptualization of the object expressed.
“Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of characteristics (*nimitta-vikalpa*)? It refers to the various attachments to the very things described, such as the mirage of a thirsty deer.
It is the discrimination of all natures based on their characteristics of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion; this is called the discrimination of characteristics.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of benefit (*lābha-vikalpa*)? It refers to the longing for various kinds of gold, silver, and precious jewels; this is called the discrimination of benefit.”

[The Buddha said: "Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of self-nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*)? It refers to the false view of discrimination that holds that self-nature exists as such and is not otherwise;
