This is the ultimate ground, the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening, which is free from the delusive imaginings of views regarding the five dharmas, the three natures, and the eight objects.

For this reason, I say that delusive imagination arises from attachment to various unreal meanings. By knowing the meaning as it truly is, one attains liberation from the various delusive imaginings of one's own mind.
It is not that discursive thought (*vikalpa*) arises once and does not arise again; rather, it means that discursive thoughts of existence and non-existence do not arise.

This directly points to those who have realized the manifestation of their own mind as the measure of reality (*svacittadṛśyamātra*): for them, all discursive thoughts of existence and non-existence do not arise. Thus, even within the present state of existence, [they remain free from such thoughts].
To claim that all natures are detached and all things are unattainable is a conceptual construction based on false imagination.

When one awakens to the fact that these are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, such notions cease entirely; this is what is called "not grasping at the existence of natures," which is equanimity and tranquil extinction.
Fools, when various signs and activities appear before them, falsely imagine them to exist, or they imagine them to be non-existent—both are merely false imaginations.
They transmigrate because they do not realize that all is but the manifestation of their own minds. Whether thoughts are stirred or stilled, they all lead back to delusion and confusion.

Therefore, it is said that if one wishes to distance oneself from the faults of "mine-ness," one must awaken to the fact that all is the measure of one's own deluded mind; one must awaken to all deluded imaginings.

All arise through the manifestation of the mind; that which is manifested is unreal. When one is detached from the perceptions of one's own mind, one immediately attains the transformation of that non-awakened body and mind.
Following the wisdom of self-awakening, one illuminates all the stages (*bhūmi*) and reaches the stage of the Tathāgata, wherein all five dharmas and their intrinsic natures are realized.
All these are conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). False imagination (*vikalpa*) arises from clinging to various unreal objects.

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), however, is realized through knowing the suchness of self-nature; it is liberation by its very essence, wherein false imagination does not arise. This is the definitive conclusion.
△ Fourth: Summary Verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Causes and conditions give rise to this world; Through false imagination, one clings to the four extremes.
They do not understand my penetrating realization: The world is neither born from existence, Nor is it born from non-existence;
It is not born from both existence and non-existence, Nor is it born from neither existence nor non-existence. How can causes and conditions [give rise to anything]?"
Foolish conceptualization is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it both existent and non-existent. One who observes the world in this way turns the mind and attains selflessness.
All natures are unarisen because they arise from conditions; all that is produced by conditions is not self-existent.
An entity does not produce itself as an entity, for there would be the fault of duality, and because there is no fault of non-duality, it is not existent.
The nature [of the effect] cannot be apprehended (the Tang translation says: "An effect does not produce itself as an effect, because there would be the fault of two effects;
since there are no two effects, its nature cannot be apprehended").

This statement that "all worlds arise from causes and conditions" refers merely to the false conceptualization of the four extremes of existence and non-existence by those who do not understand dependent origination.
Yet, in this very world, there are in truth no four extremes to be found; these all arise from the deluded imaginings of fools who fail to penetrate this principle.
If one can contemplate thus with discernment, one will finally realize that all things are without self and lack intrinsic nature.
They do not arise independently; they all arise from conditions. Yet these conditions themselves are non-existent. Both the agent and the acted-upon lack any real nature;

one should immediately and completely transcend them. A phenomenon does not produce itself; "phenomenon" here refers to the resultant phenomenon, meaning that an effect necessarily depends on a cause, and the cause brings about the effect.
Thus, there is no nature of self-arising. In short, the initial mind is unaware and cannot be self-governing; it errs.

Following causes and conditions, it appears as if there is arising and ceasing. Fools do not know this and falsely conceptualize existence and non-existence; upon awakening, they are suddenly freed from these notions, for its fundamental nature is originally without reality.

Observing all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), which are free from the grasper (*ālambaka*) and the grasped (*ālambana*), and which are a mind-measure (*citta-mātra*) devoid of mind—I call this "mind-measure.
This measure is the locus of self-nature; it is free from both objectivity and subjectivity. Its nature is ultimately wondrously pure; I call this "mind-measure."

The preceding discourse on worldly dependent origination—that which arises dependently has no inherent nature—is intended for those who have emerged from the measure of their own mental constructs (*cittamātra*).

By simply being able to detach from the subject-object relationship of grasping and the grasped, and by directly becoming mindless, one accords with the measure of the mind; that is to say, the self-nature of this very mind.

Fundamentally, there is neither the subject that perceives nor the object perceived; this is ultimately perfect and sublime. If one has even the slightest attachment to anything external to the mind, one immediately falls into deluded conceptualization, which is not the original direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The self is a conventional designation for worldly truth; it has no substantial reality. The aggregates are likewise designated as "aggregates," yet they too lack any substantial reality.
There are four kinds of equality: [equality] of characteristics, of causal nature, of arising, and thirdly, of selflessness; the fourth concerns the cultivation and the cultivator.
The preceding passage spoke of the mind-measure (*cittamātra*) of intrinsic nature, which is free from all phenomena and is, in its very essence, wondrously pure.

This present passage concerns the provisional designation of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), whether as persons or as dharmas, even down to the characterized and the uncharacterized, the arisen and the unarisen, and the self and the non-self.

The capacity for cultivation and that which is cultivated are both entirely equal; they possess no substantial nature. This reveals that the self-nature is merely the measure of mind-only (cittamātra), and there is nothing else external to it.

Conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) establishes what is called the characteristic of the person (pudgala-lakṣaṇa), while the aggregates (skandha) establish what is called the characteristic of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa).

There are four kinds of equality: namely, the equality of characteristics (lakṣaṇa), causes (hetu), self (ātman), and cultivation (bhāvanā). "Characteristics" refers to the characteristics of the five aggregates; the five aggregates are non-existent... [text truncated]
In reality, characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*) are equal. Characteristics must have a cause;

this cause is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) among the Four Noble Truths, namely, the cause for the arising of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Since the characteristic of the fruit is empty, arising and non-arising are equal.
When cause and effect arise in succession, they possess the sense of a self (*ātman*); when cause and effect do not arise, then self and non-self are equal. Thus one understands [the truth].
It is not the self; this is what is called cultivation. When there is nothing to be realized, then cultivation and non-cultivation are equal.
When the habitual tendencies of false imagination revolve, various kinds of minds arise and objects manifest externally; this is the conventional measure of the mind.
"External appearances exist but are not real; the mind perceives them as various things. The establishment of the body and possessions—I declare these to be the measure of mind (*cittamātra*).
This refers to the conventional measure of mind, which, driven by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), gives rise to false discrimination, appearing as if there were external objects."
To realize this is to turn [the mind] back toward the mind-only nature of self-nature (*svabhāva-cittamātra*). External manifestations do not exist; that is to say, they do not exist separately.
Because of the deluded perceptions of the mind, the sense organs, the body, and the objective world—all that appears is but the mind itself.
Free from all views, and free from both thought and that which is thought; without attainment and without arising—this I call the measure of mind (*cittamātra*).

It is neither existence nor non-existence, for it is entirely free from both existence and non-existence (the Tang translation says: "neither existent nor non-existent, free from both existence and non-existence").
That which is called the liberation of the mind, I call the measure of mind; it is suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of emptiness (*śūnyatākoṭi*), and nirvāṇa.
As well as the dharma-realm and the various mind-born bodies—I declare these to be the measure of mind (*cittamātra*).

"Various views" refers to the two views of self, namely the self of persons and the self of phenomena. "The perceiver and the perceived" refers to the subject that perceives and the object that is perceived.

To be free from these is to attain one's own original mind; it is not something newly acquired, and is therefore called "non-attainment. When the measure of mind manifests before one, one does not grasp at existence.
As for its nature, the causes of birth are simultaneously severed; hence it is called "non-arising. The two dharmas of existence and non-existence are produced by the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Once one is detached from these four propositions, there is immediate liberation. Suchness, the limit of emptiness, nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm all refer to the true purity and perfection of the mind-measure (*cittamātra*).
Even the various types of mind-born beings possess a marvelous unity of essence and function; in brief, they are all [the mind].

The nature reaches the ultimate. ○ First, the initial section demonstrates the two types of penetration—of the doctrine and of the teaching—and concludes with the distancing from deluded thoughts and attachments.

Second, it demonstrates the meanings of words and the cognition of wisdom to reveal the function of the penetration of the doctrine. This is divided into five parts. First, demonstrating the meanings of words, which is further divided into five.
△ First, in response to Mahāmati’s question, the characteristics of words are first demonstrated.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be skilled in words and meanings.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being skilled in words and meanings? What is 'word' (vākya)? What is 'meaning' (artha)? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well. I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati replied: [Please teach us.]
The Buddha said, "Excellent. "World-Honored One," [Mahāmati] replied, "We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "What is speech?
It refers to the conjunction of words, syllables, and conceptualization (*vikalpa*). It arises based on the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, palate, cheeks, and jaws;
it is produced through the attachment to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of conceptualizing discourse regarding 'self' and 'other. This is called speech."
"Words" refers to the verbal teachings of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle as expounded by the Tathāgata.

"Meaning" refers to the sphere of practice of the noble ones' ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This sphere of practice of the noble ones' ultimate truth is that which is entered through verbal expression;

by entering this sphere of practice of the noble ones' ultimate truth, one is able to remain far removed from all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of verbal expression and the realm of discursive cognition. This is due to the cause [of such entry].

Regarding the meaning of "entering through words": it refers to illuminating and realizing [the truth], yet it does not mean that meaning arises dependent upon words, for that would conversely fall into conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

First, one must distinguish between the two types of essential characteristics of words and meaning; only then can one say that one enters meaning through words, just as a lamp illuminates forms, yet the lamp is not itself the form.
This school’s adherents demonstrate its fundamental tenet by using verbal expression as a means of entry, yet one must not rely upon those words.

This is merely a description of the distinct characteristics of conceptual attachment and deluded imagination (*vikalpa*). The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of deluded imagination, in conjunction with the seven factors of the throat, constitute the essential nature of speech.
This is spoken according to worldly convention; however, according to the sacred teachings, it is the wondrous mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

He has skillfully revealed this; therefore, what follows consists of words whose meaning is not different from the principle itself. One discerns the meaning through words and enters the meaning by means of words—this is what is called the teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Now, the habitual tendencies of deluded thought and the wondrous mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) are identical in essence though different in name;

both are merely transformations resulting from delusion or awakening. Thus, one should know that while the "penetration of the essence" (*zongtong*) is what is revealed, it is that which is entered through verbal expression. It is not...
This is the realm of false conceptualization. △ Second, showing the characteristics of the meaning.
Mahāmati, what is meant by "meaning"? It refers to that which is free from all characteristics of false conceptualization and characteristics of verbal expression; this is called "meaning."

Mahāmati, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, regarding such meanings as these, dwells alone in a quiet place and, through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, takes self-realization as their object and heads toward the city of nirvāṇa;
having undergone the transformation of the body of habitual tendencies, they perceive the realm of self-realization and contemplate the characteristics of the superior progress between each stage.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skill in meaning.
This demonstrates the essential nature and characteristics of the meaning (*artha*), yet it does not specify what constitutes that meaning;

it simply states that being free from all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and verbal expressions is what is called "meaning. This is intended so that people may attain self-realization within the state that transcends both verbal expression and conceptual construction.
By virtue of this self-realization, one is finally able to suddenly comprehend the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation while dwelling alone in a quiet place.
Dedication to Nirvana means that the body of habitual tendencies is entirely transformed into the realm of self-awakening.
By means of the wondrous wisdom of self-awakening, one illuminates the various stages (bhūmis), progressing higher and higher without depending on another. This is the characteristic of its meaning.

Because one perceives the Tathāgata’s ultimate, wondrous mind, he skillfully reveals it so that people may discern the meaning through words and enter the meaning by means of words—namely, that the words do not differ from the meaning. This will be further elaborated in the following text.
△ Third, showing how to enter the meaning by means of words.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skilled in words and meaning contemplates that words and meaning are neither different nor not different.
He contemplates meaning and words in the same way. If words were different from meaning, then meaning could not be discerned by means of words.

One enters into the meaning by means of words, just as a lamp illuminates forms (the Tang translation says: "by means of the lamp of words, one enters the realm of self-realization that transcends verbal expression").
This correctly clarifies that the "Principle of the School" (*zongtong*) reveals what has been entered. All its chapters and sentences are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Skillful in Language and Meaning observes the words to know the meaning; [the meaning] is neither different from nor not different from the words.

If it were different, one would not discern the meaning by means of the words; rather, one must enter the meaning through the words until reaching the state of self-realization, which is attained beyond language. Thus...
They understand all verbal teachings and illuminate the source of the mind; yet they remain detached from the realm of conceptual proliferation and verbal expression.

Shrouded by the habitual tendencies of sentient beings, they are unable to know their true home through words; instead, they rely on verbal expression and calculate according to existence and non-existence.
This is not a fault of the holy teaching. △ Fourth, taking the meaning based specifically on the words:
Furthermore, Mahāmati, [concerning] non-arising and non-ceasing, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nirvāṇa, the three vehicles, the one vehicle, mind, self-nature (*ātman*), and so forth...

Just as one becomes attached to the meanings of verbal expressions, one falls into the views of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*). This is distinct from superimposition and distinct from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*);
it is like the manifestation of various false conceptualizations that are like illusions. (The Tang translation states:

"If there are those who grasp at the meaning according to the words regarding non-arising, non-ceasing, intrinsic nature, *parinirvāṇa*, the three vehicles, the one vehicle, the five dharmas, the various minds, self-nature, and so forth, they then fall into superimposition.")

And there is the view of slander, because one gives rise to conceptual discrimination by treating things as different from them. It is like various illusions, which ordinary, foolish sentient beings falsely imagine to be real, whereas the noble sages do not.

This means that fools are unable to enter into the meaning by means of words. Regarding the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena, such as their lack of arising and ceasing in their own-being (*svabhāva*), they lack clear comprehension.
Instead, relying on verbal expression, they become attached to the conceptual objects of what is spoken, falling into the extremes of existence and non-existence.
Thus, they construct [views] that differ from the ultimate suchness of the own-being of all phenomena.
It stands that all false conceptualizations arise through discrimination, just as they do based upon illusions.

Therefore, one should know that all phenomena are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), appearing equally to both the noble ones and ordinary beings; yet, the distinction lies between delusion and awakening.

For those who awaken to the manifestation of their own mind, they depart from the characteristics of verbal expression and the characteristics of mental objects, directly attaining the essence of the Dharma. Only then do they believe that daily life is no different [from the ultimate], just as it was for him.
Devas and humans share the same vessel for food; yet, according to the thickness or thinness of their merit, what they perceive differs. V. Summary Verse:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Those who engage in false conceptualization regarding speech establish various dharmas.
Because of those establishments, at death they fall into the hells. Within the aggregates (skandhas) there is no self; the aggregates are not [the self]."
This is indeed the self; it is not like that false conceptualization, nor is it a non-self. All things possess an intrinsic nature, yet it is not as the foolish and ignorant falsely imagine.
If it were as they perceive it, then everyone would see the Truth. All phenomena lack an intrinsic nature, and both purity and impurity do not exist at all.
It is unreal as they see it, yet it is not a mere nothingness.

This refers to how non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), relying on conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), establish existence and non-existence. Because they see these causes of false teachings, they will certainly fall [into error].

However, while the followers of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) maintain that there is no self within the aggregates (*skandha*), and thus do not hold the delusion that the aggregates themselves are the self, they fail to realize that "no-self" (*anātman*) is likewise not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Ordinary non-Buddhists do not distinguish between delusion and awakening.
To mistake the false for the true is one error; for the practitioners of the Two Vehicles to counteract their perverse attachments by discarding the true as being identical to the false is another.

Both fail to realize the nature that is inherently present and do not perceive the reality without departing from delusive thoughts. If one must depart from delusion, how does this differ from mistaking the false for the true?
Therefore it is said: if it were as they perceive it, then everyone should see the truth—namely, that the selflessness of the two vehicles is not the ultimate reality.
Thus one knows that all truly real dharmas are fundamentally without intrinsic nature; all that exists, whether pure or defiled, [is likewise so].
All arise from views. By merely eliminating unreal views, reality manifests before one. This is what is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the suchness of the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
It is a state of silent resonance and accord, free from grasping or rejecting. This is the realm of self-attainment;
it is not a mere nothingness, yet it cannot be expressed by the conceptual proliferations of speech. The final verse provides a subtle indication of this.

...is it not? [End of section] The first part, showing the meaning of the terms, is concluded. Second, the discernment of wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). This is divided into three parts. △ First, showing the characteristics of the three kinds of wisdom.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness shall now be explained. If you and [others] can skillfully discern the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness...
All bodhisattvas are thus able to penetrate the characteristics of knowledge and consciousness, and swiftly attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mahāmati, that knowledge is of three kinds: namely, worldly, supramundane, and the highest supramundane.
What is mundane knowledge? It refers to all non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings who cling to the notions of existence and non-existence. What is supramundane knowledge?
It refers to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who fall into the clinging of hoping for and conceptualizing self-characteristics and common characteristics.
What is the supreme supramundane knowledge? It refers to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas who contemplate the dharma of non-existence and perceive that which is neither born nor extinguished.
Free from the categories of existence and non-existence, the stage of the Tathāgata consists of the selflessness of persons and phenomena, which arises through personal realization.
All sentient beings are unable to attain this personal realization because they fail to understand the two aspects of wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Taking what is actually consciousness to be wisdom, they develop overweening pride (*adhimāna*). For this reason, the Tathāgata has repeatedly revealed and demonstrated [this truth].
Furthermore, among the three kinds of knowledge, "worldly knowledge" refers to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). They are also called "wise" because these non-Buddhists consider themselves wise.

Those of the Two Vehicles realize that the aggregates (*skandha*) are without self, yet they still cling to the phenomena of the aggregates, failing to understand that all are manifestations of one's own mind—what is known as the longing for individual and common characteristics. Buddhas and Bodhisattvas awaken to their own minds.
Manifesting, one realizes that all phenomena are entirely non-existent, transcending existence and non-existence, arising and ceasing; their intrinsic nature is suchness (*tathatā*).

Therefore, on the stage of the Tathāgata, both person and phenomena are forgotten, and realization arises spontaneously from within, not being compared for superiority with the views of existence or non-existence, self or other, or hope and expectation held by outsiders (*tīrthika*) or those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
△ Second, showing the distinction between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and wisdom (*jñāna*).
Mahāmati, that which arises and ceases is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which is neither arising nor ceasing is wisdom (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, that which falls into the categories of the characterized and the uncharacterized, as well as the various causal signs of existence and non-existence, is consciousness; that which transcends the signs of existence and non-existence is wisdom.
Furthermore, that which nourishes and develops characteristics is consciousness; that which is not a characteristic of development is wisdom.
Failing to realize that all is a manifestation of one's own mind, one falsely perceives the arising of all phenomena and falsely perceives the cessation of all phenomena.

When one realizes that all is a manifestation of one's own mind—that what appears is but mind alone—there is neither arising nor cessation. This is the distinction between wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Based on this, one conceives of the characteristics of arising and ceasing, existence and non-existence, and their causes; because these function as consciousness (*vijñāna*), one is able to transcend them, which constitutes wisdom (*jñāna*).
"Nurturing" has the meaning of "producing": when it acts as the productive cause (*janana-hetu*) for all phenomena, it is consciousness;

when it acts as the revealing cause (*parijñāna-hetu*) for all phenomena, it is wisdom. Such is the nature of the Tathāgata’s thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).
Furthermore, the six pāramitās and all immeasurable pāramitās serve as the *vijñapti-hetu* (revealing cause) and not as the *janana-hetu* (generating cause).
Moreover, there are three kinds of wisdom: namely, knowing arising and ceasing, knowing specific and general characteristics, and knowing non-arising and non-ceasing. Furthermore...
Next, the characteristic of non-obstruction is wisdom (*jñāna*); the characteristic of various obstructed objects is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Furthermore, the characteristic of the means (*upāya*) arising from the conjunction of the three factors is consciousness; the characteristic of the self-nature of the means when there are no [external] objects is wisdom.

Furthermore, the characteristic of attainment is consciousness; the characteristic of non-attainment is wisdom. Because one personally attains the sphere of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), which neither issues forth nor enters, it is like [the reflection] in water.

"Arising and ceasing" refers to the dependent origination through delusion regarding the truth; it means that all ordinary beings and non-Buddhists are deluded about their own true nature, and this gives rise to all causes and conditions for arising and ceasing.

"Self-characteristics and common characteristics" refers to the dependent origination through stagnation in the truth; it means that the followers of the Two Vehicles are stagnant regarding phenomena (*dharma*).
[Objection: It is not understood that all that arises—whether characterized by self-nature or common characteristics—is the causal condition for weary detachment. [Response:

Non-arising and non-extinction is precisely the gathering of one's own true conditions. This means that a Bodhisattva of the Initial Teaching perceives their own true nature as never departing from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
It is the cause of all dharmas of bodhi that arise, which are neither born nor extinguished. To know these three types is what is called wisdom.
To be able to know the three types, yet to know them as not being three types—this is what is meant by the purity of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

It is unimpeded; this refers to the meaning of the four kinds of unimpededness in the *Avataṃsaka*, namely: unimpededness with respect to principle (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), unimpededness with respect to phenomena (*arthapratisaṃvid*), and unimpededness with respect to both phenomena and principle (*niruktipratisaṃvid* and *pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).

All phenomena are unimpeded; this is the unimpeded true exposition. Should one harbor even the slightest sense of self-importance or grasping, one immediately falls into the realm of the conscious mind.

Regarding the "three things," these refer to the sense organs (*indriya*), their objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). One must realize that both the sense organs and their objects are transformations of internal consciousness appearing as such; thus, no actual sense organs or objects can be found.

All conceptualization is itself non-conceptual wisdom; that is to say, while conforming to the characteristics of all phenomena through conceptualization, one remains unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
"Characteristics" refers to the characteristics of all form, mind, and so forth. One awakens to these as manifestations of one's own mind.
There are no characteristics to be apprehended; that is to say, no characteristic can be grasped. All these are the sphere of the noble wisdom of self-realization.
Like the moon in water, they are neither existent nor non-existent, neither emerging nor entering, and cannot be demonstrated; they can only be realized through personal experience.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The accumulation of karma constitutes consciousness; non-accumulation constitutes wisdom (*jñāna*).
Examining all phenomena, one penetrates their non-existence. Attaining the power of mastery—this is what is called insight (*prajñā*).
Being bound to objective realms is the mind (*citta*); the arising of conceptualization is wisdom. Non-existence and excellence—insight is [thus defined]."
From this arises [what the Wei translation calls] "the signless and the supreme object, which are the dwelling place of wisdom. This portion is "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
Regarding "knowledge" (*jñā*), it refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) that awakens to one's own mind and does not follow the grasping of the conceptualizing consciousness.
Regarding "wisdom" (*prajñā*), it refers to the non-discriminative wisdom that attains all places through differentiation and enters into Samantabhadra.
The practice of the Dharma is the spontaneous adornment. Regarding "being bound by objects": this refers to being bound by all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.
When one awakens to the mind that perceives these bound objects, it is fundamentally perfect and pure; it is merely due to deluded thoughts, yet none of these can ultimately be found.

It is also subsumed within fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Through awakening, one is able to comprehend; yet, in comprehending, there is nothing to be comprehended. Reaching the state of signlessness (*animitta*), it becomes increasingly superior through successive stages.
It is also subsumed within the differentiated [wisdom]. "Signless" refers to the sphere of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). "Superior" refers to the stage of the Tathāgata.
Mind, mentation, and consciousness are far removed from conceptualization; one attains the state of non-conceptual phenomena. Such is the Son of the Buddha, not a śrāvaka;
through tranquil and supreme progress in patience, the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom arises within the excellent ultimate truth, and all that is practiced is utterly transcended.
This is precisely the mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). By attaining the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom, one reaches a state beyond the reach of the Two Vehicles.

Mind, thought, and consciousness are, in their very essence, entirely empty. By being able to abandon all conceptual discrimination and attain the non-conceptual nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one is able to enter the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*) and reach the ground of the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom. Through this Tathāgata’s purity...
Wisdom arises entirely from the dharma of non-discrimination. This dharma of non-discrimination is precisely the sublime ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

This sublime, non-discriminative dharma is the very essence of conceptual thought and discrimination. Through delusion, one gives rise to falsehood based upon this essence; through awakening, the essence and its perceptions merge and come to rest.
What was originally present manifests before one, and all mental activities are suddenly exhausted. This is called the supreme non-discrimination.

This is also the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). There are five types of patience (*kṣānti*): the patience of subduing (*vinirjita*), the patience of faith (*śraddhā*), the patience of conformity (*anuloma*), the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda*), and the patience of cessation (*nirodha*).

From the stage of the three worthies (*trividha-ārya*) up to the stage of Buddhahood, these represent the realizations attained at varying depths. The patience of cessation constitutes the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*);

it encompasses both the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) and the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*vimala-buddhatva*), wherein all afflictions are completely severed. All of these are included within this patience.
I possess three kinds of wisdom that are noble, developed, and true. Contemplating those perceptions, they fully encompass all natures.
They are not shared with the followers of the two vehicles; this wisdom is free from all that exists. It arises from the Śrāvakas who are attached to intrinsic nature.
Transcending all mental measures, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is pure.
"The three kinds" refers to the three types of long-standing knowledge regarding arising and ceasing, and so forth. This is the knowing capacity of these three kinds.
This is precisely the essence of the Tathāgata’s true, pure wisdom. Due to deluded conceptualization, various forms of grasping arise;
this is merely the grasping of all phenomena. To be inconsistent with such grasping is to belong to the stage of the Two Vehicles.

If one realizes that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is non-existent, then grasping is suddenly abandoned, and one becomes identical to noble wisdom. Therefore, know that the Two Vehicles [merely dwell] within the non-existent.
There is. Through the false arising of conceptual attachment, one ultimately forms the "mind-measure" (*cittamātra*). To transcend this is immediately to be fundamentally pure;

it is not that there exists some other, separate Tathāgata-wisdom. [Section] 3: Showing that the transformations of non-Buddhists do not depart from the delusion of consciousness. This is divided into two parts. △ First:
Presenting the names and characteristics of the transformations of non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are nine kinds of theories of transformation among the non-Buddhists, from which the views of transformation arise among them.

They are: transformation of form and location; transformation of characteristics; transformation of cause; transformation of accomplishment; transformation of view; transformation of nature; transformation of the manifestation of conditions;
transformation of the manifestation of what is produced; and transformation of things. Mahāmati, these are called the nine kinds of transformation.
Regarding the perception of transformation: all non-Buddhists (tīrthika) give rise to theories of existence, non-existence, birth, and transformation based on this.

What is meant by the transformation of shape and location? It refers to the perception of differences in shape and location; for example, when gold is transformed into various vessels, various shapes and locations manifest, yet the nature of the gold does not change.
The transformation of all natures is likewise. Or there are some non-Buddhists who assert as follows:
These are false imaginings, even down to the false imagining of the transformation of phenomena. They are neither identical nor different because they are false imaginings.

Regarding the nine kinds of transformations of the non-Buddhists, the body composed of the four great elements and aggregates, and all conditioned phenomena of the world—such as the causes and effects, arising and ceasing, success and failure, suffering and pleasure, and various shifts currently perceived before one’s eyes—they [the non-Buddhists] falsely believe these to be truly existent.
Thus it is. To hold such views is to establish them as fixed doctrines. One fails to realize that these are manifestations of one's own mind. It is like gold fashioned into vessels:

the gold does not possess the nature of the vessel, yet the vessel is not separate from the gold; they are neither identical nor different, neither existent nor non-existent. Due to delusion, they appear vividly real; through awakening, they are seen to be like illusions.

This is what the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) refers to as "changing according to conditions while remaining unchanging, and remaining unchanging while changing according to conditions. Thus the Tathāgata has shown.

Although this [teaching] arises from the false conceptualizations of non-Buddhists, it serves to eliminate for all sentient beings and practitioners of future generations the obstacles of superficial proliferation (*prapañca*) before their eyes, so that they may realize that what is manifested by one's own mind has no inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
"Form" refers to the aggregate-body (*skandha-kāya*); this body transmigrates through the six realms, and its appearances vary between the beautiful and the ugly.

It is established that form and appearance have causes; when the causes are complete, the fruit is accomplished. The perceptions of youth and old age shift repeatedly, and the natures of suffering and pleasure change abruptly.

The conditions from which things arise are clearly evident, and the phenomena produced by those conditions are fully discerned. Once both the agent and the object are present, the process of arising is manifest.
These nine types of transformation are relied upon by non-Buddhists to establish their views of existence and non-existence as being without cause. Furthermore...

To take up the matter of physical forms: they are fully encompassed within nine types. Using the metaphor of a golden vessel, to speak of the vessel apart from the gold, or to speak of the gold as being identical to the vessel—neither identity nor separation, or both identity and identity-separation—is all equivalent to frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*). All such views arise from deluded thought (*vikalpa*);
this, too, is subsumed under consciousness (*vijñāna*). Second, showing that transformation lacks intrinsic nature, all of which arises from the delusion of consciousness. Together with a verse:
In this way, all transformations of nature should be understood as being like the ripening of milk into curd, wine, or fruit;

the transformations imagined by the non-Buddhists do not actually exist as either existent or non-existent. Mahāmati, these external natures and non-natures are merely manifestations of one's own mind.
Thus, Mahāmati, ordinary and ignorant beings arise from the habitual cultivation of their own false imaginings. Mahāmati, there is no dharma that is ever born.
If they were to cease, it would be like seeing the forms produced by illusions or dreams.
Furthermore, all phenomena are seen to undergo transformation, such as milk turning into curd, wine, or fruit;
because non-Buddhists rely on this, they give rise to the false imagination of transformation. However, in reality, all phenomena lack the nature of transformation. Milk...

There is no inherent nature in curd; there is no inherent nature in wine as a fruit. Whether through causes and conditions or through transformation, whether existent or non-existent, all are manifestations of one’s own mind and lack intrinsic nature.
Just as one perceives all forms in a dream or an illusion, they neither arise nor perish, and are neither existent nor non-existent.
The foolish and ignorant do not understand this; they take them to be produced by their own habitual practice and falsely perceive them as real dharmas.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The transformation of shape, location, and time, The four great elements and the sense faculties— The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises gradually;
Such false imaginings belong not to the wise. The Supreme One [teaches] dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) Is not like those false imaginings;
Yet worldly dependent origination Is like a city of Gandharvas."

To perceive the four great elements and the various sense faculties, their forms, locations, and the signs of transformation, as well as the gradual growth of the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*), is all mere false imagination and not the wisdom of the enlightened. Worldly dependent origination is like a city of the *gandharvas*:
it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither one nor different. The Buddhas and Tathāgatas certainly do not [assert] existence or non-existence within dependent origination.
The arising of discrimination is as it is falsely conceptualized. "Present birth" refers to the preceding aggregates (*skandha*); "subsequent birth" refers to the succeeding aggregates.

Having abandoned present birth and not yet having reached subsequent birth, the intermediate state body manifests; this is called the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*). The above concludes the second section, the discernment of consciousness and wisdom.
Third, separately relying on words to grasp meanings, which establishes the adherence to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, divided into five parts. △ First, Mahāmati requests.
Question:

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the meaning of the continuity of all dharmas and the meaning of liberation.
If you skillfully distinguish the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas, then I and [others]..."

All Bodhisattvas skillfully understand all continuities (*saṃtāna*) through their mastery of expedient means (*upāya-kauśalya*), and they do not fall into the continuity of attachment to the literal meaning as it is spoken.

(The Tang translation says: "I pray that the Tathāgata will explain for me the profound and secret meaning of all dharmas, as well as the characteristics of those meanings, so that I and all other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may thoroughly know these dharmas and not fall into grasping them according to the words.")

[They possess] deep and subtle attachment to the meaning [of phenomena], yet they are skilled in the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas, as well as in the awakening that transcends the conceptualization of words, letters, and speech.

They travel through all Buddha-fields and immeasurable assemblies, possessing the power of mastery, supernatural penetrations, the seal of *dhāraṇī*, various transformations, and radiant illumination. Their awakened wisdom skillfully enters the ten [stages].
This is the stage of exhaustion. Without employing expedient means, it is like the sun, the moon, a mani-jewel, or the four great elements;

in all lands, one is free from the marks and views of one's own deluded imaginings. One perceives all phenomena as being like illusions, dreams, and so forth, and enters the body of the Buddha-ground.
Within the realms of all sentient beings, one preaches the Dharma according to their needs and guides them, causing them all to dwell securely in the state of omniscience.

All phenomena are like illusions, dreams, and so forth; they are free from the categories of existence and non-existence, as well as the conceptualizations of arising and ceasing that differ from the meaning of verbal expression.
His body becomes increasingly sublime.

This refers to his realization that he has transcended attachment to the meanings of words and expressions, desiring that the World-Honored One further clarify the attainment of the entry into the realm of verbal expression.
The single meaning is the noble and blissful sphere of practice, by which one proceeds toward the ultimate and does not fall into divergent paths.

Because the objects grasped through verbal expressions are profound and subtle, and because conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is not severed, it is called "continuous" (*saṃtati*). Both the Two Vehicles and the One Vehicle share this obstacle, namely, attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
For example, based on the sacred teaching that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are without self, the followers of the Two Vehicles take this as their object of focus.

One enters the contemplation of non-self and realizes the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*). Yet, one still perceives the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as truly existent dharmas and the realized dharma of non-self as truly existent.
This obstacle persists until the seventh stage; even upon entering the eighth stage, it cannot yet be avoided.

As for the subtle object of knowledge regarding the non-self of dharmas (*dharma-nairātmya*), it is only at the stage of Buddhahood that it is finally exhausted. "Object of knowledge" refers to that which is realized.

Regarding the principle of emptiness and the empty wisdom that realizes it, if there remains even the slightest trace of that which is understood, one has not yet reached perfection within the sphere of the noble bliss of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This is because one must exhaustively reach the end of even the subtlest characteristics of the mental continuum.

Nevertheless, if a bodhisattva can skillfully understand expedient means (*upāya*), they will not fall into the realm of conceptualization and discursive speech regarding awakening, and thus attain liberation.
Maintaining awakened wisdom, one travels through all Buddha-fields by means of this awakened wisdom and supernatural transformations.
Ultimately, one is able to ride upon the ten inexhaustible vows, illuminating the ten directions like the sun, moon, mani-jewels, and the four great elements.
Dwelling nowhere and clinging to nothing, one traverses all stages, leaves behind all marks and views, realizes that all phenomena are like illusions, and reaches the ultimate body of the Tathāgata.
Having first established this foundation, he then guides sentient beings according to their individual capacities.

Just as he himself has understood it, he causes them to suddenly eliminate existence and non-existence, as well as arising and ceasing, thereby transcending all conceptual proliferation of speech and delusive thought.

Thus, one should know that both the non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles, due to their unskillful means, cling to the conceptual proliferation of speech and are unable to bring forth the awakened wisdom of liberation.
This is the point from which wisdom and consciousness diverge; it is the pivot upon which delusion and awakening must be turned. This was the intent of Mahāmati’s request:

the essential mechanism is indeed subtle. Regarding the ten inexhaustible phrases (*daśākṣayapada*), Bodhisattvas on the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, give rise to vows as vast as the Dharma-realm and achieve fulfillment through these ten inexhaustibles. These ten phrases are [the means by which] the finite is transcended.
Then my vows would come to an end; because these ten items are inexhaustible, my vows are likewise inexhaustible. First, the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible.
Second, the realm of worlds is inexhaustible. Third, the realm of space is inexhaustible. Fourth, the realm of phenomena is inexhaustible. Fifth, the realm of nirvana is inexhaustible.
Sixth, the realm of the appearance of Buddhas is inexhaustible. Seventh, the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is inexhaustible.
Inexhaustible: eighth, the inexhaustibility of the objects of the eight mental factors; ninth, the inexhaustibility of the sphere of entry for the Buddha’s wisdom;

tenth, the inexhaustibility of the revolution of the world, the revolution of phenomena, and the revolution of wisdom. It is like the sun, the moon, the *maṇi* jewel, and the four great elements: the sun and moon travel through space without support;
the *maṇi* jewel manifests colors according to its surroundings and possesses no inherent nature; and earth, water, fire, and wind pervade everywhere.
The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is without obstruction. △ Second, the exposition of the eleven kinds of continuous and profound mysteries.
The Buddha addressed Mahāmati: "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for your sake."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"Regarding the infinite nature of all dharmas as explained according to their meaning, there is a continuous attachment to characteristics. That is to say: the continuity of attachment to characteristics; the continuity of attachment to conditions;
the continuity of attachment to existence and non-existence; and the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of arising and non-arising, and cessation and non-cessation."

The continuity of attachment to signs; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of vehicles and non-vehicles; the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of the conditioned and the unconditioned;

the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination of the specific characteristics of each stage; the continuity of attachment to the uninterrupted false discrimination of one's own [subjective] constructions;

the continuity of attachment to the false discrimination based on the dualistic views of existence and non-existence held by externalists; and [the continuity of attachment to] the three vehicles and the one vehicle.
The "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the continuous succession of uninterrupted false conceptualizations and attachments;

this includes both the characteristics of the five aggregates as clung to by the two vehicles, and the characteristics of the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena in the ten stages—all of these are "characteristics.

The "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to causal conditions, which are likewise clung to by the two vehicles, as well as the conditions for self-awakened realization, which involve a slight degree of [subject-object] differentiation.

"Reliance" refers entirely to that which takes phenomena as its object. "Nature" is synonymous with "phenomena. Whether nature or non-nature, arising or non-arising, ceasing or non-ceasing, vehicle or non-vehicle, conditioned or unconditioned—all these are attachments to the dualistic oppositions between the mundane and the supramundane. As for the specific characteristics of each stage:
In each stage (*bhūmi*), there are no real dharmas. In the *Avataṃsaka*, a single stage already encompasses all stages;
furthermore, each stage enters into every other stage, like the jewels in Indra’s net, mutually containing one another and devoid of self-nature (*svabhāva*).

If there were any characteristic of a stage to be realized, there would then be a self-characteristic of a realizing subject—what is called one's own deluded imagination. This is the category of existence and non-existence.

Those who previously relied on existence and accepted the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, yet later claim they are non-existent, all rely on the words of the Sages while developing overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

Such individuals destroy the Buddha-dharma and are identical to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, regarding the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle, which are both taught in the holy scriptures, those who do not understand skillful means (*upāya*) take the literal words as the definitive meaning and cling to them as real dharmas; these are all included within the category of "successive attachment" (*saṃtati-parigraha*).
△ Third, showing how the continuity of deep-seated secret [delusions] destroys oneself and others.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, these and other ordinary, ignorant beings have a continuity of their own delusive imaginings (*parikalpita*).

Because of this continuity, the delusive imaginings of ordinary, ignorant beings are like a silkworm making a cocoon; with the threads of delusive imagining, they entangle themselves and entangle others. Whether existent or non-existent—
They are attached to the characteristics of continuity.
Building upon the previous extensive analysis, there are further immeasurable kinds of profound and secret attachments. Bound by these themselves, they bind others;

all of this arises from grasping at meaning based on words, falsely giving rise to divergent characteristics which they take to be "secrets. Thus they destroy themselves and destroy the Dharma for the sake of the multitude.
The arising of obstacles is deeply pitiable; it is for this reason that the Tathāgata heaves a sigh.
△ Fourth, showing that all phenomena are quiescent, being far removed from both continuity and non-continuity.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, therein there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity, because one perceives all dharmas as tranquil and false conceptualization does not arise. Thus, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives all dharmas as tranquil.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, having realized that external natures are without nature and that the appearances manifested by one’s own mind do not exist, one should conformingly observe what is manifested by one’s own mind.
[This is] the measure. All natures, whether existent or non-existent, are signless (*animitta*).

Because the continuity of views is stilled, there is neither continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity regarding all phenomena. Furthermore, Mahāmati, therein there is neither bondage nor liberation;
others who fall into [error] due to not awakening to reality as it is, perceive bondage and liberation. Why is this? It is because they [perceive] existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena.

Because no sentient beings can be apprehended, there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity. Furthermore, this is taught for the sake of those who conceive of non-continuity.

Having attained the realization of the primary truth (*paramārtha*), one perceives all phenomena as quiescent; thus, false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise. [There is] neither continuity nor...
Continuity is entirely a conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Why is this so? Because one awakens to the fact that all external phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);

they are manifestations of one’s own mind, like illusions and dreams, and are utterly non-existent. By observing them as they truly are, one realizes the measure of one’s own mind (*svacittamātra*), wherein both existence and non-existence are extinguished.
This is pure, singular stillness, devoid of the characteristic of continuity; therefore, there is also no characteristic of non-continuity.
This is the continuity of characteristics. If there were bondage or liberation, both would fall into non-realization of things as they truly are;
they would not be the self-characteristic *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena. The self-characteristic *tathatā* of all phenomena is neither existent nor non-existent, and it has no master.
This is the primary meaning realized through self-awakening, wherein the internal and external correspond.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three continuities for the foolish: namely, greed, hatred, and delusion; as well as craving for future existence accompanied by delight and pleasure.
Because of these continuities, there is the continuity of the realms of existence. That continuity, Mahāmati, continues the five destinies. Mahāmati, [this is so].
Regarding the severance of continuity: there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, when one clings to the means of the threefold conjunction of conditions, consciousness arises in uninterrupted succession. Through clinging to such means, there is continuity;
when the consciousness resulting from the threefold conjunction of conditions is severed and the three liberations are realized, no further continuity arises.
Fools have three kinds of continuity; the two vehicles rely upon this continuity to realize non-continuity and establish the view of non-continuity.

Therefore, the Tathāgata specifically addressed them, saying: "Those who read 'the severance of characteristics' possess neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity.
Greed, anger, and delusion are the causes of continuity; these causes arise from the non-enlightenment of ignorance."

This gives rise to the perception of characteristics; persons and phenomena appear distinct. Afflictions arise based upon this, from which craving and future rebirth emerge together with greed and delight.
Through this continuity, the five destinies are ultimately formed. Although those of the Two Vehicles have severed the causes of this continuity, [the seeds remain].

Yet they do not realize that ignorance and non-awakening are entirely like dreams and illusions; they mistakenly perceive them as having characteristics that can be severed, which is what is called "attachment to dharmas" (*dharmagrāha*).

Regarding the phrase "the arising of consciousness through the expedient attachment to the conditions of the threefold conjunction": the "threefold conjunction" refers to the sense organ (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Although this consciousness encompasses all eight consciousnesses, in the context of this specific definition, it refers specifically to the seventh consciousness, the *manas*, which is characterized by the grasping of a self (*ātman-grāha*).

By means of this consciousness, the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) sever only the grasping at a person—that is, an external self. Once this external self is severed, there is no one who undergoes appropriation;
thus, the cause for birth within the three realms is naturally severed. However, because ignorance has not been severed, the internal self of the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) still persists.
This internal self is precisely the self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*). Because this self of phenomena exists, when the cause of birth is severed, they conceive the notion that it will not continue.

This is not true liberation. If one completely severs the seven types of selfhood both internally and externally, and perceives the three gates of liberation of the Mahāyāna, then all continuities will no longer arise.
Even when the two vehicles manifest the characteristic of non-continuity, this is still a case of grasping at meaning based on causal explanations.
This continuity is even more profound and subtle; it can only be permanently severed upon the realization of liberation.
The three liberations are emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Wishlessness is especially the true medicine for the two extremes.
Therefore, by entering this gate, all phenomena are stilled. △ Fifth: Summary Verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Unreal conceptualization is said to be the characteristic of continuity.
If one knows that reality, the net of continuity is severed. Lacking knowledge of the various natures, one grasps according to verbal expressions;
just as a silkworm spins a cocoon and entangles itself, so too are fools bound by the continuity of their own conceptualizations."
"Not observing.
The meaning of the verse is that upon entering the true ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the continuity [of existence] is spontaneously severed;

there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity. Fools, however, do not skillfully observe while within the bonds of present continuity, and thus rely [upon them].
Regarding the explanation of grasping at meaning: they falsely give rise to divergent characteristics and, desiring liberation, instead bind themselves.

All this arises from failing to attain the first principle of self-awakening (*pratyātma-adhigama*). The above three sections have concluded the detailed discussion on how relying on words to grasp meaning results in deep-seated attachments.

Commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* by the Dharma-heir Śramaṇa Śīlajin (now lost; now verified). Part Four:
Demonstrating that the Wisdom of the Sage is Empty in Order to Destroy Erroneous Conceptions. Divided into six sections. △ First: Mahāmati’s Interrogation of All [Matters].
"The Dharma is subject to cessation.
Mahāmati spoke again to the Buddha, saying: "As the World-Honored One has taught, by means of various conceptualizations (*vikalpa*), one conceptualizes various natures (*svabhāva*);
yet those intrinsic natures do not exist, for they are merely the nature of conceptualization itself. (The Tang translation says: "By means of various minds...")
[He] distinguishes all dharmas. No dharmas possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); this is merely a false conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

"World-Honored One, if it is only the imagined intrinsic nature and not an intrinsic nature that exists in mutual dependence, would this not be a fault for the World-Honored One’s teaching that afflictions and purification are without intrinsic nature?
For all dharmas are of an imagined intrinsic nature and lack an [actual] nature. (The Tang translation says: "World-Honored One, if...")
However, for those who falsely conceptualize that all phenomena do not exist, there would be the total destruction of both defiled and pure phenomena.

All phenomena are manifestations of one's own mind; they are neither existent nor non-existent. Due to delusion regarding one's own mind, one falsely gives rise to the conceptualization and attachment to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena.
As the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, once said: "All phenomena lack intrinsic nature; there is only delusion."

[Because they are] of the nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Therefore, Mahāmati raises an objection: "If there were only the nature of conceptualization and no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena, then all pure and impure phenomena would be utterly destroyed.
This doubt concerns the annihilation of phenomena. [The Buddha explains that] one does not realize that phenomena are manifestations of one's own mind and lack intrinsic nature;
the deluded do not know this, and thus see them as existing through conceptualization. In order to depart from [this view]...

Because of such false attachments, it is said that the intrinsic nature of noble wisdom is empty. This emptiness does not fall into the extreme of existence, yet there is that which is known by noble wisdom;
furthermore, it is not the destruction of phenomena. The subsequent text repeatedly investigates and clarifies this point, providing a general demonstration of this principle. II.
Showing that while all dharmas lack an inherent nature, it is not that the knowledge and vision of noble wisdom is non-existent.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said. Mahāmati, it is not like the reality of the self-nature of things as imagined by the ignorant.
This imagined self-nature does not possess the characteristics of a real self-nature. (The Tang translation says:
"All foolish commoners discriminate among all phenomena, yet the nature of phenomena is not as they imagine. This is merely false attachment; it does not exist.")

It is thus, Mahāmati. Just as there is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of noble wisdom—known by the noble ones, seen by the noble ones, and perceived by the noble eye of wisdom—in this same way, one knows that intrinsic nature.
I agree with what Mahāmati has stated: it is only the nature of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that is non-existent regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), and not their total annihilation.

This means that while all phenomena lack a fixed nature of either affliction or purity, they are not without nature. Therefore, it is said that according to noble wisdom there is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
such is the intrinsic nature as perceived by the noble ones through their noble knowledge, noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom.

This is known. It is because the noble wisdom possesses the nature of self-nature; thus, by means of noble knowledge, noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom, it accords with the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as it is—internal and external in correspondence, without separate realms.

It is not like the deluded discriminations falsely produced by ignorant people, who falsely engage in conceptual reckonings. [Objection: Third, [it may be argued that] if all phenomena are not non-existent, then noble wisdom would fall into existence.
This is divided into two parts. △ First, the doubt that what is known by noble wisdom is identical to the manifestation of deluded thought.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "If it is as you say—that the noble ones, through their noble knowledge, see with the noble eye of wisdom rather than the divine eye—"
It is not by means of the fleshly eye that one knows the nature of self-nature (*svabhāva*) in this way; it is not as the false imaginings of foolish commoners do.

World-Honored One, how do foolish commoners abandon such false imaginings? Because they do not perceive the reality of the noble nature. World-Honored One, they are neither inverted nor non-inverted. Why is this?
Because they do not perceive the reality of the noble nature of self-nature, and thus they do not see that which is free from existence and non-existence.

Because of [the absence of] marks (the Tang translation says: "because one does not see the dharmas seen by the noble ones"; for the noble eye is far removed from the marks of existence and non-existence).

It is that which is known by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), not as it is in false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). That is to say, what is known by noble wisdom is not like the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) of false conceptualization.
This is because ordinary fools do not depart from false conceptualization and do not awaken to the nature of the noble ones; thus, although their spheres differ, [the object remains the same].
However, the identity of the seer and the identity of the seen are precisely what one wishes to be free from through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Yet, the sense faculties and their objects (*indriya-viṣaya*) of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) remain vividly present. This is the point of Mahāmati’s difficulty; his intention is to ask:

since foolish ordinary beings currently possess false conceptualization and discrimination, how can they be free from it? Furthermore, while the realm of noble wisdom currently exists, it is not perceived as it truly is.
It is known that it cannot be called "awakening. However, the nature, self-nature, and characteristics known by noble wisdom appear in the same manner as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
That is to say, when the world speaks of a "cow," the noble ones also speak of a "cow"; when the world speaks of a "horse," the noble ones also speak of a "horse.
Although their attachments and conceptions differ, they circulate in the same way. Therefore, it is said that this is not a delusion, nor is it not [a delusion].
It is a perversion. One does not see that which is free from the marks of existence and non-existence; this is precisely what is called "not awakening to the holy reality.

That is to say, it is not that there is no perversion. Now, regarding this nature and its intrinsic characteristics: in one case, one sees that which is free from existence and non-existence; in another case, one does not see that which is free from existence and non-existence.

There are, in fact, no two distinct dharmas, yet their perceived realms differ. It is based on this that difficulties arise, and it is by means of this very point that the fundamental principle is clarified.
The Buddha and the Bodhisattvas interact through the resonance of their spiritual capacities; there is truly no other underlying principle.
World-Honored One, even the Sage does not perceive things in this way as they appear through deluded imagination, for he does not take the realm of self-characteristics as his objective realm.
World-Honored One, that too is the manifestation of the nature of self-nature through the nature of deluded imagination; it is not said to have a cause.

Because there would be no cause; that is to say, it would fall into the view of [inherent] nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa-dṛṣṭi*). If it were different from its object, there would be such an infinite regress as those [previously mentioned].

World-Honored One, this is because one does not realize the self-nature and characteristics of the nature itself. World-Honored One, furthermore, the self-nature and characteristics of the nature of the causal state of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)—how could that be "imagined" rather than "not imagined"? It is by knowing imagination as it truly is... (The Wei translation says: "World-Honored One...")

"World-Honored One, it is not because there is a substantial nature or characteristic of phenomena through conceptual discrimination that phenomena exist. World-Honored One, how should one discriminate them?
One should not discriminate them as they are discriminated; rather, one should discriminate them as they truly are."

Furthermore, it is said that although noble wisdom does not perceive things in the same manner as deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), all phenomena have never failed to manifest in the same manner as deluded conceptualization. This sphere of experience is not distinct from phenomena;
yet, while it manifests in the same manner as deluded conceptualization, phenomena do not cease to exist because of noble wisdom. They are one and the same phenomena. And...
In the realm of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one seeks only to speak of emptiness; yet in the realm of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), one does not disdain falling into existence.

This is what is challenged in the following passage. When it says, "The noble ones do not perceive things as they appear in deluded conceptualization," it means that noble wisdom awakens to the manifestation of one's own mind, and thus does not take the appearances manifested by one's own mind to be real objects. Nevertheless, it is not that there is nothing manifested.
The nature of these things is the manifestation of the self-nature of false imagination.

However, noble wisdom does not speak of causes or causelessness, for that would fall into the views of intrinsic nature and characteristics, resulting in the infinite faults of self-arising distinctions as found in the realm of the ignorant.
Because fools do not realize that the characteristics of the self-nature of things arise from the manifestations of their own minds, they fail to understand these characteristics of self-nature.

Such characteristics are known by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) to be identical to the manifestations of false discrimination (*vikalpa*). Therefore, it cannot be said that they exist because of false discrimination;
hence it is said that the characteristics of self-nature are also not caused by false discrimination. Since the characteristics of self-nature are not caused by false discrimination...

If there is existence, it is merely what is conceptualized by deluded thought; it is not that which is conceptualized by deluded thought, yet it is just like what is conceptualized by deluded thought.
This refers generally to all phenomena being identical [in nature]. However, that which is known by noble wisdom is precisely what is conceptualized by deluded thought;

thus, while the following text refutes false conceptualization by speaking of emptiness, the sphere of noble wisdom would conversely fall into the view of existence. △ Second, the doubt regarding the noble ones.
“Wisdom falls into existence, Blessed One.
False imagination is different, and the characteristic of self-nature is different, Blessed One; they are not similar, because of the characteristic of the self-nature of false imagination.”
How is it that these things are each non-conceptualized, yet the foolish do not know them as they truly are?
Nevertheless, for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon conceptualization, it is taught that the characteristics of conceptualization do not exist as they truly are.

Blessed One, why do you prohibit sentient beings from clinging to the self-nature of objects through views of existence and non-existence, and from clinging to the sphere of activity of noble wisdom, thereby falling into the view of existence? Please explain.
The dharma of emptiness is not a self-nature (*svabhāva*), yet it is described as the objective reality of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
This summarizes the aforementioned characteristics of the nature of self-nature (*svabhāvalakṣaṇa*): different views appear as the same.

This is taught by the Tathāgata to negate false conceptualization (*parikalpita*) and is said to be unreal; it reveals noble wisdom and describes its sphere of activity. Nevertheless, this still falls into the extremes of emptiness or existence. Self-nature...

Characteristics do not exist because of deluded conceptualization; therefore, it is said that deluded conceptualization is distinct from the characteristic of self-nature. Being distinct, they are not similar.

Since they are not similar, yet one perceives the characteristic of self-nature due to deluded conceptualization—this is because foolish people do not know, as it truly is, the respective characteristics of their own self-natures, and because each lacks the sphere of deluded conceptualization. Nevertheless, since they have become [deluded] for the multitude...

Birth arises from the conceptualization of existence through false imagination (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, it is said that the sphere of activity of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) is the emptiness of what is desired by false imagination;
this is the sphere of activity of the self-nature of noble wisdom, which is entirely without fault.

One does not realize that all phenomena appear identically to both the noble and the ordinary. Those who awaken to their own mind do not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence. Therefore, it is said: "All..."

Dharmas have no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Failing to realize that they are one's own mind, people falsely conceptualize them as existing or as non-existing; both deviate from the true essence of dharmas.
Out of compassion for this, the Tathāgata taught the doctrine of emptiness, stating that there is no intrinsic nature of dharmas, but only false imagination (*parikalpita*).
If one knows that the essence of dharmas is fundamentally void and that false conceptualization is not real, then the very realm of false imagination becomes the sphere of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
Momentary transformation is non-dual and undifferentiated; it does not mean that by negating this, one falls into the opposite extreme there.
That truth and falsehood possess distinct natures, or that existence and non-existence are mutually dependent, is not what is revealed by those who dwell in self-awakened observation.

[The Buddha said: "The three preceding objections [imply] that all phenomena are not non-existent; thus, noble wisdom would fall into the extreme of existence. 4. Showing that the reality of noble wisdom is empty and free from existence and non-existence.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not my teaching that phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Nor do I teach that noble wisdom falls into the view of existence."

Regarding the matter of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): however, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings to leave behind phrases that provoke fear. Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been attached to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of things (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).

As for the object of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna-vastu*), they hold views based on attachment to intrinsic nature. Therefore, I teach the Dharma of emptiness. Mahāmati, I do not speak of the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of things.

Mahāmati, I abide in the reality of the emptiness of the Dharma as it is personally realized (*pratyātma-adhigata-yathābhūta-śūnyatā-dharma*), which is free from the characteristics of delusive confusion.
He sees. He sees that which is free from the perception of the existence or non-existence of what is manifested by one's own mind. (The Tang translation says:

"For the sake of sentient beings, I have, since beginningless time, been attached to existence. Regarding the quiescent Dharma, I shall speak of it through noble matters so that, having heard it, they may not give rise to fear;
