they may be able to realize the quiescent and empty Dharma as it truly is, leave behind the marks of delusive confusion, enter the principle of *vijñapti-mātra*, and know that what is seen has no [independent] reality.")

Regarding external phenomena, one attains the three liberations, which are sealed with the seal of reality as it is. With respect to the intrinsic nature of things, one attains a dwelling in the observation of self-realized wisdom, free from the views and signs of existence and non-existence.
The Tathāgata speaks of emptiness and speaks of the self-nature of noble wisdom as being primordially quiescent.

This is because sentient beings, due to beginningless habitual tendencies, cling to all internal and external natures and characteristics; [the Tathāgata] wishes to cause them to distance themselves from these.

Furthermore, fearing that they might give rise to fear on their own account, he therefore speaks of the dharma of the emptiness of the self-nature of the objects of noble wisdom—namely, abiding in the emptiness of reality as it is attained by oneself.

This is the Dharma. It is the Dharma of suchness-emptiness (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*). It is free from the manifestations of one's own mind, yet it does not fall into non-existence. It attains the seal of liberation (*vimokṣa-mudrā*), yet it does not fall into existence.
Regarding the three liberations—namely emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—only upon attaining these liberations does one first know the reality of the emptiness of self-nature.

This is the seal of the Dharma of suchness, primordially existent and primordially quiescent; it is the true nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*), to be personally realized through contemplation.
Examine this: it is far removed from all marks of existence and non-existence, as well as the delusions of views.

○ Fifth, demonstrating that the reality of noble wisdom is empty and does not establish a formal tenet, divided into three parts. △ First, demonstrating that one should not establish a tenet of non-arising.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should not establish the thesis that "all dharmas are unarisen. Why is this?
Because such a thesis would imply that all natures are non-natures, and because it relies on the characteristics of causes and arising to assert the thesis that all dharmas are unarisen;
thus, that thesis itself would be undermined. If that thesis—that all dharmas are unarisen—is undermined, then [the position fails].
Because that thesis arises in dependence [on something else], and because that thesis does not enter into all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), its characteristic of non-arising is not established.
(The Tang translation says: "Furthermore, that thesis enters into all phenomena, for even the characteristic of non-arising does not arise.
For one who establishes the thesis that all phenomena are unarisen, their own statement is thereby subverted. Mahāmati, neither existence nor non-existence arises.
Thesis: That thesis enters into all natures; the characteristics of existence and non-existence are unapprehendable.

Mahāmati, if that thesis were such that it does not arise, yet one establishes a thesis based on the non-arising of all natures, then that thesis is undermined. This is because the characteristics of the natures of existence and non-existence do not arise;

therefore, one should not establish a thesis. Furthermore, because the five-membered syllogism contains many faults, and because there are mutually differing characteristics in the reasons, and for the sake of...

Because it is a [mere] fabrication, one should not establish a thesis-position, namely: "all phenomena are unarisen," "all phenomena are empty," or "all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. One should not establish such a thesis.
"All dharmas are unborn; this is what the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time have taught in unison. This is for the sake of those who lack awakening, not for those who possess it.
For one who awakens to the manifestation of their own mind, all delusions are suddenly stilled; this is an internal self-realization that can never be pointed out."
Except for the purpose of causing sentient beings to abandon all attachments, one speaks of the nature of non-arising;
and except for the purpose of removing all terrors, one speaks of the fact that noble wisdom has the nature of emptiness. However, these should not be established as tenets.

To establish the tenet that "all natures are non-natures" is precisely to trace all natures back to their original lack of a nature of arising; yet to establish the tenet of non-arising is itself born of false perception.

Therefore, it is said: "Because that characteristic arises from causes. Since one has already stated that characteristics do not arise because they are produced by false views, yet establishes this very [non-arising] as a thesis, that thesis is then undermined;
for non-arising is posited in contrast to arising, and thus stands in dependence upon it.
Furthermore, this school [asserts] that it enters into all phenomena (*dharma*). Since all phenomena are unarisen, there should likewise be no characteristic of non-arising.
If there still exists a characteristic of the phenomenon of non-arising, then phenomena are not unarisen; such is the reason this doctrine is refuted.
The unchanging characteristic is non-arising; the Tang translation states that the characteristic of non-arising is also non-arising. This refers to the emptiness of the noble nature (āryadhātu).
To avoid attachment and fear, one should not establish this as a formal thesis (*pakṣa*). [To do so] would be based on false conceptualization of existence.

Therefore, it is said that there is no arising. To establish existence based on non-existence as a cause—to posit the two characteristics of being and non-being—within all phenomena, is to find their intrinsic nature unattainable.
If one were to establish such a thesis, it would merely deviate from the true nature of dharmas.

Just as in the five-membered syllogism, where the mutual progression of thesis and reason results in various distinct characteristics, all of which pertain to conditioned origination, this only leads to manifold fallacies. Thus, one comes to know that all dharmas are unarisen.
In order to abandon attachment, it is held that all phenomena are empty and all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

When measured against their actual specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), none of these [propositions] exist at all; therefore, one should not establish a thesis (*pakṣa*). According to the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the syllogism of inference (*anumāna*) consists of three members:

first, the thesis; second, the reason (*hetu*); and third, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). When combined with the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*), these form the five-membered syllogism. Regarding the thesis, there are nine fallacies (*doṣa*).

There are fourteen fallacies regarding the reason (*hetu*), five fallacies regarding the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and five fallacies regarding the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), totaling thirty-three fallacies;

these are established by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, if one employs the "self" (*ātman*) as the property (*dharma*) [of the subject], there is also one fallacy regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*, *pratijñā*), namely, that the essential nature of the property (*dharmasvarūpa*) cannot be established.

The reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are employed to establish the thesis (*pakṣa*). If there is a fault in the thesis, then the reason and the example will follow one after another, resulting in even more divergent characteristics.
What is meant by "not attaining the essential nature of phenomena" (*dharmatattva*)? For instance, if one formulates a syllogism as follows: the thesis is that "all phenomena are unarisen";

the reason is "because they lack intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatvāt*); and the example is "like a plantain tree. When the fault is challenged: "Which phenomena are unarisen? the answer is: "The mind."

Regarding all phenomena that appear: all phenomena are manifestations of the mind and possess no nature of arising. [The opponent] challenges: "If the mind has no nature of arising, does it have a nature of non-arising? [The respondent] answers:
"Because it is called the 'nature of non-arising,' it is said to be unarisen; how could there be anything further? [The opponent] concludes with a refutation:
"If there is nothing further, then by establishing the thesis of 'non-arising,' one does not attain the essence of the dharma. Nevertheless, this is a skillful means regarding self and dharmas."
To sever that attachment, there are no real dharmas. Once that attachment is severed, one naturally realizes the initial mark of the mind and returns to what was originally attained.
Thus, through authentic self-realization, the great function manifests before one; conceptual clinging suddenly ceases, and both arising and non-arising [are seen as equal].

Both [of these] are redundant explanations; therefore, one should not establish a formal thesis (*pakṣa*). What the Tathāgata does is directly reveal the source of the mind, which is realized without depending on others.
△ Second, showing what is seen by noble wisdom: it is like an illusion and free from fault.

Mahāmati, nevertheless, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas teach that all dharmas are like illusions and dreams because of the appearance and disappearance of their characteristics, and because of the faults perceived in [ordinary] vision and cognition.
Thus, one should declare that all dharmas have the nature of illusions and dreams; however, this is excepted for the sake of removing the cause of fear in the minds of the ignorant.
Mahāmati, the ignorant fall into the views of existence and non-existence; do not cause them to be terrified and thereby lead them away from the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).
Paramārtha: Illusions and dreams are not real; they cannot be said to exist. Yet illusions and dreams appear vividly; they cannot be said to be non-existent.

They are neither existent nor non-existent, and whether they manifest or do not manifest depends entirely upon conceptual perception. For this reason, it is said that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams regarding their essential nature.
It is certainly without error. It can also awaken those wise ones so that they may know where to return in that very place and realize the fundamental state of non-action;

therefore, it is taught as appropriate. However, this excludes those foolish people who seek to avoid fear, for such fools fall into the views of existence and non-existence, each having their own point of reliance.

When they hear it said that things are like dreams and illusions, they become utterly bewildered and find no basis for understanding, thereby giving rise to terror and distancing themselves from the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, all discourses concerning the nature of the Sage, or regarding parinirvāṇa, belong to the realm of skillful means (*upāya*).

If one attains the severance of the path of words and the cessation of the sphere of mental activity, and awakens to this state of vast openness, only then will one know that the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood on a certain night and entered nirvāṇa on a certain night;
that in the interval between these two, he did not speak a single word. This silent resonance is difficult to manifest or display.
If one wishes to point toward the present state, there is nothing but non-illusion with which to serve as a metaphor. △ Third, the summary of non-arising as being like an illusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Without self-nature, without speech, without objects."
There is no continuity. (The Wei translation says: "There is no self-nature, no consciousness, and no *ālaya*-consciousness.
That is the deluded imagination of fools, like a corpse with evil thoughts. All phenomena (*dharma*) are unarisen; this is not the tenet of those external paths. Ultimately, nothing is produced.
Accomplished through the nature of conditions, all phenomena are unarisen; the wise do not form conceptions regarding them. Their tenet arises from causes.
Therefore, the awakened one completely eliminates and extinguishes them.
The Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally without self-nature and cannot be demonstrated through words; all eight consciousnesses are like flowers in the sky.
Neither possesses any substantial reality. All sacred teachings are merely for the purpose of guiding those who are lost. Fools, lacking wisdom, do not comprehend these skillful means;
this constitutes their deluded imagination and evil views. All phenomena are unarisen; all phenomena are ultimately without arising.
Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, they are like illusions and dreams. A wise person should not form conceptualizations regarding them. Indeed...
Because they teach non-arising based on the causes of external paths and then cling to this as a real dharma, all these dharmas are non-arising;
this is not like the explanations of the external paths. Once awakened, all such expedients are entirely eliminated. "Matter" (vastu) refers to characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and continuity (saṃtati).
"Flowing on" and "the appearance flowing on" together refer generally to the arising and ceasing of the eight consciousnesses; they are like an illusion and cannot be apprehended.
It is, for example, like one with cataracts seeing the appearance of dangling hairs; the nature of such clinging is likewise so. It is the false conceptualization of the deluded.

Designations are established within the three realms of existence; yet there is no intrinsic nature to things. To designate an intrinsic nature to things is to give rise to delusive conceptualization through reflection.

When signs and things are used to establish verbal teachings, the mind becomes distracted and violently agitated. The Son of the Buddha is able to transcend this and remain far removed from all such delusive conceptualizations.

The falling hairs seen by one with cataracts serve as a metaphor for the deluded perceptions of ordinary beings. Due to these deluded perceptions, various conceptualizations arise, leading to the provisional establishment of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*).

Furthermore, based on these provisional names and characteristics of the three realms, they grasp them as having a real nature, giving rise once more to false imaginings and establishing verbal teachings.

These factors cause one another in succession, resulting in a distracted mind and chaotic speech. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "In every instance of cognition and vision, there is a desire to retain..."
In this world, the course of karma constantly shifts across lands; the world of deluded thought arises and perishes from moment to moment.
If one can awaken to this, within a single kṣaṇa, its very substance is quiescent—truly inconceivable.
Perceiving water where there is no water is a sensation born of craving; thus are the delusions of the foolish. For the noble ones it is not so;
the noble ones perceive purity, which arises from the three liberations and samādhis. Remaining far removed from arising and ceasing, they wander in the state of non-existence.
Cultivating the practice of non-existence, there is neither nature nor non-nature; the equality of nature and non-nature gives rise to the fruits of the noble ones.

That which is not water yet is perceived as water is the point of delusion for the foolish, yet it is the point of awakening for the sages. Through the pure samādhi, one realizes the ultimate destination indicated by this teaching.
Abiding in the ocean of the mind by means of the three gates of liberation, one acts in accordance with the true nature, free from birth.

Extinction: that which moves toward is unimpeded. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* verse says: "Unattached to the world like a lotus flower, always skillfully entering the practice of emptiness and stillness;
penetrating the characteristics of all phenomena without hindrance—I bow my head to him who, like space, has no dependence."
This true nature and non-nature are equal; the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit penetrates to the source of the cause. Thus one knows there is no differentiation.
What is meant by "nature" and "non-nature"? What is meant by "equality"? It is said that when the mind does not know, it is utterly tossed about between the internal and external.
If one can destroy that [dualistic grasping], the mind perceives with equanimity.
To abide within existence and non-existence while failing to realize equanimity is simply due to not understanding that all phenomena are unborn.

When one understands that what manifests is but the appearance of one's own mind, and that this manifestation is ungraspable, it is quiescent in its very place; therein, there is neither equality nor inequality. This is...

This is because it is a mind of equanimity. [End of section] The preceding five points have demonstrated that the phenomena of empty holy wisdom do not establish a formal thesis; this concludes the section.
△ Sixth, demonstrating that holy wisdom is far removed from the objects of knowledge.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, regarding the objects of perception, wisdom does not apprehend them.
This is the establishment of designations based on the measure of designations. That which is grasped has no intrinsic nature, and the act of grasping likewise has no intrinsic nature.
Because there is no grasping, wisdom does not arise; it is merely a designation by name."
The realms of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena are merely provisional designations; they are not the domain of wisdom.

Only when one awakens to the fact that these are the manifestations of one’s own mind does one first realize that all established constructs—the false conceptualizations of subject and object—are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.
Once grasping has ceased, this great wisdom manifests before one; all objective realms are like ice melting in hot water, such that no more ice remains.
"One who knows the melting of ice" refers to one who dwells in the world and follows its conventional flow, yet remains free from inversion.
To clarify this meaning, Mahāmati first cites the words of the Sage, after which he raises an objection.

"The object of apprehension" refers to the various phenomena of existence and non-existence in the world. "That which is grasped" refers to the objective realm; "grasping" refers to the subjective grasper.

When the mind perceives that both the grasper and the grasped are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature, cognition does not arise; this means that cognition does not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding these objects.

"How so? World-Honored One, is it because the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the nature of non-awakening are neither different nor non-different that cognition does not apprehend them?
Or is it because the various natures and intrinsic characteristics of self-characteristics and common characteristics are obscured that cognition does not apprehend them?

Or is it because of obstructions such as mountains, cliffs, rocky walls, earth, water, fire, and wind that cognition does not apprehend them? Or is it because they are extremely distant or extremely near that cognition [does not apprehend them]?"
"Is it not possible? It is because they are old, young, blind, ignorant, or lack the full sensory faculties. Is it that wisdom does not attain [its object]?

World-Honored One, if wisdom does not attain its object because it does not perceive whether self-characteristics and common characteristics are different or not different, then one should not call it 'wisdom'; one should call it 'non-wisdom'."

Because it cannot be apprehended due to the presence of an object. Furthermore, if wisdom were unable to apprehend because the self-characteristics and common characteristics, or the intrinsic natures and their marks, are mutually obscured, then that too would be non-wisdom; it would not be wisdom, World-Honored One. Wisdom arises because there is such an appearance (*tathatā*);
it is called wisdom because it accords with that appearance through the absence of intrinsic nature. (The Tang translation says: "Because one knows the object, it is called wisdom.")
It is not because of a lack of knowledge. If one does not perceive due to mountain crags, rocky walls, earth, water, fire, or wind; or due to being extremely distant or extremely near;
or due to being old, young, blind, or having impaired faculties—this too is not wisdom. It should rather be called a lack of wisdom, because there is an object that cannot be perceived.
Wisdom cannot be attained due to three kinds of obstacles: first, lack of clear realization because wisdom is incomplete;

second, the mutual concealment of phenomena because the objects of knowledge are difficult to know; and third, being obstructed by mountains, cliffs, rocks, walls, the elderly, children, or the blind, whereby one does not know.
These three types of non-knowing are all not the state of a wise person, for they are excluded from it.
The following passage states that it is because one knows [the truth] that the matter cannot be attained;

it is not that the matter cannot be attained because of ignorance. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not that there is a lack of wisdom; rather, it should be understood as wisdom, not as non-wisdom. I do not speak with such concealment.

It is when one relies on objective phenomena (*ālambana*) that wisdom cannot attain them; this is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) established for the purpose of realization. One must awaken to the fact that these are merely the manifestations of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*)."
There exists neither existence nor non-existence of external nature or lack of nature; though one knows this, the objective entity is not apprehended.

Because it is not apprehended, cognition does not arise regarding that radiance (*tathatā*), conforming to the three doors of liberation. Even cognition is not apprehended. For one who is free from false conceptualization, there is the beginningless nature and lack of nature, which is a deceptive habituated cognition.
To know in this way is to know that [the other] does not know.
The first three difficulties involve failing to attain the objective due to a lack of wisdom; what the Tathāgata has taught must be wisdom, not a lack of wisdom.
If one fails to attain it due to a lack of wisdom, it is merely because it was spoken in an obscured manner. Therefore, he further says:

"When the object of focus is not attained through wisdom, it is merely established as a provisional designation. This is the realization that [all things] are the manifestation of one's own mind; it is the realization of the measure of one's own mind.

Then one realizes that all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, as manifested by the mind, lack intrinsic nature. Regarding the objects of perception, one deeply penetrates their fundamental source, and conceptual discrimination ceases instantly.
Although this accords with the three gates of liberation, even so, no noble wisdom (āryajñāna) can be apprehended;

it is called abiding in the ocean of the mind’s primordial quiescence and illumination, which differs from the false awakening of externalists that follows along with beginningless [habitual tendencies].
The habitual tendencies regarding the objects of knowledge—whether internal or external—are precisely what is called "true non-cognition.

Therefore, one continues to harbor false imaginings regarding the characteristics and the existence or non-existence of external objects and locations; these are merely established as the manifestations of one's own mind.
They speak of grasping through attachment to the characteristics of "self" and "what belongs to the self," failing to realize that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds.

They give rise to false conceptualizations regarding the radiance of gnosis; because of such conceptualization, they fail to perceive external natures as being either existent or non-existent, and thus fall into the view of nihilism.
This correctly demonstrates that they do not understand. Although all things in every place are devoid of intrinsic dharmas, their present deluded thoughts remain uninterrupted;
they all arise from the manifestation of their own minds, establishing subject and object, grasping and becoming attached.

When traced to their origin, they are nothing but non-awakening; thus, regarding non-conceptual wisdom, they spontaneously give rise to conceptualization based upon the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Various delusive thoughts arise, falsely reckoning existence and non-existence, and observing existence and non-existence. Birth and cessation have no source; they further result in annihilationism.
If one can know this, then wisdom will manifest before them, and all objects of attachment will suddenly cease at once.
This is what is meant by "knowing the object, yet the object is not attained," for wisdom does not give rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) therein.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When there are objects of perception, if wisdom does not discern them, this is called 'non-wisdom' rather than 'wisdom'; such is the teaching of those who hold false imaginings.

When one does not discern the nature of non-differentiation through wisdom, regarding obstructions, distance, and proximity—this is termed 'perverse wisdom. In the case of the old and the young whose faculties are dull, their cognition..."
Wisdom does not arise; yet, in reality, such a radiance exists. This too is called false knowledge.
The verse states that what is obtained from the first three kinds of knowledge is entirely non-intellectual.

Knowing that those are not true knowledge, one’s wisdom then does not give rise to attachment toward grasping, but remains merely a conventional designation, the domain of mind-only, and not an objective realm.
This may be discussed. (The preceding four sections demonstrated the emptiness of the objects of noble wisdom;

having thus concluded the refutation of false conceptualizations, the fifth section—due to [the opponent’s] failure to understand their own school and their false adherence to expedient means—re-establishes its own tenet to refute worldly doctrines. This is divided into three parts.
△ First, rebuking the foolish who cling to expedient teachings, which gives rise to Mahāmati’s request.)
Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings are turned around by beginningless false, evil, and perverse conceptualizations.
While being thus turned around, they do not skillfully understand the penetration of one's own school (*svapratyātma-gati*) or the penetration of the teaching (*deśanā-gati*).

Because they are attached to the external natures and characteristics manifested by their own minds, they cling to expedient teachings and fail to properly discern the pure characteristics of the fourfold logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) within their own school. Mahāmati.

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is truly as Your Majesty has taught. I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for my sake, analyze and explain the *sūtrānta* (the teaching) and the *tathāgatagarbha* (the principle).
May I and other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas become skilled in these two penetrations, so that future ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas may likewise do so."
They do not perceive its deficiency.
This is because these foolish persons do not properly understand the general characteristic of the purity of the four alternatives within their own school;
hence they pose this question. Because they do not understand the purity of the four alternatives in their own school, [they misinterpret] the expedient teachings of the Noble Doctrine.
They give rise to false conceptualization and are driven by the flow of habitual tendencies and evil thoughts; this school explains this thoroughly to reveal what is to be attained.
The "four phrases" refer to the four alternatives of existence and non-existence. By departing from these four phrases, one attains the purity of the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This is the characteristic of the pure penetration. △ Second, showing that the fundamental teaching does not fall into the views and characteristics of ordinary beings.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it. I shall speak for your sake."

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of doctrinal penetration (*dharmapraveśa*):

namely, the penetration of discourse (*deśanā-praveśa*) and the penetration of one’s own school (*svapratyātma-gotra-praveśa*). As for the penetration of discourse, it refers to that which accords with the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings.”
To teach various sūtras concerning the manifold requisites is called the "communication of the teaching" (deśanā-āgama).

As for the "thorough penetration of one's own school" (sva-pratyātma-āgama), it refers to the practitioner’s departure from the various delusive imaginings manifested by their own mind; that is, not falling into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither;

transcending all mind, thought, and consciousness; realizing the noble realm of self-realization; and being free from the characteristics of views formed through causes. [This applies to] all non-Buddhists and śrāvakas...
"It is that which cannot be known by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who have fallen into the two extremes. I call this the 'Dharma of the Self-System' (svaśāstranaya).
Mahāmati, these are the characteristics of the Self-System and the Teaching-System (deśanānaya); you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should practice and study them."

The *sūtras* are precisely what is taught in the ninefold division of scriptures; that is to say, they accord with principle and accord with phenomena, all serving as guides based upon the minds of sentient beings. There are no real dharmas here;
this is the penetration of the fundamental tenet (*mūla-yukti*) through skillful means (*upāya*), wherein reality does not abandon provisional expediency.

Therefore, one must transcend words to grasp the essential meaning. Furthermore, it is by means of the practitioner’s causal discourse that they reach the fundamental tenet. One must depart from the various manifestations of one's own mind.

Regarding "false conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) and so forth: this refers to the false discrimination of all things—existence, non-existence, and the four logical alternatives (*catuskoṭi*)—which are manifestations of one's own mind.

All of these arise from being deluded regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*, appearing falsely in accordance with the mind, the thought, and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Following such false appearances, one gives rise to discrimination.
Once one awakens to one's own mind, false conceptualization does not arise, and discrimination is forever stilled. This is the domain of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

The sphere of practice is free from all characteristics of views associated with causes and conditions; this is called the characteristic of the ultimate realization of one's own school (*svatantra-siddhānta*).
Because it does not follow any conventional expressions or skillful means, it cannot be known by outsiders (*tīrthika*) or those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse: "I speak of two kinds of penetration: the penetration of the ultimate principle (zongtong) and that of verbal expression (yan-shuo).
The verbal expression is for the sake of instructing the ignorant; the ultimate principle is for those who practice."
This is the same sacred teaching. The simple-minded may speak of it, but through practice one attains its essence. It is not that the Tathāgata truly possesses two kinds of discrimination;
rather, what I have spoken from time to time as "unanswered questions" is merely according to what [the questioner] perceives.

3. Refuting Worldly Discourse to Reveal One’s Own School. This section is divided into six parts. △ First, showing that worldly discourse does not enter into one’s own realization and can bring about [suffering].
[This leads to] delusion and suffering, and the destruction of the compiled [teachings].
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One once said:

'Regarding the various discursive arguments of worldly treatises, you must be careful not to study or associate with them. If one studies or associates with them, it will lead to the grasping of desire and the failure to grasp [the truth].'..."
Regarding the teaching on sensation: Why, World-Honored One, do you speak in this way? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The various phrases and expressions of worldly discourse, adorned with the collection of causes, conditions, and parables, are used to entice and delude foolish ordinary people.
They do not enter into the true self-realization; they fail to awaken to all phenomena, and through false imagination and inversion, they fall into the two extremes—foolish and ignorant."
Deluded, they bring about their own destruction; they continue through the various realms of existence and fail to attain liberation.
Unable to realize that all is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, they do not depart from the false conceptualization and attachment to the intrinsic nature of external objects.

Therefore, despite the various discourses and eloquent explanations of worldly treatises, they remain unable to escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, affliction, deception, and delusion.

This reason is explained as follows: because one should be proficient in both internal and external treatises to support one’s delight in debate, he recalled a former instruction of the World-Honored One, and thus harbored doubts regarding the apparent contradiction between earlier and later passages.

"Worldly treatises" refers specifically to the scriptures of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), which are composed as established doctrines based on various false views; or they are those that provide indirect or circuitous explanations, merely embellishing their names.
The principle is like the finger of heaven and earth, or the myriad things as a single horse;

to extend such meanings and flavors only deludes the mind and consciousness, and thus runs directly counter to the true phrase of self-attestation. Indeed, the inner realization of the awakened mind is far removed from the knowable;

the nature of consciousness delights in seeing and easily forms objective realms. All intellectual understandings are like the bird’s path—profound and subtle—yet they remain within the sphere of awakening-thought and conceptual activity.
It is translated as "secret. This kind of deep attachment is even more difficult to liberate from than coarse and heavy sensual desires.
There are those who, while relying on their own school and taking the sacred teachings as their model, treat the subtle words of the ultimate learning as established treatises for malicious views.
As it is said: "There is no meaning within the words; the meaning lies within the words. Such statements originate from this sort of person, and they have entirely come to be a mere imitation.

Regarding speech: within the subject and object of a phrase, how can the categories of affirmation (*vidhi*) and negation (*pratiṣedha*) be identical? Negation is equivalent to non-existence; affirmation ultimately falls into existence.

If negation and affirmation are not distinguished, the entire substance is ignorance. When negation and affirmation occur simultaneously, names and characteristics proliferate, manifesting spontaneously as soon as the mouth opens.

To attempt to transcend this by means of metaphysical abstractions results in obstruction; to speak of a "vague and subtle departure from the manifest" is a deceptive fabrication of phrases and sentences—this is a failure to penetrate the truth.
Our own school, though situated within the True Dharma, is similar to worldly discourse.

This is precisely what will lead to the destruction of the Council fifty years hence—namely, the cause of evil discernment rooted in false views. Those who realize that all is a manifestation of their own mind should observe this carefully:
whatever arises as external to the mind is entirely inverted, increasing deluded consciousness and perpetuating the causes of birth and death; one must not fail to be cautious regarding this ground.
"Upholding" refers to the cultivation of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), including all internal and external fields of knowledge, medicine, and arts and crafts.
These are the long-enduring great Bodhisattvas whose *ālayavijñāna* is luminous and clear; they enter into all worlds and guide sentient beings in accordance with their minds.
It is not appropriate to use this as a pretext to abruptly relax the sacred prohibitions; rather, you should reflect upon yourself, for only then will you truly know the proper time.
Mahāmati, Śakra Devendra was extensively learned in various treatises and himself composed a work on phonology (*śabda-śāstra*).

Among the followers of that worldly philosophy (*lokāyata*), there was a disciple who assumed the form of a dragon and went to the palace of Śakra to establish his own philosophical tenets, intending to destroy Śakra’s thousand-spoked wheel.
...the wheel. "If I am not equal to you, I shall sever each of my heads to atone for my defeat. Having made this vow, he immediately subdued Śakra by means of the Dharma of Śakra.
Śakra fell into defeat, whereupon [the opponent] destroyed his chariot and returned to the human world. Thus it is, Mahāmati:
worldly discourse, adorned with causes and similes, can even be employed by animals through various phrases.
This savor deludes those devas and asuras, causing them to become attached to views of arising and ceasing; how much more so for humans?
Therefore, Mahāmati, one should distance oneself from worldly discourse, for it brings about the causes for the arising of suffering. Be careful not to cultivate or frequent it.
I cite this as a warning against associating with worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). Worldly discourse uses metaphors for ornamentation and employs the utmost skillful rhetoric;
its applications are inexhaustible and it is difficult to refute. This is merely the mind’s illusory transformations, deceiving what is heard and seen.
It does not expound correct principles, obstructs one's own school, and gives rise to the suffering of birth and death—nothing is more harmful than this.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the proponents of worldly treatises (lokāyatika) speak only of the realm of bodily sensation. Mahāmati, there are hundreds of thousands of such worldly theorists;
however, in the future, during the final five hundred years, their collections will be destroyed due to the causes and views of evil discernment.
Thus it is that evil disciples receive [these teachings]. In this way, Mahāmati, the worldly treatises (lokāyata) destroy the collected [teachings].

Adorned with various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies, they speak of the matters of non-Buddhists (tīrthika), clinging to their own causal conditions and lacking any self-attained realization (sva-prativedha).

Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists have no treatise of self-attained realization; regarding other worldly treatises, they extensively expound immeasurable hundreds of thousands of categories of things, yet they possess nothing [of true realization].

This is self-communication. Furthermore, one does not realize that these are the foolish worldly discourses concerning the body’s sensory experiences—the objects of the five aggregates traversed through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
One may either give rise to discourse based on seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, or [realize] the emptiness and stillness of what is perceived by seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
The subtle, profound, and mysterious realm constitutes its fundamental tenet. "Destroying the compilation" means destroying the Tathāgata’s compilation of the true teaching;
these are those who study the True Dharma yet fall into false views. Were it not for such as these, they could never destroy the true teaching.
"Self-conditioned causes" refers to the realm realized by one's own body. Regarding that which he composed:
These [teachings] do not transcend what is seen, heard, sensed, or known; they do not take non-appropriation as their intrinsic nature.

Instead, they abandon [the truth] to resort to the void and the mysterious, relying on their own private interpretations. In reality, they are identical to heterodox schools. While spreading through the present age, they mislead those yet to come.
Having themselves fallen into ruin, they cause others to fall as well. Their discourses are endless, and their delusions are doubly severe—this is truly to be pitied. △ Second.
[The Buddha] showed that this was the Tathāgata’s teaching according to his own specific terminology (*sva-saṃvṛti*). At that time, Mahāmati said to the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, if the various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies used by non-Buddhists in their worldly treatises (*loka-vāda*) lack any self-terminology and are merely attachments to their own particular objects, then why does the World-Honored One also speak of worldly treatises for the sake of those of various [capacities]?"

"Furthermore, the various assemblies of devas, humans, and asuras gathered from other regions who extensively expound immeasurable varieties of phrases and expressions—do they not also possess their own realization?
Or do they fall within the category of the wisdom and discourse of all non-Buddhists? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
I do not speak of worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*), nor is there coming or going; I speak only of neither-coming-nor-going.

Mahāmati, "coming" refers to the gathering and arising [of phenomena], while "going" refers to their dispersal and destruction. That which neither comes nor goes is that which is neither born nor extinguished.
The meaning I have taught does not fall within the categories of worldly discourse or deluded conceptualization. Why is this? Because it does not involve attachment to external natures.
The nature of things is the locus of what is manifested by one's own mind; it cannot be turned away from by the false imaginings of the two extremes.

Since the characteristics of objects have no inherent nature, when one realizes that they are manifestations of one's own mind, the false imaginings of one's own mind cease to arise. When false imaginings do not arise, there is emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
one enters the three gates of liberation, which is called emancipation.

The World-Honored One has also, on various occasions, extensively expounded for the assembled multitudes from other regions, as well as the eight classes of devas and humans, the *Itivṛttaka* (Past Deeds), the *Jātaka* (Birth Stories), and the *Adbhutadharma* (Marvels); in all these, he has fully explained immeasurable causes, conditions, phrases, and meanings.
Therefore, some suspect that the Tathāgata also teaches worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*).

They do not realize that all the causes and conditions taught by the Tathāgata are for the purpose of establishing one’s own understanding of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), or that he speaks of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by means of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). People fail to understand this and are deluded into thinking it is merely conventional truth.
The World-Honored One does not clarify this point explicitly here, but simply says: "I do not teach worldly discourse," and so forth.

If it does not state what specific matters constitute non-worldly discourse (*alokavāda*), then one knows that all the teachings manifested by the Tathāgata in the present are entirely non-worldly discourse.
Furthermore, it says: "There is also no coming or going," referring to the assembly of people gathered from various directions.
It appears as if there is coming and going. However, the Tathāgata directly points it out within his own direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, he says: "I teach only that there is no coming and no going. Thus one should know that all sentient beings fail to realize the realm present before them;
they cling to the false imaginings (*vikalpa*) of their own mental direct perception, taking them to be truly existent coming and going. Therefore, [he speaks] again...

The Emperor issued this decree: "That which comes gathers and gives rise to existence; that which goes disperses and destroys it. This is birth and extinction. That which neither comes nor goes is without birth or extinction.
This clarifies the meaning of what I have taught: it does not fall within the reckoning of worldly conventions or deluded imaginings.
The Tathāgata, through his own realization, abides in the direct perception of his own mind-manifestation, seeing that all external natures are non-natures and are not existent."
It cannot be turned back by the spheres of the two extremes. Abiding among humans and devas, it speaks of the three periods of time according to its own sphere.
Humans say that the Tathāgata speaks of the three periods of time, yet for the Tathāgata there are truly no three periods of time.
He speaks of the three vehicles and of humans and devas; humans say that the Tathāgata speaks of the three vehicles and of humans and devas, yet for the Tathāgata there are truly none.
The followers of the three vehicles and the gods and humans follow worldly perversion in asserting the existence of the three times and the existence of the three vehicles, gods, and humans.

Desiring that sentient beings may realize the penetration of their own fundamental principle (sva-śāstra-yukti) and attain the Tathāgata’s realm of self-mastery—which is not dependent on verbal expression—I have repeatedly and earnestly instructed them, saying:
"When you awaken to what is manifested by your own mind, then regarding that which is manifested by your own mind, false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) will no longer arise."
When birth occurs, the non-arising of deluded thoughts constitutes the gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; entering these three gates of liberation is what is called "liberation.
These three gates of liberation are most perfectly accordant with the samādhi that exists fundamentally within the realization of the measure of one’s own mind.
This is what the Tathāgata has repeatedly exhorted us to recognize. 3. Showing the Tathāgata’s Cessation of Discourse.
"Mahāmati, I recall that once, while I was dwelling in a certain place, a world-theorizing brāhmaṇa came to where I was.
Without first seeking my leave, he immediately asked me: 'Gautama, is everything created? At that time, I replied:
'Brāhmaṇa, everything is created. This is the first world-theory. He then asked again: 'Is everything uncreated?'"
I replied again: "That 'everything is uncreated' is the second worldly doctrine. They asked further: "Is everything eternal?
Is everything impermanent? Is everything born? Is everything unborn? To this, I replied:
This is the sixth worldly doctrine (*loka-vāda*). Mahāmati, they further asked me: "Is everything one? Is everything different?
Is everything both? Is everything neither? Does everything manifest through birth due to various causes?
I replied to them: "This is the eleventh worldly doctrine. Mahāmati, they further asked: "Is everything indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? Is everything determinate (*vyākṛta*)?"
"Is there a self? Is there no self? Does this world exist? Does this world not exist? Does another world exist? Does another world not exist?
Is there liberation? Is there no liberation? Are all things momentary? Are all things non-momentary?
Is it space? Is it analytical cessation? Is it nirvāṇa? Gautama, is it created? Is it uncreated? Does it exist?"
"Is there an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), or is there no intermediate state? Mahāmati, I then replied to him:
"Brāhmaṇa, such statements as these are all merely worldly discourse (*lokavāda*); they are not what I teach. They are your worldly discourse."

Furthermore, non-Buddhists raise questions from within their worldly treatises (*loka-vāda*), whereas the Tathāgata answers correctly from the perspective of his own realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
That which is produced arises from causes; that which is unproduced arises without cause.

All such positions—whether regarding the eternal or the impermanent, arising or non-arising, identity or difference, or both—are merely the province of worldly treatises; they do not pertain to the ultimate truth.
This is beyond the scope of their own systems. The Tathāgata refers to both the first-worldly discourse and the two-worldly discourse;

he teaches this directly, without concealment. The outsiders do not understand it and raise many questions; one might say they are passing him by face-to-face. From beginning to end, the Tathāgata has taught directly, saying:
"Those who speak thus are all proponents of worldly discourse; this is not what I have taught. This is your worldly [discourse]."
Treatise: Formerly, a Brahmin asked the World-Honored One: "I do not ask about that which can be expressed in words; I do not ask about that which cannot be expressed in words.
After the World-Honored One remained silent for a long while, the Brahmin said: "The World-Honored One’s great compassion has cleared away the clouds of my delusion, enabling me to enter [the Way].

This is like a fine horse seeing the shadow of the whip. I, the Tathāgata, have often said: "Cease the discursive theorizing. I speak of this from time to time; therefore, one should know how to construct [the meaning].
It is merely that their disposition is difficult [to deal with]. O Brahmin, those who emerge from the five regions of India claim that their ancestors were born from the mouth of Brahmā;
thus they take the name of the Brahma-clan, which is the same as "Brahmacārin. Their lineage is haughty and prone to contention.

Whether they have left the household life or remain at home, they maintain a succession of established practices and possess many sūtras and śāstras. They do not seek out leisure for contemplation, yet they are singularly haughty in this regard. To the west—

In the ritual protocols of the region, all requests must first be submitted for approval; this is termed "requesting a vacant interval" (*kṣaṇa*). A *kṣaṇa* refers to a subtle moment of arising and ceasing.
Space (*ākāśa*), nirvāṇa, and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—these three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are the existence of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
"Created or uncreated" refers to the inquiry as to whether these three unconditioned phenomena are produced or not.
I teach only that the various evils arising from beginningless false conceptualization and habitual tendencies are the cause of the three realms of existence.

Failing to realize that all is a manifestation of one’s own mind, one gives rise to false conceptualization and clings to external natures, as do the followers of non-Buddhist paths who claim that cognition arises from the conjunction of the sense organs, their objects, and consciousness.
I do not hold such a view, O Brāhmaṇa; I do not speak of causes, nor do I speak of [conditions].
There is no cause; it is only the nature of the grasped and the grasper, which is designated as dependent origination through false conceptualization.
This cannot be realized by you or others who have fallen into the continuity of the notion of a self. Mahāmati, nirvāṇa, space, and cessation are not of three kinds;
there are only three enumerations.
Deluded regarding the Tathāgatagarbha, it becomes ignorance; through non-awakening, there is delusive movement. This is the beginningless habit-energy of falsehood.
All worlds—the sense organs, the physical body, and the receptacle world—take this falsehood as their cause. Because of this falsehood...
Unable to realize that these are manifestations of their own minds, they give rise to false attachments and grasp at external phenomena.
Thus, the non-Buddhists erroneously claim that the three—sense organs, objects, and consciousness—arise through conjunction.

Not realizing that the present triad of sense organs, objects, and consciousness is a delusion of one's own mind, they falsely reckon that internal consciousness transforms into these appearances and that all phenomena arise from them as if they were truly existent. This is...

Regarding the theory of causal origination: one observes arising and ceasing closely and perceives the exhaustion of causes; yet others reckon that there is no cause. This is not what the Tathāgata has taught.
The Tathāgata teaches only that there are false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) which falsely grasp at subject and object as provisional designations (*prajñapti*). Therefore, it is said:
"This cannot be perceived by you or by others who have fallen into the continuity of the self-notion (*ātma-saṃtati*). This is the continuity of the self.

This refers to the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). Regarding the dharmas of the two vehicles, my realization of selflessness is not yet exhaustive; I still do not know the initial signs of ignorance giving rise to karma.

Furthermore, I clearly perceive that the three unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛta-dharma) lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and are certainly not objects of attachment to dharmas—how much less so for those of the external paths?
Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time the Brahmin of Worldly Discourse again asked me:
"Is the existence of the three realms of being caused by ignorance, craving, and karma, or is it without cause? I replied to him: "Both of these views are merely worldly discourse."
He asked again: "Do all natures enter into their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common-characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)? I replied: "This too is worldly discourse (*lokavāda*), O Brahmin.
Even up to the mental stream’s false conceptualization of external objects—all these are worldly discourse. Furthermore, Mahāmati,"
At that time, the Lokāyatika Brahmin asked me again, "Is there anyone who is not a proponent of worldly discourse? I am the preeminent leader among all non-Buddhists;
I speak with various phrases, flavors, causes, conditions, and embellishments through parables. I replied to him, "Brahmin, there is.

There is one who does not belong to you, who has no [worldly] existence, who has no [worldly] purpose, who has no [worldly] doctrine, and who neither speaks nor fails to speak various [worldly things]."

Regarding the phrasing and meaning: it is not that it is not adorned with similes. The Brahmin asked, "What is it that is not worldly discourse (*lokāyata*), not a non-doctrine, and not a non-exposition?

I replied to him, "Brahmin, there is a discourse that is not worldly, which you followers of external paths cannot know, because of your false attachment to the unreal conceptualizations of external natures. That is to say, conceptualization is..."
Birth. One who fully realizes that existence and non-existence are the manifestations of one’s own mind does not give rise to false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Not receiving external objects, false conceptualization is forever stilled; this is called "non-worldly discourse. This is my teaching, not yours, O Brahmin.
To speak briefly of that consciousness: whether coming or going, dying or being born, pleasure or pain, sinking or seeing, contact or...

"Attachment to various characteristics—whether to characteristics of combination or continuity, or to attachment through craving or causal calculation—O Brahmin, such as these are your worldly doctrines;
they are not mine. Mahāmati, when the Brahmins of worldly doctrine ask me such questions, I answer them in this way.
They then remain silent and withdraw without further argument, reflecting upon their own positions."

He thought to himself: "The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has strayed outside of the common world; he teaches non-arising, signlessness, and causelessness, [claiming that] one awakens to the fact that the manifestation of signs is one's own deluded imagination, and thus deluded imagination does not arise."
The World-Honored One replied again, summarizing it within the two characters "worldly discourse" (*loka-vāda*). He then added further:

"Even until the consciousness slightly stirs and subtly engages with external objects, all of these constitute worldly discourse. This single phrase may be said to provide a thorough and comprehensive analysis.
When he says, "There is that which is not worldly discourse, yet it is not known by you," this also expresses the intent of being far removed from fear. As soon as—

It is said that it is neither non-action nor non-explanation; yet it is also not the case that various phrases and expressions are not spoken, nor that they are not adorned with analogies and illustrations.
This strips away what is grasped, yet does not depart from what is grasped. There is another universal path, namely: neither identical to nor separate from [the grasping];
it can only be realized through self-awakening. Failing to realize that external natures are unreal and that all things arise from falsehood, one then falls into delusion.
When thoughts arise, one perceives the existence or non-existence of all phenomena as entirely originating from one's own mind, rather than through external conditions;
thus, false conceptualization will forever cease. Furthermore, one should bring the ordinary lack of self-awareness found among followers of external paths to a state of self-awakening.

From beginning to end, one should maintain this mindfulness so that they remain free of wounds; do not cause them further injury. Moreover, regarding the deluded consciousness postulated by those external paths, one should ultimately instruct them [as follows].

He said: "Whether coming or going, whether dying or being born, whether pleasure or pain, whether drowning or seeing, whether touching or clinging—these various marks, whether as compounded continuities or as attachments to causes and conditions—all such things as these belong to your worldly treatises (*loka-vāda*).
Having utterly overturned them all and having completely destroyed them, only then do you withdraw."

He thought to himself: "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have strayed outside of the common consensus; they speak of non-arising, signlessness, and causelessness, claiming that what appears as a sign is merely one's own deluded conceptualization, and that when such conceptualization does not arise, [reality is realized]. Yet these outsiders describe this and, conversely, slander it, asking:
'Does the Tathāgata say that the fruit can be exhausted, or does he say it cannot be exhausted? If they consider it to be inexhaustible, then their words are certainly [contradictory]."
It appears as such, and one takes it to be the ultimate; yet this is merely the self-communication of the Tathāgata, which stops at this point.

As for what is called the supreme secret intent of the ancestors, how could it be fathomed by the mere words of a Brahmin treatise? △ Fourth, showing that worldly treatises embrace greed and do not embrace the True Dharma.

"Mahāmati, this is precisely what you asked me just now: 'For what reason do you say that those who cultivate and rely on various worldly treatises and modes of debate embrace desire but do not embrace the Dharma?
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, 'World-Honored One, what is the meaning of the phrases "embracing desire" and "embracing the Dharma"?
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! You are indeed able to act for the sake of the future."
“Sentient beings contemplate and inquire about the meaning of such phrases. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon them well;
I shall speak for your sake. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“That which is called ‘craving’ refers to grasping or rejecting, contact or tasting—being bound by attachment to external objects and falling into the views of the two extremes, thereby giving rise again to the aggregates of suffering. Birth...
Aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress—all such afflictions arise from craving.

This results from associating with worldly discourse and those who engage in worldly discourse; I and all the Buddhas call this "greed. This is what is called "embracing desire and not embracing the Dharma."
The dharma of craving consists solely of the two minds of grasping and rejecting; it encompasses the entire sphere of bodily sensations and exhausts that sphere of bodily sensations.

Whether it be the characteristics of present phenomena, or the mind’s empty conceptualization of all things—such as the illusory appearances of tortoise hair or rabbit horns—it is all contained therein.

Whether they be phenomena or principles, all are termed objective realms (*viṣaya*). Following after these objective realms, whether one grasps them or abandons them, one falls into the views of existence and non-existence.
This entire mass of suffering results from craving; craving is the cause, and birth-and-death is the fruit.

This worldly discourse (lokāyata) should not be approached or cultivated. △ Fifth, showing the reception of the True Dharma and distancing oneself from worldly discourse: "Mahāmati, what is the reception of the Dharma?
It means to skillfully awaken to and know the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind, and to perceive the selflessness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya) and..."

The Dharma is without the marks of self; false conceptualization does not arise. One skillfully knows the progressively higher stages (*uttarottara-bhūmi*), is detached from mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*), and receives the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) of the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Fully possessing and upholding the ten inexhaustible phrases (*daśākṣaya-pada*), one attains mastery over the non-arising of all phenomena.
This is called the Dharma; that is to say, it does not fall into any views, any fabrications, or any...
"Conceptual construction, all natures, and all two extremes—O Mahāmati, many foolish outsiders fall into these two extremes of either permanence or annihilation.
Those who are not wise, having accepted the doctrine of causelessness, give rise to the view of permanence when external causes are destroyed."

If causes and conditions were not of the nature of reality, one would give rise to the view of annihilationism. Mahāmati, because I do not perceive arising, abiding, or ceasing, I designate them as "dharmas.
Mahāmati, this is what is called desire and the dharma; you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should practice and study it.
The manifestation of one's own mind is devoid of self and other; whatever is perceived is entirely illusory.

To understand this deeply and with firm conviction, the two selves of person and phenomena will be instantly liberated. At all times and in all places, do not grasp at the existence of intrinsic nature;
when conceptualization completely dissolves, one illuminates the various stages (*bhūmi*) without relying on mental constructs, becoming inseparable from the wisdom of all Buddhas.
As for the distinction: one is able, by means of the ten inexhaustible phrases, to spontaneously increase in excellence with sovereign ease, without exerting effort.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that one does not fall into the false and deceptive nature-characteristics of existence and non-existence as held by various views: this is because non-Buddhists fall into these, giving rise to attachments to annihilationism and eternalism.
This is the specific distinction of the universal awakening of the self; it is profoundly penetrating and clearly manifest. Thus, he spoke with great reverence: "I..."

That which is not seen to arise, abide, or perish is called the Dharma. That which the Tathāgata manifests for people is the total embodiment of great function within the state of sudden self-extinction;

its purport is subtle. To accept the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*) is to point toward the causes of arising clung to by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), thereby giving rise to the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
To say there is no cause means that the cause is not a cause; this is what is meant by "causelessness."

Perceiving that the cause of birth has been exhausted, they further give rise to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Thus, both the theory of causality and the theory of no-cause ultimately result in nihilism.
VI. Summary Verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "All worldly treatises and those of the non-Buddhists..."
This is a false teaching. Those who hold that there is a creator and a created object have no school of their own;
I alone possess my own school. Free from creator and created, I teach it to my disciples. It is far removed from all worldly doctrines. The mind-only is invisible; one does not observe two minds.
Subject and object are without intrinsic nature. It is free from both extremes of annihilation and permanence, until the flow of the mind ceases. This is...
This is the worldly discourse (*lokavāda*). For one whose false imaginings (*vikalpa*) do not arise, such a person perceives their own mind: that which "comes" is called the arising of phenomena;
that which "goes" is the non-appearance of phenomena. Clearly knowing this coming and going, false imaginings no longer arise.
Whether permanence or impermanence, the created or the uncreated, this world or the other world—all these are encompassed by worldly discourse.

The first two verses mean that non-Buddhists have no school of their own; they are all driven by the grasping of subject and object, and thus wander in the flow of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
The Tathāgata’s own school differs from that of the non-Buddhists in that it also merely remains far removed from subject and object, with no further distinct tenet.
The third and fourth verses demonstrate that when one is far removed from subject and object, one is naturally silent.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "One does not engage in the perception of characteristics; that is to say, all things lack true reality, and one does not perceive them as true.
If one were to perceive them as true, such perception would be entirely non-true. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If one does not grasp at 'non-illusion,' then even non-illusion does not arise.
From where could illusory phenomena be established? This refers precisely to this inconceivable mind-measure (*citta-mātra*), which one knows and has confidence in for oneself.
One no longer gives rise to further observation. At once, all views—whether of existence or non-existence, the abandoned or the permanent—are entirely unattainable.
If one reaches this limit, the slightest involvement with subtle thought leads immediately to transmigration and turns back into worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*).
Therefore, it is said that "if deluded thoughts do not arise, this person sees their own mind. This may be called a most earnest admonition. [The latter two...]
Verse: Furthermore, it is shown to people that regarding all phenomena encountered in daily life, the characteristics of coming and going are transparently clear:
they come from nowhere and go nowhere; they are like clouds and lightning, like shadows and echoes. This is the realization of one’s own mental measure (*cittamātra*);
therein self and others are not separated, and the present and the past are viewed as equal. This is not like the "eternal" [entities] asserted by worldly theories.
Impermanence, the conditioned and the unconditioned, this world and the other world—these are various views and cognitions. (End of section.
The above two [sections] have demonstrated the meaning of the words and the function of consciousness and wisdom to clarify the utility of the universal penetration of the doctrine.
Third, demonstrating the liberation of the True Dharma, which far transcends the ignorant outsiders, divided into three parts. △ First, listing false conceptions and nirvana.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what is called 'nirvāṇa,' what dharma do you designate as nirvāṇa?
For various non-Buddhists each give rise to their own deluded conceptions. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall explain it for you. As for the nirvāṇa imagined by various non-Buddhists, it is not their delusion [that constitutes true nirvāṇa]."

[This is] the perception that accords with *nirvāṇa*. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Yes, we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “There are some non-Buddhists who [advocate for] the cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*);
who are free from desire regarding objective spheres; and who perceive the impermanence of phenomena, whereby the categories of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) do not arise.”
Not recollecting the objects of the past, future, or present, all aggregates of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) are exhausted—like the extinguishing of a lamp’s flame or the destruction of a seed.

When false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise, those who are thus disposed conceive of this as *nirvāṇa*. However, Mahāmati, it is not by the destruction of views that it is called *nirvāṇa*.
(The Wei translation states: "Mahāmati, when those non-Buddhists see such dharmas, they give rise to the thought of *nirvāṇa*; it is not [the result of] seeing...")
"Because it is extinguished, it is called nirvāṇa.
The preceding section clarified the inclusion of dharmas; this, however, distinguishes the correct fruit based on the correct cause. The initial passage states:
"Just as various non-Buddhists falsely imagine nirvāṇa," and further states: "It is not that false imagination conforms to nirvāṇa; rather, false imagination follows [it]."

[The categories of] "conformity" (anuloma) and "deviation" (viloma) are clearly distinguished. The various items listed below do not transcend delusive thought (*vikalpa*). Until the True Dharma emerges, [the mind] correctly clarifies what it means to "conform.

What is meant by "conforming"? It is conforming to one's own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This original intrinsic nature is pure, yet because it is obscured by adventitious defilements, it does not manifest.
If one awakens to the measure of one's own mind (*cittamātra*), the true Path of the Sages arises, and [defilements] are severed.
That which is manifested by the removal of hindrances is called *nirvāṇa*; that is to say, it is the designation of being free from hindrances in accordance with *tathatā*.

Regarding the "extinction of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), and the detachment from sense objects": this means that one observes these phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and bases as ultimately impermanent and does not crave sense objects.
Since one no longer craves sense objects, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) do not manifest before one.
Therefore, there is also no thought of the three periods of time—past, present, and future. This is like a lamp being extinguished or a seed being destroyed;

it serves as a metaphor for the cessation of the realm of sensation. This particular type of false discrimination involves only the destruction of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), rather than the destruction of views (*dṛṣṭi*). As for the destruction of views:

Contemplate the manifestation of one’s own mind and understand the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases. These are falsely manifested as objective realms due to delusion regarding one’s own mind;

fundamentally, they have neither arising nor cessation. When the views of arising and cessation are abandoned, false conceptualization ceases instantaneously, and this is the nirvana of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nirvāṇa*), rather than the nirvana resulting from the contemplation of the impermanence of phenomena or the mere cessation of perception and feeling through false calculation.
Mahāmati, some consider the transition from one direction to another to be liberation; the cessation of the perception of objective realms is like the subsiding of the wind.

Others consider the destruction of the vision of the perceiver and the perceived to be liberation. Still others, seeing the permanent and the impermanent, form the notion that this is liberation (the Tang translation says:
some say that not giving rise to the discrimination of views regarding permanence and impermanence is called attaining nirvāṇa). Or they see...

The perception of various marks is the cause that brings about the arising of suffering. Having reflected upon this, one fails to correctly realize that [the world] is merely the manifestation of one's own mind;
thus, fearing marks, one perceives the markless and develops a deep attachment to it, conceiving it to be nirvana.

"From direction to direction. The ancient commentary cites a treatise which states: "The second type of non-Buddhist proponent asserts that direction exists primordially. From direction, the world and human beings arise;

humans are born within heaven and earth, and through successive cycles of dissolution and disappearance, they return to direction. This [direction] is declared to be eternal and to serve as the cause for *nirvāṇa*.
However, the Vaiśeṣika masters establish six categories (*padārtha*) as the causes of arising; among these, within the category of substance (*dravya*), [direction is included].
There are nine factors: earth, water, fire, wind, space, time, direction, self, and mind.

The masters of the *Vaiśeṣika* treatise maintain that Mahābrahmā, time, direction, the primal limit (*ādi*), nature (*svabhāva*), space, and the self—these seven factors—are eternal and capable of producing all phenomena.

These three types of explanations regarding direction are all devoid of intrinsic essence or characteristics; they falsely speculate that the various phenomena appearing before them have no source from which they arise.
Regarding the cause of birth: it arises from the void, just as the primordial limit of natural space is given various names, yet all lack substantial reality.
Furthermore, the commentary states that "fang" (方) signifies "kind" (類). From one kind to another, there is no change in essential nature;

as the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says, "knowing humans give birth to humans, and awakening birds give birth to birds. Even throughout eighty thousand kalpas, there is no alteration or shift; they follow their own kind.

The "Ultimate Category" does not lose its original nature; this, moreover, is the doctrine of the Naturalists (Svabhāvavādins). Of these four, the first three arise from spatial directions and return to those directions upon cessation.
The latter one, however, has no loss of its original nature and is sovereign in all places; based on this, they falsely calculate it to be eternal.
They hope for the extinction of all objective realms and conceptualizations, like the sudden stilling of the wind, and reckon this to be Nirvana.
"Seeing the destruction of the perceiver and the perceived" means not seeing the perceiving mind and the perceived object;
this is called "seeing their destruction. "Seeing the permanent and the impermanent" means not giving rise to views of permanence or impermanence.

According to these two types, they seem close to the [teachings on] "separating from the grasper and the grasped" and "distantly severing the two views of permanence and annihilation"; yet, they do not arise through discursive cognition (*buddhi*).

Knowing that what appears is but the manifestation of one's own mind, one falsely suppresses it and falls entirely into the duality of subject and object. To perceive the cessation of perceptions is merely termed "delusive thought" (*vikalpa*).
Seeing various signs brings about the causes of suffering and gives rise to a mind of fear; yet, one must see into signlessness (*animitta*).

This class of followers of the Two Vehicles contemplates impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, and forms the notion of a non-self. They adhere to a partial *tathatā* (suchness) and delight in empty stillness.

Because they do not skillfully awaken to the fact that all things are merely the manifestations of their own minds, they fail to understand that all natures and characteristics are transformations of internal consciousness and lack any real substance.
Consequently, they falsely give rise to fear, abandoning one thing and grasping at another; thus, they do not transcend deluded conceptualization.
Some perceive that the internal and external dharmas possess their own and common characteristics, and that their nature remains unimpaired throughout the past, future, and present;
they conceive of this as nirvana. Others claim that the self, persons, sentient beings, and life-span, as well as all dharmas, undergo destruction; they conceive of this as nirvana.
Or, because their wisdom has been scorched by the evil of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), they perceive primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa).

They hold that these two are distinct, and that what is produced by the person is called primordial nature, similar to the analogy of primordial darkness. They conceive of the transformation of the guṇas as the agent, and imagine this to be nirvāṇa.
Or they claim it is the exhaustion of merit and demerit; or the exhaustion of all afflictions (kleśa); or they claim it is wisdom. Or...
They perceive Īśvara as the true creator of saṃsāra (the Chinese translation says: "or they conceive that Īśvara is the real creator"), and they form the notion that he is nirvāṇa.

To perceive that all internal and external phenomena possess an indestructible nature is to identify the "self" within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which is termed "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
This is like the aforementioned perception of a permanent body; it is the calculation of permanence.
