To claim that the self, persons, sentient beings, and life-span—all phenomena—are destroyed is to say that the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) perish and vanish like empty space; this constitutes the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Intrinsic nature refers to the primordial darkness...

The "Truth" (satya) and the "Person" (puruṣa) are the same as the "Self" (ātman). Because the person emerges from primordial nature (prakṛti), it is said to be comparable to the "dark beginning" (tamas).
"Guṇa" is translated as "reliance" (āśraya); this means that the Self relies upon the dark beginning to undergo transformation and arise.

This "reliance" is the agent who conceives the notion of nirvāṇa—namely, relying on non-existence to produce existence, and existence returning to non-existence. This is likewise the same as the view of annihilationism (ucchedadṛṣṭi). Merit is not...
The exhaustion of merit means that there is neither sin nor merit; all things are unimpeded, and there is no cause and effect.
Some say it is the exhaustion of all afflictions (*kleśa*); some say it is wisdom (*prajñā*). They regard afflictions and wisdom as two distinct entities.
Others say that one exhausts the afflictions by relying upon wisdom; still others say that afflictions are exhausted spontaneously, not through being severed by wisdom. All [of these views]...
This is not a correct reason. Some perceive Īśvara as being none other than Mahābrahmā;
the teachers of the Lokāyata school reckon that Mahābrahmā is able to create the birth and death of sentient beings, and thus they take this capacity for creation to be eternal.
Some claim that birth and death arise through a continuous succession of mutual production, and that there is no other cause for them.
Such a view is an attachment to causality, yet those fools are unable to perceive this. Because they do not know it, they conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa*.
Or there are non-Buddhists who say they have attained the path of True Reality and conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa*. Or they see the union of merit and that which arises from merit. (Wei Translation)
They say: "There is the agent and the acted-upon, which are in mutual conjunction—neither identical nor different, neither both nor neither. They conceive of this as *nirvāṇa*.

Or, they see the nature arising from itself (the Tang translation says: "or they calculate that all things arise from spontaneity"), such as the variegated patterns of a peacock's plumage, various miscellaneous jewels, sharp thorns, and so forth; having seen these, they conceive of them as *nirvāṇa*.

They arise in succession from one another: the father gives birth to the son, and the son gives birth to the grandson; thus life continues in an uninterrupted stream. There is no other cause for this:
they do not realize that the flow of craving becomes the seed and the formation of conceptualization becomes the womb.

Grasping at ignorance, delusion, and karma constitutes the root of birth and death, from which there is no liberation. Because they do not understand this, they remain settled in birth and death while imagining it to be nirvana, just as is the case now.
In the world, fathers and sons, grandfathers and grandsons, succeed one another in birth and death; this is mistakenly taken to be the natural order (*dharmatā*).

The "Ultimate Truth" (*tattva*) is the "Dark Ultimate" (*tattva-avidyā*); this is the grasping of the Dark Ultimate as the Way. "Merit" and that which arises from merit are the agent and the object of action.
Doubting the union of agent and object gives rise to views of identity, difference, both, or neither; none of these transcend the four alternatives.
This is a [false] proposition. That which arises from its own nature is said to be produced spontaneously; it is likewise equivalent to being without cause. For example:
"Crows have always been black, and cranes have always been white. Humans and devas are originally upright, while animals are originally horizontal. Pines are straight and thorns are crooked;
the plumage of birds and beasts, and all various precious gems, are all produced spontaneously, without cause or effect."
Mahāmati, some perceive twenty-five truths and, being kings who protect their nations, receive the *Ṣaḍdharmapravibhāga-śāstra* (Treatise on the Six Virtues), conceiving it to be *nirvāṇa*.
(The Tang translation says: "Some claim that by understanding the twenty-five principles, one immediately attains *nirvāṇa*;
others say that by receiving the six divisions [of the teachings] and protecting sentient beings, one attains *nirvāṇa*"). Or they see time as the creator, [claiming] "Time..."

Restraining the world, those who perceive it in this way conceive of nirvana; some call it existence, some call it non-existence, and some claim to know both existence and non-existence (the Tang translation says:

some grasp at the existence of things as nirvana, some reckon the non-existence of things as nirvana, and some reckon the attachment to both existence and non-existence as nirvana); or they see there is awakening and...

The differentiation of nirvāṇa; conceiving the notion that it is nirvāṇa (the Tang translation says: or reckoning that all things are no different from nirvāṇa, thereby conceiving the notion that they are nirvāṇa).
The twenty-five realities refer to the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) of the Sāṃkhya school. The six virtues refer to the six categories (*padārtha*) of the Vaiśeṣika school.
Their previous reckoning held that the twenty-five primordial principles (*prakṛti-tattva*) and the six categories constitute *nirvāṇa*;

however, this [system] holds that it is through the capacity for awakening and the capacity for experiencing that one attains *nirvāṇa*. As for the King protecting the state, it means receiving a sixth portion [of the harvest] to protect all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are those who immediately disperse the heterodox attachments that hold all phenomena arise from time (*kāla*).

They observe the flourishing and withering, the blooming and falling of grasses and trees, and reckon time to be eternal, unitary, and the cause of the myriad things, as well as the cause of *nirvāṇa*.
Nature is a thing. Whether there is a thing or no thing, whether it is neither existent nor non-existent, these are all subsumed under the categories of "causation" and "uncaused.

Awakening, the conceptualization of awakening, and the fluctuation of conceptualization—these are contrasted with the stillness of nirvana. To claim they are distinct, or to calculate that they are not distinct, is merely a single instance of false conceptualization.
There are various such delusions of this kind, as taught by the non-Buddhists; they fail to establish what is to be established and are rejected by the wise.
Mahāmati, all such things fall into the two extremes and are conceived as *nirvāṇa*.
Among these various non-Buddhist delusions regarding *nirvāṇa*, there is absolutely no arising or ceasing (the Tang translation says: "in this, there is no abiding").
Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding each of those various non-Buddhist nirvāṇas, when examined through the wisdom of their own treatises, nothing at all is established.
Like those false imaginings, their minds come and go, drifting, racing, and flowing; thus, among them, there is not a single one who attains nirvāṇa.
To conclude: the various notions of nirvāṇa conceived by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are all merely views born of false imagination; they do not constitute true nirvāṇa.
This is because they do not transcend the two extremes of existence and non-existence—whether they involve remaining within or emerging from them—they entirely lack any real meaning.

They are all merely the drifting and fluctuating movements of the mind and its mental factors. Even if these were ultimately extinguished, there would still be no one who truly attains nirvāṇa. All of these...

Because one perceives that all things are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, and because one follows these mental manifestations with false discrimination lacking the wisdom of reality as it is, all actions whatsoever fail to be established. △ Second, showing how the Tathāgata accords with nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati, as for what I have called "nirvāṇa," it means: to be well-awakened to the manifestation of one's own mind;

to be unattached to external natures; to be free from the four extremes (catuṣkoṭi); to see the state of reality as it is; not to fall into the two extremes of false conceptualization regarding the manifestations of one's own mind;

to find that neither the grasping subject nor the grasped object can be apprehended; and to see that all forms of measurement fail to establish anything real. Since the foolish are ignorant of the truth, they should not cling to such views.

Having abandoned those, one attains the noble Dharma of self-awakening, realizes the two kinds of non-self, becomes free from the two kinds of afflictions, purifies the two hindrances, and is forever liberated from the two kinds of death.
This refers to the progressively higher stages, the stage of the Tathāgata, and various profound samādhis such as those like shadows and illusions.
Being free from mind, thought, and consciousness, this is designated as nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, you and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should...
You should practice this. You should swiftly distance yourselves from all views of nirvana held by non-Buddhists.
That which is the manifestation of one's own mind is itself primordially pure nirvana. This nirvana is [the nature] of all sentient beings.
It is equally shared by all; its nature is fundamentally quiescent. It is realized within oneself only by true sages, and is therefore called "awakened knowledge.
Having awakened to this, one sees that the fundamentally quiescent nature and all phenomena are neither identical nor different.
This means not clinging to external natures, being free from the four extremes, and seeing the state of reality as it is. Seeing the state of reality as it is is the principle of *tathatā*.

It is revealed as being free from all marks and all conceptualization; that is to say, it does not fall into the two extremes of the false imaginings of what is manifested by one's own mind, for neither the grasper nor the grasped can be found. When the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is revealed, both thought and its marks are stilled;

thus, the path of discursive inquiry is cut off and the way of names and words is severed. This means that among all measures of cognition, nothing established is perceived, for the ignorant are deluded regarding the truth.

Indeed, one should not grasp at them. For in the state of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*), there is no convergence of speech or thought; to do so would merely lead to delusion, and therefore one should not grasp at them.
The two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*) refer to the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). The two kinds of afflictions (*kleśa*)...

This refers to the primary and secondary [afflictions], the two obstacles—namely, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—and the two types of death—namely, death by segmentation (*pariccheda-maraṇa*) and death by transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*).
These four pairs are perceived all at once from the realization that they are merely the manifestations of one's own mind.
Only upon attaining the non-abiding nirvāṇa do they become fully perfected. This nirvāṇa is precisely the principle of *tathatā* (suchness), which transcends the knowable.
Obstructed by these, Great Compassion and Prajñā-pāramitā constantly provide support and protection.

Consequently, one does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, but brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future, acting while remaining eternally quiescent. This is what is called the profound samādhi, which is free from mind, thought, and consciousness.
These two types of nirvāṇa—both in the causal stage and upon the attainment of the fruit—are equally present; they exist only in the Tathāgata.

Together with the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder) and the *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder), there are four types [of truths], all of which the Tathāgata fully possesses.
Although the Tathāgata has no actual basis of dependence, he manifests as if there were; therefore, it can be said that the Tathāgata possesses all four.

While the ultimate truth revealed by the two vehicles through the severance of the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) still possesses a subtle basis for suffering, because those two delusions are eternally extinguished, it is likewise [considered nirvana].
They attain *nirvāṇa with remainder*. As for *nirvāṇa without remainder*, it both exists and does not exist for those of the two vehicles.
Based on their failure to perceive the intrinsically pure nature of the fundamental source (*prakṛti-viśuddha-svabhāva*) and their lack of a non-abiding state, it is said that they do not possess it.

However, based on the truth revealed by the exhaustion of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which is free from characteristics, profound, quiescent, and blissful, and is no different from that of a Buddha, it is said that they do indeed possess it.
There is. △ Third, the general verse summary.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The views of nirvana held by the non-Buddhists are each but the arising of deluded thoughts.
These arise from the workings of the mind; they lack the skillful means for liberation. They are ignorant regarding both the bonds and those who are bound. [They] remain far removed...

Skillful means and the notion of liberation held by non-Buddhists never give rise to actual liberation. Though their various wisdoms lead to different destinations, what the non-Buddhists perceive is merely a commonality;
they possess no liberation at all, because of their foolishness and deluded conceptualization.
These various notions of nirvāṇa conceived by the non-Buddhists all arise from false imagination; they possess no skillful means for liberation.
To lack the skillful means for liberation means to fail to realize that which is the manifestation of one's own mind.
Failing to realize that it is the manifestation of one's own mind, one perceives both the binder and the bound. Seeing a binder, one then conceives of a mind that can be emptied.
If there were wisdom that could be extinguished, or if one saw something by which one was bound, then there would be dharmas to be severed and objects to be abandoned;
this is what is called "ignorance. Various people grasp at things and each calls themselves wise, yet in reality they possess no wisdom and lack the principle of liberation.
All deluded non-Buddhists falsely perceive the agent and the acted-upon; they hold arguments concerning existence and non-existence, yet none among them possess liberation.
The foolish delight in false imaginings and do not hear the wisdom of reality. Language is the root of the three sufferings; reality is the cause for extinguishing suffering.
Just as an image in a mirror appears yet does not exist, so too within the mirror of the deluded mind, the ignorant perceive duality.
Failing to recognize the mind and its objects, they give rise to dualistic conceptualization; when they thoroughly understand the mind and its spheres, such conceptualization no longer arises.
The mind is itself manifold. It is far removed from both the characteristic and the characterized. Though phenomena appear, they do not truly appear;

yet, like the false imaginings of the ignorant, there is the act and the actor, which are precisely the causal characteristics that are conceptualized. The "acted upon" refers to the dharmas produced by causes;

these all fall into the two categories of existence and non-existence, and thus lack the factors conducive to liberation. This is because the nature and desire of consciousness seek to perceive the marks of form; therefore, everything exists [in this conventional sense].
There are no objective realms; they are all merely what is delighted in by conceptualization. To delight in conceptualization is necessarily to be deluded regarding reality.
This means that where there are afflictions, there is no wisdom; where there is wisdom, there are no afflictions.

All such reckonings of existence and non-existence merely invite karmic causes and effects; they are entirely devoid of substantial reality and consist only of words. Therefore, it is said: "Words are the threefold suffering."
Fundamentally, if one perceives reality, all delusions will suddenly cease, thereby extinguishing the cause of suffering. The mirror is a metaphor for one's own mind;
the images are metaphors for all objective realms of form and mind manifested by that very mind. Mind and its objects are non-dual in their essential nature.
The nature of non-duality is precisely the measure of mind (*cittamātra*). When this is realized, all manifold phenomena are seen as mind; both subject and object are forgotten.
They manifest yet are without manifestation, like illusions or lightning—neither existent nor nonexistent.

The three realms of existence are merely conceptual construction; external objects do not exist at all. Conceptual construction manifests in various ways, yet the ignorant and foolish cannot comprehend this.
Sūtra after sūtra speaks of conceptual construction, for it never transcends names. If one were to depart from verbal expression, there would likewise be nothing to be expressed.

The three realms of existence are merely conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). This means that all phenomena within the three realms arise through the internal consciousness manifesting as if there were external objects;
in reality, there is no separate referent. Fools fail to understand this and falsely perceive various things.

The conceptual constructions described in all the *sūtras* are said to be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and to exist only as names. If one is separated from these names, there is no conceptual construction at all.

It can be attained. Since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is already empty, its verbal expression is likewise non-existent. Furthermore, one must not rely on the sacred teachings in a manner that turns them into a source of attachment—this is what is meant by "taking the medicine and contracting the illness.
The Tathāgata’s instruction to people contains no meaning beyond the truth itself. The preceding five sections demonstrate the dual penetration of the doctrine and its exposition;

through the function of skillful speech, meaning, consciousness, and wisdom, they distinguish the ignorant from outsiders and support the progress of both self and others within the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
The Liberation is concluded.
Phonetic Glossary for Volume Six of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-hṛdaya-mudrā*.
Chǎng (cut by Chāngliǎng: the appearance of being bewildered and losing one's composure). Diào (cut by Túliǎo: to move and shake). Chù (cut by Qīlù: to watch and spy).
The Heart Seal of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Volume Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master and Śramaṇa Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
Recorded by the thirty-fourth generation descendant of Cao Dong, Shibo, the third generation descendant of Shishen, and Leifeng Sha.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Heart of All Buddha-Speech by the Monk Śramaṇa Śī (now Jìnmù Jìnmèi),
Disciple in the Lineage of the Dharma of Master Shì Hánshì; Part Four.

○ Six: Showing that Perfect Enlightenment is neither cause nor effect; it is taught as being free from arising and ceasing, manifesting true permanence and stainlessness, and transcending all stages instantaneously.
This is divided into seven parts. First, showing that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is neither cause nor effect. This is further divided into seven. △ First:
Questioning whether the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is a cause or a phenomenon.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain the *Samyaksaṃbuddha* for me and for the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, so that we may become skilled in the self-nature of the Tathāgata, awakening ourselves and awakening others.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Ask whatever you desire; I shall explain it to you according to your questions. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
"Venerable One, regarding the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: is he the agent or the non-agent?
Is he the object or the cause (the Chinese translation says: is he the fruit or the cause)? Is he the characteristic or the characterized?
Is he the speaker or the spoken? Is he the awakening or the awakened? Regarding such terms as these, are they different or not different?"
This is intended to reveal that the Tathāgata’s awakened nature is neither cause nor fruit, but is ultimately pure white, singular, and without fault.
*Samyaksaṃbuddha* is translated as "Equal and Perfectly Awakened One" (*Dengzhengjue*) and is also called "Right Universal Knowledge.
It is the third of the ten titles: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. This question concerns the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body; by citing these three, all the other titles are encompassed.

"Action" (*kṛti*) has the sense of arising through performance; it takes that which is the basis for arising as its cause (*hetu*), and that which is accomplished through performance as its objective (*vastu*).

This objective is the fruit (*phala*). The characteristic of the cause is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of the fruit is the characterized (*lakṣya*). "Exposition" (*ākhyāna*) refers to the expositor, the exposition itself, and the principle being expounded.
"Awakening" (*bodha*) refers to the person who knows and the object known. Such are the terms and phrases.
"Are they different or not different?"—referring to such propositions as "this action" versus "non-action," and so forth—all such formulations result in four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).

This is intended to reveal that the Dharmakāya transcends the four alternatives and is ultimately pure and white. △ Second, showing that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is neither cause nor effect, and is far removed from the four alternatives.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding such terms as these, is neither an effect nor a cause.
Why is this? Because both [positions] entail faults. Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were an effect, he would either be something produced or impermanent;
because he would be impermanent, all effects would then be the Tathāgata. (The Tang translation says: "If the Tathāgata were something produced...")
If it were thus impermanent, then all conditioned phenomena would be the Tathāgata; this is something neither I nor the Buddhas desire.
If it were not a product of conditioning, then because nothing could be attained, skillful means would be empty. (The Tang translation says:)

If it were not produced through conditions, it would have no essential nature; the skillful means one cultivates would all be empty and useless, like the horns of a rabbit or the son of a barren woman, because they do not exist.
Mahāmati, if there is neither object nor cause, then it is neither existent nor non-existent.
That which is neither existent nor non-existent transcends the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). These four propositions are merely worldly discourse.
If one emerges from the four propositions, one does not fall into the four propositions. Because one does not fall into the four propositions, it is that which is taken up by the wise.
The meaning of the phrases of all Tathāgatas is also like this; the wise should know this.

In sum, all the aforementioned questions do not transcend the two meanings of cause and effect; therefore, only the causal basis of phenomena is cited to clarify that the Tathāgata’s self-nature *dharmakāya* is neither cause nor effect.

If it were a produced phenomenon, it would be something created and thus not the Unsurpassed True Reality (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), unlike the impermanent practices of the mundane world. If it were not a produced phenomenon, it would obstruct the realization of non-attainment.
Furthermore, the adornment of its own nature—the immeasurable and subtle merits manifested through the removal of obscurations—is not empty or meaningless.
Therefore, one should know that what is not produced is "without activity" (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Yet, it is also not the case that it is not produced;

rather, it is obtained through skillful means and arises from causes. It is the primordially existing essence of awakening (*bodhi-tattva*), which is attained through realization, not through birth. This is...
It is without cause; being without an object and without a cause, it does not involve existence or non-existence. It is suddenly free from the four propositions.
Since it is free from the four propositions, it is beyond the reach of all verbal expression whatsoever; it is a pure state of meaning realized by the wise.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "Although the Buddha-nature exists, it is not like empty space. Why?
Because although the worldly void cannot be seen despite immeasurable skillful means, the Buddha-nature can be seen; therefore, although it exists, it is not like empty space.
Although the Buddha-nature is non-existent [in certain senses], it is not like a rabbit's horn. Why? Because [unlike a rabbit's horn,] tortoise hair..."
Although the horns of a rabbit cannot be produced even through immeasurable skillful means, the Buddha-nature can be produced;

therefore, although it does not exist [in a conventional sense], it is not the same as the horns of a rabbit. This subtle and esoteric principle of the Buddha-nature is realized only within by true sages.
Such a nature is neither existent nor non-existent, neither cause nor effect, and transcends all measurement and calculation.
It should be understood in this way. *Bandha* translates as "stone-woman" (*vandhyā*); a "son of Bandha" refers to the son of a stone-woman.
△ Third, demonstrating that the Dharmakāya is the true self, eternally quiescent.
As I have taught that all dharmas are without self, you should understand this meaning: the nature of being without self is itself non-self.

All dharmas possess their own-nature (svabhāva) and lack other-nature (parabhāva). (The Wei translation states: "Now, as for 'non-self,' it is because there is no self within the internal body; therefore, it is non-self.
Mahāmati, all dharmas exist as their own bodies, while other bodies are non-existent. It is like [the case of] an ox or a horse. Mahāmati...

Wisdom. For example, the nature of a horse is not that of a cow, and the nature of a cow is not that of a horse; in reality, they are neither existent nor non-existent, yet it is not that they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In this same way, Mahāmati, all phenomena do not lack their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);

they possess their own characteristics, but these are not something that can be known by foolish people who are deluded regarding the self, because of their false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Thus, all phenomena are empty, unarisen, and unceasing.
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should be understood in this way:
the Tathāgata has taught that the *dharmakāya* as intrinsic nature is neither cause nor fruit, yet it is not annihilated.

Therefore, he further cites the phrase "the selflessness of phenomena" (*dharmanairātmya*) to reveal the true self (*ātman*) of the Tathāgata. For the true self of the Tathāgata’s intrinsic nature is... [ever-present].

Because they are shrouded by the self of phenomena (*dharmātman*), it is said that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*). This is for the purpose of revealing the true characteristic of the *tathatā* of the intrinsic nature *dharmakāya*.
If one perceives the true characteristic of the *tathatā* of the intrinsic nature *dharmakāya*, one will further know the true characteristic of the *tathatā* of all phenomena;
internally and externally there will be no obstructions, and all will be profoundly and eternally quiescent. All phenomena, by their own...
What appears is manifested by the mind; because all phenomena arise from the manifestation of one's own mind, they are all devoid of self-nature, and thus are called "selfless" (*anātman*).

What is manifested is merely mind; that is, all phenomena possess their own nature (*svabhāva*) and lack the nature of another. However, this absence of the nature of another is precisely the state of being selfless.
Thus, one speaks of the selflessness of all phenomena, and with respect to all phenomena as the manifestation of one's own mind, one speaks of their selflessness.
It is also thus. Therefore, all teachings that state that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty, unarisen, and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) do not differ in their ultimate intent.

What is meant is that there is only true consciousness (*vijñāna*), and no other consciousness exists. This is the ultimate realization reached by those who have awakened to the fact that [all things] are merely the manifestation of one's own mind.
Just as the nature of a horse is not that of an ox, and the nature of an ox is not that of a horse, this illustrates the absence of "other-nature" (*parabhāva*), not the absence of "self-nature."
If there were no other, it would not be existent; if existence were intrinsic, it would not be non-existent. Being neither existent nor non-existent is the self-characteristic of *tathatā*.
It is realized only within the inner realization of true sages; it is simply not the domain of the conceptualizations of fools.
△ Fourth, showing that the manifestation of the *dharmakāya* is neither identical nor different.
In this way, the Tathāgata and the aggregates (skandhas) are neither different nor not different. If he were not different from the aggregates, he would be impermanent.
If he were different, skillful means would be empty. If there were these two [possibilities], there would have to be a difference, as in the case of the horns of an ox.
Because they are similar, they are not different; because they differ in length, they are different. All phenomena are likewise, Mahāmati. It is like the right horn of an ox.
The left horn is different from [the right]; the left horn is different from the right horn. In this way, length, shortness, and various colors are each distinct. (The Tang translation says:
"Just as a cow's right horn is different from the left, and the left horn is different from the right; their lengths differ and their color-appearances are each distinct, yet they are not different.
Mahāmati, regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, the Tathāgata is neither different nor non-different [from them].
This reveals that the *dharmakāya* manifests as neither one nor different; it is not something known by ordinary or ignorant beings.

From this point onward, [the text] generally explains that seeing the true self (*ātman*) which is the very nature of the Tathāgata—namely, the single [reality of] the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*, transcending bondage and liberation, equalizing the cognitive obstructions, being *prakṛti-nirvāṇa*, and surpassing all numerical categories—is precisely what is meant by the "aggregates" (*skandha*). That is to say, the *dharmakāya* and [the form bodies].
The form-body (rūpakāya) and the dharma-body (dharmakāya) are neither identical nor different. If they were identical, then when the form-body perishes, the dharma-body would also perish;

if it perished, it would be impermanent. If they were two distinct things, then the dharma-body would be something obtained through expedient means (upāya), and thus entirely empty and devoid of meaning.
Yet, the thousand-fathom Vairocana, as well as all infinite responsive and transformational bodies, manifest with truly existent wondrous marks and secondary characteristics. That is to say:
By extinguishing impermanent form, one attains the eternally abiding true form. The similarity of the horns of an ox illustrates the first [point];
the distinction between their length illustrates the second. Yet, they are collectively called "ox horns," being neither identical nor different.

Thus, it is said that the Tathāgata, in relation to the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas), is likewise neither identical nor different. △ Fifth, showing that the Dharmakāya and liberation are neither identical nor different.
In this way, the Tathāgata’s liberation is neither different nor not different. Thus, the Tathāgata is designated by the name "liberation. (The Wei translation states:
"Thus, because he relies upon liberation, he is called the mark of the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.

If the Tathāgata were different from liberation, he would be constituted by material form (*rūpa*); being constituted by material form, he would be impermanent. If he were not different [from liberation], then cultivation...

The practitioner attains the sign (nimitta) and should be free from conceptual differentiation (avikalpa); yet the practitioner perceives it as differentiated. Therefore, it is neither different nor not different.
The three virtues of nirvāṇa—dharmakāya, vimukti, and prajñā—are like the three dots of the syllable *I*: they are neither vertical nor horizontal, yet [they exist].
This statement means that the *dharmakāya* and liberation are neither identical nor different. It is by virtue of liberation that the Tathāgata is so named.
If they were different, then the liberation realized by the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya* would be like material form (*rūpa*) and would consequently be impermanent.
[The ignorant] do not realize that the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya* is itself liberation, and that liberation is itself the *dharmakāya*. Pure...
Purity is stainless; its essence is non-dual. If they were not distinct, then for a practitioner, there would be no difference between the subject that realizes and the object realized.

Yet, a difference is observed, as in the case of the ten true suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*). Although these are attained from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) onward, the realization and practice remain incomplete.
To bring them to perfection, they are established in successive stages, each with its own depth and degree of distinction.
They are seen as distinct; therefore, they are neither one nor different. △ Sixth, showing that the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is neither one nor different:
"In this way, wisdom (*jñāna*) and its objective field (*jñeya*) are neither different nor not different.

Mahāmati, that wisdom and its objective field are neither different nor not different means they are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither an agent nor an object of action, neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."

Awakening is not that which is awakened to; it is not a characteristic, nor is it that which is characterized; it is not the aggregates, nor is it distinct from the aggregates; it is not speech, nor is it that which is spoken;
it is not identical, nor is it different, nor is it both, nor is it neither. Because it is not identical, not different, not both, and not neither, it is entirely free from all measures of cognition.

It was stated above that the *dharmakāya* and liberation are neither identical nor different. Here, it should likewise be stated that the *dharmakāya* and *prajñā* are neither identical nor different.

As for the statement that *prajñā* and the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are neither identical nor different, this refers to the *ādikṣaṇika-bodhi* (initial awakening) of *prajñā*, which arises from the *mūla-bodhi* (original awakening) of the *dharmakāya*. To speak of "initial" implies it is no different from the "original. If [it were] the objects of knowledge...
Regarding the hindrances: up to the eleventh stage (*bhūmi*), there still remain two types of extremely subtle ignorance;

it is only upon reaching the stage of the Buddha’s wondrous enlightenment that these are suddenly and completely exhausted. This wisdom and these hindrances are clearly distinct as two, yet they are said to be neither identical nor different.

This is because there are no hindrances apart from wisdom, and no wisdom apart from hindrances. Thus, the nature of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is further revealed herein, and the Tathāgata himself...
The true nature of the self (*ātman*) transcends the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) and exceeds all measure and number; it is not something known through discursive thought.

The mention of "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*), "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), and so forth, serves as a general summary of the preceding questions, as these categories are fully subsumed within the transcendence of the four propositions. △ Seven:
Summary Conclusion that the Dharmakāya Transcends All Faculties and Measures, along with a Verse.
Being free from all means of valid cognition, there is no verbal expression. Being without verbal expression, there is no arising.

Being without arising, there is no cessation. Being without cessation, there is quiescence. Being quiescent, there is nirvāṇa by its very nature. Being nirvāṇa by its very nature, there is neither object nor cause.
Without phenomena and without causes, there is no object of clinging. Without an object of clinging, one transcends all falsity.
To transcend all falsity is to be the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Mahāmati, this is called the Samyaksaṃbuddha Buddha. Mahāmati, as for the Samyaksaṃbuddha Buddha, he is free from [the notion of] oneness.
The measure of severing the root:
this fruition, the Tathāgata’s own-nature *dharmakāya*, transcends all calculation and measurement. It is realized within oneself;
it is not the essence of any conventional designation whatsoever. One who realizes this essence finally knows that both arising and ceasing are non-existent, and that there is only...
Quiescence is what is called intrinsic nirvāṇa. Intrinsic nirvāṇa is neither cause nor effect. All stirring thoughts have ceased; the mind of ideation has stilled.
At the primordial limit of ignorance, there is ultimate liberation. It is devoid of falsehood;
it is the true Dharmakāya, the Body of Equality, forever transcending the spheres of all the sense faculties. Thus, the Tathāgata, regarding...

Entering parinirvāṇa, he addressed Mahāmati universally, saying: "With my profound prajñā, I have observed all the mountains, great oceans, the earth, and sentient beings within the three realms and the six destinies. Thus, these three realms are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature."
Ultimately quiescent, it is identical to the mark of emptiness. It is without name and without consciousness; it has forever severed all modes of existence (*bhava*).
It is primordially equal, free from notions of high or low. It is without seeing or hearing, without perception or cognition.
It cannot be bound and cannot be liberated. There is no sentient being and no life-span. It is neither born nor arisen, neither exhausted nor extinguished; it is not of the world.
It is not that it is not the mundane; for both nirvana and saṃsāra are unattainable. These two limits are equal, because they are equal to all dharmas.
Dwelling in seclusion and tranquility, there is nothing to be performed. Ultimate establishment is absolutely unattainable.
From the dharma of non-abiding, the activity of the dharma-nature cuts off all marks; there is nothing at all. Such is the characteristic of dharmas. Its...
One who knows this is called a world-transcender; one who does not know this matter is said to be at the root of birth and death.

This is precisely the Tathāgata’s self-nature liberation, which dwells together with all phenomena at the fundamental limit of True Suchness (*tathatā*). It is eternally free from all faults, both internal and external.
All sentient beings likewise possess this, yet they are merely obscured by adventitious defilements for a single thought-moment.
To be aware of this is identical to attaining the original state.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Completely free from the measures of the sense faculties, there is neither object nor cause.

Having already transcended the awareness and that which is known, one also transcends the characteristic and that which is characterized. Regarding the aggregates, conditions, and so forth, the Perfectly Enlightened One [is beyond] oneness or difference."
None can see it. If there is no seer, how can one make distinctions? It is neither created nor uncreated; it is neither an effect nor a cause.
It is not the aggregates (*skandha*), nor does it reside within the aggregates, nor is it something else distinct from them, nor does it possess various intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
Just as it is seen through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one should know that it is likewise not non-existent. This Dharma and its phenomena are also thus.
This general verse concerns the Dharmakāya’s transcendence of the four tetralemmas regarding cause and effect, subject and object, the vessel and its contents, and identity and difference.

There is no one who perceives it as being separate, nor does it possess a self-nature of dharmas, yet it is also not the case that there are no dharmas. This may be called truly attaining the essence of the Dharma;
upon awakening to this, it should naturally subside into extinction.
Because of existence there is non-existence; because of non-existence there is existence. If it were non-existent, one should not grasp it; if it were existent, one should not conceptualize it.
Whether regarding self or non-self, one remains entangled in mere verbal conventions, sinking into the two extremes; thus destroying oneself and destroying the world.
Liberated from all faults, one correctly observes the penetration of the self; this is called right contemplation. One does not disparage the Great Teacher.

If it were non-existent, it should not be accepted; if it were existent, it should not be conceptualized. This means that if it were non-existent, it would be ultimately non-existent and could not become existent;

if it were existent, it would have been existent from the beginning and could not become further existent. Since existence and non-existence depend upon each other, their intrinsic nature is non-existent.

There is none. Failing to penetrate my penetration, they lack right view; lingering in the two extremes, they destroy themselves and others, slandering the Tathāgata—nothing could be more extreme than this.
The World-Honored One once said: "If one says 'it exists,' wisdom should not be stained by it;
if one says 'it does not exist,' that is false speech. If one says 'it exists,' one should not remain silent; nor again..."

One should not engage in frivolous speculation or contentious debate; its purport is subtle indeed. The first section concludes the demonstration that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is neither cause nor fruit.
The second section demonstrates that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is neither born nor extinguished and is beyond verbal expression. This is divided into four parts.
△ First, it is shown that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is not devoid of intrinsic nature.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said that the sūtras uphold [the doctrine of] non-arising and non-ceasing, and as the World-Honored One has further stated that 'non-arising and non-ceasing' is another name for the Tathāgata—how is this so?"
“World-Honored One, is it because they lack intrinsic nature that you speak of non-arising and non-ceasing? Is this another name for the Tathāgata?
The Buddha told Mahāmati, “When I say that all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, it is because the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, if all dharmas are non-arising, then the grasping of dharmas cannot be apprehended, because all dharmas are non-arising.
If there is any dharma within names, we pray that you will explain it for us. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “Excellent, excellent!
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it. I shall analyze and explain it for you. Mahāmati replied:
The Buddha said, "So be it; I shall accept your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not say that the Tathāgata is without nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Nor is it the case that he does not give rise to or cease, yet encompasses all phenomena. Furthermore, it is not because he depends on conditions that he is neither born nor extinguished, nor is it that he is devoid of meaning."
This refers to those who, outside of what is merely manifested by their own minds, cling to the notion that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, thereby raising objections.

This is intended to clarify for those who follow after names while losing sight of their true meaning. The Sūtras establish that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);
this is not said because they possess an intrinsic nature. Furthermore, it is stated that [the term "unborn"] is another name for the Tathāgata.

Thus, it is not that they lack intrinsic nature; rather, while currently falling into the category of existence, one speaks of the non-existence of phenomena. This results in falling into both existence and non-existence—this is the purport of Mahāmati’s objection.
The World-Honored One replied: "I teach that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, and that the categories of existence and non-existence do not manifest.

Mahāmati did not realize that this teaching of non-arising and non-extinction was spoken from the perspective of what manifests as the measure of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya-pramāṇa*), and thus he failed to immediately transcend existence.
[The interlocutor says: "No. Since all dharmas are neither produced nor extinguished, they should not be further subsumed under the category of 'existent dharmas.

If you claim that 'Tathāgata' is merely another name [for non-existence], and since a name must have a referent, this would mean it is subsumed under existent dharmas. Therefore, the World-Honored One further said: "I do not say that the Tathāgata is without nature.
Only then does one know that the original mind is a mental construction (*cittamātra*) and is not like a rabbit's horn; it exists based on non-awakening (*abodhi*).

Meaning (*artha*): It appears as all phenomena, yet fundamentally there is no arising and no ceasing. This non-arising and non-ceasing refers to the fact that phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
it does not mean that all phenomena are entirely non-existent. One should not grasp at existence and wait for conditions to be exhausted before seeing non-arising.
Nor is this a meaning of non-existence; rather, it refers to the meaning of the self-mind being truly non-arising as it is.
Furthermore, they fail to realize the meaning that their own minds are, in reality, non-arising.

They merely take the phrases "unborn" and "unextinguished" as a basis for the false attachment that there is no nature (niḥsvabhāva) and that existence should not be subsumed [within reality]. Thus, the word "existence" would be devoid of meaning; therefore, the following text explains this extensively.
△ Second, showing that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is both "to-be-born" and "unborn."
Mahāmati, that which I call the Tathāgata by the name of the Mind-born Dharma-body (manomaya-dharmakāya) is that which is unborn;
it is not within the sphere of experience of any outsiders, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage.
Mahāmati, that which is unborn is simply another name for the Tathāgata. Mahāmati, it is just as with the various designations such as Indra, Śakra, and Prajāpati.
Each individual thing has many names, yet it does not possess multiple natures simply because there are many names for it; nor is it devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

(The Tang translation states: "For example, Indra, the earth, space, and even hands and feet—each such object has many names, yet it is not because of the multiplicity of names that it has multiple entities, nor is it without entity.")
This is precisely the teaching that birth is non-birth, intended to reveal the profound and esoteric principle. One must certainly not follow the literal name while losing the underlying meaning.
For the mind-born Dharma-body (*manomaya-dharmakāya*) is itself non-arising; thus, it is called another name for the Tathāgata.

This meaning of non-arising is not within the realm of the two vehicles or the seventh stage. Prior to the seventh stage, one merely exhausts the causes of birth but does not yet penetrate [this truth].

The self-nature of the Tathāgata is unborn; the self-nature of the Tathāgata is unborn. It is the equality of true thusness (*tathatā*), which, at all places and at all times, is devoid of the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
Because it does not manifest through the exhaustion of conditions, it cannot be comprehended by those who cling to the notion of non-arising.
Indra, Śakra, and Purandara are all synonymous names for Śakra; they are not distinct [deities].
Regarding "having multiple natures despite being a single name," this means that while the substance is one, the names differ. Furthermore, it is not that there is no intrinsic nature;

rather, it means that although many names are used to designate a single substance, one must still rely upon the names to realize the substance. △ Third, showing that the various names for the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya refer to a single essence.
"It is so, Mahāmati. In this Sahā world, I have three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names.
Fools hear them all and each speaks of my name, yet they do not understand that these are different names for me, the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati, there are some sentient beings who know me as the Tathāgata; some know me as the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*); some know me as the Buddha; and some know me as the Savior."
Regarding the World (*loka*): there are those who know it as Self-Awakened; those who know it as the Teacher; those who know it as the Broad Guide;
those who know it as the Guide of All; those who know it as the Sage (*ṛṣi*); those who know it as Brahmā; those who know it as Viṣṇu;

those who know it as Īśvara; those who know it as the Victorious One (*jina*); those who know it as Kapila; and those who know it as the Limit of Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). There are those who know it as... [the text continues].
Regarding the moon: there are those who know it as the sun; those who know it as the king; those who know it as non-arising;
those who know it as non-ceasing; those who know it as emptiness; those who know it as suchness; those who know it as the truth; those who know it as the limit of reality;
those who know it as the nature of phenomena; those who know it as nirvāṇa; those who know it as permanence; those who know it as equality; and those who know it as non-...
Second, there are those who know me as the Signless (animitta), those who know me as Liberation (vimukti), those who know me as the Path (mārga), and those who know me as the Mind-born (manomaya).
Mahāmati, these and hundreds of thousands of other names, numbering three asaṃkhyeyas, neither increase nor decrease.
In this world and in all other worlds, they all know me to be like the moon in water—neither emerging nor entering.
In the Sahā world-system, the Tathāgata has indeed infinite hundreds of thousands of different names;

according to the minds of sentient beings and in accordance with the measure of their knowledge, there are various distinct designations. Yet they do not know the true meaning of the Tathāgata’s own nature.
It is like the moon in water: it neither emerges nor enters; it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Those who do not understand the various names of the Tathāgata are said to be all sentient beings who know only to grasp at meaning based on names.

They do not understand that although the Tathāgata has many names, they express only a single essence—namely, the self-nature purity of the Tathāgata—which is realized only through personal realization and correspondence, and is not [merely] a name.
It describes that which is reached as being like the moon in water: it cannot be said to exist or not to exist; it cannot be near or far; it cannot be pointed out or demonstrated;
and it cannot be measured. In truth, it is not devoid of nature, yet it does not fall into the categories of existence, non-existence, quantity, or measure.
Those foolish people cannot know me because they have fallen into the two extremes; yet they all pay me respect and make offerings to me.

However, they do not skillfully understand the meaning of words and phrases, nor do they discern their designations. They do not understand my self-evident realization, but instead cling to various verbal expressions and textual passages.
Regarding that which is neither born nor extinguished, they conceive of it as being without intrinsic nature, failing to recognize the true name of the Tathāgata.
Distinctions—such as Indra, Śakra, and Brahmā—are not understood through their own inherent communication; they ultimately converge at the ultimate limit.
Regarding all phenomena, one becomes attached to them according to how they are described.
Fools do not know the Tathāgata’s intrinsic nature, the Dharma-body; they falsely perceive existence and non-existence, and they relish and cling to verbal designations.
Consequently, regarding the phrase of the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena, they conceive of them as being without intrinsic nature.

This is a failure to understand self-attestation, whereby they falsely grasp all phenomena as being non-arising and non-ceasing. All names and designations explain a single essence; it is because of names [that this is so].
To penetrate the essence is to realize that the essence transcends verbal expression; this is what is meant by "converging upon the ultimate.

Failing to understand this meaning and merely engaging in verbal explanations based on names, one creates a separate conceptual framework for the principle of reality; this only serves to increase one's erudition and nourish the view of self. IV.

Demonstrating that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body transcends words to reveal the truth. This section is divided into two parts. △ First, demonstrating that the true meaning of the Dharma-body does not fall into the realm of letters.
"Mahāmati, those foolish people speak thus: 'The meaning is identical to the expression; there is no difference between the meaning and the expression. Why is this?
Because they claim that meaning has no body [of its own], and that apart from the expression, there is no further meaning, but only the expression itself.
Mahāmati, those of corrupted wisdom do not know the self-nature of expression, nor do they know the arising and ceasing of expression; yet they claim that meaning does not arise."
"Extinction. Mahāmati, all verbal expressions fall within the realm of letters, but the meaning does not fall therein, for it is free from both existence and non-existence.

There is no rebirth and no body. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata does not speak of dharmas that fall within letters, because the existence or non-existence of letters cannot be apprehended—except for those [dharmas] that do not fall within letters (the Tang translation says: 'excepting only those that do not fall within letters')."
This statement refers to those who are ignorant and fail to comprehend the true meaning of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

They claim that meaning has no substantial essence, and thus exhaust all the flavors of meaning through the conceptual objects of speech and cognition. Therefore, it is said that there is "only speech.
This is not merely a failure to understand meaning; it is also a failure to understand the intrinsic nature of speech itself. Speech depends upon meaning, yet fundamentally, [meaning] does not exist.

The intrinsic nature [of phenomena] is of the nature of arising and ceasing; this refers to the nature of verbal expression. Meaning transcends verbal expression, and its nature is neither arising nor ceasing, nor does it belong to existence or non-existence.
Since it is already free from arising, ceasing, existence, and non-existence, it is also free from that which "leaves" them. As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* says:
To know these as flowers in the sky is to be without cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). There is then neither body nor mind to undergo birth and death;
this is what is meant by "no rebirth and no body. Furthermore, it is said: that which perceives is like empty space, and that which perceives empty space is the appearance of a flower in the sky.
Yet, one cannot say that the nature of perception is non-existent; this is what is meant by "excluding the non-... (i.e., excluding only that which is not).

They fall into [the trap of] words. The Tathāgata’s self-nature *dharmakāya* is without birth and without body; it does not fall into words, yet it is not that there is nothing which does not fall [into them].
Those who are deluded and lack wisdom do not distinguish the meaning of what is taught, but instead falsely indulge in their own attachments;
they are truly to be pitied. 2. Showing that the Tathāgata establishes verbal expressions in order to dispel verbal expressions.
Mahāmati, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata teaches a dharma that falls within the realm of words, that would be a false statement, for the dharma is beyond words.
Therefore, Mahāmati, we Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas do not speak a single word, nor do we answer with a single word. Why is this?
Because the dharma is beyond words. It is not that there is no benefit in speaking; rather, it is through speech that the meaning is conveyed.
This is because sentient beings have false conceptualizations. (The Wei translation says: "All dharmas are without words;
they rely on meaning and are without speech, yet they are spoken based on discrimination. Mahāmati, if all dharmas were not taught, then the teaching would perish.
If the teaching perishes, then there would be no Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas. If these did not exist, who would teach, and for whom?
All the speech of the Tathāgata is for the sake of meaning; it is through provisional speech that one enters the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Thus, by means of speech, he speaks of the ultimate truth that transcends speech.

Therefore, from his own attainment of Buddhahood until his parinirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken between them—meaning that not a single utterance fell into the conceptual mark of letters—yet this was not without benefit.

It is for the benefit of sentient beings that [the Buddha] provides detailed explanations. If there were no benefit in providing detailed explanations for sentient beings, then from what basis would those of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas be established? How could they enter into the meaning of reality?
In such a case, the holy teachings would perish; who would then teach whom? Therefore, one should know that all verbal expressions are devoid of substantial reality; this is the foremost [truth].

There is meaning, yet there is teaching and demonstration. By means of teaching, one enters into meaning; when meaning is revealed, teaching is transcended. Teaching is itself no-teaching, and demonstration is itself no-demonstration.
Therefore it is said that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not speak a single word.

Therefore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should not be attached to verbal expression. One should extensively expound the Dharma through skillful means as appropriate, because the aspirations and afflictions of sentient beings are not uniform.

Thus, I and the other Buddhas teach various dharmas for the sake of those sentient beings with diverse understandings, so that they may become detached from mind, thought, and consciousness; it is not for the sake of attaining the noble self-realization.

The Abode of Wisdom (the Tang translation states: "Both I and all Buddhas expound [the Dharma] according to the various differences in the afflictions, understandings, and desires of sentient beings, thereby transforming the mind, intellect, and consciousness;
it is not for the purpose of establishing a domain of noble self-realization").
Furthermore, this teaches and instructs bodhisattvas to extensively expound the Dharma according to the faculties, consciousnesses, and cognitions of sentient beings.

One should not become attached to verbal expressions. All such verbal expressions are intended to eliminate the various hopes, various afflictions, and various divergent interpretations of sentient beings, thereby causing them to depart from beginningless falsehood and to transform the mind, thought, and consciousness. Self-...
One knows self-realization. There is absolutely no teaching that points toward the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

This so-called noble wisdom of self-awakening is free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of mental objects; it is realized within oneself and is not something displayed by the conceptualizations of verbal discourse.
Therefore, one should know that the Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma is like a physician treating a cataract: its sole purpose is to remove [the obstruction].

The method for removing cataracts and visual distortions exists, yet there is no method for augmenting the light; the explanation and its meaning, as well as the existence or non-existence of an intrinsic nature, are clearly distinguished of themselves.
“Mahāmati, regarding all phenomena as non-existent, one awakens to the fact that they are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind and becomes free from the two kinds of false discrimination.

All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely on the meaning and not on the words. If good sons or good daughters rely on the words, they will destroy the ultimate truth for themselves and will be unable to awaken others;
they fall into a succession of evil views and become [leaders] for the multitude.”

It is said: "Those who do not correctly understand all dharmas, all stages, and all characteristics, and who do not know the words and phrases, are unable to find delight through the true signless joy.

However, those who are proficient in all dharmas, all stages, and all characteristics, who have mastered the words and phrases, and who are endowed with the meaning of the nature of reality, can indeed find delight through the true signless joy and establish sentient beings in the equal Mahāyāna."
The aforementioned discourse on verbal expression does not pertain to the attainment of the state of self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

This statement regarding the attainment of self-realized noble wisdom refers to one who has profoundly penetrated the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and all established systems, such that they naturally do not fall into the sphere of conceptual proliferation (*vikalpa*) concerning words and letters.
Indeed, it is words and letters that delude people; they are the sphere of conceptual proliferation regarding the existence or non-existence of all phenomena as they are explained.

This is the realm of the ear. If one realizes that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and are merely manifestations of the mind, having transcended the two types of conceptual boundaries—existence and non-existence—then what kind of contemplation should be applied to that which is indicated by words?
Thus, whenever reliance on words fails to express the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and instead tends to destroy it, it is because one has not properly understood.
The suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, all stages, and all characteristics, at their primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), likewise cannot be known through the words and phrases of the holy teachings.
Therefore, the establishment of all phenomena, all stages, and all characteristics is entirely that which is revealed by being free from characteristics;

it is the perfection of the meaning of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*). Thus, one should have faith that the holy teachings are beyond words, intended for the purpose of eliminating conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

He uniquely reveals that there is only mind (*cittamātra*). Internally, he personally realizes and dwells in the bliss of the Dharma; externally, he establishes the equality of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

This is the sphere of activity of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), which the Tathāgata has profoundly and earnestly taught for the sake of bodhisattvas who rely on the meaning.
"How could it be something shallow or trivial?
Mahāmati, to embrace the Mahāyāna is to embrace all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
To embrace all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas is to embrace all sentient beings. To embrace all..."
Sentient beings are those who uphold the true Dharma. Those who uphold the true Dharma ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed.
When the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed, one is able to understand and attain the sublime state of entry.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who know how to attain this sublime state of entry are always born by transformation; they establish the Mahāyāna, possess the ten powers of mastery, manifest various forms and appearances, and penetrate all things.
One understands the various forms, inclinations, and afflictions of sentient beings and teaches the Dharma according to reality. "According to reality" means it is not otherwise.
"According to reality" means it is characterized by neither coming nor going; all fabrications have ceased—this is called "according to reality.
Mahāmati, sons and daughters of good family should not grasp at or adhere to what is spoken according to conventional expression. The ultimate truth is free from words and letters.
The Mahāyāna is precisely the single vehicle of the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
To abide securely in this single vehicle of the noble wisdom of self-awakening is to be sustained by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
It is from this noble wisdom of self-awakening that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emerge; if one can abide therein, one is of the same essence as all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
It is also a gathering-in. It is able to gather in and sustain sentient beings, so that they rely upon it and obtain happiness and benefit.
It is also able to gather in and sustain the True Dharma, remaining unshaken by any worldly discourse and such that no heterodox practitioners can find its flaws.
Upholding the Tathāgata’s seal of the ultimate reality of self-nature, this is indeed the seed of the Buddha.
This self-nature, the ultimate reality mind (*paramārtha-citta*), is supreme in all respects; that is to say, it is the attainment of the Great Dharani.
Having attained the Great Dharani, one spontaneously manifests through transformation wherever one is, establishes the Mahayana, and accomplishes the ten powers (*daśabala*).
Appearing in physical form (*rūpakāya*) before beings, one delivers them according to their afflictions (*kleśa*) by means of suchness (*tathatā*). Without...
The flavor of the Dharma of signs consists in abiding in disciplined mastery and bringing all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) to rest;

therefore, one who practices the precepts should not grasp at verbal expressions, but should instead grasp only the truth. This is attained apart from words and is not the domain of discursive consciousness;
it is here that the wise should exercise their own discernment.
Mahāmati, it is like using a finger to point at an object for a fool; the fool looks only at the finger and does not grasp the actual meaning.

In this same way, fools follow the finger of verbal expression, grasping and becoming attached to it, never letting go until the very end, and thus they can never attain the supreme, ultimate reality that lies beyond the finger of verbal expression.
Mahāmati, it is like an infant who should eat food that has been cooked, and should not eat what is raw.
If one eats raw food, it causes madness, because one does not know the sequential methods for cooking it.
Mahāmati, in the same way, that which is neither born nor extinguished is unwholesome if it is not cultivated through skillful means. Therefore, one should cultivate skillful means well.
Do not follow after words, just as one does not look at the tip of a finger.
This further means that one should transcend words to attain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The finger is a metaphor for words; the object is a metaphor for the ultimate truth.
That is to say, the ultimate truth is that which is entered by means of words, but words themselves are not the ultimate truth, nor is it [the case that] what is not words is the ultimate truth.

What has been taught is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). If one relies on verbal expression to give rise to the realm of conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-buddhi*), this is a profound and secret attachment that causes people to go mad;
for they take that very realm of conceptual cognition to be the ultimate truth, thereby losing the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
This is merely to delude oneself and others. For instance, when it is said that "all dharmas are unarisen," this is a verbal expression.

One should personally employ skillful means to investigate: which dharma is unarisen? In what manner is it unarisen? By investigating through skillful means, one immediately realizes that all dharmas are merely manifestations of one's own mind.
Being deluded regarding one's own mind, one falsely perceives what appears; these appearances arise from the vision of delusion and are not [ultimately real].

There is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). When one awakens to the measure of one’s own mind, delusive error is suddenly stilled. All things are not distinct; there is absolutely no grasping or rejecting.
In the state where there is no grasping or rejecting, the self-nature is true suchness (*tathatā*), tranquil both internally and externally;
this is the primary ultimate reality. This constitutes the skillful cultivation of means. If one hears that all phenomena are unarisen, then regarding all phenomena...

To analyze atoms until they reach non-existence is also a characteristic of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). This is because one reckons existence within non-existence and reckons non-existence within existence;
thus, regarding the reality of things as they are (*yathābhūta-dharma*), one separately gives rise to objective spheres (*viṣaya*). This constitutes the characteristic of differentiation.

Even when hearing the teaching of "mind-only" (*cittamātra*), if one uses conceptual awareness to perceive one's own mind and clings to it as something profound and secret, this too [is a characteristic of differentiation].
To manifest delusion through delusion is not to depart from discursive thought; it is to rely on verbal designations, like looking at the tip of one's finger.
Therefore, there is the aforementioned analogy of food giving rise to life. Without skillful means, this would instead increase one's madness.
Therefore, Mahāmati, you should practice skillful means regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha*). The true meaning is subtle and tranquil; it is the cause of nirvana.
Verbal expression is conjoined with false discrimination (*vikalpa*); false discrimination accumulates birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Mahāmati, the true meaning is obtained from those who have heard much (*bahuśruta*). Mahāmati, "having heard much" refers to being skilled in the meaning, not being skilled in verbal expression.
Regarding "one who is skilled in meaning": they do not follow any of the scriptures or treatises of the non-Buddhists; they do not follow them themselves, nor do they cause others to follow them.
This is what is called being a virtuous one of great learning. Therefore, those who seek the meaning should draw near to such great learning—namely, that which is skillful in meaning.
That which is contrary to this, namely, attachment to mere words, should be avoided.
That which is cause but not fruit is called *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature). That which is fruit but not cause is called *nirvāṇa*.
That which is neither cause nor fruit is called *buddhadhātu*. That which is neither cause nor fruit is called *mahāparinirvāṇa*. These are all the words of the Tathāgata;
though the expressions differ, their meaning is one. As for the true meaning: intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) is the cause, and ultimate quiescence is...
Quiescence is the fruit. However, this is not something reached by those who rely on verbal expressions. One must know that the self-nature is fundamentally pure;
it is quiescent without arising, devoid of causal characteristics, and quiescent within its own nature. It is not obtained through cultivation, nor does it possess the meaning of a "fruit.
This realization of the measure of one's own mind is known and realized by oneself; it does not follow any false verbal expressions.
It is merely the realm of conceptualization. If one follows verbal expressions, it increases false discrimination and accumulates the causes of birth and death;
this is not what the Tathāgata calls "much learning. The Tathāgata has said that if one hears only the two words "eternal abiding" and deeply understands their meaning, that is called "much learning.
Even if one reads all the twelve divisions of the sūtras, if one does not hear of eternal abiding, it is said that—
Regarding the absence of hearing [the Dharma], one should draw near to those who are learned. As for what is well-meaning yet not well-spoken, one must examine it with careful scrutiny.
The first two sections have demonstrated that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is neither born nor extinguished, and is beyond verbal expression.

Now, thirdly, to demonstrate that the Tathāgata’s non-birth and non-extinction differ from those of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), there are six parts. △ First, the objection that the Tathāgata is identical [to the non-Buddhists].

Regarding the four types of causal characteristics held by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), at that time Mahāmati Bodhisattva, further empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, there is nothing extraordinary about the World-Honored One’s demonstration of non-arising and non-ceasing. Why is this? For the causes [posited] by all non-Buddhists are likewise..."

They are neither born nor extinguished. The World-Honored One also speaks of space, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the realm of nirvāṇa as being neither born nor extinguished.

World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) say that causes give rise to all worlds; the World-Honored One also says that ignorance, craving, karma, and false discrimination serve as conditions for the arising of all worlds.
These causes and these conditions differ only in name. External objects likewise have causes and conditions.

It is thus. There is no distinction between the World-Honored One’s discourse and that of the non-Buddhists. The nine categories—such as atoms (*paramāṇu*), primordial matter (*pradhāna*), the supreme spirit (*īśvara*), and the Lord of Beings (*puruṣa*)—are neither born nor extinguished;
likewise, the World-Honored One also teaches that all natures (*bhāva*) are neither born nor extinguished, and that existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.
The non-Buddhists also maintain that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are indestructible and that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is neither born nor extinguished.
"The four great elements are permanent; these four great elements, even as they circulate through the various realms of existence, do not abandon their own nature.
What the World-Honored One has taught is likewise so. Therefore, I say there is nothing extraordinary about this. I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the distinctions for us."
This is why he is extraordinary and surpasses all non-Buddhists. If there were no distinction, then all non-Buddhists would also be Buddhas, because they too are neither born nor extinguished.
Yet the World-Honored One has said that many Buddhas appear in a single world-system.
This is impossible. As previously stated, there would have to be many Buddhas in a single world because there is no distinction [between them].
These four objections are intended for the Tathāgata to clarify why he differs from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

The first objection concerns the non-Buddhists' reckoning of a creator-cause that is neither born nor extinguished, which they claim is identical to the Tathāgata’s three unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and space (*ākāśa*). That is to say:

Space is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is the unconditioned phenomenon of non-analytical cessation; nirvāṇa is the unconditioned phenomenon of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Not knowing that externalists postulate [these] as causes is a deluded and false calculation within [the cycle of] birth and death, which is subsumed under the category of arising and ceasing.
Even "neither-arising-nor-ceasing" is a false calculation. What is called the "characteristic of arising and ceasing" is not the same as the three unconditioned phenomena. As it is said:

Come to realize that the measure of one's own mind is by nature quiescent. Second, [this addresses] the difficulty of the non-Buddhists' reckoning of a creator as the cause for the arising of all worlds, which they claim continues through the three periods of time like the Tathāgata’s twelve links of dependent origination.

They do not know that what they reckon as "arising from nature" is actually a false condition. All dependently arisen phenomena are entirely manifested through delusion; they arise neither from themselves nor from another.
It is not that they do not exist together. These three—the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), the supreme nature (*pradhāna*), and so forth—these nine entities are neither born nor extinguished.

This is likewise as the Tathāgata has taught: all phenomena (*dharma*) are neither born nor extinguished. How could one know that the *dharmatā* of the Tathāgata and the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of true thusness (*tathatā*) remain thus by their very nature, whether a Buddha appears or not? They are not like the constructs of the false imaginings of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). No.
There is indeed a true meaning. The four objections concern the non-Buddhists' reckoning of *svabhāva* (self-nature) as being eternal and unitary.
