This is similar to the Tathāgata’s teaching that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) pervade the ten directions of space without obstructing one another.

However, they do not understand that the Tathāgata teaches these are neither caused nor conditioned, neither produced by combination nor by conjunction, nor are they spontaneous; rather, they manifest through deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). This is precisely the *Laṅkāvatāra*.
What I, Yan, call "the seer and the conditions for seeing," along with the perceived characteristics, are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent.
This seeing and these conditions are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi. There are not many Buddhas within a single world-system;
if non-Buddhists were identical to the Buddha, there would be many Buddhas. [This statement] generally refutes the claim that non-Buddhists are identical to the Buddha, thereby revealing [the truth].
This is merely a distinction. II. Showing that the Tathāgata awakens to the measure of his own mind and that false discrimination does not arise.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "What I call 'non-arising and non-ceasing' is not the same as the non-arising and non-ceasing of the non-Buddhists. Why is this?
Those non-Buddhists maintain that there is a self-nature (*svabhāva*) which, by its very nature, attains the characteristics of non-arising and immutability. I do not teach in such a manner."
[They] fall into the categories of existence and non-existence. Mahāmati, my [teaching] is free from the categories of existence and non-existence, free from arising and ceasing;
it is neither a nature nor a lack of nature. Because it appears like various illusions and dreams, it is not a lack of nature. Why is it not a lack of nature?

It is because the characteristics of form are grasped as lacking intrinsic nature, due to their appearing and not appearing, and being grasped and not grasped. (The Tang translation says: "Why is it not a lack of nature? Like illusions and dreams...")
Because form is seen in various ways, how could it not exist? It is because the self-nature of the characteristic of form does not exist as a reality;

it is because it is seen and yet not seen, and because it is grasped and yet not grasped. For this reason, all natures are neither existent nor non-existent; they are merely the manifestation of what appears from one's own mind.
When false discrimination no longer arises, there is peace, security, and happiness, and worldly affairs are forever stilled.
The non-Buddhists are deluded regarding the measure of their own minds; from the place where things manifest from the mind, they calculate that there is an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

This is because they do not understand the cause of the flowing stream [of existence]. Seeing the continuity of this stream, they perceive a characteristic of non-arising and non-ceasing, and thus they fall into the view of existence.

Because they posit a creator, they treat the cause as a non-cause, and thus they likewise fall into the view of non-existence. The Dharma of the Tathāgata is neither existent nor non-existent, being free from these extremes.
All that arises and ceases—namely, the various forms and appearances—is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature, like a dream and like an illusion. Dreams and illusions are not non-existent;
yet, being without intrinsic nature, they are not existent. When there is seeing and grasping, one cannot say they are non-existent; when there is no seeing and no grasping, they are not existent.

It cannot be said to exist; it is neither existence nor non-existence, being entirely free from both. One merely awakens to the fact that all is the manifestation of one’s own mind, and that what appears is but mind alone.
There is absolutely nothing to be grasped or rejected; with both grasping and rejecting forgotten, one dwells peacefully in the ocean of the mind, tranquil and free from sorrow.
They wander through the world as if it were merely a pleasure garden. △ Third, [it is shown that] the false conceptualizations of outsiders are unreal;
they are the products of the deluded imaginings of ignorant ordinary people, not those of the noble sages. These unreal imaginings are like a city of the *gandharvas* or like magically conjured men.
Mahāmati, just as with a city of the *gandharvas* or magically conjured men, so too are the various sentient beings.

When merchants enter and exit, foolish people give rise to false imaginings, claiming there is actual entering and exiting; yet in reality, there is no one who exits and no one who enters—it is merely due to their false imaginings.
In this same way, Mahāmati, ignorant ordinary beings give rise to delusions regarding non-arising and non-ceasing.

For them, there is neither the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It is like a person born from an illusion: in truth, there is neither arising nor ceasing, for such is the nature [of phenomena].
Because there is no intrinsic nature and nothing exists, all phenomena are likewise free from arising and ceasing.
Foolish ordinary beings fall into untruth and give rise to the delusive conceptualization of arising and ceasing; this is not the case for the noble sages.
This is an extreme statement regarding the causal factors (hetu) postulated by non-Buddhists; they are like illusions and transformations, lacking any real meaning.
"Performing an act" refers to the causal factor, which is precisely the nature and characteristics of the intrinsic essence (svabhāva) they postulate.
To say that the intrinsic essence they postulate is not for the wise, but is rather unreal conceptualization, is like a city of the Gandharvas or a magical illusion—[the view of] the foolish.
They falsely perceive coming and going, yet in reality there is neither one who comes nor one who goes.
Since self-nature (*svabhāva*) is not truly existent, it likewise lacks the characteristics of non-arising and non-ceasing.

Thus, even their conceptualization of arising as non-arising and non-ceasing cannot distinguish what is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and what is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is because the self-nature they conceptually construct does not [exist].
In reality, even the characteristics of arising and ceasing belong to deluded thought and cannot be pointed out.
Whether conditioned or unconditioned, they are all equally like illusions and transformations. Furthermore, turning the discourse back upon what you have calculated, it is said:
in truth, whether there is arising or ceasing, or nature and non-nature, these do not exist; all dharmas are likewise free from arising and ceasing.
This is because one desires to realize one's error in the present moment, to attain the true characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and to perceive quiescence.

The following passage specifically points to this self-characteristic of quiescence: it is to attain the reality that is no different from deluded thought; it requires nothing more than a single awakening.
△ Fourth, showing that the true nature of false imagination is itself ultimate tranquility.

It is not as those who do not see things as they truly are claim. Just as with the self-nature of phenomena, false imagination is not different from it. If false imagination were different [from that nature], [it would not be so].
To be attached to the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is to fail to see tranquility. One who does not see tranquility never transcends conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, Mahāmati, the vision of signlessness (*animitta-darśana*) is superior, not the vision of signs (*nimitta-darśana*). The vision of signs is the cause for undergoing rebirth; therefore, it is not superior.
Mahāmati, that which is signless is the non-arising of conceptual construction; it is neither arising nor ceasing. This, I say, is *nirvāṇa*. Mahāmati.

Nirvāṇa is that which, according to the vision of ultimate reality, is free from the prior deluded thoughts and mental factors, and has attained the noble wisdom of the Tathāgata’s self-realization; this I call nirvāṇa.

To continue from what was said above: those who are foolish and fall into non-reality are unable to realize that all phenomena are not different from the nature of their own conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
Indeed, the nature of all phenomena is like the nature of conceptual construction; yet they cannot directly penetrate and illuminate the self-nature of such construction.
Following after delusion, they give rise to calculations and discriminations, as if there were distinct dharmas, and thus the characteristics of subject and object arise. This is what is meant.
One does not perceive tranquility; one does not perceive tranquility, and consequently remains unable to distance oneself from deluded thoughts.
This is entirely due to ignorance of the self-nature of deluded thoughts. This, then, directly points out that the self-nature of deluded thoughts is itself reality.
One simply realizes for oneself that there is no perception of signs; this is itself nirvāṇa. Those who perceive signs act as the cause for rebirth.
Being deluded regarding reality, they are unable to abide [in it]. All these sentient beings are originally pure, yet have been obstructed by adventitious defilements.
Therefore, know that what is revealed through the severing of obstructions is the non-dual *tathatā* (suchness), which is itself.

Nirvana by nature refers to the severing of hindrances; that is, the severing of these hindrances of subject-object perception (*nimitta-dṛṣṭi*). If these hindrances are severed, one directly perceives the true nature of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).
One then immediately and completely detaches from the preceding mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) at their very source.
This detachment is itself the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), which has no separate essence; it is merely what the Tathāgata calls "nirvana. 5. Showing the Absence of Cause.
This is to manifest the meaning of non-arising.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "I have expounded such a Dharma To eliminate the theories of arising And establish the principle of non-arising;
Yet the foolish are unable to understand it. All dharmas are unarisen, For they lack intrinsic nature."

There is nothing at all. Gandharvas, illusions, and dreams—those things that possess an intrinsic nature have no cause; they do not arise and lack self-nature. For what reason should emptiness be explained?
Because it is free from combination, the nature of cognition does not manifest; therefore, emptiness is unarisen. I teach that there is no self-nature:
that which manifests as an intrinsic nature within each individual combination does not truly exist. When analyzed, there is no combination; it is not as [it appears].
The view of the non-Buddhists is that all phenomena, due to delusion regarding one's own mind, suddenly appear without being perceived; they possess no intrinsic nature.
This is why the Tathāgata speaks of non-arising and emptiness. He speaks of non-arising in order to refute the theory of arising, and he speaks of phenomena...
"Emptiness" is taught to refute the view of existence; yet in reality, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Like a *gandharva-city*, a dream, or an illusion, although their nature appears, they fundamentally lack a cause. Appearing without a cause, they possess no sense of arising, for they have no nature of self-origination.
Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, they adhere to the nature of cognition and appear as if manifest before one.

If one were separated from these combinations, there would be no basis for perception or conceptualization; what form, then, would manifest? Within the combination of a dream, things remain perfectly present in their respective places.
After awakening, who is it that remembers the causes and conditions? Therefore, know that emptiness and non-arising refer to all phenomena:
they do not suddenly appear through lack of awareness, yet they possess no self-nature; nor are they unilaterally non-arising, stubbornly empty, and inert.
Each and every [phenomenon] is a composite; its nature is like a shadow or an echo—manifest yet non-existent.
It is not like the "real productive cause" asserted by the non-Buddhists, which must be subjected to analytical dissection before one realizes it does not exist.
Like dreams, illusions, and falling hair; like mirages and the city of the Gandharvas—various phenomena in the world appear without cause.

To refute those who argue for the existence of causes, the meaning of non-arising is proclaimed. When the meaning of non-arising is proclaimed, the stream of the Dharma flows on forever without interruption.
Blazing forth, this doctrine of causelessness strikes terror into all non-Buddhists.

It repeatedly declares that all phenomena are like dreams, illusions, floating hairs, mirages, and castles in the air; they have no cause for their arising, yet the manifestations of things appear vividly.
By means of this, it subdues those who maintain theories of causation, and by this very same means, it proclaims the teaching of non-arising. Indeed, such is the nature of dharmas.

Abiding in the station of the Dharma, the world is eternally constant. When the Dharma-eye suddenly opens, then the daily activities of the common people—bending, raising, turning, and moving—are all capable of continuing the lineage.
Therefore it is said that to "elucidate non-arising" means that the flow of the Dharma is forever uninterrupted.
Furthermore, the very means by which external paths (tīrthikas) are subdued is also found herein; for it is because external paths falsely conceptualize all phenomena.
If there were a cause for arising, it would fall into two errors: first, that things do not arise from themselves, because they are manifestations of false conceptualization;

second, that they cannot produce others, because they lack an inherent nature of production. If there were a cause for arising, then all phenomena would possess a fundamental basis and could not be suddenly realized.
Yet, there are those that are seen and those that are not, and those that are included and those that are not; this is merely due to the arising of delusion, and is not [the case otherwise].
It is not understood all at once. The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cannot awaken to this; they merely hear of "no cause" but do not understand where to turn for refuge.

Thus, being utterly bewildered and without support, it is known that they must surely be terrified. 6. Extensively demonstrating the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). This is divided into two parts.
△ First, a direct demonstration of non-arising.
At that time, Mahāmati asked in verse: "What is it? What is its cause? For what reason does it arise?
In what place do they combine to establish the doctrine of causelessness?"
Because the Tathāgata previously taught the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*), he now asks again:
"Ultimately, what is the cause and where do all phenomena come together? To which the Tathāgata replies that they are without cause.
At that time, the World-Honored One again answered in verse: "Observing conditioned phenomena, one sees they do not exist without a cause, but possess a cause;
thus, the views of those who propound arising and ceasing are extinguished."

The teachings of the non-Buddhists all arise from false views. If a wise person can observe that all conditioned phenomena are merely the delusive manifestations of one's own mind due to a lack of awakening— being like dreams and illusions, having neither causal characteristics nor being causeless—
then this view will suddenly cease, and one will immediately accord with the unborn.
At that time, Mahāmati spoke in verse, asking: "What is meant by 'non-arising'? Is it the absence of intrinsic nature?
Or is it the observation of conditions such that a phenomenon is called 'non-arising'? A name should not be without meaning; pray explain this for my sake through analysis."

This question concerns non-arising (*anutpāda*). Does it refer to the total absence of phenomena, or does it depend upon the convergence of conditions? Since it is called "non-arising," the name must necessarily have a meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse: "It is not non-arising because of the absence of nature, nor is it due to looking toward conditions; it is not existent."
It is a nature that receives a name; yet the name is not without meaning. It is not within the realm of any of the non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or those at the seventh stage;
this is called the characteristic of non-arising.
All phenomena arise from the manifestation of the mind. This manifestation is not devoid of nature; it does not depend on external conditions; and its manifestation is not an inherent self-nature.

Nevertheless, this does not mean that there is no principle of the "mind-measure" (cittamātra). This meaning of the non-arising of the mind-measure is not within the realm of the two vehicles at the seventh stage, much less that of the non-Buddhists.
Far removed from all causes and conditions, and likewise free from all phenomena, there remains only the subtle mind abiding;
with both the perceiver and the perceived abandoned, the body undergoes transformation—this I call the Unborn.
Regarding causes and conditions: this refers to the harmony of worldly causes and conditions. "All matters" refers to all resultant matters;

that is, it means to be free from views concerning the existence or non-existence of cause and effect within the harmony of worldly causes and conditions, and to possess only the subtle and profound mindfulness of the present moment.
Abiding in tranquility, one transforms the entire body of subject-object conceptualization into the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
Although delusion and awakening function differently, they possess no distinct essence; this is what is meant by "the mind is fundamentally unborn."
There is no external nature, nor is there non-nature; nor is there any mental apprehension. Having severed all views, I declare this to be non-arising.

Thus, regarding the absence of intrinsic nature, emptiness and so forth should be distinguished. It is not because of being empty that it is called "empty," but because of being non-arisen that it is called "empty."
Regarding this statement, "awakening to the manifestation of one's own mind," it means simply to realize that all external phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

When there is no mind grasping at objects and all views are severed, this is precisely non-arising (*anutpāda*). This term "non-arising" shares the same meaning as "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) and "lack of intrinsic nature":

they both refer to the fact that what is about to arise does not arise; it does not mean that all things are entirely non-existent. Therefore, it is said: "It is not empty, yet it is spoken of as empty. It is not...
It is because of arising that emptiness is taught. △ Second, showing the dharma of dependent origination to eliminate views regarding causes:
When the various factors of dependent origination combine, there is arising and ceasing; apart from these various factors of dependent origination, there is no separate arising or ceasing.
Apart from the enumeration of causes and conditions, there is no other distinct nature. To speak of identity or difference is the false imagination of the non-Buddhists.
The nature of existence and non-existence does not arise; it is neither existent nor non-existent. Apart from the transformation of these enumerations, none of these can be found.
The preceding statement that non-arising is itself arising within the present life is the Tathāgata’s indication of the principle of non-arising.

This declares that arising and ceasing are fundamentally based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), thereby clarifying the reason for the transmigration of sentient beings. However, once one realizes that transmigration is itself dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), one abandons causes and conditions;
there is then no further talk of identity or difference, existence or non-existence. [This is unlike] the false views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

These constitute four propositions. Thus one comes to know that delusion perceives arising and ceasing due to causes and conditions, whereas awakening accords with non-arising due to causes and conditions.
If arising and ceasing were to exist apart from causes and conditions, then the doctrine of non-arising would likewise destroy the meaning of causes and conditions;
it would not be the case that they are neither produced nor unproduced. Therefore, the following text explains this in detail.
There are only various conventional designations that function as a chain of mutual dependence. Apart from this causal chain, the meaning of "arising" cannot be found.

Since arising lacks intrinsic nature, it does not originate; thus, one avoids the errors of the non-Buddhists. We speak only of the chain of conditions, yet the ignorant and foolish are unable to comprehend it.
If there were a nature of arising that existed apart from the chain of conditions, this would be a doctrine of causelessness that destroys the meaning of the chain of conditions.

Just as a lamp reveals various forms, if the manifestation of the chain of conditions were likewise [independent], then there would be various natures existing separately, apart from the chain of conditions.
The various conventional designations refer to the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of sentient beings, like a chain of hooks and links that is never severed.
If one suddenly detaches from those very causes and conditions, then no arising or ceasing can be found. This is the immediate absence of birth;
at once, the views of dharmas do not arise, and one naturally avoids the errors of the non-Buddhists. It is simply by means of this teaching of causes and conditions [that one attains liberation].

This is certainly not something that the ignorant and foolish can comprehend. For when one is free from the hook and the chain, there is neither arising nor ceasing; when one is free from the hook and the chain, there is likewise no non-arising.
Delusion and awakening share the same path, yet it is easy to give rise to divergent views. If there were arising and ceasing apart from the hook and the chain, [then such views would hold].
This is the Tathāgata’s discourse on the absence of causes. Furthermore, it shall dismantle the hook and chain while demonstrating something further:

just as a lamp reveals various forms, yet the lamp is not the forms themselves; if the manifestation of the hook and chain were likewise [to exist inherently], then apart from the hook and chain there would be a separate, distinct nature, which would constitute the doctrine of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika). Thus, the Tathāgata establishes the meaning of neither arising nor non-arising.
Furthermore, what is it that is clearly manifest?
It is without intrinsic nature and without arising, having the self-nature of empty space. If one is free from the hook and the chain, wisdom has nothing to differentiate.

Furthermore, there is another non-arising, which is the dharma attained by the noble ones (*ārya*). That which is the arising of that [non-arising] is precisely the patience toward non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
This correctly reveals the meaning of non-arising within what is about to arise; it refers to being without nature while being within nature, and being without arising while being within arising.
Amidst the causal conditions of the present, which are like a chain of links, it is luminously clear as the self-nature of space, never departing from it.
At that very place, one realizes and knows for oneself that the dharma-patience attained by all other noble ones is of a single, non-dual intent.
If those in the world were to observe this hook-and-chain, they would all be freed from the hook and chain; from this, they attain samādhi.
Ignorance, craving, various karmas, and so forth—these are the internal hook-and-chain. The fire-drill, the lump of clay, the potter’s wheel, seeds, and so forth are called external.
If there were a nature other [than these], yet it were produced from causes and conditions, that would not possess the meaning of a hook-and-chain; thus, it would not be established.
If that which arises has no self-nature, for whom would it serve as a hook or a lock? Since things arise through mutual succession, one should understand the meaning of causes and conditions.
Once again, I exhort the world: if one can simply observe that these hooks and locks lack self-nature, they will not give rise to other phenomena.

In that very moment, there is a sudden flash of realization, free from all further obstruction. The original, inherent meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) immediately manifests before one; thus, one comes to know all things.

Ignorance, delusion, and karma are like fire-drills and clay wheels; the deluded perceive phenomena as if they truly exist, yet awakening does not come from another. As these states arise one after another in succession, who is the creator?
What is called "mutual perception" lacks inherent nature, being like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other; such is the meaning of dependent origination.
Such is the nature of things.

Regarding the phenomena of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion, the ignorant give rise to false conceptualizations. Apart from these enumerations, there is no distinct phenomenon; this is what is meant by "the absence of intrinsic nature."
Taking solidity, moisture, motion, and warmth as examples, one should see that all phenomena likewise arise from false imagination and appear as a continuous succession;
apart from this, nothing else exists. This is what is meant by "the absence of intrinsic nature."

Just as a physician treats various ailments without having multiple treatises, but devises diverse cures according to the differences in the diseases, so too do I, for the sake of those sentient beings, destroy their various afflictions;
knowing the superiority or inferiority of their faculties, I preach to them the gateways of liberation.
It is not that the roots of affliction differ, such that there would be various distinct dharmas; rather, it is by teaching only the Single Vehicle Dharma that this constitutes the Mahāyāna.
To conclude: the Tathāgata extensively expounds the causes and conditions for the sake of all sentient beings, destroying their afflictions and establishing the gateways of liberation.

Although there appear to be various differences in the teachings and principles according to the differing faculties and desires [of beings], it is as if the Tathāgata himself possesses a variety of pedagogical methods.

Know that the Tathāgata has only one vehicle, which is the manifestation of what is measured by one’s own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*). Though there are many gates of skillful means (*upāya*), they return to a single source without duality.
The preceding three sections have demonstrated that the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished, differing from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Now, the fourth section demonstrates that the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is neither eternal (*nitya*) nor impermanent (*anitya*), differing from the non-Buddhists. This is divided into two parts. △ First, the question concerning the non-Buddhists.

[The Buddha said: "The path of false conceptualization regarding impermanence—whether it be heterodox or orthodox—at that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, all non-Buddhists give rise to the false imagination of impermanence.
World-Honored One, you also say that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and are subject to arising and ceasing. What is the meaning of this? "
What do you mean? Is it false or is it correct? How many kinds of impermanence are there?

Since [the teaching of] permanence through non-arising and non-ceasing differs from that of the non-Buddhists, this question is raised because the dharma of impermanence itself also possesses both false and correct aspects.
Speaking from the perspective of one's own mind, it is neither permanent nor impermanent.

Failing to realize that what appears is but one's own mind, which manifests falsely, ceases from moment to moment without abiding, and possesses no master—then all phenomena of form and mind, internal and external, are like a lamp, like a flame, like lightning, and like a shadow.

Neither their prior limit nor their subsequent limit reach one another; this is the True Dharma’s teaching on impermanence. Indeed, the true nature of self-characteristics is difficult to awaken to instantaneously.
I preach impermanence for them so that they may gradually awaken. Those followers of external paths perceive all phenomena outside the mind as truly arising and truly ceasing;
their calculation of permanence is certainly not the true cause, and their notion of impermanence is likewise not true quiescence.
This is what Mahāmati urgently seeks to have elucidated. II. Listing the impermanence of non-Buddhists in order to reveal that the True Dharma is neither permanent nor impermanent;
this section has eleven parts. △ First, a general listing of seven kinds of impermanence.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "All non-Buddhists maintain seven kinds of impermanence, which do not belong to my teaching.
What are these seven? Some say that once something has been created, it is then abandoned; this is called impermanence. Some say that the destruction of form and location is impermanence.
Some say that form itself is impermanence. Some say that the interval during which form undergoes transformation is impermanence."
It disintegrates spontaneously and without interval, like milk turning into curd; its transformation during the intermediate stage is imperceptible.
Impermanence destroys all natures and causes them to shift. Some say that nature itself is impermanent; some say that both nature and non-nature are impermanent;
others say that the non-arising of all phenomena is impermanence, which penetrates all phenomena.

"Having performed [an action] and then relinquishing it" means that there is an impermanent nature capable of producing the great elements (*mahābhūta*), while the great elements themselves are permanent;

having performed the act of production, they are subsequently relinquished, thus being impermanent. "The destruction of shape and location" means that one reckons that the four great elements and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)—both the producers and the produced—are not destroyed;
rather, it is only when analyzed that the shapes, such as length and shortness, are seen to be destroyed. This refers to form (*rūpa*).

This means that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which act as the creators are eternal, while the derivative forms (*upādāyarūpa*) they produce are impermanent. Regarding the transformation of form during the interval:

this refers to the fact that between the primary and derivative elements there exists an impermanent nature that transforms moment by moment, just as milk turns into curd and so forth, changing spontaneously.
Regarding the impermanence of nature: this means that there is an impermanent intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that is indestructible, yet it is capable of destroying all [other things].
Regarding phenomena (*dharma*): they are like staffs, tiles, or stones, possessing a nature capable of destruction. As for "nature" (*svabhāva*) and "non-nature" (*asvabhāva*) being impermanent:

"nature" refers to the creator (*nirmātr*), while "non-nature" refers to that which is created (*nirmita*). Once the creative nature has finished creating, it immediately perishes; the phenomena that were created likewise perish accordingly.
This reckoning holds that both the creator and the created perish together. Regarding the impermanence of the non-arising of all phenomena: this refers to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
All dharmas are unarisen; yet, by means of this non-arising, they pervade all things—this is impermanence.
These seven types are listed here and will be extensively refuted in the following text; their sequence is not fixed. △ Second, the impermanence of nature and the absence of nature.
Mahāmati, as for the impermanence of existence and non-existence, it refers to the destruction of the specific characteristics of the four great elements and their derivatives;
the self-nature of the four great elements cannot be apprehended, for they are unarisen.
The four great elements are called the "producers," while all phenomena are called the "produced. They calculate the specific characteristics of the producer and the produced;
yet once the production is finished, all is destroyed. However, the intrinsic nature of the four great elements cannot be apprehended through form or appearance.

They do not arise, nor is it known that the four great elements are formed by false conceptualization. Falsehood is fundamentally non-arising and likewise has no cessation; they exist precisely within causes and conditions.

The hook and the lock both lack a creator. When that which is capable of creating and that which is created are destroyed, would there not further be the non-arising of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the four great elements?
△ Third, the impermanence of the non-arising of all phenomena.
Regarding that "non-arising impermanence": it is not the impermanence of [mere] non-existence. All phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—are non-arising. (The Wei translation says:
"That which is called 'not permanent' is therefore impermanent; one sees that all phenomena are neither arising nor non-arising.
Even when analyzed down to the subtlest atom, they cannot be perceived; this is the meaning of "non-arising. It is not arising; this is called the characteristic of non-arising impermanence. If...
Those who perceive this fall into the view of all non-Buddhists that birth is impermanent;
yet "neither permanent nor impermanent" is what the non-Buddhists themselves calculate. They maintain that all phenomena arise neither from existence nor from non-existence.
When analyzed down to the finest atom, it cannot be seen; this is the meaning of "non-arising. It is not that it arises and then ceases to be non-arising and impermanent.

Rather, one fails to realize that what we call the "non-arising" of self and dharmas is simply because the deluded manifestations of one's own mind are like shadows and lightning—beyond being existent or non-existent—and are not merely things that vanish when analyzed. Furthermore, since...
It is said that there is a nature of non-arising which enters into all phenomena; this is precisely what constitutes arising, because it is characterized by an agent.

One should therefore speak of "the impermanence of arising," yet one speaks of "the impermanence of non-arising. Thus, taking arising as non-arising is to fail to understand the meaning of non-arising;
taking non-arising as impermanence is likewise to fail to understand the meaning of impermanence. If one does not awaken to this, [one remains deluded].
This would immediately fall into the heterodox view that asserts the meaning of non-arising as impermanence, yet mistakenly takes it to mean that non-arising itself is impermanent.

△ Fourth, the impermanence of nature (*svabhāva*). Mahāmati, as for the impermanence of nature, it is a conceptual construction of one’s own mind; it is not a nature characterized by permanence or impermanence. Why is this so?

This means that the nature of impermanence itself is indestructible. (The Tang translation says: "Regarding things that are impermanent, it refers to the state of being neither permanent nor impermanent, wherein one gives rise to conceptual discrimination.
What is its meaning? That which establishes impermanence does not itself perish or disintegrate, yet it is capable of destroying all phenomena.
Mahāmati, this is the matter of the impermanence of the existence and non-existence of all natures; apart from impermanence, there is nothing else that can [accomplish this].
Regarding the statement that "the nature of all phenomena is non-nature": it is like using a staff, a tile, or a stone to destroy various objects.
As for the claim that "nature is impermanent," this refers to the calculation of externalists who assert that there is an impermanent intrinsic nature capable of destroying all phenomena.
First, one must investigate their obscuration: in a state where there is neither permanence nor impermanence, they falsely give rise to discrimination, asserting that there is impermanence.
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indestructible. Below, the [opponent’s] calculation is set forth: it is claimed that all these natures are non-existent and impermanent;

it is not the case that there exists an impermanent intrinsic nature capable of destroying phenomena, for such a thing could certainly not render the nature of all phenomena non-existent and impermanent.
It is like a staff, a tile, or a stone, which possess the power to destroy; this [staff, etc. is what can destroy.
That which is destroyed appears as if it were two distinct things; therefore, [the text] refutes this below.
What is perceived is that each is not different from its nature; this nature is impermanent. It is not the case that there is a distinction between the agent and the acted-upon.
This is impermanence; this is the thing. If there were no difference between the agent and the acted-upon, then all natures would be eternal and devoid of causality, Mahāmati.
The fact that all natures are devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) has a cause; it is not something known by ordinary fools.

Following the preceding [argument], if one were to claim that there exists an impermanent intrinsic nature that is indestructible yet capable of destroying all phenomena, there would necessarily be a distinction between two separate entities.
Therefore, it is refuted as follows: we clearly perceive before our eyes that all things characterized by impermanence lack any agent capable of destruction or any object to be destroyed.

The distinct characteristics of the destroyer and the destroyed can certainly be pointed out; namely, that "this is impermanence, the nature that destroys," and "this is the entity destroyed by impermanence.
If the agent and the object were not distinct, then all natures would be permanent and would lack causal nature.
It means that all phenomena are eternally quiescent by their very nature; there is no cause capable of destroying this causal nature. The Tathāgata further spoke in turn, saying:
"The state of all natures being without nature is a matter of impermanence that also has a cause, yet it is not something known by the foolish and ignorant."
What is meant by "having causes"? It refers to all phenomena (*dharmas*), which, due to beginningless non-awakening, falsely appear;

they possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Moment by moment, thought after thought, they do not abide. What is called the abiding of all phenomena in their dharma-position, and the eternal persistence of the characteristics of the world—this is not something known by the ignorant and foolish.
It does not arise from causes that are dissimilar. If it were to arise [from such], then all natures would be entirely impermanent;
this would be a case of dissimilarity. There would be no distinction between the agent and the acted-upon, yet a difference is clearly perceived.

(The Tang translation says: "Mahāmati, a different cause should not produce a different effect. If it could so produce it, then all different phenomena should arise simultaneously. Those phenomena... )

If this dharma were such that the producer and the produced were non-different, there would be no distinction between them; yet we clearly perceive that there is a distinction. How, then, could a different cause produce a different effect?
If its nature were impermanent, it would fall into the category of being a causal agent (*kāraka-hetu*); if it were to fall into that [category], then all natures would be non-final.
If all natures were to fall into the characteristic of being produced by causes, then that which is itself impermanent would have to be impermanent;
yet because the impermanent is impermanent, all natures would not be impermanent and would consequently have to be permanent.
This reason follows from the preceding discussion on the causes for the non-existence or existence of all natures;
it clarifies that falsely imagined diverse causes cannot produce diverse effects. Non-Buddhists falsely imagine that there is a self-nature of impermanence capable of destroying all phenomena;
this is merely like producing a diverse effect from a diverse cause. If such production were to occur, then since the cause is already impermanent, [the effect would likewise be so].
If all dissimilar and distinct phenomena were likewise impermanent, then humans could also give birth to animals, and animals could also give birth to humans;

the producer and the produced would be entirely confused and indistinguishable. Yet we clearly observe that humans produce humans and animals produce animals—how could such distinct causes produce such distinct effects? This is merely [an argument] based on...
The false conceptualization that cause and effect are dissimilar is refuted by exposing the internal contradictions of their own assertions;

however, the underlying intent is actually to reveal that both the agent and the object are non-existent, thereby manifesting that all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are unborn at their very locus. Therefore, it further states:

"If nature were impermanent, it would fall into the category of being a produced cause, etc. This means that if the nature of the cause is impermanent, and since it is said to be capable of destruction, [it cannot be the permanent nature].
It would then fall into the category of being produced by causes, and thus would not be ultimately eternal.

Since all natures are not ultimately eternal—because the characteristic of a cause can be destroyed by impermanence—and because that [cause] itself is impermanent, it follows that everything should be impermanent.
Since all things are impermanent, yet that which is perceived is not impermanent, it must therefore be permanent.
All natures are eternally quiescent; there is no distinction between the agent and the action. This is what is meant by "all natures are eternal," which is the state of being causeless.
If impermanence were to enter into all natures, they would fall into the three periods of time. That past form is accompanied by destruction; the future does not arise because form does not arise.
Present form is accompanied by the characteristic of destruction. Form is a specific accumulation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);

the self-nature of the four great elements and their derivative forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) is indestructible, because it is free from being either different or non-different. [Thus say] all the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
All four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are indestructible. (The Tang translation states: "All non-Buddhists reckon that the essential nature of the four great elements is indestructible.

'Form' (*rūpa*) is simply a differentiation of the great elements; because the great elements and the derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*) are neither different nor non-different, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) likewise does not perish.
All four great elements and derived forms within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) arise and cease among objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), yet they are [ultimately] detached from them.
Regarding the four great elements and derived matter (*mahābhūta-upādāya-rūpa*), what is it that all non-Buddhists contemplate as being impermanent in nature?
[They hold that] the four great elements are not produced, because their intrinsic nature and characteristics are indestructible. (The Tang translation states:

"Within the three realms of existence, there is nothing among the primary and derived elements that does not possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing. How could there be any further nature of impermanence that could produce things and yet not itself perish?")
Beyond this, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain that there is an impermanent self-nature (*svabhāva*) which is indestructible because it enters into all phenomena.

They further claim that all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) fall within the three periods of time, and while all material phenomena of the three times belong to the characteristic of destruction, the self-nature that enters into them is indestructible;
where, then, would it abide? Furthermore, the non-Buddhists constantly maintain that the essential nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is indestructible.

[This view] is refuted; it is shattered by this reason. That is to say, they conceive of form (*rūpa*) as a specific accumulation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), [consisting of] the primary elements and their derivatives (*upādāya-rūpa*), which are neither different nor non-different from one another.
They do not understand that all three realms of existence (*tribhava*) presently manifest—the four great elements and their derivatives—are subsumed under arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya*).
If one were to exclude the form derived from the four great elements, what else would there be for them to contemplate as being distinct and impermanent?

The nature of these [elements] enters into the four great elements, yet it is said that their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indestructible. Above, one exhaustively investigates that there is no dharma capable of destroying them;
here, one further exhaustively investigates that even this [intrinsic nature] lacks indestructibility. Both subject and object are non-existent.
This is what is meant by "all natures and characteristics are, in their very place, unborn. △ Fifth: Abandoning impermanence after having acted.
Regarding the impermanence of that which is devoid of initial creation: it is not that the four great elements (mahābhūtas) are distinct from other four great elements;

for each has its own distinct characteristic by virtue of its own intrinsic nature (svalakṣaṇa), and no differentiation can be found therein. Since they are without differentiation, these do not undergo further creation, nor are they produced through the two types of conditions.
One should know that this is impermanent.
Furthermore, these non-Buddhists reckon that the nature of impermanence is the creator; it creates the four great elements and, having created them, immediately abandons them as impermanence.
It is not the case that the four great elements again produce other four great elements; they say that they cannot create one another.
They mutually produce one another, as fire produces water and water produces earth; each has its own distinct characteristic and cannot produce the other.
Nor do they produce themselves, for their own characteristics possess no differentiation. These elements likewise do not produce further [elements];

if they were to produce further [elements], it would constitute joint production. Regarding the non-activity of the two skillful means: this refers to the arising of fire and water in conjunction, though their essential natures are divergent.

This clarifies that they are not created collectively. Now, since they are neither created by mutual interaction, nor created by themselves, nor created collectively, one should know that the great elements (mahābhūta) arise suddenly as false illusions due to delusion. In their midst there is no master; this is true quiescence.
One should not regard them as impermanent merely because they are newly created and then subsequently abandoned. 6. Impermanence through the Destruction of Form and Location.

Regarding the impermanence of the destruction of shape and location: it refers to the fact that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) do not undergo destruction; they remain ultimately indestructible.

Mahāmati, "ultimately" means that when analyzed down to the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*), even upon observation, one cannot find any difference in the shapes and locations of the four great elements and their derived matter, nor can one perceive length or shortness.
It is not that the four great elements themselves are destroyed; rather, it is the manifestation of the destruction of shape and location that falls within the realm of numerical reckoning.
Treatise:
Regarding shape and location—this refers to the shapes and locations of the four great elements (mahābhūta), such as length and shortness.

One perceives the cessation of the shapes and locations of the four great elements, yet the essence of the four great elements themselves, as well as the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) they produce, does not cease. This is what the Sāṃkhya school maintains regarding the permanence of the four great elements.

This is a treatise. Even when analyzed down to the finest atoms and observed with precision, one can only destroy the visible characteristics of form, shape, length, and shortness produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

It does not destroy the four great elements themselves; that is to say, the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the four great elements and their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is absolutely indestructible—it is only their form and location that are destroyed. Regarding this, the Tathāgata merely says that [such views] fall into the realm of numerical calculation.
Treatise: It has already been demonstrated in great detail that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) which they constitute have no creator.
△ Seventh, matter itself is impermanent.
Regarding "matter itself is impermanent," this means that matter is precisely impermanence; it is the spatial form (*saṃsthāna*) that is impermanent, not the four great elements.

If the four great elements were impermanent, they would not be conventional designations; if conventional designations lacked intrinsic nature, one would fall into the worldly view (Lokāyata), seeing all natures as being merely verbal expressions and failing to perceive the manifestation of their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
"All material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are manifestations of mind alone; they are entirely of an impermanent nature. This is what the Tathāgata has taught.
Externalists reckon that matter itself is impermanent, but [they attribute this] only to its spatial form and not to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

If the four great elements were impermanent, they would not be conventional designations (*saṃvṛti*). That which is said by conventional designation to lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is truly a non-existent dharma."
If that were so, one would fall into the nihilistic worldly doctrine (*lokāyata*), for there would be mere verbal expression without the self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of dharmas.

Therefore, know that the self-characteristics of all dharmas—the true reality as it is—can only be attained through internal realization via the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the manifestation of one's own mind.
This is beyond the reach of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). 8. The impermanence of transformation within the eight substances.

Regarding impermanence as transformation: this refers to the manifestation of a different state of form (*rūpa*), not of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). It is like gold being transformed into an ornament;

it manifests through transformation, yet the nature of the gold is not destroyed. Only the configuration of the ornament is destroyed. In the same way, the transformation of other natures and so forth is also like this.

The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon that between the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), there exists an impermanent nature that undergoes transformation at every moment, just as milk transforms into curd and a different color and nature manifest.

As for those things that are not the four great elements, they are likewise like the forms and locations of the four great elements seen to perish, yet the essential nature of the four great elements does not perish; it is like gold being fashioned into ornaments—it merely manifests through transformation.
It is not that the nature of gold is destroyed; rather, it is other natures [that change]. This means that the transformation of all phenomena is likewise entirely so.
△ Ninth: Summarizing the seven kinds of false conceptualizations regarding impermanence.

In this way, when the fire of false discrimination belonging to various non-Buddhists who hold the view of impermanence burns the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not burned.

As for the claim that "if each of their own specific characteristics were to be destroyed," then the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced by the four great elements would be annihilated. (The Wei translation states:
"The non-Buddhists say: 'If fire could burn the great elements, then the great elements would be cut off and perish; therefore, it does not burn them.'")

These comprise seven types of false discrimination in total. Roughly speaking, apart from what manifests as the forms of the four great elements, there exists a separate self-substance of the four great elements that cannot be burned by fire.
If it were capable of being burned, then both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) would all be annihilated;
this would mean they are half-born-and-ceasing and half-unborn-and-non-ceasing. This is truly due to the failure to realize that [all things] are one's own mind.
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not realize that all phenomena are mind-only, fundamentally without arising and without ceasing. Yet, through deluded vision, one perceives arising and ceasing;

through delusion, one differentiates between essence and attributes; and one constantly takes the permanent to be impermanent and the impermanent to be permanent—this constitutes nothing but total inversion.
10. Showing that what the Tathāgata has taught regarding the non-permanent and the impermanent is intended to reveal that which is the direct perception of one’s own mind.
Mahāmati, the arising of my teaching is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why is this? It is because external objects are not determinate;

I teach only the subtle mind of the three realms of existence, and do not speak of the arising and ceasing of various marks, nor of the combinations and distinctions of the four great elements and the derivative forms produced by them.
Thus, the two kinds of things—grasping and the grasped—are subsumed within false imagination. (The Wei translation says: "Only...")

These are the four great elements (mahābhūta) in combination; neither the elements nor the objects (viṣaya) are substantially real dharmas. By means of the deluded mind, one discriminates between these two kinds of dharmas—the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka).

One should know these two kinds of false imagination (vikalpa), abandon the two views of external existence and non-existence, and awaken to the manifestation of one’s own mind as the measure of reality (svacittadṛśyamātra).
False imagination arises from mental activity (saṃskāra); it does not arise without activity. It is apart from the mind.
The conceptualization of existence and non-existence—whether mundane, supramundane, or the highest supramundane—all phenomena are neither eternal nor impermanent.
Failing to realize that these are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, one falls into a continuous succession of dualistic and evil views.
All non-Buddhists fail to realize their own false imaginings; such ordinary people lack any fundamental basis, whether regarding the mundane, the supramundane, or the highest supramundane.
In the interim, [the teaching] is supreme. It arises from the discourse on false discrimination and is not something perceived by ordinary fools.
The various dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are neither permanent nor impermanent; this is because he does not grasp at external natures as having arising and ceasing.
He teaches only that the three realms of existence are mind-only. This is the same fundamental intent of all Tathāgatas throughout the three periods of time. This is because, through various...
Arising and ceasing occur through the conjunction of causes and conditions among the four great elements and derived matter; thus, there appears to be differentiation.

However, in reality, there is neither a creator nor that which is created. Since beginningless time, due to non-awakening, these have manifested all at once. This is what is meant by "the three realms of existence are mind-only.
Failing to realize that they are mind-only, one gives rise to the two kinds of false imaginings—the subject and the object—and thereby falls into the extremes of existence and non-existence.
Upon seeing and realizing this, one immediately becomes detached; there is only the measure of the single mind.

Therefore, know that all dharmas—the four great elements, internal and external forms, and the mind—arise from deluded conceptualization, and from these arise all karmic actions. These various karmic actions...

There is no such thing as truly existent arising, nor does it depend upon non-existence. Rather, when one is free from the two kinds of conceptual discrimination—existence and non-existence—then that which is the manifestation of one's own mind appears directly before one. This is why the Tathāgata speaks of neither permanence nor impermanence;
he teaches the three types of discriminative dharmas—mundane, supramundane, and the most excellent supramundane—based on deluded thought, yet these cannot be called permanent.
It is precisely through conceptual construction that the three kinds of non-discriminative wisdom—the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane—are manifested.

It cannot be said that these are impermanent; rather, the two types of evil views held by non-Buddhists arise solely from the failure to realize that all things are the manifestation of one's own mind.

Because one cannot, amidst false conceptualization and discrimination, realize enlightenment in the present moment and attain the fundamental wisdom of non-discrimination, the Tathāgata has established three kinds of dharmas based on the discriminations of sentient beings to explain expedient means;
these are not perceived by the ignorant and deluded. △ Eleven: General Summary Verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Detached from initial creation, as well as from differences in form and location, and regarding nature and matter as impermanent—these are the deluded imaginings of the outsiders. All natures are indestructible; the Great Elements abide in their own self-nature.
The outsiders, with their notion of impermanence, are submerged in various views. Those various outsiders do not [possess] such [wisdom]."
If birth were to cease, the great nature would be eternal; what then would be meant by the perception of impermanence? All is but the measure of the mind.
Two kinds of mind flow forth: the grasper and the grasped. There is no self, nor anything belonging to a self. Brahmā is the root of the tree;
its branches extend everywhere. Thus I have taught: it is solely the measure of that mind.
The verse states that all that is conceived by non-Buddhists as impermanent is merely deluded by false imagination. In reality, all dharmas possess no characteristic of destruction;
the natures of the great elements each abide in their own dharma-position, and all arising and ceasing [are likewise devoid of inherent nature].
The suchness of specific characteristics arises precisely from not knowing the measure of the mind, mistakenly taking it to be impermanent, and being submerged by views.
If one knows that all things are mind-only, then the circulation of the two views is also a manifestation of mind-only. At this very moment, subject and object are subsumed within emptiness;
there is no creator. It is entirely delusion and entirely truth—how could there be anything else? Therefore, it is right within what they themselves calculate.
This means that Brahmā is regarded as the root of the tree, capable of producing all sentient beings throughout the three realms;

yet the Tathāgata teaches that these various forms of delusion and falsehood are all merely the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*). To awaken to this is itself Bodhi; there is no need for further transformation.

This is taught by the Tathāgata to show people how, even regarding the false calculations of non-Buddhists, if they suddenly realize their error, they are identical to what was originally attained. Thus does the Tathāgata instruct humanity.

This may be called profoundly compassionate. ○ The preceding four sections demonstrate that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is neither eternal nor impermanent, concluding the section on how this differs from the heterodox paths.

The fifth section demonstrates that the Tathāgata’s ultimate meaning (paramārtha) instantaneously eliminates all stages (bhūmis), uniquely revealing Mind-Only (cittamātra). This is divided into five parts.
△ First, in response to Mahāmati’s question regarding meditative absorption (samāpatti), he first demonstrates the characteristics of the practices of the seventh and eighth stages.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) of all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

If one is skilled in the characteristics of this sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi, I and the other bodhisattvas shall never recklessly abandon the gateway to the bliss of cessation-samādhi, nor fall into [the state of] one-ness."
[To all] Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the deluded followers of external paths, the Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I pray that You will explain it for us. The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the sixth stage, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the seventh stage enter meditative absorption moment by moment, which is free from the characteristics of the self-nature of all phenomena; this is not the case for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fall into the awakening of active practice and enter the meditative absorption that extinguishes the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper. Therefore...

In the seventh stage, there is no meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of mindfulness; one attains the non-differentiated characteristic of all phenomena, which is beyond the scope [of lower vehicles].

One attains the nature of various characteristics and awakens to the meditative absorption regarding the wholesome and unwholesome natures and characteristics of all phenomena. (The Wei translation states:

"Therefore, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot enter the seventh stage moment by moment into the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas give rise to alarm...")

It is because they fear falling into the state where all phenomena lack distinct characteristics; rather, by perceiving the various distinct characteristics of all phenomena—such as existent and non-existent dharmas, wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, and similar and dissimilar characteristics—they enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). For this reason, in the seventh stage, there is no meditative attainment of wholesome thought (*kuśala-smṛti-samādhi*).
Mahāmati, in the eighth stage, the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of the mind, intellect, and consciousness of Bodhisattvas, as well as those of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, [cease].
The characteristics cease;

one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). This exists in all three vehicles. It serves generally as an antidote to the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) of ordinary beings, merely to distance oneself from all conceptual thoughts of "self" and "what belongs to self. However, those of the two vehicles do not realize that these are the manifestations of their own minds.
Like an illusion and like a dream, through the application of antidotes, they are established as real dharmas. Regarding the dharma of samādhi, they have not yet forgotten subject and object;
because there is still conceptualization and effort, this is not equal to the moment-to-moment right reception (*samāpatti*) of a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage.
Although those from the first to the sixth stages certainly cannot match the moment-to-moment right reception of the seventh stage, by means of entering the Mahāyāna...

Regarding the section on the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*): although there is an antidote (*pratipakṣa*), one has not yet abandoned conceptual activity (*vikalpa-caryā*). Nevertheless, all of this belongs to the stage of skillful means (*upāya*) and does not constitute actual reality (*bhūtadharma*).

Thus, one knows that the reason the seventh stage attains meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in every thought-moment is that, by realizing that which appears as one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*), one has already relinquished skillful means;

having departed from the characteristics of the self-nature of all phenomena (*sarvabhāvasvabhāvanimitta*), one attains non-discriminative wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*). These two—[the abandonment of means and the attainment of non-discrimination]—are...

This is because the vehicle [of the two vehicles] is not the proper portion [for this]. To "attain the various characteristics and natures" and "awaken to the characteristics and natures of good and evil in all dharmas while entering samādhi" specifically refers to those of the two vehicles who fear falling into the undifferentiated characteristic;

they wish to attain the various characteristics and natures of good and evil and enter samādhi, yet they abandon birth and hasten toward extinction, their discrimination not yet forgotten. This is what is meant by: ...with the so-called... (the remainder of the passage is omitted as per instructions).

The profound stillness merges with profound stillness, returning to the limit of consciousness; therefore, there is no wholesome mindfulness or meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in the seven stages.

"Wholesome mindfulness" refers to every moment of thought, which is also non-thought. As for the statement that only in the eighth stage can the delusive imaginings of the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*) of the two vehicles be extinguished:

this means that upon reaching the eighth stage, one attains the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), and the mind and consciousness finally come to an end. From the first stage up to the seventh stage—

Although one realizes that all is but the manifestation of one's own mind and is thus able to transcend the mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), this is only fully perfected upon reaching the eighth stage;

therefore, it is said that [the defilements] are extinguished in the eighth stage. While from the seventh stage onward there is no longer any conceptualization of expedient means and one attains meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in every moment, it is not said that they are extinguished in the seventh stage because the power of meditative absorption is so preeminent that the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) has not yet been fully manifested, and due to the greatness of one’s original vows.
It is pitiful that one must still rely on recollection; therefore, it is not said to be "ultimate extinction.

Yet, even upon reaching the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one must still rely on the support of the mind of awakening through samādhi before being able to ultimately fulfill the stage of a Tathāgata—how much more so for the seventh stage!

Mahāmati, having already distinguished between the false and the correct based on the preceding marks of permanence and impermanence, he now requests instruction regarding the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the various stages, desiring to obtain...

This clarifies the distinction between the Mahāyāna and the Two Vehicles, as well as the distinctions between the various stages (*bhūmi*) of the Bodhisattva, so as to illuminate the progress of all practitioners.
△ Second, it shows the similarities and differences between the first through the seventh stages and those of the Two Vehicles.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from the first stage up to the seventh stage contemplate the extent of the mind, mentality, and consciousness within the triple world.
They are free from the notions of "I" and "mine," yet they still practice based on their own false imaginings and fall into the various marks of external natures.

Fools are caught by the two aspects of their own minds—the grasper and the grasped—and thus turn toward ignorance; they fail to realize that they have been perfumed by the beginningless faults of evil and the deceptive habitual tendencies.
Regarding the passage from the first stage up to the seventh stage: both the Wei and Tang translations state that it extends from the first to the sixth stage.

This is because the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) possessed by Bodhisattvas are the same as those of the Two Vehicles up to the sixth stage; thus, the original translation records what was perceived by the Bodhisattva only up to the sixth stage.
This distinguishes it from the Two Vehicles; therefore, it is called the "seventh stage. The following text immediately presents the characteristics of the eighth stage.

Because the Bodhisattva realizes that all is the measure of his own mind, he is able to observe that everything within and without the triple world is manifested through the non-awakening of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Fundamentally, there is no "mine" (*mama*); it is merely one's own deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that perceives external natures and characteristics. This is not the case for the Two Vehicles.
Failing to realize their own minds, they fall into the two extremes of existence and non-existence and give rise to the objective and subjective grasping of objects;

therefore, although they share the same meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) as those on the sixth stage, the Bodhisattva enters absorption by thoroughly realizing that all natures lack the characteristic of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), whereas the followers of the Two Vehicles enter absorption by awakening to various distinct characteristics and their aspirations. One [the Bodhisattva] does so through the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*).
To purify present habits: first, because of non-awakening and lack of knowledge, one is driven by beginningless, false habitual tendencies;
thus, the provisional and the real are clearly distinguished in what is realized. △ Third, showing the maintenance of awakening through the samādhi of the eighth stage.
Mahāmati, regarding the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the eighth stage: the bodhisattva is sustained by the awakening of samādhi.
Therefore, because of the bliss of the gate of samādhi, they do not enter parinirvāṇa. If they were not so sustained, the stage of the Tathāgata would not be fulfilled;
for, by abandoning all conditioned activities for the sake of sentient beings, the lineage of the Buddhas would be severed. Thus, the Buddhas...
World-Honored One, in order to demonstrate the inconceivable and immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata, [it is said that] Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
being led by the pleasure obtained through the gates of samādhi, give rise to the notion that they have attained nirvāṇa.
Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage also possess the gate of the samādhi-bliss of the two vehicles;
yet, by the power of their original vows, although they abide in samādhi, they are sustained by awakening and therefore do not enter parinirvāṇa.

If they were not so sustained, they would be unable to fulfill the stage of the Tathāgata, would abandon sentient beings, and the lineage of the Buddhas would be severed. Thus, in the *Avataṃsaka*, it is said that up to the eighth stage of the Bodhisattva...
"Sā. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions exhorted him with one voice, saying: "That which you have attained is also shared by those of the Two Vehicles;

you should therefore contemplate the immeasurable and inconceivable merit [of this state]. Thus, one knows that the arousal of the eighth stage is entirely due to the spiritual power of all Buddhas, so that one does not fall into the intoxicated bliss of the samādhis of the Two Vehicles. Although it is the spiritual power of the Buddhas, it is described as "samādhi."

Regarding "Awakened Sustenance": when a Bodhisattva first abides in the stage of initial resolve, by awakening to the fact that all is the manifestation of one's own mind, they enter the awakening of the Tathāgata.
Through this shared essence, they are sustained and there is a mutual resonance between cause and response. Within samādhi, the Buddha’s own self-awakening spontaneously stirs; it is inconceivable.
△ Fourth, showing the relinquishing of samādhi in the seventh and eighth stages. Skillfully... [self...]

"O Mahāmati, regarding the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*), I have established the seven stages (*bhūmi*) for those who have well cultivated the characteristics of the mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*); who have well cultivated the grasping of 'I' and 'mine';

who have well cultivated the non-selfhood of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*); who have well cultivated arising and ceasing, as well as specific and general characteristics; and who have attained mastery in the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the power of certainty, and the gates of samādhi."

The sequential continuity of the stages (*bhūmi*) is established as a method for entering the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), so that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas do not fail to perceive their own and common characteristics, nor become unskilled in the seven stages and fall into the wrong paths of externalists.

Therefore, Mahāmati, the sequential continuity of the stages and the triple world are established; yet, in reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing, except for what is the manifestation of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*).

Various types of conduct are not perceived by the foolish. That which is not perceived by the foolish refers to what I and all Buddhas have taught regarding the sequential continuity of the stages (*bhūmi*), as well as the various types of conduct within the three realms.
"Distinction" means to analyze and expound in detail. The Tathāgata analyzes and expounds this regarding the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).

This refers to the fact that at the seventh stage, the causes for rebirth have already been severed, making it similar to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); because it is particularly prone to defilement, he provides this detailed analysis.

If one skillfully distinguishes mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*) as all being manifestations of one's own mind, there is neither self nor what belongs to a self. When there is no self, then [the mind] is gathered.
When there is no person and no object, one then grasps the non-existence of dharmas. When there is neither person nor dharma, one is free from the longing for common or distinct characteristics.
Because those of the two vehicles perceive various distinct characteristics, they long for and easily attain meditative absorption (samāpatti) and nirvāṇa.

If one can skillfully master this, then one will be able to fully comprehend the meaning of the Dharma of the One Vehicle and become proficient in the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) regarding the gates of samādhi.
Sustained by the power of definitive self-awakening, one illuminates the various stages (*bhūmi*) and advances in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

Therefore, it is said that one must not allow the bodhisattva to remain unaware of the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), nor to become unskilled in the seven stages and fall onto the deviant paths of externalists.
This is the intent behind the Tathāgata’s establishment of the stages; he was especially meticulous regarding the seventh stage, fearing a fall into error.

This is merely a brief summary. Furthermore, it is said that there is truly neither arising nor ceasing, apart from what is manifested by one’s own mind—namely, the sequential succession of the stages (*bhūmi*) and the various practices within the triple world (*tridhātu*).

From beginning to end, the Tathāgata has upheld the Dharma-gate of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*), asserting that it is only one’s own mind; there are no successive stages, nor is there anything at all in the triple world.
As for the mode of practice: having realized that all is but the measure of one's own mind, one attains non-existence; from this state of non-existence, one establishes all dharmas.
This is for the sake of delivering those who have not yet awakened, and not for the sake of those who are already awakened.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, intoxicated by the intoxication of the bliss of the cessation-samādhi (nirodha-samādhi) in the eighth Bodhisattva stage, are unskilled in the manifestation of their own minds.
Obstructed by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of self-characteristics and common characteristics, they fall into the view of grasping at the non-existence of persons and phenomena.
They conceive of a false nirvana, which is not the awakening of the wisdom of true cessation. Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva perceives...
The joy of the gate of the samādhi of cessation; the fulfillment of great compassion through the pity of original vows; knowing and discerning the ten inexhaustible phrases;

not conceiving the notion of nirvāṇa through false imagination—because such false imagination does not arise, he has already entered nirvāṇa. Being free from the false imagination of grasping and that which is grasped, he realizes the manifestation of his own mind as the only measure;
false imagination regarding all phenomena does not arise, and he does not fall into the realm of mind, thought, or mentation.
