There is no difference between sentient beings, wisdom, and its radiance (*jñāna-tathatā-jvālā*). All phenomena are entirely quiescent; it is merely that one does not recognize one's own...
The mind manifests as false conceptualization; thus, false conceptualization arises.
If consciousness is extinguished, the original limit of birth and death is itself the original limit of nirvana.

Because one does not know how to accord with this, false views arise, whereby the characteristics of birth and death appear distinct from the characteristics of nirvana, resulting in the fault of habitual tendencies. If one knows that [all] is manifested by one's own mind, [birth and death cease].
Death and nirvana are fundamentally not two distinct boundaries. When the causes of deluded habituation are extinguished, one perceives that external phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
thus, one is able to transform the body of false conceptualization and accord with the cycle of birth and death—this is called liberation, and it is not annihilation.
Therefore, it is said to be "boundless. This does not mean that there is absolutely no fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).

It is simply because one does not know this fundamental limit that one falsely perceives birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, giving rise to the notion of being "bounded. To counteract such false conceptualization, the "boundless" is taught.

This is intended to lead one to observe that both internally and externally, apart from false conceptualization, there is no such thing as the name "sentient being," nor are there any dharmas such as cognition (*jñāna*) or its radiance (*jvālā*).
All phenomena are entirely quiescent. Thus one knows that the birth and death of sentient beings all arise from deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

If one does not know that [the world] is a manifestation of one's own mind, then deluded conceptualization arises; if one knows it is a manifestation of one's own mind, then deluded conceptualization ceases.
When it ceases, one accords with the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). Birth and death and nirvāṇa are both like dreams and illusions. △ Tenth: General Verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Observe all the Guides, who are like the sands of the Ganges:

They are neither destroyed nor do they depart, Nor are they ultimately [non-existent]; this is what constitutes equality. Observe all the Tathāgatas, who are equal in number to the sands of the Ganges:
They are entirely free from all faults; though they flow along with the stream, their nature is eternal. This is..."
The Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, is neither destroyed nor departed. If there were yet another ultimate state, then nirvāṇa and saṃsāra would not be equal.
If they were not equal, then it would belong to the category of conditioned causes; that which is conditioned is impermanent and entails many faults and afflictions.

Therefore, know that if one merely eliminates the causes of delusive thoughts, one will attain the true nature as it flows along and perceive the Tathāgata’s realm of self-awakening, which is identical to the limit of birth-and-death, quiescent and eternally abiding. This realm of the Tathāgata is established through the analogy of the sands of the Ganges as a self-evident realization;
it transcends the faults of verbal expression. Although there are words and metaphors, it is ultimately inconceivable. ○

The first section above concludes by demonstrating that the Dharmakāya transcends worldly perspectives. Second, it demonstrates that the Dharmakāya is untainted (*anāsrava*) and does not possess the nature of momentariness (*kṣaṇika*).
This is divided into two parts. First, it demonstrates the momentariness of all phenomena, which is further divided into two.
△ First, prior to demonstrating the meaning of momentariness and non-momentariness, it first enumerates all phenomena.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the characteristic of the momentary destruction of all dharmas.
World-Honored One, what is meant by 'all dharmas are momentary'? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall speak for your sake. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "'All dharmas' refers to those that are wholesome, unwholesome," and so forth.
Wholesome; indeterminate; conditioned; unconditioned; mundane; supramundane; faulty; faultless; with outflows; without outflows.

"Perception" and "non-perception"—these questions regarding the meaning of *kṣaṇa* (moment) are intended to reveal that which is not momentary. That which does not abide from moment to moment is called *kṣaṇa*;
it is also termed the "characteristic of disintegration" and the "characteristic of emptiness. That all phenomena are momentary means they are manifestations of one's own mind.

All internal and external phenomena do not abide for even a single moment. Because they do not recognize that their own minds are not subject to the principle of momentariness (*kṣaṇika*), they perceive only what appears to them as arising and ceasing moment by moment and failing to abide for an instant;

thus, they erroneously conclude that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are likewise subject to extinction, giving rise to the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). They fail to realize that while all phenomena are momentary, there are those that are not momentary.
This is not something discerned by the followers of the Two Vehicles. Through a series of questions and answers, this essential point is elucidated in its entirety.
First, all dharmas are listed to await their subsequent clarification.

Mahāmati, in brief, the mind, the thought, the mental consciousness, and the habit-energies (vāsanā) are the causes of the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha). These are the mind, the thought, and the mental consciousness...
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of consciousness are nurtured by the false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) of the ordinary and ignorant regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome.

To speak briefly of the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*): all phenomena arise from the five aggregates, and these five aggregates, in turn, are nurtured by having the habitual tendencies of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as their cause. The ordinary and ignorant [conceive of] the wholesome and unwholesome through false conceptualization.
"Perception" refers to the tainted, deluded perceptions of the six classes of ordinary beings within the three realms; this constitutes the meaning of "momentariness.

Mahāmati, that which consists of dwelling in the bliss of the present life through the meditative absorption of the bliss of samādhi and the correct reception of samādhi is called the virtuous, untainted state of the noble ones.
The characteristic of the untainted cause of the noble ones of the Three Vehicles is not momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
It is manifested through dwelling in the bliss of the Dharma attained by practicing samādhi, and is subsequently elucidated. △ Second, showing the meaning of "momentary."
“Mahāmati, as for the wholesome and the unwholesome, they refer to the eight consciousnesses. What are these eight?

They are the Tathāgatagarbha, which is called the ‘storehouse consciousness’ (ālayavijñāna), along with the mind (manas), the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses. These are not what is taught by the non-Buddhists.

Mahāmati, the five groups of sensory consciousnesses, together with the mind, the mental consciousness, and the manas, possess both wholesome and unwholesome characteristics; they undergo successive transformation and disintegration, yet they flow on in a continuous stream, giving rise to an indestructible body.”

They arise and they cease. Failing to realize that these are manifestations of one's own mind, as each preceding moment ceases, another consciousness arises. It grasps at the distinctions of forms and characteristics;
it arises in conjunction with the mental consciousness and the five sensory consciousnesses. Not abiding for even a single moment is called "kṣaṇa" (moment).
This refers to wholesome, unwholesome, and impure consciousnesses. They possess an original indestructible body, yet they erroneously follow along with arising and ceasing;

therefore, they are momentary (*kṣaṇika*). This is stated in order to reveal that [the Tathāgatagarbha] is not momentary. The Tathāgatagarbha is called the "consciousness-store" (*vijñānagarbha*); it is not what is taught by non-Buddhists.
This is because non-Buddhists do not know that the consciousness-store is the Tathāgatagarbha. Thus, when the five consciousnesses rely upon the mind, [it is this store that is meant].
When the signs of good and evil arising from the mind and mental consciousness undergo successive transformation and destruction, that continuity of the stream does not perish;
it likewise arises together with the body along with the various consciousnesses and perishes together with the body.

Because one fundamentally fails to realize that what appears is merely the manifestation of one’s own mind, one is unable to abide within the sequential cessation of these manifestations, and thus further consciousnesses continue to follow.

That which is emphasized by long-standing habituation gives rise to various forms and appearances. This, in turn, draws forth the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), wherein the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*) correspond to form the meaning of a *kṣaṇa* (moment). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The first is the root of beginningless birth and death, which is that very攀緣心 (*pān-yuan-xin*, the攀緣心) you and all sentient beings now take as your own nature. The second is beginningless bodhi..."
The essence of nirvāṇa is fundamentally pure; it is your present fundamental clarity of consciousness that is able to give rise to all conditions.
That which is lost amidst these conditions is due to sentient beings having discarded this original clarity; thus, though they act all day long, they remain unaware of it.
They enter the various realms of existence in vain. This unbroken continuity arises because they fundamentally lack awakening and erroneously follow the cycle of arising and ceasing;

are they not those who, being left behind by the conditions that give rise to all phenomena, enter the various realms in vain? Truly, this is to be pitied. The first section above concludes the demonstration that all dharmas are momentary.
The second section demonstrates that untainted habitual tendencies (*anāsrava-vāsanā*) are not momentary; it is divided into five parts. △
First, he demonstrates the meaning of the momentary (*kṣaṇika*) and the non-momentary.
Mahāmati, "momentary" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*, the *tathāgatagarbha*, and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the co-emergent mental consciousness (*manas*).

The "non-momentary" refers to the untainted habitual tendencies (*anāsrava-vāsanā*). This is not realized by ordinary, ignorant people because they are attached to the doctrine of momentariness; thus, they do not perceive the One.
All phenomena are both momentary and non-momentary; this is because the view of annihilation destroys unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
This precisely clarifies the meaning of being both momentary and non-momentary.

When one is deluded regarding the *tathāgatagarbha* and it becomes the *ālayavijñāna*, there arises the co-emergent consciousness of the mind (*manas*), which forms habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); this constitutes the momentary. However, if one penetrates the co-emergent consciousness of the mind...
They exist due to delusion, yet fundamentally lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, the *ālayavijñāna* is transformed into the *tathāgatagarbha*.

These untainted habitual tendencies (*anāsrava-vāsanā*) do not possess the characteristic of momentariness (*kṣaṇika-artha*), a truth that is not perceived by ordinary, ignorant people. Such ordinary, ignorant people perceive all phenomena as merely momentary;
they do not know that among all phenomena, some are momentary while others are non-momentary. They thus recklessly employ the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) to destroy [the Dharma].
Because it is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), we know that all sentient beings fail to awaken to and fail to understand this, mistakenly following along with birth and extinction.
This is why the Tathāgata [teaches] the *asādhāraṇa-siddhānta* (the non-common tenet). △ Second, showing that the Tathāgatagarbha is not momentary (*akṣaṇika*).
Mahāmati, the seven consciousnesses do not undergo transmigration; they do not experience suffering or pleasure, nor are they the cause of nirvāṇa.

Mahāmati, the tathāgatagarbha experiences suffering and pleasure, is accompanied by their causes, and undergoes birth and cessation; it is intoxicated by the four stages of dwelling and the stage of ignorance.
Ordinary fools do not awaken; their minds are perfumed by the perceptions of false conceptualization in every moment.

The seven consciousnesses, arising through non-awakening, falsely give rise to the perceived portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) and grasp it as their own essence. Since this false essence is fundamentally empty, it is not the cause of *nirvāṇa*.
While the Tathāgatagarbha exists within the state of delusion, one falsely experiences suffering and pleasure, yet it remains identical to *nirvāṇa*.
Due to the conjunction of causal characteristics, although they arise and perish together with all sensations, the causal characteristics themselves do not perish.

Because they are intoxicated by the five abodes, ordinary fools do not perceive this and merely give rise to the view of momentariness. As for that which does not transmigrate: the seven consciousnesses depend upon the eighth consciousness and perfuse it moment by moment;
though there appears to be a real self, it does not abide for even a single moment. This continues until the state of fainting, where only...

There are eight consciousnesses; therefore, it is said that they do not transmigrate. Until one reaches a state of fainting or unconsciousness, there is always a potentiality capable of summoning suffering or pleasure, yet while knowing suffering and knowing pleasure, these are not what is being experienced by those [consciousnesses]; therefore, it is said that they do not receive suffering or pleasure.

Deluded views perceive arising and ceasing, which do not abide for even a single moment; from beginning to end, they simply remain unaware. The four abidings belong to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); [this refers to] ignorance (*avidyā*).
[The section on] "Abiding" belongs to the Two Vehicles. This concludes the commentary on the "Manifestation" chapter.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, just as gold, vajra, and the relics of the Buddha possess extraordinary qualities and are never destroyed, so it is, Mahāmati.
If there were such a thing as a momentary interval between attainments, then the noble would cease to be noble; yet the noble have never ceased to be noble. As...
O Vajra of Gold, though it passes through kalpas, its weight does not diminish.
Why do the foolish and ignorant, being unskilled in my hidden teaching, conceive of all internal and external phenomena as being momentary?
Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgatagarbha, the untainted realized Dharma, is not of a momentary nature.
The gold-vajra and the Buddha-relics—these two extraordinary and indestructible substances—are used as metaphors for the uninterrupted true nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Not following the momentariness of all phenomena, the ignorant and foolish, lacking wisdom, do not understand the secret treasury of the Tathāgata;
they consider it identical to all other phenomena and conceive of it as being momentary. This is why they destroy the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
△ Third, showing that the mundane and supramundane *pāramitās* are not separate from momentariness.

The Bodhisattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said that one attains perfect enlightenment by fulfilling the six pāramitās, what are these six?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are three kinds of distinctions regarding the pāramitās."
That is to say: the worldly, the world-transcending, and the world-transcending supreme. Mahāmati, as for the worldly *pāramitās*:

they involve attachment to the grasping of "self" and "mine," and the grasping of the two extremes; they lead to various places of rebirth because one delights in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and textures.
Thus one fulfills the *dāna-pāramitā*. The same applies to morality, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
The supernatural powers of ordinary beings and birth in the Brahma heavens are due to the preceding illumination;
thus, the meaning of "non-momentariness" is established. Here, he again asks about the six *pāramitās*, intending to say:
if they were not momentary, there would be no six types; if they belonged to the momentary, they could not bring fulfillment for that which is non-momentary.
This is the cause. There are three kinds of *pāramitās*. First, regarding the mundane: I am the giver, that which is given is the object, and the act of giving is the means;
by grasping at these as subject and object, one does not depart from the two extremes of existence and non-existence.

Seeking a superior rebirth, this is the causal process of outflows (*sāsrava*) performed by ordinary beings. As for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), these refer to the five superknowledges of devas and humans.

Mahāmati, as for the supramundane pāramitās: because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fall into the grasping of nirvāṇa, they practice the six pāramitās while delighting in their own personal nirvāṇic bliss.
The supramundane *pāramitās*, although they do not embrace worldly causes and effects, nevertheless embrace *nirvāṇa* as a means for the bliss of self-deliverance;
yet this is also not ultimate. △ Fourth, showing that the supreme-supreme supramundane *pāramitās* are not of a momentary nature.

Regarding the supramundane, supreme-to-the-supreme *pāramitā*: because one awakens to the fact that the measure of false discrimination manifested from one’s own mind is comprised of both [subject and object], and because one realizes that these two are of one's own mind, one does not give rise to false discrimination.
One does not grasp at the various realms of existence as being real, and does not cling to the forms and marks of one’s own mind.
For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, one gives rise to the *dāna-pāramitā* and initiates the supreme-to-the-supreme skillful means. Thus...
The precept in which conceptualization does not arise regarding those objects is the *śīla-pāramitā*.
The patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is that very non-arising of conceptualization through knowing the grasped and the grasper.

The *vīrya-pāramitā* is the non-arising of conceptualization through diligent application during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, and through practice in accordance with skillful means. When all conceptualizations have been completely extinguished...
To be gathered within the nirvāṇa of the śrāvaka is the dhyāna-pāramitā. To observe with wisdom that the false imaginings of one’s own mind lack intrinsic nature,
thereby not falling into the two extremes, and to attain the noble realization of self-awakening through the successive transformation of the body into something superior and indestructible—
this is the prajñā-pāramitā.

The supreme *pāramitā* consists in awakening to the fact that all is the manifestation of one’s own mind, and in thoroughly understanding the duality of subject and object within conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Within the measure of one’s own mind, these two do not reach one another; it is only due to non-awakening that they appear. Once awakened, they do not arise.

Therefore, one does not grasp at the various realms of existence as belonging to oneself, nor does one give rise to attachment toward external forms apart from one’s own mind. This is for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
That which is born as the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is that which counteracts stinginess and greed, and is also able to remedy the stinginess and greed of others.
Practicing generosity in accordance with its own nature is the supreme skillful means (*upāya*).

Reaching the state where conceptual proliferation (*vikalpa*) does not arise, one accords with the nature of non-defilement and accomplishes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). One accords with the nature of non-anger and knows...
The grasper and the grasped are both unattainable; this is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

During the first, middle, and last watches of the night, one accords with the suchness of the original limit of self-nature, giving rise to no conceptual discrimination; this is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

Within the fundamental self-nature, one does not produce divergent characteristics and does not follow the samādhis of the two vehicles that involve the subject-object duality of grasping; this is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). To thoroughly penetrate all things is [the perfection of wisdom].
Delusive thoughts lack intrinsic nature; they do not create obstacles where they arise, nor do they abide in their original positions where they do not arise.
Free from all existence and non-existence, solitary and without companion, the body of wisdom does not perish. By means of this, one accomplishes the noble path of self-awakening;
this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). According to these six perfections, when they are present in the world, they serve as the fields [of merit].
Because of those causes, the characteristics of the resulting fruits are entirely established as momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

Although the cause for transcending the world is not momentary, when measured against the nature of nirvāṇa—which is devoid of subject and object—it is likewise subsumed within the momentary; it is exclusively the supreme transcendence of the world.
There is only one’s own mind. Apart from one’s own mind, there are no six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā). When function arises in accordance with the nature, the function returns to the essence;
this is not a matter of momentariness (kṣaṇika). To fulfill the intent of the question, all is fully contained beyond words and can be understood through principle.
△ Fifth, the summary conclusion on the equality of momentariness and non-momentariness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Empty, impermanent, and momentary—these are constructed by the deluded thoughts of the foolish.
Like a river, a lamp, or a seed, they give rise to the notion of momentariness. When moments cease their turbulence, there is tranquility and freedom from activity;
all phenomena are unborn—this is the meaning of 'moment' as I teach it."
These two verses explain why the Tathāgata speaks of the *kṣaṇa* (moment).

It is intended to point out that the conditioned phenomena of the deluded world are like a flowing river, like the flame of a lamp, and like seeds that perish rapidly; this is done so that one may conceive of them as *kṣaṇas*.
If one penetrates the nature of the *kṣaṇa*, then afflictions will naturally subside, one will attain a state of tranquility, and will remain far removed from delusive conceptualization.
Only now do I realize that all phenomena are entirely manifestations of the mind alone; they possess no intrinsic nature and are, in their very essence, unarisen.
This is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s teaching regarding the momentary (kṣaṇika).
When things arise, they are subject to cessation. (The Wei translation says: "That which first arises is subject to cessation. This is not taught for the sake of the ignorant.
It is the nature of uninterrupted continuity, perfumed by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), with ignorance (*avidyā*) as its cause;

from that, the mind arises. Until form (*rūpa*) has yet to arise, what division exists in the interval? (The Tang translation says: "Before one can discern the coming of form, what is there in the interim?")
When a thing arises, it is subject to cessation; that is to say, a thing perishes at the very moment of its initial arising.

Because one does not understand the Tathāgatagarbha, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). Through the non-awakening of ignorance, there is deluded movement that constitutes karma—this is what is meant by "initial arising."
If one does not realize that movement is illusory, then the nature of non-arising arises; yet this non-arising is itself extinguished in the very moment it occurs.
The deluded do not understand this, and thus there is uninterrupted continuity. This is what is perfumed by ignorance and false conceptualization.

Ignorance acts as the cause, and the deluded mind arises in dependence upon it. Tracing back to the time before ignorance and illusory movement had attached themselves to form, there is nothing whatsoever upon which they can rely.
One awakens to this realization: it certainly does not flow on to a second moment.
As the preceding [moment] ceases in succession, another mind arises following it. Since it does not abide at the time of the form, upon what object could it arise?
Because it arises from that [preceding moment], it does not arise from a cause that exists as it truly is. How, then, can it be established that it perishes momentarily?
This further clarifies that in the uninterrupted succession [of moments], there is in reality no arising. Since it arises without being real, its cessation likewise cannot be apprehended.
Indeed, the mind in its continuity arises and ceases simultaneously; when causes and conditions assemble, another mind [arises].
If birth occurs again, yet the causes and conditions have not yet converged, upon what could this birth depend?

If you claim it arises immediately from that [prior] mind, then since that mind is illusory and arises without awareness, the substance of birth cannot be established; if so, what is there to perish when it ceases? Thus, one says that its cessation has no locus.
Therefore, know that birth fundamentally has no cause, and cessation likewise has nothing upon which to depend. At this point, one realizes the original non-arising.
The intrinsic nature is quiescent;
it is the meditative absorption of the practitioner. It is the diamond-like relics of the Buddha, the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, and the indestructible reality of the world.
Abiding in the True Dharma, one attains it; the Tathāgata is endowed with wisdom. The bhikṣu attains equanimity. How can one perceive moments (kṣaṇa)?
Like a gandharva-city or a magical illusion, form has no such moments. Regarding these unreal forms and so forth, one views them as if they were real.
(The Tang translation says: "The great elements have no real nature; how can one speak of their being the creators?")
This verse [demonstrates] that untainted habitual tendencies (*anāsrava-vāsanā*) are not momentary (*akṣaṇika*).

It cites the cultivation of right concentration, the Vajra, Śāriputra, and the palaces of the Light-Sound Heaven (*Ābhāsvara*) as metaphors for those who abide in the True Dharma—namely, the four unshakeable worldly and supramundane matters.
The noble wisdom attained by the Tathāgata is equal for all bhikṣus; it is not momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Like gandharvas, illusions, and so forth, form (*rūpa*) has no momentariness.
This refers to those who abide in the True Dharma, extending even to all phenomena as they are perceived.
All are like illusions and so forth; thus, even form (rūpa) lacks the meaning of momentariness. For what reason, then, do you regard unreal dharmas of form as if they were real?
This [passage] refutes the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) who cling to the four great elements (mahābhūta) and others as the productive causes of arising.

The above two points have demonstrated that the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), being untainted (anāsrava), does not possess the characteristic of momentariness. Third, [the text] demonstrates the Dharma...
The body is the true Buddha; it is the limit of equality. It shatters doubt and leaves behind transgression. This is divided into seven parts. Part One: Mahāmati’s Request Regarding Six Doubts.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has prophesied that Arhats shall attain [Buddhahood]...”
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is equal and without distinction from that of all bodhisattvas.
No dharma of any sentient being enters nirvāṇa; who, then, attains the Buddha-way?

From the initial attainment of Buddhahood until parinirvāṇa, not a single word is spoken during that interval, nor is there any response. Because the Tathāgata is eternally in samādhi, he neither reflects nor investigates.
The manifested Buddha performs the deeds of a Buddha. For what reason do you speak of the mark of the momentary, successive destruction of consciousness?

Why does the Vajrapāṇi always follow and guard you? Why do you not establish the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*)? You manifest Māra and the works of Māra, as well as the retribution of evil karma—such as the case of the Māṇava Cañcā and the woman Sundarī, and your emerging with an empty bowl. When such obstacles of evil karma appear, how can it be said that the Tathāgata has attained [the ultimate]?
Although one realizes all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), one does not depart from various faults.
Regarding the six doubts you have asked, as explained in this sutra and other sutras, there is that which is spoken by the Dharma-Buddha and that which is spoken by the Transformation-Buddha.

There appear to be mutual discrepancies; therefore, I wish to clarify them. First, there is the doubt that the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) cannot attain Buddhahood through their own nirvana, yet for what reason does the Tathāgata bestow predictions of enlightenment upon them, no differently than he does for bodhisattvas?

Second, there is the doubt that sentient beings, due to their false imaginings, fail to realize that which is manifested by their own minds, yet for what reason does the Tathāgata further speak of all [phenomena]?
Once all sentient beings have attained parinirvāṇa, there is no further nirvāṇa; once one has already become a Buddha, who else reaches the path of Buddhahood?

Thus, there are three doubts regarding the Tathāgata’s distribution of the Three Vehicles: for what reason did he further say that on a certain night he attained Buddhahood and on a certain night he entered parinirvāṇa?

Within this interval, there is neither speaking nor showing. There are four doubts: first, if the Tathāgata is always in meditative concentration, without thought or examination, then what work do the manifested Buddhas perform? Second, [the doubt that] all sentient beings have already attained Buddhahood. Third, [the doubt that] the Buddha-body is eternal and unchanging. Fourth, [the doubt that] if the Buddha-body is eternal and unchanging, how can it enter parinirvāṇa? Fifth, [the doubt that] once all sentient beings have become Buddhas, there would be no further recipients for the Buddha’s teaching. Sixth, [the doubt that] if there are no further recipients for the teaching, the Buddha’s great compassion would be exhausted. Seventh, [the doubt that] if the Buddha’s great compassion were exhausted, he would not be able to manifest various transformations. Eighth, [the doubt that] if he could not manifest various transformations, he would not be able to save sentient beings. Ninth, [the doubt that] if he could not save sentient beings, his original vow would be unfulfilled. Tenth, [the doubt that] if his original vow were unfulfilled, he would not be able to attain the ultimate fruit. These ten doubts are the reason why the Tathāgata must preach the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. This is called the "Chapter on the Ten Doubts. Furthermore, there are five kinds of doubt regarding the meaning of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*: first, the doubt concerning the nature of the Tathāgata; second, the doubt concerning the nature of the Dharma; third, the doubt concerning the nature of the Sangha; fourth, the doubt concerning the nature of the Great Vehicle; fifth, the doubt concerning the nature of the Three Jewels. These five doubts are the reason why the Tathāgata must preach the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. This is called the "Chapter on the Five Doubts. Furthermore, there are three kinds of doubt regarding the meaning of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*: first, the doubt concerning the nature of the Tathāgata; second, the doubt concerning the nature of the Dharma; third, the doubt concerning the nature of the Sangha. These three doubts are the reason why the Tathāgata must preach the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. This is called the "Chapter on the Three Doubts. Furthermore, there are two kinds of doubt regarding the meaning of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*: first, the doubt concerning the nature of the Tathāgata; second, the doubt concerning the nature of the Dharma. These two doubts are the reason why the Tathāgata must preach the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. This is called the "Chapter on the Two Doubts. Furthermore, there is one kind of doubt regarding the meaning of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*: the doubt concerning the nature of the Tathāgata. This single doubt is the reason why the Tathāgata must preach the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. This is called the "Chapter on the Single Doubt. Furthermore, there is no doubt regarding the meaning of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. Why? Because the Tathāgata has already preached the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* extensively. Furthermore, there is no doubt regarding the meaning of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. Why? Because the Tathāgata has already preached the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* extensively.
