For what reason, moreover, is it said that the seven consciousnesses do not circulate and are not the cause of *nirvāṇa*, being subject to momentary, successive destruction?
[The Buddha] resolved six doubts by establishing his own authority (*svapravacana*), abiding in the fundamental limit (*koṭi*), free from obstruction, and devoid of all faults and afflictions.

For what reason, moreover, is the Vajra Guardian mentioned? Why is the primordial limit (koṭi) not established, yet the Māra, the deeds of Māra, the retribution of those deeds, and various such calamities are manifested?
As for "Māra," when the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment, the armies of Māra came to disturb him. As for "the deeds of Māra":

The Buddha showed him the royal palace where he had experienced sensual pleasures for ten years. The Brahmin woman Ciñcā Mānavikā tied a wooden bowl to her belly to slander the Buddha as having illicit relations with her.
Sundarī killed a girl and buried her in a vacant space within the monastery grounds, falsely accusing the Buddha of committing adultery and murder.
While begging for alms in the village of Bālinā, he returned with an empty bowl and later ate horse fodder, suffering from pain in both his head and back.

Being wounded by wooden splinters, falling into pits of fire, and poisoned rice—these are various manifestations of retribution. 2. Removing Doubts Concerning the Bestowal of the Prediction of Arhatship.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively! Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha:
He said, “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“It is for the sake of *nirvāṇa* without remainder, and to encourage and advance those who practice as bodhisattvas, that I speak thus.

For those practicing as bodhisattvas in this and other worlds who take pleasure in the *nirvāṇa* of the Śrāvaka vehicle, in order to cause them to leave the Śrāvaka vehicle and advance toward the Mahāyāna, the transformation buddhas bestow predictions of enlightenment upon the śrāvakas.”
"Mahāmati, it is not because they are Dharma-Buddhas. For this reason, Mahāmati, I declare that the Śrāvakas and the Bodhisattvas are not different.
Mahāmati, 'not different' means that the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Tathāgatas have severed the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and their liberation is of one single taste;

it does not mean they have severed the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Mahāmati, as for the cognitive hindrance, it is the seeing of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), which is supreme and pure. As for the afflictive hindrance..."

First, by practicing the realization of the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), one eliminates the seven consciousnesses and attains liberation from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). When the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) are extinguished, there is ultimate purity.
This answers the first doubt regarding the bestowal of the prophecy of Arhatship. There are three meanings to the bestowal of the prophecy of Arhatship. First:
First, they cause those of the two vehicles to attain *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Second, they entice those of the two vehicles to resolve upon the bodhisattva path.

Third, they demonstrate to the bodhisattvas of this realm and other realms that they must not fall into the meditative pleasures of the two vehicles. These are the provisional inducements of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, not the teachings of the *dharmakāya* Buddha.
Furthermore, by distinguishing between the differences and non-differences of the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas, the true teaching of the two [vehicles] is clarified.
The vehicle [of the two vehicles] severs the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and the liberation thus attained is no different from that of a bodhisattva.

However, because the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) has not been severed, it differs from the bodhisattva. Since the two vehicles do not perceive the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), they do not sever the cognitive hindrance;

yet, because the sevenfold self of the perceiving aspect (*darśanabhāga*)—arising from habitual tendencies—is separated from its grasping nature within the three realms, they sever the afflictive hindrances. And...
The internal self, which is the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) upon which the seven consciousnesses rely, has not yet been eliminated.

Once this self is extinguished, the body of the consciousness-store’s habitual tendencies undergoes transformation, and one immediately attains ultimate purity. Thus, it is known that the Śrāvaka who dwells in the bliss of samādhi shall attain the most supreme body of a Tathāgata.
△ Third, the removal of the doubt regarding the non-existence of a single word.
Because of the principle of the eternally abiding dharma (*pūrvasthita-dharma*), there is no nature [of arising] in the preceding or succeeding moments. (The Wei translation says:
"I always abide by the essence of the fundamental dharma and do not further give rise to dharmas. The Tang translation says: "I rely on the eternally abiding dharma and speak these secret words;
it is not different from the Buddhas of the past that there is further teaching later, for such written characters were already complete previously.)
This answers the third doubt, concerning the non-utterance of a single word. "Primordial Abiding" (benzhu) refers to the eternally abiding fundamental nature.
Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, the Dharma is naturally so; it is without antiquity or modernity, and without verbal exposition.

Therefore, it is said that "before and after are not the nature. "Nature" (xing) here means the Dharma. This signifies that from beginning to end there is only the single primordial abiding, and not a single dharma that can be apprehended. △
Fourth, the removal of doubt regarding the absence of reflection and investigation:
because his fundamental vows are inexhaustible, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma without reflection or investigation, for he is transformed by right wisdom.

Because mindfulness is non-erroneous, there is no discursive thought (*vitarka*) and no investigation (*vicāra*). Because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the four stages of abiding and the stage of ignorance (*avidyā*) have been severed, the two afflictions are abandoned.
One is freed from the two kinds of death, realizes the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*), and the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) are severed.
This answers the fourth doubt concerning the absence of reflection (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*). The Tathāgata expounds the Dharma without reflection or investigation;

he transforms beings through right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), not through deluded thought (*asat-saṃjñā*). Therefore, although these are performed by the transformation-buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), they are all free from reflection and investigation.
It is said that the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind.

However, the Tathāgata truly has no mind that conforms to their types; it is simply that those who possess the karmic affinity perceive it differently. [This concerns] the five abodes and the two deaths.
The two afflictions, the two selves, and the two obstacles—these five kinds of habitual tendencies have been severed by the Tathāgata for a long time;

therefore, he attains eternal constancy and freedom from deliberation. Relying solely on his original vows, he manifests through transformations according to the perceptions of beings, appearing like the moon reflected in water.
△ Fifth: Dispelling the doubt that sentient beings’ attainment of Buddhahood involves the destruction of consciousness in each moment.

Mahāmati, the seven—mind, intellect, mentation, and the visual consciousnesses, etc.—have the habitual tendencies of moments as their cause; they are excluded from the category of the wholesome and the outflow-free.

They no longer undergo cyclic existence. (The Tang translation says: "Mahāmati, the manas, the mental consciousness, and the seven [consciousnesses] such as the visual consciousness have habitual tendencies as their cause;
they are of a momentary nature. Apart from untainted goodness, they are not dharmas that flow on.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of cyclic existence and nirvana, and of suffering and pleasure. It cannot be realized by foolish ordinary people whose wisdom is distracted by emptiness.

This is a general response to the second point regarding the attainment of Buddhahood by sentient beings, and it addresses the doubt concerning the destruction of the fifth consciousness in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

As for the mind, the mental faculty (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), and so forth, the reason they are said to be momentary is that they take the habitual tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*) as their cause.

Turning their backs on untainted awakening (*anāsrava-bodhi*), they falsely cling to a self-substance (*ātma-tattva*). This substance is unreal; it perishes moment by moment and does not undergo transmigration.
Therefore, although all sentient beings exist within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), there is no birth and death to be found.
If we speak in terms of the *tathāgatagarbha*, although it manifests as the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), it contains the causes for both *nirvāṇa* and suffering and pleasure.

Ordinary beings, through their deluded conceptualizations and attachments, are shrouded by suffering and pleasure; they do not know that the capacity to experience suffering and pleasure and the capacity to realize *nirvāṇa* are non-dual in nature.
Furthermore, the practitioners of the Two Vehicles, as an antidote to ordinary beings, extinguish the sensations of suffering and pleasure. Moreover, for...
Disturbed by emptiness, they abandon the causes of suffering and pleasure and seek a separate nirvana, yet fail to recognize that their own nature is itself nirvana;

this is uniformly termed "non-awakening. Awakening, however, is realized immediately as it is, with nothing else existing apart from it. In a single moment of the seven consciousnesses, sentient beings attain Buddhahood; fundamentally, there is no mutual obstruction.
The original translation lists the mind, thought, mental consciousness, and the six sensory consciousnesses—eye consciousness and so forth—as the seven. (The Tang [translation]...)

The meaning of the translation is as follows: regarding the seven consciousnesses, including the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), and so forth, it is stated that these seven do not undergo transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
However, in the original translation, the term "mind" (*citta*) is employed specifically to reveal that the Tathāgatagarbha’s true nature is indestructible.

This refers to what is called the "extinction of the characteristics of mind" (*cittalakṣaṇanirodha*), rather than the extinction of the substance of mind (*cittasvabhāvanirodha*). It is because delusion (*moha*) alone is extinguished that the characteristics of mind are extinguished accordingly; this is not without purpose. In summary:
The seven consciousnesses fundamentally take the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] as their substance.

Therefore, when it is said that the seven consciousnesses are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), it need not be explicitly stated that the mental phenomena (*citta-lakṣaṇa*) of the eighth are also momentary. Now, regarding the statement that the Tathāgatagarbha is non-momentary, yet it is called the cause of suffering and pleasure:
since the experiencing of suffering and pleasure must necessarily arise from discrimination, these belong to the six consciousnesses which are momentary; this is also immediately evident.

There is a meaning that is not momentary (*akṣaṇika*). One knows that when deluded, one points to false cognition as being momentary; thus it is said that the seven consciousnesses do not undergo transmigration.
When awakened, one points to the true nature as being non-momentary; thus it is said that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the cause of both nirvāṇa and suffering and pleasure.
In reality, the seventh consciousness is the eighth consciousness, and the eighth consciousness is the fifth and sixth consciousnesses. This is not a destruction.
The characteristics of destruction mutually serve as causes for one another; all arise from delusion and awakening, and there is no reality of multiple substantial entities. △ Sixth:
Eliminating doubts regarding the Vajra attendants and all karmic retributions.
Mahāmati, those who are followed and protected by the Vajrapāṇi-guards are merely transformation Buddhas (nirmāṇa-buddha); they are not the true Tathāgata.
Mahāmati, the true Tathāgata is beyond all faculties and measures (pramāṇa). All the faculties and measures of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists are extinguished;

having attained the bliss of the present dharma (dṛṣṭadharma-sukha), he dwells in the patience of the knowledge of the uninterrupted dharma (anantarya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti). Therefore, he is not [protected] by the Vajrapāṇi-guards.
That which is protected: all emanation-buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) are not born of karma. An emanation-buddha is neither a Buddha nor separate from a Buddha.
He teaches the Dharma by means of signs produced by sentient beings, such as a potter’s wheel; he does not teach the realm of self-realization from his own direct realization.
This and the following section both answer the sixth question of the Vajra Attendant regarding doubts concerning the faults and afflictions of all karmic retributions.

The True Buddha establishes his own realization and directly reveals to sentient beings the realm of self-awakening, which transcends the cognitive measures of all ordinary people and followers of the two vehicles.
It is the attainment of dwelling in the bliss of the present dharma and the patience of uninterrupted wisdom; it is not something that can be grasped by the Vajra.

Protection. Vajra-protection refers to the manifested Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*). The manifested Buddha appears solely through the power of compassion and vows, manifesting a physical body like the moon reflected in water;
it is neither identical to nor different from [the Dharmakāya]. Since it is not born of karma, there is no fault of karma.
All manifestations are solely for the sake of sentient beings. Just as a potter uses a wheel, string, clay, and water to create various vessels, each suited to its purpose.
Its function is to manifest in accordance with conditions as an analogy; it is not something produced by a conscious mind.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish people give rise to the view of annihilation based on the cessation of the seven consciousnesses, and because they do not realize the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), they give rise to the view of permanence.
(The Wei translation states: "All ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas perceive the cessation of the six consciousnesses.")

Falling into the view of annihilationism, they do not perceive the *ālayavijñāna* and fall into the view of eternalism; because of their own false conceptualization (*parikalpita*), they do not know the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).

Through the cessation of the wisdom of their own false conceptualization, they are liberated; the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the four stages of dwelling and the stage of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) are severed.
Therefore, all faults are severed.

This also answers the sixth doubt. It specifically clarifies that the fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is free from fault; it is only because ordinary, ignorant people do not realize this that they falsely perceive distinctions.
If the seven consciousness-bodies are extinguished, one can then thoroughly comprehend the fundamental limit and will no longer give rise to the view of annihilationism.

This statement regarding the extinction of the seven consciousnesses should be understood as an observation of the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (evolving consciousness), which does not abide from moment to moment.

Because one fails to realize that it is one's own mind, the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) arises. Both the Wei and Tang translations maintain that the six consciousnesses share this same meaning.

Due to delusion regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is the *ālayavijñāna*. If one seeks the mind apart from consciousness, it belongs to the partial truth of the two vehicles; therefore, [one should] take consciousness itself as...

The mind further falls into the view of an externalist agent. This arises from failing to understand the *ālayavijñāna*, mistakenly taking it to be real, and seeing through one's own deluded imaginings;
thus, one does not know the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). If deluded imagination is extinguished, the habitual tendencies of the five abodes are severed all at once;
then all faults are eliminated. How could there then be various karmic retributions? Therefore, one should know that it is by being deluded regarding the *tathāgatagarbha* that...
As the ālayavijñāna, it conforms to false conceptualization and serves as the fundamental limit of saṃsāra; one neither awakens to nor understands this.
If one realizes that the ālayavijñāna is the tathāgatagarbha, then it conforms to right gnosis and serves as the fundamental limit of nirvāṇa—untainted and stainless.
All manifestations are solely for the sake of sentient beings; they are not established for one’s own personal realization, being the realm of self-awakened awareness.
...and so forth. △ Seven: Conclusion and General Response.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse: "The three vehicles are also not vehicles;
the Tathāgata is not subject to extinction. That which is recorded by all Buddhas is said to be free from all faults and evils, for the sake of those with uninterrupted wisdom, and..."

The "remainder-nirvāṇa" is taught as an inducement for those of inferior capacity; therefore, it is spoken of in a concealed manner. The wisdom arising from the Buddhas distinguishes and explains the paths:
that which is not a vehicle is not a vehicle, and that which is not such is not nirvāṇa. Desire, form, existence, and views—these are said to be the four stations of abiding.
They arise from the mental consciousness; consciousness is the house and the mind is what dwells therein. By severing the mind and the visual consciousness and so forth, [one attains liberation].
To those who speak of impermanence, he may teach eternal abiding so that they may form a view of nirvana;
to those who regard the Three Vehicles as not being vehicles, he teaches that the Tathāgata does not perish. These two statements alone have fully answered all six doubts.

It means that the Tathāgata has personally realized that there is no characteristic of a vehicle, that there is no parinirvāṇa, and that [the nature of reality] is fundamentally pure and free from all defilements and evils.
If one can thoroughly understand this, there is nothing further to be said. Inferior sentient beings cannot believe this;
therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of "right knowledge" and "nirvāṇa" as a means of first inducing them forward, and only thereafter reveals this secret.
This is the meaning: that which the Tathāgata has attained is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
He has analyzed and expounded it without any further ulterior intent, teaching only that there is neither a vehicle nor nirvāṇa, so as to lead beings to self-confidence and self-realization.

If one were to claim that the mere cessation of the four abodes of existence constitutes nirvāṇa, this would not be the eternal [state]. What the Tathāgata has taught is that there is neither vehicle nor nirvāṇa.

The fundamental nature is pure; it is eternally quiescent, which is what is meant by "permanently abiding. The seven mental faculties arise based upon the eighth consciousness and abide by means of that very eighth consciousness.

One does not take the transformation of the substance of consciousness as the ultimate goal, but rather takes the temporary cessation of the mental faculty (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five sensory consciousnesses to be *nirvāṇa*. This is equivalent to annihilationism. It is merely...
This increases false views. ○ The above three sections have demonstrated that the Dharma-body is the true Buddha and that the fundamental limit is equality;

thus, the refutation of doubts and departure from faults are complete. Fourth, the demonstration of the Tathāgata’s correct cause and correct fruit as being ultimately pure is divided into four parts.
△ First, Mahāmati asks about the sins and blessings of eating meat versus not eating meat.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati asked in verse: "Those bodhisattvas who are resolved to seek the Buddha-way—how should they consume alcohol, meat, and onions?
I pray that the Unsurpassed Honored One will, out of compassion, explain this for us."
That which fools greedily crave is foul, filthy, and brings no renown; it is what tigers and wolves delight to eat—how could it be fit for human consumption?

For those who eat it, various faults arise; for those who do not eat it, there is merit and goodness. I pray that you will explain to me the transgressions and blessings of eating and abstaining from food.
After Mahāmati Bodhisattva had spoken these verses in question, he addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will explain for us the merits and faults of eating and not eating meat.

I and the other bodhisattvas, in the present and the future, shall expound the Dharma in various ways for those sentient beings who desire to eat meat, so as to cause those beings to regard one another with a heart of compassion."
Having attained a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), each will clearly understand their respective stages of abiding and swiftly attain ultimate, unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, having brought their own stages to rest, shall also quickly achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.

As for those followers of heterodox paths who propound evil and false doctrines—those with wrong views who are inverted in their attachments to the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism—even they still possess prohibitions that forbid the consumption of [certain] foods.
How much less, then, would the Tathāgata—the protector of the world who has perfected the True Dharma—consume meat?
An ancient commentary states: When the Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma within the palace of a king of the ghosts, the yakṣas and other spirits thought their mealtime had arrived;
they eat nothing but meat. Mahāmati, wishing to inspire compassion in these kings of the ghosts, therefore requested the Tathāgata...

To speak of the faults of eating meat: while this indeed accords with the capacities of sentient beings, it should be further corroborated by the meaning of the three gradual stages from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which is the path of the Tathāgata’s true cultivation.

Regarding the fifty demonic states of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, one attains a nature of empty luminosity within that state of enlightened clarity. Within this, suddenly—

Yet, they take refuge in eternal extinction and deny cause and effect, entering exclusively into emptiness. When the mind of emptiness manifests before them, the demon of emptiness enters their vitals;
they then slander the observance of precepts, labeling it as "Hīnayāna," claiming that since Bodhisattvas realize emptiness, what need is there for observing or violating precepts?
Such individuals constantly consume alcohol and eat meat, and engage extensively in sexual misconduct, all while receiving offerings from faithful donors.
Due to the power of demonic influence, they ensnare those before them, causing them neither to give rise to doubt nor to slander [the Dharma].

Once the spirit’s mind has long entered them, they may consume excrement and urine, treating them as identical to wine, meat, and the like—all being equally empty. Thus they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code, erroneously lead others into sin, and lose right concentration (*samādhi*), destined for a downward fall.
The holy instructions are profound and strict; those who know the Dharma stand in awe. Now, in this late and declining age, we look upon...
If one speaks constantly in this manner, using the phrase "zealous in the vehicle but lax in the precepts" as a pretext for indulging one's own whims, various forms of destruction will ensue;

it is truly lamentable that such behavior does not stop at the consumption of meat. Furthermore, regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, even giving rise to a single thought of anger toward sentient beings can sever one’s spiritual lineage (*gotra*);
how much more so when it comes to killing and eating them? Those who aspire to this path should protect their right view and must not [act otherwise].
This is to be understood as being misled by error. △ Second, showing the many faults of eating meat.
The Buddha addressed Mahāmati: "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it. I shall speak for your sake."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat.

However, I shall now briefly explain them for you: all sentient beings have, from the very beginning, been related to one another through successive causes and conditions, having at times been one’s own six kinds of kin. Because they should be regarded as kin, one should not eat meat. (The Wei translation says: "I observe...")
Sentient beings cycle through the six realms of existence, all equally dwelling within birth and death.

They give birth to one another and mutually raise one another, serving in turn as fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, sons, or daughters, as well as paternal and maternal relatives, distant kin, and members of the inner and outer families. Or they may be born into other realms, whether the good paths or the evil paths.
They have always been my kin. For this reason, when I observe sentient beings devouring one another’s flesh, there is not one who was not once my relative.

Driven by a craving for the taste of flesh, they devour each other in turn, constantly giving rise to harmful intent, increasing their karma of suffering, and wandering through birth and death without finding liberation.
When the Buddha spoke these words, all the malevolent rākṣasas heard what the Buddha had said; they completely abandoned their evil intentions and ceased eating.

They exhorted one another to give rise to a heart of compassion and to protect the lives of sentient beings more than they protected their own bodies. Renouncing all kinds of meat, they abstained from eating it.

Weeping with tears streaming down, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, having heard the Buddha’s teaching and observed the six realms of existence with discernment, we realize that the flesh we have eaten has all been our own kin.
Thus we know that eating meat is a great enmity toward sentient beings and severs the seed of great compassion."
"Long-unwholesome karma is the root of great suffering, World-Honored One. From this day forward, I shall abstain from eating meat;
I shall also prohibit my attendants from eating it. As for those disciples of the Tathāgata who do not eat meat, I shall personally approach and protect them day and night."

If there are those who eat meat, I shall bring them great harm. Mahāmati, even rākṣasas and evil spirits who constantly eat meat, upon hearing what I have said, will give rise to a heart of compassion and abandon meat, refusing to eat it; how much more so should my disciples who practice the wholesome Dharma?
"You should listen to [the teaching on] eating meat. You should know that those who eat meat are great enemies of sentient beings and sever my noble lineage.
Mahāmati, if my disciples hear what I have taught yet eat meat without careful reflection, you should know that they belong to the caste of *caṇḍālas*;
they are not my disciples, nor am I their teacher. Therefore, Mahāmati, if one wishes to act as my..."
Regarding "relatives": one should not eat any kind of meat whatsoever.
My Buddha has constantly exhorted his kinsmen to cultivate a heart of filial piety and compassion; he was indeed most earnest and sincere.

Yet, as a child of the Buddha, because one deeply understands that all things are of one essence, one still contemplates their deliverance even when they belong to different species—how much more so, then, for those who are one's own kin?

Regarding this trivial physical existence, you still indulge your palate and allow yourself to inflict injury and destruction at will. Even upon hearing of past lives, you cannot be moved to great compassion;
yet toward those currently existing as your kin and fellow beings, you alone feel such deep affection and harmony. Why do you not consider that those of the future will view the present as we do now?
According to the Dharma, among those who study Buddhism in recent times, many are seen to belong to the faction of Māra; I especially wish for all under heaven to [avoid this].

Those who possess right knowledge and vision strictly observe the holy teachings and bequeath them to future generations; with this single thought, they look up in reverence within the great radiance of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
One should not eat the flesh of donkeys, mules, camels, foxes, dogs, oxen, horses, humans, beasts, and so forth, because butchers sell them mixed together.

One should not eat meat because it grows from impure elements. One should not [eat meat] because when sentient beings smell its odor, they all become terrified, just as the *caṇḍālas* and *tāpasa*s [flee];
and because dogs, seeing it, loathe it and bark in a pack out of fear. Therefore, one should not [eat it].
Eating meat. (The Wei translation says: "O Mahāmati, it is like a *caṇḍāla*, a hunter, a butcher, or a fisherman or bird-catcher.
Wherever they go, living beings see them from afar and think: 'I am now certain to die; this person who comes here is a great evildoer.
He does not recognize sin or merit, but severs the lives of sentient beings, seeking only immediate profit. Now he has come here to seek me out.'"")
...and so forth. Now our bodies are all covered with flesh; therefore, having come here now, we shall certainly die.
Mahāmati, because people eat meat, it causes all sentient beings who see them to give rise to such fear and terror.
Mahāmati, all sentient beings in the void and upon the earth, seeing those who eat meat, become terrified and conceive doubts, thinking: "Am I going to die now?"
For the sake of survival, such evil persons do not cultivate a mind of loving-kindness; they wander through the world like jackals and wolves, constantly seeking meat to eat.
Like oxen devouring grass or dung beetles chasing after excrement, they know no satiety. My own body is flesh; it is precisely their food.
One should not encounter them; rather, one should abandon them and flee, departing to a great distance, no different from a person who fears a rākṣasa.
Mahāmati, those who eat meat cause all sentient beings who see them to give rise to such terror and fear. You should know, therefore, that eating meat [is thus].
It is a great enemy to sentient beings. Therefore, the Bodhisattva practices loving-kindness and compassion to gather in sentient beings;
he should not consume the flavors eaten by those non-noble and evil persons, for such things spread an evil reputation and are censured by the noble ones.
For this reason, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva, for the sake of gathering in all sentient beings, should not eat meat.
"Selling miscellaneous goods" refers to the indistinguishable nature of human and animal flesh and blood. "Impurity" refers to the impurity of pus and blood.
It is not fitting for those of pure companionship to associate with such foulness; how much less should they consume it? As for the fear of death, all creatures are no different;
the inability to bear the sight of a trembling victim is what a gentleman cherishes, yet such a sentiment is often absent from the world today.
Externally, how could one still be called a vessel for the Way?
Furthermore, because it prevents the practitioner from generating a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one should not eat meat.

Because it is the object of craving for the foolish and ignorant, being foul-smelling, impure, and lacking a good reputation, one should not eat meat. Because it causes various mantras and incantations to fail to achieve success, [one should not eat meat].
One should eat meat, because those who kill living beings perceive the form and give rise to consciousness, and thus deeply relish and become attached to it.
One should not eat meat, because those who eat meat are abandoned by the devas. One should not eat meat, because it causes the breath to stink.
One should not eat meat, because it causes many evil dreams. One should not [eat meat], because tigers and wolves will smell its scent in empty forests. One should not...
Eating meat leads to a lack of moderation in eating and drinking; therefore, one should not eat meat. Eating meat causes practitioners to fail to develop a sense of weary detachment from the world;
therefore, one should not eat meat. I have often said that regarding whatever food and drink one consumes, one should conceive of it as the flesh of one's own child or as medicine;
therefore, one should not eat meat. There is no possibility that I would ever permit the eating of meat.

Seeing the form, consciousness arises. "Form" refers to the physical body; "consciousness" refers to the mind of consciousness. It is said that long-standing habituation can cause the mind of consciousness to undergo transformation, becoming deeply attached and defiled.
"Abandoned by the devas" means that because [those who eat meat] harbor anger and theft, they are abandoned by the devas.
This causes practitioners not to give rise to revulsion and renunciation. [It is said: "If my disciples do not cease eating meat, then..."
It enables all who resolve their minds to practice not to give rise to thoughts of weariness or aversion.

Regarding whatever food and drink they consume—specifically regarding "leftover food"—they should remain free from greedy attachment, even to the point of regarding it as the flesh of their own son or as medicine for a disease.
"How could one ever eat meat again? Such a thing is impossible.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, in the past there was a king named Siṃhasaudāsa who ate various kinds of meat until he eventually came to eat human flesh.
His ministers and subjects could no longer endure this, so they plotted against him and cut off his stipend, for those who eat meat are like this."
For these reasons, one should not eat meat.
Generally, the fruit of killing living beings lies in the hells; this refers to the present age, as it pertains to retribution in this very life.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, whenever those who kill for the sake of profit slaughter and sell living beings, those foolish meat-eaters use money as a net to catch various meats. As for those who kill, if they do so by means of wealth or goods...
If one uses hooks and nets to capture those beings that move through the air, water, or on land, and then slaughters, sells, and trades them for profit in various ways— Mahāmati,
there is no such thing as fish or meat that exists without being taught, sought after, or imagined. For this reason, one should not eat meat.

There is nothing that does not involve teaching, seeking, or conceptualizing. This means that when there is meat-eating in the world and the trade in slaughter is flourishing, this is precisely "teaching others to kill.
Using wealth to purchase various meats constitutes "seeking," and perceiving the physical form to give rise to consciousness constitutes "conceptualizing.
Since it is impossible to obtain fish or meat without these three factors, one should not eat them. △ Third, showing this sutra.
In ultimate reality, all [meat-eating] is entirely abandoned.
Mahāmati, at times I have spoken of prohibiting five kinds of meat, or restricted ten kinds;
but now, in this sutra, by means of skillful means, I exclude them in every way and at all times, so that all is entirely abandoned. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha...

The Awakened One does not even consume [ordinary] food, much less eat fish or meat; nor does he teach others to do so. Because he is preceded by great compassion, he regards all sentient beings as his only child.
Therefore, he does not permit the eating of one's own child's flesh.

There are five kinds of meat that are permitted: those which one has not heard of being killed for oneself, those one has not seen being killed, those one suspects were not killed for oneself, those left over by birds, and those that died of themselves.
There are ten kinds that are prohibited: human, camel, elephant, horse, dragon, fox, pig, dog, lion, and monkey.

Regarding these two categories of permission and prohibition, when the World-Honored One first attained Buddhahood, because the capacities of sentient beings were not yet mature, he provisionally allowed them to eat such meat out of compassion; however, they were all [of a supernatural nature].
This is a transformation through supernatural power; it possesses no life-force. It is only within this sutra that the true meaning is revealed: that all [killing] is utterly severed.
Regarding all sentient beings as if they were one's only child, the World-Honored One does not permit the eating of a child’s flesh.
His demonstration to people of the urgency of our shared essence (samatā) may be called profoundly compassionate. Nevertheless, according to principle, we are equal in abiding in the single source.
Although their physical forms differ, their consciousness is the same; one must not fall into confusion, but should instead examine this with careful scrutiny.
△ Fourth, a summary conclusion detailing the faults and perils of practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse: "All have once been our kin;
they are base, filthy, and impure. Born from the impure, the mere scent of them strikes terror into the heart.

All meats, along with onions, leeks, garlic, and the like, as well as various intoxicating liquors—those who practice the path should always keep far away from these. They should also always avoid sesame oil and all such things."
The perforated bed: because those various minute insects find it utterly terrifying within it.
Onions, scallions, leeks, and garlic provoke anger when eaten raw and arouse lust when cooked; therefore, they should be abandoned together.
The ancient commentary states that this refers to foreign customs, where the pounding of hemp inevitably produces insects; perhaps this differs from the practices of our own land. The bed has holes.
Cracks abound where many insects gather; sitting or lying there, one is struck with alarm and fear. How could you not feel shame that the Noble One’s compassion extends even to this?
Food gives rise to negligence; negligence gives rise to various discursive thoughts; from these thoughts arises craving. Therefore, one should not eat.
From food arises sensual desire; desire causes the mind to become deluded and intoxicated. This delusion and intoxication increase craving, so that one is not liberated from birth and death.

This applies by extension to all other foods and drinks: if one becomes deeply attached to their flavors, they can all cause the body and mind to become lax and negligent, giving rise to many discursive thoughts until one reaches the state of sensual desire and intoxication, becoming entangled in birth and death. It is all due to the mouth and belly; for a single moment of indulgence—
Sentiment: The cause may be subtle, but the fruit is manifest; how can one not be cautious?
To kill sentient beings for profit, or to ensnare various meats with wealth—both are evil karmas; at death, one falls into the Raurava Hell.
If there were no perception of [the animal] being killed for one's sake, then the three kinds of pure meat would not exist; yet they do not arise without a cause. Therefore, one should not eat them.
For this reason, all those practitioners have completely distanced themselves from them, and all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, unanimously censure such eating.
Passing from one to another, they devour each other; upon death, they fall among the species of tigers and wolves. Foul and loathsome, they are born ever ignorant and dull-witted.
They are mostly born as Caṇḍālas, hunters, or Tāmbas; or they are born as Dāyinīs, or among those whose nature is to eat flesh.

Rākṣasas, wildcats, and the like are born everywhere within this world. For the sake of the Bound Elephant, Mahāmegha, Aṅgulimāla, and this Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, I have strictly prohibited the eating of meat.
Dāyani is a rākṣasī. Baddhagaja, Mahāmegha, and Aṅgulimāla are all names of sūtras.
Those who are rebuked by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas, yet remain shameless after eating [the flesh], will always be dull-witted and ignorant throughout their successive births.

It was previously stated that those who have seen, heard, or suspected [the killing] have already abandoned all meat; yet, through deluded thoughts and lack of awareness, they are born in places where meat is eaten.
Just as with the faults of lustful desire, these obstruct the noble liberation. Alcohol, meat, scallions, leeks, and garlic are all obstacles to the Noble Path.
Sentient beings of future ages will speak out of ignorance regarding meat, saying: "This is pure and blameless; the Buddha permitted us to eat it.

One should eat with the thought that it is like taking medicine, or like eating the flesh of one's own son. Being content and giving rise to revulsion, one should practice the way of begging for food.

For one who dwells securely in a mind of loving-kindness, I say they are always free from aversion; even tigers, wolves, and all other malevolent beasts may constantly dwell and roam together with them.
Yet, when various flesh and blood are consumed, all sentient beings are filled with terror. Therefore, the practitioner of loving-kindness does not eat meat.
Those who eat meat lack compassion and wisdom; they turn their backs forever on true liberation and contravene the outward signs of the noble ones. Therefore, one should not eat meat.
By abstaining from eating meat, one will be born into the lineage of brahmins, in various places of spiritual practice, or into families of wisdom and prosperity. This is all due to not eating meat.
They obstruct noble liberation; they all serve as hindrances to the Noble Path. Those who eat meat lack a compassionate heart and forever turn their backs on true liberation.
The Tathāgata has repeatedly and earnestly issued these strict and formal admonitions for the sake of practitioners.

This was because he pitied future generations who would claim that the Mahāyāna is without restraint, recklessly propounding false doctrines and falsely accusing the Tathāgata of permitting the eating of "pure" meat, thereby leading them into delusion.
This class of people who disrupt their original resolve is largely characterized by negligence and a lack of shame; they are truly the dregs of hell.

Even those born as brahmins, those who practice cultivation, and those possessed of wisdom and nobility still rely upon the cessation of meat-eating—how much more so must this be true for the Tathāgata’s ultimate liberation?
In this sutra, the Buddha directly points to the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) as being the *tathāgatagarbha* (womb of the Tathāgata).

It is simply that once one attains full realization, all delusion is immediately the truth. This is not the domain of any of the followers of the Two Vehicles or of Bodhisattvas at the provisional stages;
thus, regarding the virtue of the precepts, he offers particularly profound admonitions. Therefore, we know that untainted, true purity admits no mundane things.

From beginning to end, from root to branch, it is ultimately pure and white, leaving nothing behind. Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, all Tathāgatas share this same secret.
The Great Way is like the sun; there is no meaning in it that can be doubted.
